practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the conflicting interests of Jews and Arabs within the British Mandate (c1920–45) for the end of the Mandate in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why these conflicting interests mattered for the end of the Mandate. Identifies several specific consequences (e.g. the 1936–39 Arab revolt forcing the 1939 White Paper; loss of British control over Jewish armed groups after 1945; UN referral 1947) and links each to evidence from the period (Balfour Declaration; aliyah numbers; Yishuv institutions; Holocaust survivors). Reaches a clear judgement on importance. [7–8]
Secure: Explains two or three consequences with relevant detail and uses period vocabulary correctly. Judgement on importance is clear if a little implicit. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant features of the Mandate but explanation is uneven; describes events more than analyses why they mattered for 1948. [3–4]
Emerging: Lists points about the Mandate without showing how the conflicting interests caused its end. Limited or no period vocabulary. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the 1939 White Paper for relations between Britain and the Yishuv.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses specific consequences of the 1939 White Paper for British-Yishuv relations — e.g. the cap of 1,500 immigrants per month closing escape routes during the Holocaust; Ben-Gurion’s ‘fight the war as if there were no White Paper’ line; the post-1945 turn of Haganah and Irgun against Britain. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with detail; analysis is clear but may be uneven across the time horizons. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies the White Paper’s terms but only loosely connects them to relations with the Yishuv. [3–4]
Emerging: Describes the White Paper without explaining why it damaged British-Yishuv relations. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the deepening of conflict in Palestine in the years 1936–45.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Arab revolt of 1936–39
• the 1939 White Paper
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative that uses both stimulus points AND adds at least one further development from the student’s own knowledge (e.g. the 1942 Biltmore programme; Holocaust impact on the Yishuv; Truman’s 1945 demand for 100,000 immigrants). Connects events through causation and consequence rather than just describing them. [7–8]
Secure: Narrative addresses three or more aspects with clear analytical links between events; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Narrative covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer aspects; analytical links are simple. (Capped at this band if it does not address three or more aspects.) [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive account; missing dates or sequence errors; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Balfour Declaration (1917) for relations between the Arab and Jewish populations of Palestine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct consequences, each clearly explained with specific period detail. For example: (i) it gave Zionism international legitimacy and accelerated aliyah, swelling the Yishuv to around 450,000 by 1939; (ii) Arab leaders treated it as a betrayal of the McMahon-Hussein understanding, fuelling rioting in 1920, 1921 and 1929 and the 1936–39 revolt. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but one less developed. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description than consequence. [3–4]
Emerging: A single point or restatement of the Balfour Declaration without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Nazi persecution of European Jews (1933–45) for the situation Britain faced in Palestine in 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explicitly links Nazi persecution and the Holocaust to Britain’s 1945 position. Specific consequences explained: the surge in Jewish refugees after 1933; the displaced-persons camps after 1945; Truman’s pressure on London to admit 100,000 survivors; the moral collapse of the 1939 White Paper’s immigration cap. Reaches a clear judgement on importance. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail; analysis clear but may underplay one time horizon. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the Holocaust without showing why it shaped the 1945 Mandate situation. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1936–39 Arab revolt for the British government’s policy in Palestine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) Britain deployed around 25,000 troops to crush the revolt, exposing how expensive direct rule had become; (ii) the revolt drove the policy reversal of the May 1939 White Paper, capping Jewish immigration at 1,500 a month and promising eventual Palestinian independence. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but one less developed. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description than consequence. [3–4]
Emerging: A single point or a paraphrase of what the revolt was without analysing its policy effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the First World War on Russia by early 1917. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, casualty figures, the bread ration falling to 280g, queues outside Petrograd bakeries, or the railway breakdown). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the war had broken not just the army but the home front’s ability to feed itself. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that paraphrases the source rather than inferring from it. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to a source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why opposition to the Tsar had grown so dangerous by February 1917.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Tsarina Alexandra and Rasputin
• the impact of the First World War
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. military disaster, the Tsar taking command at Stavka in 1915, the Alexandra–Rasputin scandal, food and fuel shortages in Petrograd, peasant land hunger). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — autocracy, Stavka, Duma, Okhrana — throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing the causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of Russia in 1917 without explaining why they amounted to growing opposition; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the importance of Rasputin in the collapse of the Romanov regime.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents Rasputin’s influence on policy as decisive; the other argues his actual power was small but the public scandal around him destroyed the dynasty’s legitimacy). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the importance of Rasputin.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (court memoirs versus Okhrana police reports), wrote at different times, or had different purposes (a political biography of Alexandra versus a wider social history of the home front). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) but with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the main reason the Tsar lost public support by early 1917?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of Russia in early 1917 — war casualties, Stavka, the Putilov strikes, the Rasputin murder, the bread ration — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’ rather than ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on Russia in 1917 and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the First World War was the main reason for the collapse of the Romanov regime by 1917?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the 1.7m military deaths, Tannenberg and the Masurian Lakes, Nicholas’s 1915 move to Stavka, the Putilov strike, the Petrograd bread ration, Rodzianko’s warnings — to test whether the war was the decisive factor. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (autocracy, Duma, Stavka, Okhrana). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors or no period vocabulary. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For Paper 3 inference questions on this period, focus on what a source implies about the strain on the regime — not what it states. Quote one short detail (a bread ration figure, a casualty number, a line about Rasputin) and draw one inference from it; a paragraph of paraphrase will score lower than a tight, supported point. For 12-mark causation essays on why the Tsar fell, weigh war, economic crisis and the Rasputin scandal against each other rather than describing each in turn — examiners reward a substantiated judgement on the most important cause, not a list.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the strength of the Guomindang army at the end of the Sino-Japanese War. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail from the source (for example, the GMD’s 4.3-million-strong regular army or US transport planes ferrying troops). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the GMD looked dominant on paper, but its strength was concentrated in cities. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that is closer to a paraphrase of the source than an inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to a source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Guomindang was in such a weak position by 1945, despite having a larger army and US support.
You may use the following in your answer:
• hyperinflation
• Sino-Japanese War (1937–45)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. hyperinflation, corruption, the cost of the Sino-Japanese War, GMD reliance on the cities, brutal conscription) and shows how they interacted. Uses the stimulus points and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing the causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit rather than direct. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the GMD without explaining why they amounted to weakness; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the position of the Chinese Communist Party in 1945.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents the CCP as battle-hardened and well-prepared by Yan’an reforms; the other stresses how small and exposed the party was compared with the GMD). Each side of the difference is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported than the other. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the strengths of the CCP in 1945.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (Cold War-era versus post-archival access from the 1990s); they used different evidence (CCP-published material versus revisionist Western archival research, e.g. Frank Dikötter); or they had different purposes (commemorative versus critical). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) but with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why; or names a reason without supporting it. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the relative strengths of the CCP and the Guomindang in 1945?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of 1945 China — GMD army size, hyperinflation, corruption, US aid; CCP land reform, Yan’an base, Long March mythology — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’ rather than ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations are reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used but in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on 1945 China and barely engages with the interpretations as views; or relies on the stimulus alone. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that the Long March of 1934–35 explains the strength of the CCP in 1945?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the c.86,000 marchers, c.8,000 survivors, the Yan’an Rectification Campaign, the role of Zhang Guotao, the propaganda construction of the March story by historians such as Sun Shuyun — to test how far the Long March alone explains 1945 strength. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Yan’an, Rectification, Eighth Route Army). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning; limited subject vocabulary. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors or no period vocabulary. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the spread of the horse to the Indigenous peoples of the Plains by c1835.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development that links the horse to a specific feature of Plains life.

Indicative content (any two developed):
• Nations could follow vast buffalo herds across hundreds of miles each year, sustaining a fully nomadic way of life that would not have been possible on foot.
• Horse wealth became the measure of family standing — the Comanche, for example, ran herds in the tens of thousands by the 1830s, reshaping social hierarchy.
• Mounted warfare and raiding (e.g. Lakota raids on Crow horse herds) intensified, raising the importance of warrior societies and counting coup.
• The reach and military power of the Plains nations grew, helping the Lakota expand their territory at the expense of weaker neighbours.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail and a clear link to Plains life.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two consequences listed under a single heading without development.
Emerging: A general comment about horses without identifying a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the buffalo for the way of life of the Indigenous peoples of the Plains by c1840.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the buffalo, supported by accurate detail and explicit links to subsequent Plains life.

Indicative content:
• Food security: an estimated 30 million bison sustained nomadic nations such as the Lakota and Cheyenne, providing meat that could be dried and preserved for the winter.
• Shelter: buffalo hides stretched over poles formed the tipi, the portable home that made nomadic following of the herds possible.
• Clothing and tools: hide for clothing, sinew for bowstrings, bone for tools, horn for cups, hooves boiled for glue — almost every part of the animal had a use.
• Spiritual significance: the buffalo was sacred and central to ceremonies; hunts were preceded by ritual.
• Vulnerability: because the whole way of life rested on the herds, any later assault on the buffalo (as the US Army would later promote) struck at every aspect of nomadic Plains life at once.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of the buffalo's importance across at least two strands (e.g. material survival AND wider way of life), with specific period detail (tipi, Lakota, Comanche, 30 million) and clear links forward to later events.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the buffalo without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Indigenous Plains beliefs about land for relations with American settlers from the 1840s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two developed):
• Plains nations did not recognise private ownership of land, so settler claims and fences were experienced as a violation of shared hunting territory rather than legitimate property.
• Treaties signed with one chief did not bind whole nations because authority on the Plains was decentralised — leading to repeated US accusations that Indigenous peoples had ‘broken’ agreements.
• Sacred sites such as the Black Hills could not be sold or surrendered in the way US negotiators expected, increasing the bitterness of later land disputes.
• Conflicts of belief made compromise structurally hard: two systems of property could not occupy the same ground without one displacing the other.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph, with explicit links to Plains beliefs and to later settler-Indigenous relations.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under a single heading.
Emerging: A general comment about disagreements without identifying a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the system of bands, councils and warrior societies for Plains decision-making by c1840.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of decentralised Plains leadership, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Bands of 50–500 related families were the everyday unit of life, allowing nations to spread out across vast territories without losing identity.
• Chiefs led by persuasion rather than command, so authority depended on a chief’s reputation for wisdom, bravery or generosity — losing trust meant losing followers.
• Big decisions (war, peace, moving camp) were taken by councils of elders, with warrior societies such as the Cheyenne Dog Soldiers policing camp life and leading raids.
• This system made Plains life flexible and resilient but later confused US negotiators, who signed treaties with one chief and wrongly assumed whole nations were bound.
• It explains why ‘the Lakota’ or ‘the Cheyenne’ could not always be held to an agreement signed by a single leader — a recurring source of misunderstanding throughout the period.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the structure of Plains leadership to specific consequences for Plains life and later US-Indigenous relations.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of chiefs without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Indigenous Plains practice of counting coup for the way Plains warfare was conducted.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two developed):
• Honour came from daring rather than killing, so battles often ended with relatively few deaths compared with European-style warfare.
• Touching an enemy and escaping alive became the highest mark of bravery, encouraging individual feats by young warriors rather than mass casualties.
• Plains warfare developed conventions of limited conflict — raiding for horses and revenge — rather than total destruction of an enemy nation.
• White observers, unfamiliar with these conventions, repeatedly misread Plains raids as savage anarchy, helping to justify later military campaigns against Indigenous peoples.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific period detail and clear links to Plains military life or perceptions of it.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: A general comment about Plains warfare without identifying a consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Black Hills and other sacred sites for Indigenous Plains life by c1840.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of sacred land, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The Black Hills (in modern South Dakota) were the spiritual heart of Lakota life, where the natural world was felt to be most charged with sacred power.
• Vision quests, in which a young man fasted alone awaiting a guiding vision, often took place in such sacred places, marking the passage to adulthood.
• Medicine men used sacred sites as bridges between the living and the spirit world, reinforcing community identity.
• Because the land was sacred, it could not be regarded as a commodity to be sold — explaining why later disputes over the Black Hills (after the 1874 gold strike) became so intense.
• Sacred sites helped knit a nation together across vast hunting territories, providing a shared geography of belief that bands could return to.

Mastering: Sustained explanation that links sacred sites to specific aspects of Plains life AND looks forward to their importance in later disputes.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of sacred sites without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the composition of English armies was different in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Fourteenth-century armies were built around the mounted knight and the longbow archer (1). Lords brought knights and tenants to the king under feudal duty, and archers made up most of the foot (1). By the seventeenth century the same army was made of musketeers and pikemen fighting in linked blocks (1). The New Model Army of 1645 was paid and drilled, not summoned by feudal obligation (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the longbow became the most important English missile weapon in the period c1300–c1415.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Edward III's archery law
• the Battle of Agincourt (1415).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• A trained archer could shoot ten or twelve arrows a minute to about 250 yards, far outreaching earlier missile weapons.
• Edward III made practice a legal duty: Sunday archery at the village butts, with 'wasteful' games banned by statute in 1363.
• Bows were cheap and could be used by commoners, so kings could put thousands of archers in the field for the price of a few knights.
• Battles proved its worth: massed arrows broke the schiltrons at Falkirk (1298) and stopped French cavalry at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415).
• Indentures and royal pay made it possible to keep large numbers of archers on campaign for months at a time.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the composition of English armies changed in the period c1250–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the feudal host
• the longbow.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• The feudal host tied army command to landholding, so the mounted knight began as the most important soldier on the field.
• Knight service lasted only about 40 days a year, which was useless for long campaigns in France, so kings turned to paid contracts.
• The longbow gave ordinary men battle-winning firepower, so archers grew from a support arm to the bulk of an English army.
• Armoured men-at-arms increasingly fought on foot beside the archers, as at Agincourt (1415), rather than charging on horseback.
• Gunpowder added a new specialist: gunners and their cannon, paid for by the crown rather than raised by feudal duty.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why gunpowder weapons changed warfare in England in the period c1340–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• cannon at Crécy (1346)
• castle walls.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Edward III brought small bombards to Crécy in 1346, showing that gunpowder could be used in the open field.
• Better metal casting and gunpowder milling made bigger, more reliable guns during the fifteenth century.
• Siege guns could break the high stone walls that had kept castles safe for centuries; the fall of Constantinople in 1453 showed what heavy cannon could do.
• Because guns were expensive, only the crown could pay for them, which strengthened royal power over the great lords.
• Cannon and the longbow squeezed the mounted knight from two sides: cheap missile fire in battle, and gunfire against the castle he sheltered in.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the training of ordinary soldiers was different in the fourteenth century and the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the fourteenth century training was local and part-time (1). Edward III ordered Sunday longbow practice at the village butts, and men trained in their own parish (1). In the nineteenth century training was done by the army itself (1). Cardwell's reforms put permanent depots in each regimental district, where short-service recruits were drilled full time before joining a battalion (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘Science, technology and communications were the most important factor in changing English warfare between c1250 and c1500.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the longbow
• the feudal host.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments supporting science/technology as most important:
• The longbow gave trained commoners decisive battlefield firepower at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415).
• The arrival of gunpowder and primitive cannon (Crécy 1346, Constantinople 1453) ended the high stone wall as a guarantee of safety.
• Better armour (plate), saddles and horse breeding all changed the cost and the role of the mounted knight.
• Improvements in shipbuilding and missile weaponry shaped how England fought across the Channel.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors (governments and individuals; attitudes in society):
• Government action was decisive: Edward III's compulsory archery law made the longbow available in mass numbers; Henry V's decisions at Agincourt turned a weapon into a victory.
• The feudal host was a social institution as much as a military one — knight service, the obligation to serve 40 days, was a legal/political fact, not a technology.
• Attitudes in society — the chivalric ideal, the prestige of the mounted knight — slowed the decline of cavalry even after the longbow had made it tactically vulnerable.
• Without organised muster, billeting and royal taxation to pay archers and gunners, the new weapons could not have been used effectively.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs technology against governments/individuals/attitudes, uses accurate period detail (longbow, knight service, Crécy, Agincourt) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Henry VIII’s character and aims at his accession in 1509.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Renaissance Prince image — trained in Latin, theology and music; admired by Erasmus; styled himself as warrior-scholar.
• Desire for military glory — particularly recapturing English claims in France; led to the 1513 invasion.
• Need for a male heir — married Catherine of Aragon in June 1509 to secure the Tudor dynasty.
• Belief in personal sovereignty — saw himself as God’s anointed monarch, expecting obedience from nobles, Church and Parliament.
• Dislike of administrative detail — preferred hunting and pageantry, requiring a chief minister to handle the workload.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Wolsey’s rise to power between 1509 and 1518.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Organisation of the 1513 French campaign — supplied an army of around 30,000, leading to the capture of Thérouanne and Tournai.
• Rapid Church promotion — Bishop of Lincoln (1514), Archbishop of York (1514), Cardinal (1515), papal legate (1518).
• Appointment as Lord Chancellor in 1515 — the senior office of state, giving Wolsey control of justice.
• Independent clerical wealth — income from York and other sees funded his court at Hampton Court without draining the Crown.
• Personal closeness to Henry — absorbed routine business so the king could pursue hunting, jousting and music.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague or partially inaccurate.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Henry VIII relied on Thomas Wolsey to manage government in the 1510s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Spurs (1513)
• Henry’s personal style of government
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explanation of distinct, supported reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• 1513 French campaign — Wolsey, as Royal Almoner, organised supply for an army of 30,000 men, including ships, food and ordnance. The capture of Thérouanne and Tournai and the Battle of the Spurs gave Henry the military glory he craved and proved Wolsey could deliver large-scale projects.
• Henry’s personal style — the king preferred hunting, jousting and pageantry to paperwork. A chief minister who could absorb the daily grind of council, courts and finance was indispensable.
• Wolsey’s administrative ability — he could draft treaties, chair the Court of Chancery and run foreign policy simultaneously, releasing Henry from detail.
• Wolsey’s lack of noble family — as a butcher’s son he had no rival power base, making him easier to trust than the Howards or Suffolks.
• Wolsey’s independent income — the archbishopric of York and the cardinalate funded his court without bleeding the Treasury.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on ‘why’ rather than narrative; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail; mostly explanatory; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive in places.
Emerging: General narrative of events with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Henry VIII ruled in a completely different way from his father.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Empson and Dudley
• Henry’s Renaissance education
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments that the style was different:
• Empson and Dudley, Henry VII’s most hated tax collectors, were arrested within weeks of the accession and later executed.
• Henry VIII spent on display — jousting, music and court spectacle — where his father had been careful with money.
• He wanted military glory in France and committed crown finances to war, which Henry VII had avoided.
• His Renaissance education, praised by Erasmus, made the court a place for humanist scholarship rather than account-keeping.
• He left the daily grind of council, courts and finance to a chief minister instead of doing the paperwork himself.

Arguments that much stayed the same:
• The machinery of government was unchanged: the Royal Council, Justices of the Peace, and Parliament called for taxes and major laws.
• Both kings guarded royal authority jealously and expected obedience from nobles and bishops.
• Henry VIII kept his father’s servants; Wolsey himself had begun as a chaplain to Henry VII.
• Both preferred trusted low-born administrators to great nobles for the running of business.
• Securing the Tudor dynasty through a male heir was the overriding aim of both reigns.

Overall judgement: the tone, the spending and the ambitions changed sharply from 1509, but the structures of government did not. Top-band answers weigh style against substance and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey was able to combine such great Church and state power by 1518.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the office of Cardinal
• Wolsey’s relationship with Henry VIII
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cardinal’s hat (1515) and papal legate (1518) — gave Wolsey ecclesiastical authority above even the Archbishop of Canterbury, allowing him to summon Church courts and appoint to benefices.
• Lord Chancellor (1515) — the senior secular office, putting him in charge of the Court of Chancery and royal justice.
• Henry’s confidence — the king trusted Wolsey because he delivered the 1513 French campaign and entertained him with pageantry, freeing the king from administration.
• Independent wealth — income from York, Lincoln and other sees funded Hampton Court and his diplomatic establishment without drawing on the Treasury.
• Lack of rival noble family — as a butcher’s son Wolsey had no dynasty of his own, so concentrating offices in one man did not create a rival power base.
• Pope’s willingness — Leo X granted him the legateship in 1518, hoping to use Wolsey to keep England within the Habsburg-Valois balance.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason Wolsey rose to power was Henry VIII’s dislike of administration.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Henry’s Renaissance Prince image
• the 1513 French campaign
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Henry preferred hunting, jousting and music to paperwork; council records show Wolsey routinely chairing meetings the king did not attend.
• Henry needed a manager to deliver the 1513 French campaign; Wolsey’s organisation of supply for a 30,000-man army made him indispensable.
• Henry’s Renaissance Prince image required pageantry rather than administration, leaving a vacuum Wolsey filled.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Wolsey’s personal ability — intelligent, energetic, a trained lawyer and theologian; he could not have risen without genuine talent.
• Independent clerical wealth — the archbishopric of York and bishoprics in plurality funded his establishment without depleting the Crown, making his power sustainable.
• Lack of a rival noble family — his butcher’s-son origins meant Henry could entrust him with great offices without creating a dynastic rival.
• Papal cooperation — Pope Leo X granted him the legateship in 1518, allowing Wolsey’s domination of the English Church.

Overall judgement: Henry’s temperament created the opportunity, but Wolsey’s ability and clerical wealth allowed him to fill it; without all three the rise would not have happened. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which law enforcement in England in the period c1000–c1500 was different from law enforcement in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Medieval law enforcement was unpaid and communal: every free man over twelve belonged to a tithing, and the hue and cry obliged the whole village to chase a suspect.
• Nineteenth-century law enforcement was salaried and organised: from 1829 the Metropolitan Police put uniformed constables on fixed beats under a single command.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Anglo-Saxons relied on the local community to enforce the law.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the tithing
• the hue and cry.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail from the period. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• There were no professional police, courts or prisons; the king did not have the resources to enforce law in every village.
• Anglo-Saxon society was small, rural and tightly knit — neighbours knew one another and could identify wrongdoers quickly.
• The system of tithings shared responsibility across ten men, so the whole group had a financial incentive to keep their members honest.
• The hue and cry mobilised the whole village against a criminal at no cost to the king.
• Compensation through wergild meant disputes could be settled locally, reducing the need for royal intervention.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons, each developed with specific period detail (e.g. tithing, hue and cry, wergild) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons clearly explained with relevant detail; links to the question are present but less developed.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of features without explaining why the community had this role.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which punishment in Anglo-Saxon England was different from punishment in eighteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Anglo-Saxon law leaned on compensation: wergild was paid to the victim or the victim's family, scaled by rank, to head off the blood feud.
• Eighteenth-century law leaned on death: under the Bloody Code more than 200 offences, most of them against property, could be punished by hanging.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main purpose of Anglo-Saxon punishment was deterrence.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the use of public corporal and capital punishment
• the wergild system.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting deterrence as the main purpose:
• Corporal punishments such as flogging, branding and the cutting off of a hand were carried out in public so that other villagers would think twice before offending.
• Capital punishment for treason, arson and the worst murders sent a clear public message that some crimes would cost the offender their life.
• The hue and cry made it likely that a criminal would be caught quickly, raising the perceived cost of breaking the law.

Indicative content — arguments against (other purposes):
• Wergild was about restitution rather than deterrence — it compensated the victim's family and headed off the blood feud, restoring relationships in the community.
• Tithings emphasised collective responsibility, which is closer to prevention than to deterrence after the fact.
• Retribution — the visible answer to a wrong done — was at least as central as deterrence; the law was deeply concerned with social rank and balance.
• Reform of the offender was not yet an aim, but maintaining communal harmony was.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs deterrence against at least one other purpose, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (e.g. tithing, wergild, shire reeve, hue and cry, retribution).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the responsibility placed on communities for crime in Anglo-Saxon England was similar to the responsibility placed on them in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• In Anglo-Saxon England the tithing made ten men answerable for each other; if one offended, the rest had to produce him or pay a fine.
• In Norman England the Murdrum fine made a whole village pay when a Norman was found dead and the killer was not produced.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the wergild mattered so much in Anglo-Saxon society.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the blood feud
• social rank.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• It prevented the blood feud — by providing compensation, it stopped families taking revenge through further killings, which had threatened to escalate into long cycles of violence.
• It reflected the social hierarchy — the size of the payment recognised the rank of the victim, reinforcing the structure of Anglo-Saxon society.
• It allowed disputes to be settled locally without constant intervention by the king's officials, which suited a society with no professional police.
• It combined punishment and restitution — the offender was financially harmed and the victim's family received tangible support, making the settlement feel just.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific detail (e.g. wergild scale under Cnut, prevention of feud) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of wergild without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth I’s inheritance of the English Crown in 1558.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with a precise supporting detail. For example: (1) Elizabeth inherited a Crown debt of around £300,000, much of it borrowed from Antwerp bankers after Mary I’s war with France. (2) Elizabeth’s legal position was insecure because she had been declared illegitimate by Parliament after her mother Anne Boleyn’s execution in 1536, and Catholic Europe rejected her claim.

Secure: Two features identified with at least one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given but support is general or only one is developed.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific support.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why religion was a problem for Elizabeth I when she came to the throne in 1558.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Marian bishops still in post
• the returning Protestant exiles
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own.

Mastering: A sustained explanation of at least three reasons, each supported by precise period detail (e.g. roughly 280 Protestants burnt under Mary I; Marian Catholic bishops still in post; returning Protestant exiles from Geneva and Frankfurt bringing radical ideas; Pope Paul IV refusing recognition). Reasons are linked, not listed separately.

Secure: Three reasons clearly explained with accurate detail. Some linkage between reasons.

Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified with limited detail.

Emerging: One reason, or general comments without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the French threat made Elizabeth’s position in 1558 especially dangerous.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least three interconnected reasons. Should include: France had recently taken Calais (January 1558); Henry II was hostile and allied to Scotland through the Auld Alliance; Mary, Queen of Scots, daughter-in-law of the French king, was already quartering the English royal arms and openly claiming Elizabeth’s throne; French troops under Mary of Guise were stationed in Scotland, exposing England’s northern border; English finances were too weak to fight a war. Answer reaches a clear analytical line about why these combined.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail and some linkage.

Developing: Two reasons explained, or several reasons identified without development.

Emerging: One reason, or general assertions without supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabethan society and government in 1558.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise detail. For example: (1) Elizabethan society was a strict hierarchy with the monarch at the top, then about 50 great noble families, gentry, yeomen, tenant farmers, labourers and the homeless poor. (2) Government ran outwards from the Privy Council in London to the counties, where Lord Lieutenants and Justices of the Peace, drawn from the local gentry, enforced the law on the queen’s behalf.

Secure: Two features identified with one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed feature.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Elizabeth’s personal strengths were the most important factor shaping her chances of success in 1558.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Elizabeth’s education and character
• the financial weakness of the Crown
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, analytical answer that uses BOTH stimulus points and adds at least one factor of the candidate’s own (e.g. the French threat; religious divisions; gender and legitimacy). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement with clear criteria for ‘most important’ (e.g. weighing what could be changed in the short term against permanent constraints). Uses period-specific terminology (Privy Council, debasement, settlement) accurately and consistently throughout.

Secure: Both stimulus points used and one own point added; clear judgement with some support; mostly accurate terminology.

Developing: Stimulus points used but limited additional content; judgement asserted rather than substantiated; some inaccuracy.

Emerging: Limited engagement with stimulus; description rather than analysis; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabeth’s gender created political problems in 1558–59.
You may use the following in your answer:
• John Knox’s 1558 pamphlet
• pressure from Parliament to marry
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own. Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons with precise detail. Should include: contemporary belief that women could not rule alone, illustrated by John Knox’s 1558 pamphlet The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women; pressure from Parliament for Elizabeth to marry quickly to produce an heir; the political risks attached to every marriage option (foreign Catholic prince → loss of independence; English noble → court factionalism); the fact that an unmarried queen with no heir made the succession itself a permanent threat. Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained. Emerging: One reason, or general comment without supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Reconquista for Spain’s readiness to back overseas exploration in 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Reconquista for Spain’s readiness to back overseas exploration, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Created a militarised society used to organising and funding holy war — Spain had eight centuries of mobilising soldiers, supplies and loans for crusading campaigns.
• Produced a generation of unemployed soldiers and minor nobles (hidalgos) after Granada fell in January 1492; these men became the manpower for the conquistador era.
• Cemented the ‘crusading spirit’ that fused conquest with religious conversion, making overseas expansion morally legible to Castilians as a continuation of the same project.
• Boosted Ferdinand and Isabella’s prestige and confidence, which Pope Alexander VI rewarded with the title Reyes Católicos in 1494.
• Freed royal attention and resources from a domestic war just as Columbus presented his proposal in spring 1492.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. military readiness AND ideological framing) with specific period detail (Granada 1492, Reyes Católicos, hidalgos) and clear links to overseas exploration.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Reconquista without explaining its importance for exploration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Spanish Inquisition (founded 1478) for life in Spain by 1490.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Inquisition policed the orthodoxy of conversos — Jews who had converted to Christianity — which produced a climate of fear and informants in Spanish cities.
• It strengthened the link between Crown and Church, making religious unity an arm of royal power and laying the ground for the 1492 expulsion of the Jews.
• It professionalised Spain’s capacity for ideological enforcement, training officials and inquisitors who would later operate in the Americas.
• It gave Ferdinand and Isabella the public reputation as defenders of Catholic orthodoxy that earned them the title Reyes Católicos in 1494.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the Inquisition without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of rivalry with Portugal for shaping Spanish foreign ambitions by 1490.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Portuguese rivalry, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Portuguese captains had been pushing down the West African coast for nearly a century — Cape Verde 1444, Cape of Good Hope rounded by Dias in 1488 — and held a papal monopoly over the African route to Asia.
• This locked Spain out of the wealthiest trade in the world (spices — pepper, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg) unless Spain could find another route.
• The rivalry made a westward Atlantic crossing politically attractive: Spain could outflank Portugal without breaking treaty.
• It encouraged Isabella to take a serious gamble on Columbus once Portugal had rejected his plan, because backing him cost her little if it failed but stole a march on Lisbon if it worked.
• It set up the diplomatic logic of the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) by ensuring that the moment a new western route opened, both crowns would need a way to divide the spoils.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking Portuguese rivalry to Spanish exploration, with specific period detail (Dias 1488, papal monopoly, spices) and clear chain of consequence.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Portugal’s position without explaining its importance for Spanish ambition.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella in 1469 for Spanish politics by 1490.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• United the crowns of Castile and Aragon under one royal household, even though the kingdoms kept separate parliaments and currencies — producing a single foreign policy for the first time.
• Allowed coordinated military pressure on the emirate of Granada, which fell in January 1492 and ended the Reconquista.
• Combined Castile’s wool wealth with Aragon’s Mediterranean trade routes, giving the joint monarchy more economic options than either had alone.
• Created a strong enough royal authority to found and run the Inquisition (1478) without local resistance.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the marriage without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the events of 1492 made Spain a country pointed outwards. You may use the following in your answer: the fall of Granada (January 1492), the Capitulations of Santa Fe (April 1492). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• The fall of Granada in January 1492 ended eight centuries of Reconquista, freeing royal attention, soldiers and the treasury.
• This release of resources made Isabella willing to consider a long-rejected proposal from Christopher Columbus, who had been waiting at court while the war finished.
• The Capitulations of Santa Fe (April 1492) granted Columbus extraordinary terms, signalling that the crown was prepared to gamble on overseas adventures now that domestic war was over.
• In March 1492 the expulsion of the Jews further hardened the religious unity of Spain, reinforcing the crusading mindset that would frame any new conquest as a Christianising mission.
• Columbus’s August departure was therefore not an isolated event but the next link in a chain — a kingdom that had just finished a holy war turning its energy outward across the Atlantic.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis — events are linked with phrases like ‘this in turn enabled’, ‘because of this’, ‘which provoked’. Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the existence of the hidalgo class in Spain for the future of Spanish overseas empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the hidalgo class, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Hidalgos were minor nobles trained for war and honour rather than farming or trade; the end of the Reconquista in 1492 left them without the war that defined their social role.
• They provided the manpower for early Caribbean and later mainland expeditions — men prepared to leave Spain for the chance of land, gold and noble status.
• Their presence shaped the conquistador model: small, self-funded expeditions led by a captain who recruited from this class on promise of a share of any loot.
• Their honour-driven outlook meant conquests were framed as personal services to crown and faith, not as commercial ventures — this affected how the Spanish state later treated conquests it considered ‘owed’ rewards.
• Without this surplus of fighting men, the Crown would have struggled to colonise large territories without much greater royal investment.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of hidalgos without explaining importance for empire.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. A description of Black voter registration in Mississippi in 1953.

‘In a county where Negroes outnumber whites two to one, only 121 of 12,000 eligible Negro voters appear on the rolls. Those who attempt to register are asked to interpret sections of the state constitution to the satisfaction of the registrar; their employers are visited; their homes are watched. The vote that the Constitution promised them is, in this state, a vote that very few dare to claim.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the position of Black Americans in the Southern states in the early 1950s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a precisely quoted detail from the source. (e.g. ‘Black registration was suppressed despite local Black majorities’ supported by ‘In a county where Negroes outnumber whites two to one, only 121 of 12,000 eligible Negro voters appear on the rolls.’ AND ‘Trying to register carried economic and personal risk’ supported by ‘their employers are visited; their homes are watched.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation, plus a second point that paraphrases the source.
Emerging: Paraphrase or summary of the source rather than inference. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for supporting quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Black Americans in the Southern states had so little political power by 1954.

You may use the following in your answer:
• literacy tests
• economic intimidation

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained analytical argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. poll taxes, white-only primaries, the threat of violence, the suppression of the NAACP), reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance, and uses precise period terminology (Jim Crow, ‘separate but equal’, sharecropping, grandfather clause).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; a judgement is offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of the stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement is implicit.
Emerging: Description of barriers to voting without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. Thurgood Marshall, head of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, on the strategy behind the school cases in the early 1950s.

‘We are not chasing one school district at a time. The doctrine itself must fall. Until the courts say plainly that segregation by law is unconstitutional, every victory we win in Topeka or Charleston will be undone in some other county before the ink dries.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the NAACP’s strategy in the early 1950s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘The NAACP wanted a single Supreme Court ruling against segregation rather than district-by-district wins’ supported by ‘The doctrine itself must fall.’ AND ‘Marshall feared that local victories would be reversed without a national legal change’ supported by ‘every victory we win … will be undone in some other county before the ink dries.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Interpretation 1 (from a school history textbook published in 2012): ‘Until 1954, civil rights for Black Americans was largely a story of patient legal work by the NAACP. Real change began only when the Supreme Court agreed to strike down school segregation in Brown v. Board. Before that, ordinary Black citizens were powerless and the federal government showed little interest.’ Interpretation 2 (from a historian writing about the ‘long civil rights movement’ in 2018): ‘The civil rights movement did not begin in 1954. By the early 1950s, Black newspapers, the wartime March on Washington movement, and grassroots organising by activists like Ella Baker and CORE in the North had built a network of activism across the country. The Brown ruling sat on top of decades of pressure from below.’ How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the development of civil rights activism before 1954? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 portrays change as top-down through the courts; Interpretation 2 portrays change as bottom-up through grassroots organising) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘patient legal work by the NAACP’ vs ‘decades of pressure from below’).
Secure: A clear difference is identified with a quotation from each interpretation.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the development of civil rights activism before 1954.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: the textbook in Interpretation 1 has been written for an introductory school audience and uses the dramatic 1954 ruling as a clear starting point, whereas Interpretation 2 reflects more recent academic scholarship that has used social and grassroots evidence (Black newspapers, activist networks) to show longer-running activism. Reason is anchored to wording of both extracts.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used, or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the development of civil rights activism before 1954?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, weighs them against substantial own knowledge (NAACP legal strategy, CORE’s 1947 Journey of Reconciliation, A. Philip Randolph’s 1941 March on Washington threat, Black wartime migration, voter suppression in Mississippi), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations are addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement is offered, though less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation is evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge is partial; judgement is implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 2. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the reasons migrants came to Britain in the medieval period (c800-c1500) were similar to the reasons they came in the modern period (c1900-present).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• In both periods economic pull mattered: Flemish weavers were drawn by the medieval wool trade, and Caribbean workers were recruited by the NHS and London Transport after 1948.
• In both periods the state decided who could come: Edward I expelled England's Jewish population in 1290, and Parliament opened and then closed Commonwealth entry between 1948 and 1971.
• In both periods religious or political persecution abroad pushed people out, from Jewish refugees fleeing medieval Europe to Ugandan Asians expelled in 1972.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why migration to Britain is studied across the whole period from c800 to the present, rather than from 1948.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the legal status of 'alien'
• the Huguenots.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Each wave - Vikings, Normans, Jewish communities, Huguenots, Irish, Caribbean - shaped British institutions, language and economy in lasting ways, so starting in 1948 erases most of the story.
• The legal idea of the 'alien' runs from medieval Hanseatic merchants to the Aliens Act of 1905, and only a long view makes that continuity visible.
• Black presence in Britain predates Windrush by centuries: Miranda Kaufmann has identified more than 360 Africans in England between 1500 and 1640.
• Patterns repeat across periods: religious refugees arrived after 1685 (Huguenots), after 1881 (Jewish refugees) and in 1972 (Ugandan Asians).
• The thematic study is examined across periods, so a comparison written over a century or more is what the question asks for.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the treatment of migrants by the English crown in the medieval period (c800-c1500) was different from their treatment by the British state in the modern period (c1900-present).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Medieval Jewish migrants belonged directly to the king and were taxed at his will through tallage; modern migrants are governed by Acts of Parliament such as the Aliens Act of 1905 and the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962.
• Medieval control was personal and could be reversed by one decree, as in 1290; modern control is built into permanent immigration law and border inspection.
• Medieval migrants had no route to equal legal standing, while the British Nationality Act of 1948 gave Commonwealth citizens the same right of entry as people born in Britain.
