Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Economic influences were the most important factor shaping migration to Britain across the period c800–present.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the role of the cloth industry in the 16th and 17th centuries
• post-war labour demand after 1945.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for economic influences:
• The cloth industry pulled Flemish and Walloon weavers to Sandwich and Canterbury from 1561, and Huguenot silk weavers to Spitalfields after 1685.
• Post-war Britain faced severe labour shortages; the NHS, London Transport and British Rail recruited directly in the Caribbean.
• Trade drew Hanseatic merchants to the London Steelyard and supported royal financiers such as Aaron of Lincoln.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Institutions decided the turning points: the expulsion of 1290, the Aliens Act of 1905, the British Nationality Act of 1948 and the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962.
• Religion drove the largest single waves: the stranger churches at Sandwich from 1561, the Huguenots after 1685 and Jewish refugees after 1881.
• Attitudes in society shaped reception independently of the economy: anti-Catholic hostility to Irish migrants in the 1850s, and the attacks in Notting Hill in 1958 during full employment.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (push factor, pull factor, Huguenot, Aliens Act, Commonwealth, alien).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the legal status of 'alien' mattered to migrants in Britain across the period c800-present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Hanseatic merchants
• the Aliens Act (1905).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• 'Alien' was the legal category for anyone not born under the English crown, and it carried real costs: higher customs duties, limits on owning land, and restrictions on trade.
• Hanseatic merchants at the Steelyard prospered but lived under alien status in a separate enclave, which kept them legally outside English society for three centuries.
• Jewish communities held a related but harsher status: they belonged to the king and were taxed through tallage, which left them exposed when royal protection failed.
• The Aliens Act of 1905 turned the old label into a border control, giving inspectors power to refuse entry to poor migrants while exempting those who travelled cabin class.
• The British Nationality Act of 1948 briefly dissolved the distinction for Commonwealth citizens, before the Acts of 1962, 1968 and 1971 rebuilt it.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why turning points are useful when studying migration in Britain across the period c800-present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the expulsion of 1290
• the Commonwealth Immigrants Act (1962).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Turning points mark the moments when policy or attitudes shifted decisively - 1290, 1685, 1905, 1948, 1962 - and they give a long answer its structure.
• They make change visible against continuity: the 1948 Act looks like a clean break, yet the older idea of the 'alien' survived alongside it.
• They allow comparison across periods: Huguenots after 1685 were welcomed as religious refugees, while Jewish refugees after 1881 met the Aliens Act of 1905.
• They anchor a judgement to dated evidence rather than to a vague sense that things changed over time.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of large-scale Scots-Irish and German immigration to British North America after 1713.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences, each developed with specific detail (e.g. the Scots-Irish pushed settlement west into the Pennsylvania backcountry, increasing pressure on Indigenous lands; German settlers strengthened Pennsylvania’s tradition of religious toleration). Explicit causal link: ‘this led to’, ‘as a result’.
Secure: Two consequences identified with some supporting detail; causal link present but less precise.
Developing: One developed consequence and one underdeveloped, or two general consequences without specific detail.
Emerging: General observations about immigration without clear consequence or specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of regional differences between the New England, Middle and Southern colonies for the development of colonial society in 1713.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: regional differences mattered because the South’s plantation economy entrenched enslaved labour while New England’s small-farm economy produced a more homogeneous Puritan society; this divergence shaped how each region later responded to British policy. Specific examples (Virginia tobacco, Massachusetts towns, Pennsylvania toleration) anchor each point.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail; two or more developments identified.
Developing: Some explanation of regional difference without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Description of the regions without explanation of why differences mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the social hierarchy in the colonies for relations between settlers in 1713.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the dominance of tidewater gentry in colonial assemblies meant backcountry settlers felt politically marginalised, leading to recurring petitions and unrest; the gulf between free white labour and enslaved labour created a working population whose interests diverged sharply by region.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to colonial groups.
Emerging: Restates the existence of a hierarchy without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how immigration changed the social character of British North America in the years 1713–41. You may use the following information in your answer: 
• Scots-Irish migration from Ulster 
• The forced migration of enslaved Africans 
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why the colonies became more plural rather than simply listing groups in order. Links Scots-Irish settlement to backcountry expansion and frontier tensions; links the slave trade to entrenchment of plantation labour and to growing demographic divergence between regions; weaves in own knowledge (e.g. German Lutheran settlement in Pennsylvania).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists migrant groups without explaining how they reshaped society.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of tensions between tidewater and backcountry settlers for colonial society in 1713.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: importance lay in the unequal political representation of backcountry settlers, which laid foundations for later unrest such as the Paxton Boys; importance also lay in the cultural distance between Anglican coastal elites and dissenter frontier farmers, which would shape religious revivalism in the 1730s and 1740s.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Identifies tension but explanation of importance is general.
Emerging: Mentions backcountry/tidewater without explaining significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the presence of enslaved Africans in every region of British North America by 1713.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two consequences each with specific detail. For example: the entrenchment of slavery in the Chesapeake produced a tobacco economy structurally dependent on enslaved labour, shaping Virginia’s political class; the presence of enslaved people in northern cities such as New York meant slavery was a colonies-wide institution, not a Southern peculiarity. Equal attention to both consequences with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Both consequences identified but underdeveloped, or one developed and one missing.
Emerging: General comment on slavery without specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the feudal hierarchy in England in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• The king as ultimate landlord — all land in England was held from the king; tenants-in-chief did homage directly to him.
• Knight service — tenants-in-chief owed roughly forty days of armed military service a year in return for their fief.
• Labour service — villeins worked the lord’s demesne for set days each week (week-work) and extra days at harvest (boon-work).
• Homage — the kneeling oath ceremony in which a tenant placed his hands between his lord’s and swore loyalty in return for land.
• Forfeiture — the legal seizure of a tenant’s land if he rebelled, refused service, or committed a serious crime.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of life in English towns in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Borough charters — royal grants giving towns the right to hold markets, collect tolls and choose their own bailiffs in return for an annual payment.
• Craft guilds — associations of weavers, tanners and bakers that set quality standards and trained apprentices.
• The wool trade — raw fleeces exported through Boston, Lincoln and York to Flemish and Italian buyers, the kingdom’s most valuable export.
• Small population — even London held only around 25,000 people; the kingdom had perhaps a hundred chartered towns by 1189.
• Royal taxation — towns paid an annual ‘farm of the borough’ into the exchequer and were targeted for extra levies in emergencies.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail (named towns, charters, guilds).
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague or partially inaccurate.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Anglo-Jewish community was so important to royal finances in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Christian ban on usury
• royal protection of Jews
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Christian ban on usury — Church doctrine forbade Christians from lending at interest, leaving Jewish lenders as the principal source of credit for barons, bishops and the Crown.
• Direct royal protection — Jews were legally the king’s property under his personal protection, meaning the wealth they accumulated was effectively a Crown reserve to be tapped through tallages.
• Concentration in towns — communities clustered in around twenty boroughs including London, York, Lincoln, Norwich and Lynn, putting their wealth within easy reach of royal officers.
• Restrictions on alternative occupations — bans on landholding and most craft guilds channelled Jewish economic activity into finance and trade, the very sectors that produced taxable cash wealth.
• Loans for royal projects — Jewish credit funded castle-building, royal campaigns and the rebuilding of cathedrals at Norwich and St Albans, all of which served Crown interests.
• Extraordinary tallages — Henry II had taxed the community at extraordinary rates and Richard inherited the habit; tallages produced large lump sums quickly without parliamentary or baronial consent.
• The archae system — after the 1189–90 pogroms, royal chests holding fresh copies of every loan ensured the Crown could always estimate, and tax, the community’s wealth.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Jewish communities of England suffered violent attacks in 1189–90.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Richard I’s coronation
• the role of indebted Norman gentry
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Richard’s coronation on 3 September 1189 — a Jewish delegation bringing gifts to Westminster was refused entry and beaten; rumours that the king had sanctioned an attack triggered a London mob to burn Jewish homes that night.
• Indebted Norman gentry — the York massacre at Clifford’s Tower on 16 March 1190 was led by Richard Malebisse and other gentry; immediately afterwards they rode to York Minster and burned the moneylending bonds, wiping out their own debts.
• Crusading fervour — Richard had taken the Cross; preachers framed the upcoming Third Crusade as a war against the enemies of Christ, and crowds extended that hatred to local Jewish communities.
• Religious antisemitism — long-standing prejudices, including the false ‘blood libel’ circulated at Norwich in 1144, made Jewish communities easy targets.
• Royal exploitation — heavy tallages had pushed barons and gentry to borrow from Jewish lenders, breeding resentment that erupted when royal protection seemed weakened by Richard’s departure plans.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative of events with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why labour service mattered so much to lords on a typical English manor in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the lord’s demesne
• the open-field system
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• The lord’s demesne — the home farm produced the food and wool that fed the lord’s household and generated cash; without villein labour it could not be ploughed, sown or harvested on time.
• The open-field system — ploughing, sowing and harvesting had to happen across great fields in narrow seasonal windows; week-work and boon-work concentrated peasant labour at exactly those moments.
• Cash-poor manors — coin was scarce in rural England; paying free wage labourers would have been impossible for most lords, so the customary obligation to work was the only way to get it done.
• Social control — labour service tied villeins to the manor and to the lord’s court, reinforcing the authority of the manorial system.
• Surplus for sale — what the demesne produced beyond the household’s needs went to market in nearby boroughs, providing the lord with cash for taxes, ransoms and royal service.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Religious hatred was the main reason for the pogroms of 1189–90.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Third Crusade
• debts owed to Jewish moneylenders
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Richard had taken the Cross; the Third Crusade was preached as a war against the enemies of Christ and crowds extended that hatred to local Jewish communities.
• The false ‘blood libel’ first circulated at Norwich in 1144 was repeated by preachers, casting Jewish neighbours as ritual murderers.
• The trigger event was the coronation banquet at Westminster, where Jewish leaders bringing gifts were refused entry on grounds that they could not approach the Christian rite.
• Religious feeling allowed mobs in London, Norwich, Lynn, Stamford and Lincoln to act with a sense of righteousness rather than guilt.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Debts owed to Jewish moneylenders — the York massacre was led by indebted Norman gentry under Richard Malebisse who burned the bonds at York Minster immediately afterwards, wiping out their debts.
• Royal absence — Richard was preparing to leave for the Holy Land; ringleaders calculated that royal protection would be weakened and prosecution unlikely.
• Royal exploitation — Henry II’s and Richard’s heavy tallages had forced Jewish lenders to call in loans aggressively, breeding resentment that turned violent at the first opportunity.
• Local crowd dynamics — once the London violence began, rumour and copying spread the pattern north along trading routes through the winter of 1189–90.

Overall judgement: Religious hostility provided the cover and the language, but the engine of the worst violence at York was debt politics and the calculation by indebted gentry that royal absence would shield them; without those material motives the killings would not have escalated as they did. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion using precise period vocabulary (pogrom, tallage, bonds, Crusade).

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Piracy Act (1717) for the suppression of piracy in American waters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences each developed with detail. For example: the Act's death penalty, applied in colonial trials, led to public hangings in port towns that deterred crews from joining pirate ships; and combined with the Proclamation, it split the pirate community between those who surrendered and those who fought on, isolating hard-line captains such as Blackbeard. Explicit causal language used.
Secure: Two consequences identified with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to trials, surrender, or deterrence.
Emerging: Restates that the Act suppressed piracy without showing how.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of tobacco for the development of British colonial society in the years 1713–41.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: tobacco mattered because its labour demands accelerated the growth of plantation agriculture in the Chesapeake and so the importation of enslaved Africans; and because tobacco profits paid for the British manufactured goods that bound the planter class to British markets and culture. Specific evidence (Chesapeake, 30 million pounds by the 1720s) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General comments on tobacco’s role without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Describes tobacco as a crop without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the British government suppressed piracy in American waters between 1715 and 1725. You may use the following information in your answer: 
• King George I’s Proclamation (1717) 
• Governor Spotswood’s campaign 
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence. For example: the post-1713 surge of demobilised sailors caused a piracy crisis; the Proclamation drew off less committed pirates by offering pardon; the Piracy Act sped up colonial trials; Spotswood’s expedition then targeted the most committed remaining pirate in November 1718. Concludes with the wider point that suppression succeeded because it combined pardon, courts and naval force.
Secure: Clear narrative with several analytical links between named events and the Crown’s response.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis.
Emerging: Lists pirates without explaining how the response unfolded.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of triangular trade with the West Indies for New England’s economy in the early eighteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two consequences with development. For example: the supply of West Indian molasses fed New England’s rum distilleries, which led to a profitable export industry that depended on cheap imports; and the demand for cheap molasses encouraged widespread smuggling that brought New England merchants into routine conflict with British customs officers. Specific causal language used.
Secure: Two consequences identified, at least one with supporting detail.
Developing: General observations about Caribbean trade without specific consequence.
Emerging: Lists trade goods without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the role of Governor Spotswood for the suppression of piracy in American waters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: Spotswood’s commissioning of Lieutenant Maynard’s expedition led directly to the death of Blackbeard at Ocracoke Inlet in November 1718, removing the most prominent pirate of the Golden Age and signalling the limits of pirate refuge in the Carolina inlets; his role also showed how Crown authority depended on individual colonial governors taking decisive action.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Describes Spotswood’s actions without explaining their importance.
Emerging: Names Spotswood without explaining what he did.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Navigation Acts for the relationship between Britain and the North American colonies in the years 1713–41.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Acts mattered because they channelled colonial profits into British ports and gave the Crown its customs revenue; and because they made smuggling a routine practice that normalised colonial defiance of imperial regulation. Specific examples (tobacco re-export through London, illegal molasses trade with French sugar islands) anchor each development.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Mentions the Navigation Acts without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Describes the Acts without explaining what they did to the relationship.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of an English king in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Sacred coronation — the king was anointed with holy oil by the Archbishop of Canterbury at Westminster, framing him as God’s appointed ruler.
• Defence of the kingdom — the king was expected to lead the army in war and protect his subjects from invasion.
• Dispensing justice — he was the source of all royal justice, with itinerant justices touring the shires in his name.
• Granting and levying taxes — the king summoned councils, granted charters and raised revenue through scutage, tallages and fines.
• Taking counsel — he was expected to consult his Curia Regis of great barons and bishops on important decisions.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how Richard I secured his power in 1189.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Coronation at Westminster — on 3 September 1189 he was anointed and crowned by the Archbishop, broadcasting legitimacy across the Angevin Empire.
• Sale of offices and charters — he sold sheriffdoms, confirmed baronial charters for cash, and was said to have joked that he would sell London if he could.
• Use of Henry II’s treasury — Richard spent the money his father had already raised through the Saladin Tithe of 1188.
• Reconciliation with John — he granted his brother extensive lands and a generous income to keep him quiet while away.
• Appointment of trusted ministers — chancellor William Longchamp, justiciars and bishops to govern in his name.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Hubert Walter was such an effective head of government for England 1193–98.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the offices he held
• his reforms of justice
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Combined offices — as Archbishop of Canterbury and chief justiciar he commanded both the moral authority of the senior English see and the secular authority to chair the Curia Regis, run the Exchequer and supervise the courts.
• Reforms of justice — the 1194 Articles of Eyre standardised what royal justices asked when they toured the shires, and the introduction of county coroners in 1194 created a check on the sheriffs.
• Raising the ransom — he extracted 150,000 marks of silver in 1193–94 through a quarter tax on income and moveables, the Cistercian wool clip, church plate and tallages on the Jewish community, holding the Crown’s credit at its weakest moment.
• Continuity with Henry II’s institutions — he ran a system already strong (Exchequer, eyre, sheriffs, pipe rolls), enabling effective government in the king’s absence.
• Royal trust — Richard knew Walter from the crusade and trusted him with the government of England; this confidence allowed bold policy decisions without fear of repudiation.
• Defeat of John’s 1191–94 coup — Walter (with Eleanor) co-ordinated the loyalist response, recovering John’s castles at Marlborough and Lancaster.
• Diplomatic reach — as Archbishop he could correspond with the Pope and negotiate with foreign powers, providing tools no lay justiciar could match.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why royal government in England did not collapse during Richard I’s long absence on crusade.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Hubert Walter
• the Exchequer
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Hubert Walter as chief justiciar — from 1193 he chaired the Curia Regis, ran the Exchequer and supervised the courts, providing a single, capable head of government able to make decisions in the king’s name.
• The Exchequer — Henry II’s twice-yearly accounting system, with sheriffs reporting and pipe rolls recording revenue, kept the Crown’s finances functional even when the king was overseas.
• The eyre and the sheriffs — itinerant royal justices and county sheriffs delivered justice and collected revenue in a regular pattern that did not depend on the king’s personal presence.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine — the queen-mother acted as a political fixer, holding the great barons together and helping to negotiate her son’s release.
• John’s rebellion — his attempt to seize power in 1191–94 gave loyal barons a clear enemy and rallied them around the legitimate government.
• The Church — the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Pope reaffirmed Richard’s legitimacy, deterring serious challengers from open revolt.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Church played such a central role in royal government in 1189.
You may use the following in your answer:
• coronation
• literate clerks and bishops
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Coronation legitimacy — the anointing by the Archbishop of Canterbury made the king God’s appointed ruler, sanctifying his authority over the laity.
• Literate administrators — in an age when most laymen could not read Latin, bishops and clerks staffed the Exchequer, courts and chancery.
• Free pool of officials — clerks held Church benefices that paid them a salary, so the Crown got skilled administrators without bleeding its own treasury.
• Bishops on the Curia Regis — senior churchmen sat alongside the great barons in the king’s council, advising on policy.
• Diplomatic links — bishops carried letters between courts and to Rome, providing a working diplomatic network that lay barons could not match.
• Spiritual sanctions — excommunication and interdict were powerful weapons that bound the Church into political crises (a fact John would discover in 1208).

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Hubert Walter was the main reason England held together while Richard was absent.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the ransom of 1194
• the strength of Henry II’s institutions
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Hubert Walter ran the Curia Regis, the Exchequer and the courts simultaneously, providing a single head of government able to make decisions in the king’s name.
• He raised the king’s ransom of 150,000 marks in 1193–94 through a quarter tax, the Cistercian wool clip and church plate, holding the Crown’s credit together at its weakest moment.
• He reformed the eyre and introduced coroners in 1194, strengthening institutions even while the king was away.
• As Archbishop of Canterbury he commanded the moral authority needed to keep the great barons in line.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Henry II’s institutions — the Exchequer, pipe rolls, professional sheriffs and itinerant justices were already in place by 1189; Walter ran a system he had inherited.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine — the queen-mother held the political coalition together and was central to the ransom negotiations and to defeating John in 1194.
• John’s rebellion — the very threat of his coup in 1191–94 united the loyal barons behind the legitimate government.
• Papal and ecclesiastical pressure — the Pope and bishops reinforced Richard’s legitimacy and discouraged open revolt.
• Royal absence as a stabiliser — with the king on crusade, baronial factions had little to gain by toppling a government whose most popular figure (Walter) was running things competently.

Overall judgement: Hubert Walter was indispensable, but he succeeded because he was running Henry II’s machinery, with Eleanor of Aquitaine and the Church reinforcing legitimacy and John’s rebellion clarifying loyalties. A balanced judgement weighs Walter’s talent against the institutional inheritance and political support he could draw on.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (justiciar, eyre, ransom, archae, demesne).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of UN Resolution 181 (November 1947) for Palestine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) civil war broke out from December 1947 between Jewish forces and Palestinian Arab militias, with around 100 Palestinians killed at Deir Yassin in April 1948; (ii) it provided the political basis for the Israeli Declaration of Independence on 14 May 1948 and triggered invasion by Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon. Pairs an immediate and a longer-term consequence. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, each explained, but one less developed. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description than consequence. [3–4]
Emerging: A single point or restatement of what Resolution 181 said without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the King David Hotel bombing (July 1946) for British policy in Palestine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct consequences with detail. For example: (i) Operation Shark, the cordon-and-search of Tel Aviv from 30 July to 2 August 1946, and the Haganah’s formal break from the Irgun; (ii) the longer-term shift in London under Bevin towards referring the Mandate to the UN in February 1947 because direct rule had become politically and financially unsustainable. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence; second is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates what the bombing was without explaining policy effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the events that led to the end of the British Mandate, in the years 1946–48.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the King David Hotel bombing
• UN Resolution 181
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects across the period. Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as the Exodus 1947 incident, UNSCOP’s 1947 tour or the Haganah’s Plan Dalet of March 1948. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing them. [7–8] Secure: Narrative addresses three or more aspects with clear analytical links between events; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6] Developing: Narrative covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer aspects (capped at this band if it does not address three or more aspects per the cap rule). [3–4] Emerging: A descriptive account; sequence errors; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of UN Resolution 181 (November 1947) for the creation of the state of Israel.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why Resolution 181 mattered for the creation of Israel. Identifies several specific consequences: it gave Israel an internationally recognised legal basis; it formed the framework for Ben-Gurion’s Declaration on 14 May 1948; it triggered Arab rejection and the civil war that allowed the Yishuv’s forces to expand the territory it controlled before independence; and it set the precedent for partition that has shaped peace negotiations ever since. Reaches a clear judgement on importance. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. Judgement clear if a little implicit. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive; events recounted rather than analysed for importance. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Resolution 181 without showing its consequences for the creation of Israel. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the end of the British Mandate (1948) for the creation of the state of Israel.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the timing of the 14 May 1948 declaration to coincide with the Mandate’s expiry; the absence of a transitional authority allowing the Yishuv to act before any UN trusteeship was established; the Arab states treating Mandate withdrawal as the trigger for invasion. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects (US recognition within hours; the precedent for UN involvement throughout 1949 onwards). [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Describes the end of the Mandate without showing why it mattered for the creation of Israel. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the end of the Mandate without explaining consequences. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the breakdown of the Mandate in the years 1945–47.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Truman’s 1945 demand for 100,000 immigrants
• the King David Hotel bombing
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Coherent analytical narrative addressing at least three aspects. Uses both stimulus points and adds material from the student’s own knowledge (e.g. the Jewish Resistance Movement; the Exodus 1947; Bevin’s February 1947 announcement; Britain’s post-war economic crisis). Causal links explicit. [7–8] Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6] Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4] Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little analysis. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Viking settlement in England (c800-c1066) was different from Norman settlement after 1066.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Viking migration was mass settlement by farming families across the Danelaw; Norman migration was elite migration by perhaps 200 barons who took the land and left the population in place.
• Vikings built their own legal zone with its own courts and wapentakes; Normans took over the existing English system of shires and used it to govern.
• Viking settlement left its mark mainly on place names and everyday speech; Norman settlement changed the language of law and government and the ownership of land.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Danelaw was established in England in the late ninth century.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of Edington (878)
• Scandinavian farming settlement.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Military stalemate: Alfred beat Guthrum at Edington in 878 but could not drive Scandinavian settlers out of the north and east, so a negotiated boundary was the realistic outcome.
• Religion: Guthrum's baptism gave Alfred a Christian peace partner and reduced the risk of renewed raiding.
• Economics: Scandinavian families had cleared and farmed land in eastern England since 865, and expelling them would have wrecked the local economy.
• Institutions: recognising the Danelaw let Anglo-Saxon law run in Wessex while Norse custom continued in the north, which stabilised both regions.
• Culture: Old English and Old Norse came from the same language family, which made coexistence easier than expulsion.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the impact of Viking migrants on England (c800-c1066) was similar to the impact of Caribbean migrants on Britain after 1948.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both left a permanent mark on everyday language: Norse gave English sky, law and they; Caribbean migrants reshaped London speech, music and food from the 1950s.
• Both changed the map of particular places: Danelaw villages ending in -by, and Caribbean shops and markets along Portobello Road and All Saints Road.
• Both were absorbed within a few generations while leaving distinct cultural traces, so newcomers became part of the local population rather than staying separate.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important impact of Viking migration on England was the establishment of the Danelaw.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Treaty of Wedmore (878)
• Cnut’s reign from 1016.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for the Danelaw as the most important impact:
• The agreement of 878 and the boundary treaty that followed divided England into two legal zones, which was a structural change to government.
• The wapentake gave the Danelaw its own unit of local government, and it survived long after the Norman Conquest.
• The Danelaw made permanent Scandinavian settlement lawful across Yorkshire, the East Midlands and East Anglia.

Indicative content - support for other impacts:
• Cnut's reign from 1016 to 1035 tied England into a North Sea empire and produced a stable Anglo-Scandinavian culture.
• The linguistic impact was deeper and longer lasting: around 1,500 Scandinavian place names, and everyday words such as sky, law and they.
• Viking trade networks linked York and Lincoln to Dublin, Bergen and the Baltic, widening the English economy.
• Scandinavian legal custom fed into later English common law, including oath-helping and jury-style decision making.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (Danelaw, wapentake, Anglo-Scandinavian, settlement).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cnut was able to rule England successfully after 1016.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Anglo-Saxon shires and ealdormen
• the English Church.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• He governed through the institutions already in place, keeping the system of shires and ealdormen rather than importing Scandinavian government.
• His law codes drew on earlier Anglo-Saxon tradition, so English landowners recognised the rules they were being asked to obey.
• He gave generously to English monasteries, which tied the Church to the new dynasty.
• A century and a half of Scandinavian settlement in the Danelaw meant much of England already had a mixed Anglo-Scandinavian population.
• His wider North Sea empire, which came to include Denmark and Norway, removed the threat of fresh Viking raiding.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Viking arrivals in England are described as migrants and not only as invaders.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Danelaw
• place-name evidence.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• After 865 Scandinavian families cleared and farmed land in Yorkshire and the East Midlands, which is settlement rather than raiding.
• The late ninth-century agreement recognised the Danelaw as a permanent area of Scandinavian settlement under recognised law.
• Settlers paid taxes through the wapentake system, used local courts and converted to Christianity, as Guthrum did in 878.
• Around 1,500 Scandinavian place names, especially those ending in -by and -thorpe, show permanent rural settlement.
• Viking trade linked York and Lincoln into a North Sea economy that lasted into the eleventh century.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the role of the Petrograd garrison in the February Revolution. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, Volynsky regiment soldiers refusing to fire, the seizure of the Arsenal, or the figure of c.66,000 garrison troops joining the protesters). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that loyalty had collapsed before the abdication, not because of it. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that is closer to a paraphrase than an inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to a source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Nicholas II fell from power in only eight days in February and March 1917.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Petrograd garrison mutiny
• the role of the generals
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. the women’s strike of 23 February, the Putilov lockout, the garrison mutiny on 27 February, the generals’ advice to abdicate, the long-term war and Rasputin background). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Petrograd Soviet, Provisional Committee, Tauride Palace, Stavka. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing the causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the revolution without explaining why the Tsar fell so fast; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about whether the February Revolution was a spontaneous rising or a planned political event.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents February as a leaderless, bottom-up rising of women textile workers and Putilov mutineers; the other stresses the role of liberal Duma politicians and front-line generals in finishing the regime off). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the role of the Duma politicians in the February Revolution.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (memoirs of Duma politicians like Rodzianko versus factory committee minutes and police reports), wrote at different times (an early liberal account versus revisionist social history) or had different purposes (vindicating the Duma versus restoring popular agency). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the Petrograd garrison’s mutiny in the fall of Nicholas II?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of February 1917 — Volynsky regiment, c.66,000 mutinous troops, Khabalov’s order to fire, General Alekseev’s telegram poll, the Pskov abdication — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’ rather than ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on 1917 and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the February Revolution was a largely spontaneous popular rising rather than the result of long-term failures of the regime?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the 23 February women’s strike, the c.240,000 strikers by 25 February, the Volynsky mutiny, the Tauride Palace negotiation, Nicholas’s abdication at Pskov, the long-run war and food crisis — to test how far the rising was spontaneous against how far it was the regime’s long collapse. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Petrograd Soviet, Stavka, Provisional Committee). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the definition of crime in Norman England was different from the definition of crime in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• The Normans criminalised everyday activity: inside the royal forest it became an offence to hunt deer, fell trees, gather firewood or graze pigs, on pain of fines, mutilation or death.
• Anglo-Saxon law had defined crime around harm to people, property and the king's peace, and had not treated hunting or wood-gathering on common land as criminal at all.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Norman Conquest changed the definition of crime in England.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Forest Laws
• the Murdrum fine.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• William needed to protect a small Norman ruling class in a hostile country — the Murdrum fine pressured English communities to surrender the killers of Normans.
• William wanted to enrich himself and project royal power over land — designating royal forest gave him exclusive hunting rights, and Forest Laws criminalised the use of that land by ordinary people.
• Norman ideas of justice (trial by combat) were brought across the Channel and added to existing trials.
• Existing Anglo-Saxon law (tithings, hue and cry) was kept to maintain stability — change was therefore selective, focusing on what suited the new regime.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Murdrum, royal forest, trial by combat) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Norman rule with no clear reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which royal power over crime in Norman England was different from royal power in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Norman kings created law to protect themselves and their followers: the Murdrum fine punished a whole community for an unsolved Norman death, and Forest Law reserved a third of southern England for the king's hunting.
• Anglo-Saxon kings issued law codes and took fines through the shire reeve, but enforcement stayed with tithings, oath-helpers and the local courts.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Norman Conquest brought more change than continuity to crime and punishment in England.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• William I’s Forest Laws
• tithings and the hue and cry.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments supporting more change:
• Forest Laws (from 1071) created entirely new crimes — hunting deer or wild boar, gathering wood, grazing pigs on royal forest land — punishable by mutilation or death.
• The Murdrum fine introduced collective punishment specifically for the killing of Normans, sharpening the legal divide between Normans and English.
• Trial by combat became a new method of deciding verdicts, alongside the older oath-helpers and ordeals.
• Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) strengthened royal courts and extended royal justice into the shires.

Indicative content — arguments supporting more continuity:
• Tithings and the hue and cry continued to do most day-to-day policing, especially in villages.
• The shire reeve and shire courts carried on under both Anglo-Saxon and Norman kings.
• Trial by jury and oath-helpers persisted alongside the new trial by combat.
• Capital and corporal punishments remained the main responses to serious crime; the basic philosophy of deterrence and retribution did not change.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs change against continuity, uses accurate period detail (Forest Laws, Murdrum, tithing, hue and cry), and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way verdicts were reached in Norman England was different from the way they were reached after 1215.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Norman trials could turn on divine judgement: trial by combat let the accused and accuser fight, and trial by ordeal read a burn or a ducking as God's verdict.
• After the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 withdrew the clergy from ordeals, royal courts extended trial by jury, so twelve local men weighed the evidence instead.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why William I introduced the Murdrum fine after 1066.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Norman lords and settlers
• collective responsibility.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Norman lords and settlers were a small armed minority ruling a hostile English population — the fine was designed to protect them from English revenge attacks in the years of unrest after 1066.
• Without the fine, English villages had every reason to shield the killer of a Norman; the threat of a community-wide ruinous payment turned that incentive on its head.
• It extended the older Anglo-Saxon idea of collective responsibility (already used in tithings) so that the same machinery now policed Anglo-Norman relations.
• The fine reinforced William's wider strategy: keep most Anglo-Saxon law intact, but layer on new measures specifically aimed at securing his rule and protecting his followers.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Anglo-Norman tensions, collective responsibility, William's wider strategy) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Murdrum fine without explaining why William introduced it.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the tactics used by English commanders were similar at the Battle of Falkirk (1298) and the Battle of Agincourt (1415).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Both commanders used massed archers to break an enemy who could not reply (1). At Falkirk in 1298 Edward I pulled his knights back and shot the Scottish schiltrons apart from beyond spear-reach (1). At Agincourt in 1415 Henry V put his archers behind sharpened stakes and shot into French cavalry trapped in mud (1). In both battles the archers worked with other troops rather than fighting alone (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the way battles were fought changed in England in the period c1250–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• schiltrons at Falkirk (1298)
• the longbow at Agincourt (1415).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• New formations changed what cavalry could do: the schiltron at Falkirk (1298) showed that disciplined foot soldiers could stop a charge.
• Massed longbow fire then cancelled the schiltron, because packed men who could not spread out were easy targets from beyond spear-reach.
• Commanders learned to combine troop types: Edward I used archers then cavalry; Henry V used archers, stakes and dismounted men-at-arms together.
• Choice of ground mattered more and more: Henry V fought in a narrow, muddy funnel between two woods so the French could not use their numbers.
• Gunpowder added a further change from the mid-fourteenth century, first in sieges and then, slowly, in the field.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way foot soldiers defended themselves against cavalry was different in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the fourteenth century Scottish foot soldiers packed into a schiltron (1). This was a tight ring of men holding 12-foot spears outwards, which horses would not charge (1). In the seventeenth century the same job was done by the pike block (1). Pikemen with 16 to 18 foot pikes stood beside the musketeers and covered them while they reloaded (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the role of the mounted knight in battle changed in the period c1250–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of Falkirk (1298)
• dismounted men-at-arms at Agincourt (1415).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Foot formations such as the schiltron stopped the charge at Falkirk (1298), so cavalry could no longer expect to break any line of infantry.
• Massed longbows killed horses at a distance, and a knight on foot in heavy armour was slow and exhausted, as the French found at Agincourt (1415).
• Ground and weather could cancel the charge: ploughed mud at Agincourt trapped horses and armoured men.
• English commanders therefore dismounted their men-at-arms to stiffen the line beside the archers.
• The knight kept his social rank and his place in command, so change on the battlefield was faster than change in society.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of the English commander was similar at the Battle of Falkirk (1298) and the Battle of Agincourt (1415).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both battles the king led in person and changed the plan as the fighting went on (1). At Falkirk Edward I saw his knights fail against the schiltrons and ordered the archers forward instead (1). At Agincourt Henry V chose the narrow ground, had stakes driven in and told his men-at-arms to fight on foot (1). In both cases one clear voice in command beat an enemy who had no single leader (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘The longbow was the main reason for English victory at both Falkirk (1298) and Agincourt (1415).’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Edward I’s use of archers at Falkirk
• Henry V’s decisions at Agincourt.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for the longbow as main reason:
• At Falkirk, longbowmen broke the schiltrons after the cavalry charge had failed — the arrows did the decisive work.
• At Agincourt, massed arrow fire stopped the French cavalry, killed horses and disrupted the advancing French men-at-arms.
• The longbow's range (around 250 yards) and rate of fire (10–12 arrows a minute) gave English armies a battlefield reach no other weapon could match.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Leadership and command: Edward I's decision to switch from cavalry to archers; Henry V's choice of terrain, his stake-line and his decision to dismount men-at-arms.
• Terrain and weather: Falkirk was fought on open ground that suited Edward's combined arms; Agincourt's narrow muddy funnel between two woods is what made the longbow lethal.
• Logistics: Edward had supplied his army; Wallace's was hungry. Henry V's men were ill but still better organised than the French.
• Morale and command: Wallace's army had been demoralised by weeks of evasion; the French at Agincourt had no overall commander, leading to chaotic ranks pushing each other into the mud.
• Combined arms: in both battles the longbow worked because cavalry and men-at-arms supported it — alone it could not have decided either outcome.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs the longbow against leadership, terrain, logistics and command across both battles, uses accurate period detail (schiltron, stakes, dismounted men-at-arms, named commanders) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident use of period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail across both battles; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side or one battle dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the condition of the Guomindang army during the 1948–49 campaigns. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. troops surrendering without a fight at Beijing, defections to the PLA, abandoned American equipment). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that GMD morale and command had collapsed by late 1948. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one slightly weaker than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase that does not quite reach inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or no clear use of the source. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Communists won the Chinese Civil War by 1949.
You may use the following in your answer:
• land reform
• corruption in the Guomindang
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, weighted explanation of the CCP victory drawing on at least three causes — e.g. land reform, GMD hyperinflation/corruption, PLA strategy under Lin Biao, urban student unrest, the loss of the Liaoshen/Huaihai/Pingjin campaigns. Uses the stimulus points and goes beyond them. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Confident period vocabulary. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained with supporting detail; some weighing of importance; one cause used to anchor a partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Two or more causes named but mainly described rather than explained; relies on the stimulus more than own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: A general narrative of the war rather than a causation explanation; little or no judgement. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about why the Guomindang lost the Chinese Civil War.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation blames the GMD’s internal failings — corruption, inflation, conscription — while the other emphasises CCP strengths such as Mao’s leadership and PLA discipline). Each side of the difference is supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without setting against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about why the CCP won the Civil War.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote in different periods (Cold War vs post-archival), used different evidence (US State Department papers vs Chinese-language archives, e.g. Frank Dikötter), or had different purposes (commemorative CCP narrative vs revisionist Western critique). The reason links specifically to the difference between the two views. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained with some supporting detail. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but only loosely linked to the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that Mao Zedong's leadership was the most important reason for the CCP's victory in the Chinese Civil War?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and weighs them with own knowledge — Mao’s strategic decisions and Yan’an leadership balanced against GMD self-destruction (hyperinflation, the gold-yuan failure, corruption, brutal conscription) and the role of Lin Biao in the Liaoshen Campaign. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’ rather than treating the question as ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured over the other; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted not argued. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay on the Civil War with little engagement with the interpretations as views; or rests only on the stimulus. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the role of urban unrest in the Guomindang's defeat?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the ‘Anti-Hunger, Anti-Civil-War’ student movement of 1947, the August 1948 gold-yuan reform, the collapse of the Chinese yuan, civil servants unable to buy rice, GMD police violence on campuses, the China White Paper of 1949 — to test how far urban unrest explains GMD defeat. Reaches a clearly justified judgement that weighs urban unrest against rural land reform and PLA strategy. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (Liaoshen, Pingjin, gold yuan, Outline Land Law). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
