Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement but reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly with the interpretations; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning; limited subject vocabulary. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: One interpretation described, the other ignored; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth’s religious settlement of 1559.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise supporting detail. For example: (1) The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth ‘Supreme Governor’ rather than ‘Supreme Head’ of the Church of England, a softer title designed to make her authority easier for Catholics and conservatives to accept. (2) The Act of Uniformity required all parishes to use a revised version of the 1552 Book of Common Prayer, with hybrid communion wording combining 1549 and 1552 phrasings to satisfy moderate Catholics and Protestants.

Secure: Two features identified with at least one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed feature.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the wording of the 1559 Book of Common Prayer was carefully crafted.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the communion wording
• moderate Catholics
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own.

Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons with precise supporting detail. Should include: the wish to keep moderate Catholics inside the national Church (hybrid communion phrase combining 1549 and 1552 wording so the priest’s words could be read as Real Presence or memorial); the political need to avoid a religious civil war in England; the queen’s personal preference for traditional ceremony, vestments and church furnishings; the practical need for parishes and clergy to keep functioning during the changeover.

Secure: Three reasons clearly explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained.

Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabeth chose to call herself ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church rather than ‘Supreme Head’ in 1559.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Catholic views of the Pope
• objections to a woman ruling the Church
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own.

Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: making the title acceptable to Catholics, who believed only the Pope could be head of the Church on earth; addressing contemporary objections that a woman could not be ‘head’ of the Church; distinguishing the new arrangement from Henry VIII’s 1534 break with Rome to soften opposition; and ensuring that more clergy and royal officials could swear the oath of supremacy without breaking conscience. Each reason should be supported with specific detail.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained.

Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of the Church of England in everyday life after 1559.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed. For example: (1) The parish church recorded all births, marriages and deaths after the 1559 Royal Injunctions required parish registers, making the Church the main administrative system for tracking the population. (2) Attendance at Sunday service was legally compulsory under the Act of Uniformity, with a 12 pence weekly fine for those who missed without good reason — making the Church both a religious and a policing institution.

Secure: Two features identified with one supporting detail each.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The 1559 religious settlement was a successful compromise that gave England thirty years of religious peace.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Act of Supremacy and the Act of Uniformity
• the response of Marian bishops and parish clergy
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained, analytical answer that uses BOTH stimulus points, adds at least one factor of the candidate’s own (e.g. ambiguous communion wording; Royal Injunctions and visitations; the queen’s ‘windows into men’s souls’ principle; later Puritan and Catholic challenges that show the limits of the compromise), and reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that the settlement was a successful short-term compromise that left long-term tensions which later challenges exposed. Period-specific terminology used accurately throughout (recusancy, vestments, Supreme Governor, via media, visitations). Secure: Both stimulus points used and one own point added; clear judgement with some support. Developing: Stimulus points used but limited additional content; judgement asserted rather than substantiated. Emerging: Limited engagement with stimulus; description rather than analysis; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why most parish clergy accepted the 1559 religious settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least three interconnected reasons. Should include: the settlement’s deliberate ambiguity in worship (vestments retained, hybrid communion wording) made conformity easier; the financial and personal cost of refusal — clergy who refused the oath lost their living; Elizabeth’s ‘windows into men’s souls’ principle of accepting outward conformity meant private belief was not interrogated; the absence of clear papal direction in 1559 meant Catholics had no authoritative call to resist; and the experience of repeated religious change since 1534 had made many clergy pragmatic. Reasons should be linked, not listed.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained, or several reasons identified without development.

Emerging: One reason, or general assertions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Court of Star Chamber under Wolsey.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Met in a chamber at Westminster decorated with gold stars, presided over by the Lord Chancellor and members of the king’s council.
• Heard cases involving powerful people that local common-law courts could not control — nobles, gentry, riots, jury intimidation.
• Wolsey heard around 120 cases a year, compared with about 12 under Henry VII.
• Made high-profile examples — the Earl of Northumberland (1515) prosecuted for illegal retaining; Sir Amyas Paulet humiliated.
• Was a prerogative court — based on royal authority rather than common law.

Mastering: Two distinct features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: One feature only, or no detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Eltham Ordinances of 1526.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Issued at Eltham Palace in January 1526 as a set of regulations for the royal household.
• Reduced the number of gentlemen of the Privy Chamber from twelve to six.
• Set wages, food allowances and rules of conduct for royal servants to cut waste.
• Removed several courtiers (including William Compton and Henry Norris) who had been challenging Wolsey’s influence over Henry.
• Aimed officially at efficiency and economy in royal expenditure.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey reformed royal taxation through the subsidy.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the cost of war with France
• the limits of the ‘fifteenth and tenth’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cost of war — the 1513 French campaign and the 1520s wars far exceeded what the medieval fifteenth and tenth could raise; the subsidy was needed to fund Henry’s ambitions.
• Limits of the fifteenth and tenth — this older tax raised a fixed sum regardless of how wealth had shifted, leaving the rich under-taxed and the poor over-burdened.
• Equity — Wolsey wanted a tax assessed on individuals’ actual landed and movable wealth, surveyed by commissioners, so the burden matched ability to pay.
• Royal authority — a tax based on personal assessment increased the king’s knowledge of his subjects’ wealth and tightened central government’s grip.
• Wolsey’s reforming instinct — he was a trained administrator who saw the older tax system as outdated and inefficient.

Mastering: Three or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but limited explanation.
Emerging: Mostly description of the subsidy without focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Wolsey’s changes to the law courts were his most successful domestic reform.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• equity
• over-mighty subjects
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the legal reforms against Wolsey’s other domestic measures and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Equity in the Court of Chancery gave poorer petitioners remedies the common law could not offer, and case volume roughly doubled.
• Star Chamber disciplined over-mighty subjects whom local courts dared not touch, hearing around 120 cases a year against about 12 under Henry VII.
• High-profile prosecutions, such as the Earl of Northumberland in 1515 for illegal retaining, showed that the crown could reach the greatest men.
• Cheap, fast justice was visible to ordinary people in a way that fiscal reform never was.

Arguments for his other reforms:
• The subsidy taxed real wealth rather than fixed quotas and raised far more than the old fifteenth and tenth.
• The 1517 enclosure commission gathered evidence in 28 counties and prosecuted 264 landowners, an unprecedented assertion of royal oversight.
• The Eltham Ordinances of 1526 cut household waste and reorganised the Privy Chamber.

Arguments that the legal reforms fell short:
• The courts were swamped, and common-law judges resented the encroachment of prerogative justice.
• Critics claimed Wolsey favoured petitioners who paid his clerks generously.
• Star Chamber business shrank again after his fall, so the change did not outlast him.

Overall judgement: the courts were his most visible success while he held office, but like his other reforms they depended on him personally. Top-band answers weigh the measures against each other and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey’s domestic policies created opposition by the late 1520s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1517 enclosure commission
• the Eltham Ordinances
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Enclosure commission — landowners prosecuted in Chancery resented Wolsey’s interference and bought their way out, breeding cynicism rather than reform.
• Eltham Ordinances — the courtiers Wolsey ejected from the Privy Chamber (Compton, Norris and rising Boleyn allies) became long-term enemies once they returned.
• Subsidy assessments — commissioners’ valuations and Wolsey’s £800,000 demand of 1523 angered MPs and gentry alike, fuelling parliamentary resistance.
• Star Chamber prosecutions — high-profile humiliations of the Earl of Northumberland and Sir Amyas Paulet built a reservoir of noble grievance.
• Personal style — ostentation, two crosses, palaces grander than the king’s, and unilateral decision-making invited the charge of arrogance.
• Pluralism — holding multiple bishoprics simultaneously offended ecclesiastical reformers and Common-law lawyers wary of clerical encroachment.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; argument coherent.
Secure: Three or four reasons explained with relevant evidence.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘Wolsey’s domestic policies were more successful than they were unsuccessful.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Star Chamber
• the subsidy
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs successes and failures and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘more successful’:
• Star Chamber genuinely curbed noble abuses and made justice more accessible — cases rose tenfold to around 120 a year.
• Court of Chancery offered cheaper, faster equity remedies for ordinary petitioners; case volume roughly doubled.
• Subsidy taxed actual wealth and raised around £325,000 between 1513 and 1529 — the most successful Tudor tax innovation before the Civil War.
• Eltham Ordinances cut household waste and modernised the Privy Chamber.
• 1517 enclosure commission gave the Crown a moral authority over landowners that no previous government had attempted.

Arguments for ‘more unsuccessful’:
• Enclosure prosecutions produced fines but little lasting change on the ground.
• 1523 subsidy demand triggered fierce parliamentary resistance, raising only a quarter of what was asked, and led to the disastrous 1525 Amicable Grant.
• Eltham Ordinances were quietly reversed within months as ejected gentlemen returned.
• Star Chamber overloaded itself; common-law judges resented prerogative encroachment.
• Wolsey’s methods built up enemies (Northumberland, Paulet, Boleyns) who would help destroy him in 1529.

Overall judgement: Wolsey was a real reformer whose individual measures often worked in the short term; but most failed to become permanent because his political style created enemies faster than the reforms could win allies. Top-band answers will weigh both sides explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument with multiple criteria; substantiated overall judgement; period vocabulary used precisely.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Queen Isabella’s desire to spread Christianity for the sponsorship of Columbus in 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Isabella’s religious motive, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Isabella saw a westward voyage as a way to bring new souls into the Catholic Church — an extension of the Reconquista that had just been completed at Granada in January 1492.
• The religious framing made the venture politically defensible at home and abroad: a Christian mission, not naked commerce.
• It allowed Pope Alexander VI to issue Inter caetera (1493) and underwrite Spanish claims, because Spain could be presented as evangelising rather than empire-building.
• It complemented the economic motive: profits could fund a future crusade to retake Jerusalem, openly discussed at court.
• It helped Isabella overrule the doubts of her scholarly commission, which had calculated that Columbus’s maths were wrong.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. domestic legitimacy AND papal authority) with specific period detail (Inter caetera 1493, Reconquista, Capitulations) and clear links to the sponsorship.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Isabella’s religious feeling without explaining its importance for sponsoring Columbus.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Capitulations of Santa Fe (April 1492) for Columbus and the Spanish crown.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Columbus secured the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, the right to be Viceroy and Governor of any lands found and 10% of all profits — extraordinary for a Genoese commoner.
• The Crown bore most of the upfront cost but kept its risk low — if Columbus failed, Isabella had spent little; if he succeeded, she gained a westward route to Asia.
• The hereditary nature of Columbus’s rights guaranteed that his family would later sue the Crown for unpaid shares once the lands turned out to be vastly larger than expected.
• The terms locked in a Spanish — specifically Castilian — claim to anything Columbus found, framing future disputes with Portugal.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the agreement without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Columbus’s underestimate of the Earth’s size for the events of 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Columbus’s miscalculation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Columbus underestimated the Earth’s circumference by roughly a third, placing Japan where the Caribbean actually is.
• This made his pitch sound plausible: a manageable westward voyage rather than an impossible open-ocean crossing — otherwise no monarch would have backed him.
• Portugal’s royal experts rejected the plan precisely because they did not share the miscalculation; Spain accepted partly because the Reconquista had absorbed scholarly attention.
• The miscalculation explains why landfall came when it did (33 days out, in October 1492) rather than ending with the crews stranded mid-ocean.
• It also explains Columbus’s lifelong refusal to accept that he had reached an unknown continent — he died in 1506 still believing the Caribbean was the outer rim of Asia.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the miscalculation to multiple consequences, with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the miscalculation without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Portuguese rejection of Columbus’s plan in 1485 for Spanish history.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Columbus took his proposal to Castile, where it sat in front of Ferdinand and Isabella for six years — long enough for the Reconquista to finish before they could reconsider.
• When Spain finally said yes in April 1492, it gained the westward route Portugal had refused, leapfrogging Lisbon’s African strategy overnight.
• Portugal kept investing in the African route, which paid off with Vasco da Gama’s reaching India in 1498 — meaning the two crowns now had separate, parallel maritime empires.
• Portuguese rejection set up the diplomatic problem that the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) would later have to solve.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Portuguese rejection without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the events of 1485–1492 led to Columbus’s landfall in the Bahamas. You may use the following in your answer: Portuguese rejection (1485), the Capitulations of Santa Fe (April 1492). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Portugal’s rejection of Columbus in 1485 forced him to take his plan to Castile, where it sat in front of a court still committed to finishing the Reconquista.
• The fall of Granada in January 1492 freed the Catholic Monarchs’ attention and treasury — making them, for the first time, willing to consider Columbus seriously.
• The intervention of Luis de Santángel, the royal treasurer of Aragon, persuaded Isabella that the political risk of letting Columbus take his plan to France outweighed the cost of backing him — this in turn produced the Capitulations of Santa Fe in April 1492.
• Those terms gave Columbus the authority and financing to depart from Palos on 3 August 1492; without them, no Spanish crew or supplies would have been available.
• The miscalculation of distance, combined with the Canary Islands stop and the Atlantic trade winds, then determined that landfall would come at Guanahani on 12 October — not in Asia, but in lands that would reshape Spanish history.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis — events linked with phrases like ‘this in turn enabled’, ‘because of this’. Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Pinzón family of Palos for the success of Columbus’s first voyage.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Pinzón family, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Pinzón family were experienced ship-owners and captains in Palos, the Andalusian port from which the fleet departed.
• Martín Alonso Pinzón captained the Pinta and helped recruit a reluctant crew — men of Palos, who would otherwise have refused to sail with an unknown Genoese commoner.
• His credibility within the local seafaring community gave Columbus the practical workforce his royal commission could not.
• The lookout who sighted land on 12 October 1492 was aboard the Pinta, Martín Alonso Pinzón’s ship, and the Niña (also captained by a Pinzón) was the ship that ultimately carried Columbus home with the news.
• Without the Pinzóns, the Capitulations of Santa Fe might have produced a paper title with no actual fleet behind it.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Pinzóns without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the belief in Manifest Destiny for migration to the West c1840–1860.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Manifest Destiny, supported by accurate detail and links to subsequent migration.

Indicative content:
• Provided a moral and religious justification for migration: settlers told themselves God had allotted the continent to American expansion, easing the spiritual cost of leaving home.
• Encouraged government support and rhetoric: politicians and newspapers used the language of destiny to back the annexation of Texas, the Mexican Cession (1848) and the opening of overland routes.
• Combined with Anglo-Saxonism, it justified pushing aside Indigenous nations as the ‘natural’ outcome of expansion.
• Boosted volunteer migration alongside push factors such as the 1837 Panic, by giving the journey a wider sense of purpose.
• Helped frame the 1849 Gold Rush and the Oregon Trail as part of one continuous national project rather than a series of separate moves.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. justification AND political effect), with specific period detail (1845, O’Sullivan, Texas, Anglo-Saxonism) and clear links to migration.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Manifest Destiny without explaining its importance for migration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the discovery of gold in California in 1848 for migration to the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Around 300,000 people moved to California between 1848 and 1855, transforming the population of the West Coast in a single decade.
• International migration surged, with substantial arrivals from China, Mexico, Chile, Britain and Australia — broadening the make-up of the West.
• San Francisco grew from a village of around 800 in 1848 to a port city of 25,000 by 1850, becoming the gateway to the gold fields.
• The pressure of overland routes across Indigenous Plains territory increased sharply, contributing to negotiations such as the first Fort Laramie Treaty in 1851.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific figures or named places.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the Gold Rush without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Oregon Trail from 1836 for the early settlement of the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Oregon Trail, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Opened a viable 2,000-mile wagon route from Missouri to the Willamette Valley, proven for families by Marcus and Narcissa Whitman in 1836.
• Allowed organised wagon trains of forty to a hundred families to set off each spring, supporting a migration of perhaps 4,000 a year by 1846.
• Established South Pass through the Rockies as the practical crossing point used by every later trail.
• Contributed to the eventual American claim on Oregon Territory and to the population that justified statehood.
• Created the model of seasonal, organised, family-based migration that the California Trail and Mormon Trail would adapt.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the Oregon Trail to specific consequences for settlement, with period detail (1836, Whitmans, South Pass).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the trail without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the belief in Manifest Destiny for relations between American settlers and Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Settler migration was framed as a national mission, weakening any moral check on crossing Indigenous Plains territories.
• The belief drew on Anglo-Saxonism, encouraging the view that Plains nations should be subordinated rather than negotiated with as equals.
• It justified the language of ‘empty’ or ‘wasted’ land, even though the Plains were already inhabited — preparing the ground for treaty pressure and eventually dispossession.
• It made later breaches of treaties politically easier to defend, since the wider settlement project was seen as providentially sanctioned.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with explicit links to Manifest Destiny and to Indigenous-settler relations.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on tensions without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of San Francisco and the boom of mining camps for the West in the years after 1849.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• San Francisco grew from a village of around 800 to a port city of 25,000 between 1848 and 1850, becoming the supply base and financial hub of the gold fields.
• Mining camps such as Sutter’s Mill and the Mother Lode created the boom-and-bust pattern repeated at every later strike, including the Black Hills in 1874.
• The wealth flowing through merchants and bankers (rather than diggers) helped finance later western infrastructure, including railroads and ranching.
• Diverse migrant populations (Chinese, Mexican, Chilean, European) shaped the social make-up of the post-Rush West and prefigured later legislation.
• California’s rapid statehood (1850) gave San Francisco federal weight that shaped national debates over the Transcontinental Railroad.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1849 Gold Rush for the federal United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• California became a state in 1850, faster than any territory before it — reshaping Senate and presidential politics.
• The federal government faced a new urgency to link the East with its newest state, fuelling the Pacific Railroad debate.
• Overland routes through Plains territory took on national strategic importance, prompting federal treaty-making with Indigenous nations such as the first Fort Laramie Treaty in 1851.
• Customs and gold revenue from California became significant federal income streams within a decade.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment without specific federal consequence.

practice_questions.text: Source A: From the majority opinion of the Supreme Court in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, delivered by Chief Justice Earl Warren on 17 May 1954. ‘To separate [Black children] from others of similar age and qualifications solely because of their race generates a feeling of inferiority as to their status in the community that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone … We conclude that in the field of public education the doctrine of “separate but equal” has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.’ Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Supreme Court’s reasoning in 1954.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail from the source. (e.g. ‘The court considered the psychological harm of segregation, not just material inequality’ supported by ‘generates a feeling of inferiority … that may affect their hearts and minds.’ AND ‘The court rejected Plessy’s “separate but equal” doctrine in education’ supported by ‘the doctrine of “separate but equal” has no place.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation, plus a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source rather than inference. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the impact of the Brown ruling on Southern schools was limited in the years 1954-60. You may use the following in your answer: • ‘all deliberate speed’ (Brown II) • the Southern Manifesto You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. Eisenhower’s reluctance to enforce, Prince Edward County school closures, the lack of federal funding penalties before 1964, intimidation of Black families by White Citizens’ Councils), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (massive resistance, deliberate speed, Southern Manifesto, Fourteenth Amendment).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of resistance without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Interpretation 1 (from a 1990 textbook on the civil rights era): ‘Brown v. Topeka was the turning point of the modern civil rights movement. The Supreme Court’s ruling that segregated schools were inherently unequal swept away sixty years of Plessy and gave the movement the legal and moral authority that made everything that followed possible.’ Interpretation 2 (from a 2015 study of Southern school desegregation): ‘The 1954 decision was, on the ground, a paper victory. Ten years later fewer than two per cent of Black children in the South attended integrated schools. Real desegregation arrived only with the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the federal funding sanctions it allowed. Brown’s words mattered; its enforcement did not.’ How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the impact of Brown v. Topeka? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees Brown as a transformative turning point; Interpretation 2 sees it as legally significant but practically limited until 1964) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the turning point of the modern civil rights movement’ vs ‘a paper victory’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the impact of Brown v. Topeka. You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is taken from a 1990 textbook focused on the legal and moral significance of the ruling, while Interpretation 2 is taken from a 2015 study that draws on quantitative evidence about how many Black children actually attended integrated schools. The two are written for different purposes (introducing the period vs assessing on-the-ground change) and use different evidence (court records vs enrolment data).
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used, or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the impact of Brown v. Topeka? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context. (You may include any SPaG mark separately.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge (the unanimous 1954 ruling, Brown II and ‘deliberate speed’, the Southern Manifesto, Prince Edward County school closures, Little Rock 1957, the gap between legal change and 1964 enforcement, the moral framework Brown supplied to the movement), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently and accurately throughout.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement is offered but less fully substantiated. Vocabulary mostly precise.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge is partial; judgement implicit. Some period terminology used.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. Vocabulary general. [16 marks for argument plus 4 marks for SPaG and use of specialist terminology — 20 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Source B: From a speech by Senator Harry F. Byrd of Virginia in 1956, calling for ‘massive resistance’ to the Brown ruling. ‘If we can organise the Southern States for massive resistance to this order I think that in time the rest of the country will realise that racial integration is not going to be accepted in the South. In interposition the South has its strongest weapon. The Federal Government cannot in the long run enforce a school desegregation that the people of the South are determined will not be enforced.’ Give two things you can infer from Source B about Southern political reaction to Brown v. Topeka.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Southern leaders saw resistance as a coordinated political strategy, not isolated protest’ supported by ‘If we can organise the Southern States for massive resistance’ AND ‘Byrd believed Southern resistance could overpower federal enforcement’ supported by ‘The Federal Government cannot in the long run enforce a school desegregation that the people of the South are determined will not be enforced.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Source A: From a leaflet distributed in Montgomery on 2 December 1955 by the Women’s Political Council, the day after Rosa Parks’s arrest.

‘Another Negro woman has been arrested and thrown into jail because she refused to get up out of her seat on the bus for a white person to sit down. It is the second time since the Claudette Colvin case that a Negro woman has been arrested for the same thing. This has to be stopped. Negroes have rights too … If we do not do something to stop these arrests, they will continue. The next time it may be you, or your daughter, or mother. We are, therefore, asking every Negro to stay off the buses on Monday in protest of the arrest and trial.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Montgomery Bus Boycott’s origins.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘The boycott was prepared by Black women activists in advance, not improvised after Parks’ supported by ‘asking every Negro to stay off the buses on Monday in protest’ AND ‘Parks’s arrest was framed as the latest in a pattern, not an isolated case’ supported by ‘the second time since the Claudette Colvin case’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955-56 succeeded.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Rosa Parks
• the role of Martin Luther King

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the prior planning of the Women’s Political Council, the economic weight of Black bus passengers as 75 per cent of customers, the MIA car-pool system, the federal court ruling in Browder v. Gayle), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (Montgomery Improvement Association, nonviolent direct action, Browder v. Gayle). Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated. Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit. Emerging: Description of the boycott without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1990 biography of Martin Luther King):
‘Without King, Montgomery would have remained a local protest. His preaching voice, his philosophy of nonviolent resistance and his ability to articulate Black grievance to a national audience transformed a one-day bus boycott into the founding moment of the modern civil rights movement.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 history of women in the civil rights movement):
‘Long before King arrived in Montgomery, Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council had been planning a bus boycott. They had drafted leaflets, identified test cases and built the local networks that sustained the protest for over a year. King was the public face of a movement that Black women had built.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the Montgomery Bus Boycott? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.

Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.

The two have different focuses and use different bodies of evidence.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the Montgomery Bus Boycott?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.

Gayle), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently. practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. E. D. Nixon, NAACP organiser in Montgomery and Pullman porters’ union official, recalling December 1955.

‘Mrs Parks was the kind of person we’d been waiting for. She had stature in the community. She was respected. When I called Reverend King, who was new in town, I told him: we’ve got the case we need. Mrs Parks won’t crumble under cross-examination, and she won’t apologise. The boycott begins on Monday whether you’re with us or not.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the planning of the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the relationship between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet in 1917. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, Order Number 1, the soldiers’ committees, the dependence of the new ministers on the railway and postal workers). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the Provisional Government held formal authority but the Soviet held the loyalty needed to enforce it. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrased point. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Provisional Government was unable to solve the problems it inherited in 1917.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Soviet Order Number 1
• the failed June Offensive
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. lack of popular mandate, Dual Power and Order Number 1, the decision to continue the war and the June Offensive, the postponement of land reform, the Kornilov Affair). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Dual Power, Constituent Assembly, Kadet, Soviet, Stavka. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the government without explaining its failure. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the role of Alexander Kerensky in the failure of the Provisional Government.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents Kerensky as a man trapped between irreconcilable forces who did the best he could; the other argues his decisions — the June Offensive, the leak against the Bolsheviks, the panic over Kornilov — were the immediate cause of the collapse). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Kornilov Revolt.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (Kornilov’s own memoirs and right-wing officer testimony versus Soviet-era and revisionist social history), wrote at different times, or had different purposes (defending the conservative officer corps versus tracing the rise of Bolshevik popular support). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the Kornilov Revolt in destroying the Provisional Government?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of 1917 — the rearming of the Bolsheviks, Kerensky’s loss of credibility, the September Bolshevik majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets, the wider context of the war and land question — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the war and the June Offensive were the main reasons the Provisional Government collapsed?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the Milyukov Note, the May resignations, the June Offensive in Galicia, mass desertions under Order Number 1, the July Days, the Kornilov Affair, postponed Constituent Assembly elections — to test whether the war was decisive against alternatives (Dual Power, the land question, Kerensky’s personal misjudgements). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Dual Power, Soviet, Kadet). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For Paper 3 inference questions on the Provisional Government, look for sources that hint at its lack of mandate or its dependence on the Soviet — Order Number 1, the Milyukov Note leak, soldier committees ignoring orders. For 12-mark causation essays on its failure, weigh the war (June Offensive), the postponed Constituent Assembly, the land question and the Kornilov Affair against each other rather than describing each in turn. Examiners reward students who reach a substantiated judgement on the most important cause and use period vocabulary — Dual Power, Order Number 1, Constituent Assembly, Kadet, Soviet — throughout to lift their SPaG and depth marks together.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the actions of the Donner Party led to disaster in the winter of 1846–47.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Lansford Hastings’s guidebook
• the Sierra Nevada snowstorms.
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that links events causally across the question’s timeframe.

Indicative content (chained, not listed):
• At Fort Bridger in late July 1846 the party decided to take the Hastings Cutoff, trusting an author who had never taken loaded wagons through it.
• Because of that decision they spent weeks hacking through the Wasatch Mountains, with the result that they fell behind schedule.
• Crossing the Great Salt Lake Desert dried out their oxen and split the train, deepening the delay and weakening their supplies.
• Because they were a month late, they reached the Sierra Nevada in late October, when an unusually early snowstorm fell on 28 October 1846.
• Trapped at Donner Lake without enough food, around half the party died over the winter; some survivors resorted to cannibalism before relief parties arrived in early 1847.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal connectives (‘because…then…’) chaining at least three named events; stays inside the dates; uses period vocabulary.
Secure: Two clear links between events; uses some period detail.
Developing: Lists events with limited causal linking; some period detail.
Emerging: Largely descriptive or first-person narrative with few links.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of mountain men for the early migration west to c1850.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Jedediah Smith’s 1824 location of South Pass gave wagon trains a gentle crossing of the Rockies that every later trail used.
• Jim Bridger founded Fort Bridger in 1842, providing a vital supply and repair stop on the Oregon and California Trails.
• Their maps and trail knowledge were inherited directly by the wagon trains of the 1840s.
• They built diplomatic relationships with Indigenous nations such as the Crow and Shoshone, smoothing later passage for emigrants.
• Even after the fur trade collapsed around 1840, mountain men served as guides for early wagon trains, the US Army and government surveying expeditions.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands (mapping AND infrastructure, or knowledge AND relationships) with specific named figures and period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of mountain men without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Lansford Hastings’s guidebook for the Donner Party.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identification; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• It persuaded the Donner Party at Fort Bridger to take the untested Hastings Cutoff, even though Hastings had never driven loaded wagons through it.
• The cutoff added weeks to their journey through the Wasatch Mountains and the Great Salt Lake Desert, leaving them dangerously short of time.
• The delay led to a late-October arrival in the Sierra Nevada, just as the first heavy snow of the season fell on 28 October 1846.
• Roughly half the party died over the winter, while news of the tragedy made later emigrants warier of unproven shortcuts.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail and clear links to the guidebook.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the disaster without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how Brigham Young’s leadership shaped the Mormon migration of 1846–47.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Joseph Smith
• pioneer companies and way stations.
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for analytical narrative across the timeframe.

Indicative content (chained):
• Joseph Smith’s murder at Carthage Jail in June 1844 left the Mormons leaderless and persecuted in Illinois, so Brigham Young, head of the Quorum of the Twelve, took charge.
• Because the community needed a refuge no one else would contest, Young chose the Salt Lake basin in Mexican territory.
• To make the 1,300-mile trek possible, Young sent a pioneer company ahead in 1847 to build way stations and plant crops along the route.
• Because pioneer logistics were in place, the main body of emigrants could follow in disciplined groups and arrive ready to settle.
• On arrival the community immediately began irrigation farming and a planned grid for Salt Lake City; this allowed the settlement of Deseret to become permanent rather than merely a refuge.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with at least three named events causally linked across the timeframe; uses period vocabulary; explicit second-order analysis.
Secure: Two clear causal links; uses some period detail.
Developing: Lists events with limited linking.
Emerging: Description without analysis or stays outside the dates.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the choice of the Salt Lake Valley for the success of the Mormon migration.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The valley lay in Mexican territory beyond the Rockies, so the Mormons did not have to compete with US settlers or another power.
• It was somewhere no other power wanted, removing the political pressure that had driven them out of Missouri and Illinois.
• Irrigation farming using mountain streams turned the basin productive almost at once, removing the threat of starvation.
• The geographic isolation reinforced Brigham Young’s authority and the ward system of social welfare.
• The choice meant Deseret could grow into a permanent planned settlement, with Salt Lake City laid out on a grid — not a temporary refuge.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the choice of valley to specific aspects of Mormon success across at least two strands.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the valley without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the murder of Joseph Smith in 1844 for the Mormon community.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Brigham Young, head of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, took over leadership of the Church.
• It convinced the leadership that Mormons could not live safely in the established United States, accelerating plans to move beyond US territory.
• The migration of 1846–47 followed, taking 1,300 miles to the Salt Lake Valley under Young’s organised system.
• It strengthened internal unity around a shared sense of persecution, helping the community accept the discipline of the trek.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the murder without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the course of the Arab-Israeli war in the years 1948–49.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the invasion by Arab armies in May 1948
• the 1949 armistice agreements
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects across the war (e.g. the May invasion, the Bernadotte truces, the Israeli offensives Yoav/Hiram/Horev, the Rhodes negotiations). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing them. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links between events; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Narrative covers the war but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; sequence errors; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the changing fortunes of war in Palestine in the period from May 1948 to January 1949.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Arab Legion advances in Jerusalem
• Operation Yoav
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent analytical narrative addressing at least three aspects of the war’s changing fortunes (e.g. early Arab gains in Jerusalem; the first UN truce and Israeli rearmament; the Ten Days; the autumn offensives). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material. Causal links explicit. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects. [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little analysis. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1949 armistice agreements for the Arab-Israeli conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct consequences with detail. For example: (i) the Green Line became the de facto border of Israel until 1967, with Egypt holding Gaza and Jordan annexing the West Bank; (ii) because the armistices were not peace treaties, the Arab states maintained their economic boycott and their refusal to recognise Israel, guaranteeing further conflict. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates what the armistices were without analysing effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the displacement of Palestinian Arabs (1948–49) for the future of the conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. roughly 700,000 Palestinian Arabs became refugees in camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan; UNRWA was established in 1949 to manage them; the unresolved ‘right of return’ became a permanent obstacle to peace negotiations; refugee camps later supplied recruits to fedayeen groups and to the PLO from 1964. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the displacement without showing why it shaped the future of the conflict. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of King Abdullah of Jordan’s actions during the 1948–49 war.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained: the Arab Legion seized the West Bank and east Jerusalem and Jordan formally annexed them in 1950; this prevented the creation of the Palestinian Arab state envisaged by Resolution 181; the annexation drew Palestinian resentment that culminated in Abdullah’s assassination at al-Aqsa in 1951 and shaped Jordanian-Palestinian relations through to 1970. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies actions of the Arab Legion or King Abdullah but with limited explanation of importance. [3–4]
Emerging: Names King Abdullah without analysing his role’s significance. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Israel’s military victory in 1948–49 for the Arab states.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct consequences with detail. For example: (i) the defeat triggered domestic political crises — King Farouk’s Egyptian regime fell to the Free Officers in 1952; King Abdullah was assassinated in 1951; Syria had three coups in 1949 alone; (ii) the loss strengthened pan-Arab nationalism and produced a generation of officers committed to overturning the result — setting up the rise of Nasser and the path to Suez 1956. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence; second descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions defeat without analysing effects on Arab states. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Amicable Grant of 1525.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Demanded one-third of clerical incomes and one-sixth of lay incomes.
• Was a non-parliamentary tax — bypassed Parliament after MPs had resisted Wolsey in 1523.
• Aimed to fund Henry VIII’s planned invasion of France after the Battle of Pavia.
• Came on top of the still-uncollected 1523 subsidy.
• Was given the name ‘Amicable Grant’ to suggest a voluntary, friendly contribution.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the East Anglian rising of May 1525.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Around 4,000 men assembled at Lavenham in Suffolk.
• Was led by yeomen and clothiers (e.g. John Greene, John Coxford), not just peasants.
• Driven partly by recession and unemployment in the East Anglian cloth industry.
• Rebels invoked Magna Carta and the principle of parliamentary consent to taxation.
• The Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk were sent to handle them, but negotiated rather than fought.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate names or detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Amicable Grant collapsed in 1525.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the East Anglian cloth industry
• Magna Carta
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• East Anglian recession — the cloth industry was in deep slump; taxpayers in Suffolk and Essex genuinely could not pay one-sixth of their income.
• Magna Carta and parliamentary consent — rebels and London merchants argued that direct taxation without Parliament breached a long-established constitutional principle.
• Size of the demand — one-third of clerical and one-sixth of lay income was unprecedentedly heavy, especially on top of the unfinished 1523 subsidy.
• Lack of consultation — commissioners simply fixed sums and demanded payment, with no appeal.
• Henry’s decision to retreat — once the rising began, Henry cancelled the Grant rather than risk a wider revolt, removing Wolsey’s authority to enforce it.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description of events without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Henry VIII’s desire for glory in France was the main reason for the Amicable Grant of 1525.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of Pavia
• the 1523 subsidy
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs Henry’s ambitions against other causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Charles V’s victory at Pavia in February 1525 captured Francis I and left France exposed; Henry demanded an army within months.
• Henry had wanted to recover the English claim to the French crown since 1513 and saw 1525 as his best chance.
• The Renaissance Prince image required military victory, so the money had to be found at speed.
• The deadline was Henry’s, not Wolsey’s: a campaign that summer left no time to prepare a parliamentary grant.

Arguments for other reasons:
• The 1523 subsidy was still being collected and had raised far less than Wolsey asked for, so ordinary taxation could not fund a war.
• Wolsey dared not recall Parliament so soon after MPs had resisted him in 1523.
• Crown finances were already strained by the wars of the early 1520s.
• Wolsey’s method — commissioners fixing sums with no consultation and no limit — made the demand harsher than it needed to be.
• The East Anglian cloth trade was in recession, so the same demand would have been resisted whatever its purpose.

Overall judgement: Henry’s ambition set the deadline, but the state of royal finance and Wolsey’s unwillingness to face Parliament shaped the Grant itself. Top-band answers weigh these factors and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the failure of the Amicable Grant was important for Wolsey’s position.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Henry VIII’s reaction
• the Duke of Norfolk and the Boleyn faction
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Henry’s public disowning — the king claimed he had never authorised the Grant, taking credit for clemency while leaving Wolsey to absorb the blame; this was a precedent his enemies would later use.
• Boost to Wolsey’s enemies — the Duke of Norfolk and the rising Boleyn faction now had concrete evidence that Wolsey could be defied and that the king would not protect him.
• Damage to credibility — the political nation saw that Wolsey’s authority had limits; future demands would be met with greater resistance.
• Cancellation of the French invasion — Henry got no military glory and Charles V signed the Treaty of Madrid with Francis I, exposing Wolsey’s diplomacy as worthless.
• Constitutional reassertion — the rebels reinstated the principle of parliamentary consent, which would shape Henry’s subsequent reliance on Parliament for the Reformation.
• Long-term vulnerability — historians like C.S.L. Davies treat 1525 as the start of Wolsey’s political slide, even though his fall came four years later.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Amicable Grant of 1525 was the most important reason for the decline of Wolsey’s power.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the East Anglian rising
• the failure of the divorce in 1529
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Reward sustained argument that weighs the Amicable Grant against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Arguments for ‘most important’: • 1525 was the first major public failure of Wolsey’s ministry, exposing the limits of his authority. • Henry’s public disowning of the Grant set a precedent for blaming Wolsey when policy went wrong. • The Boleyn and Howard factions gained a usable grievance and began to coordinate against him. • Cancellation of the 1525 French invasion ended Wolsey’s pose as Henry’s indispensable war minister. • It reasserted parliamentary consent, weakening Wolsey’s preferred non-parliamentary methods. Arguments for alternative explanations: • Failure of the annulment (1527–29) — far more decisive; the legatine court at Blackfriars in 1529 collapsed when Cardinal Campeggio adjourned it; Henry never forgave Wolsey for this. • Rise of the Boleyn faction — Anne Boleyn’s influence over Henry from c.1527 directly undermined Wolsey at court. • Foreign policy isolation — the 1526 Treaty of Madrid and the 1527 alliance reversal left Wolsey with no working partner in Europe. • Personal style — Wolsey’s ostentation, palaces and pluralism had built up enemies long before 1525. • Charges of praemunire in 1529 — the legal mechanism that finally removed him relied on his papal legateship, not the 1525 episode. Overall judgement: 1525 weakened Wolsey but did not destroy him; the failure of the annulment in 1529 was the immediate cause of his fall, while the Amicable Grant was an early warning shot. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion. Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout. Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached. Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the founding of La Navidad in December 1492 for Spain’s presence in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of La Navidad, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• La Navidad was the first European settlement in the Americas — built on the north coast of Hispaniola from the wreck of the Santa María after Christmas Eve 1492.
• It established a precedent for the small-garrison, gold-seeking model that Spain would carry across the Caribbean and onto the mainland: a few dozen Spaniards relying on local goodwill while hunting for tribute.
• It made it possible for Columbus to return to Spain with the claim of a settled foothold, not just a flag-planting voyage — helping secure royal support and the second voyage of 1493 of seventeen ships and around 1,200 men.
• Its destruction within twelve months — the garrison killed after kidnapping Taino women and turning on Guacanagarí’s rivals — foreshadowed the violent collapse of Spanish-Indigenous relations on Hispaniola.
• It set the geographic anchor: when Columbus returned, he founded Isabela nearby, and Hispaniola became the base from which Cuba (1511–15) and Panama (1513) were later launched.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. precedent set AND geographic anchor) with specific period detail (Hispaniola, Diego de Arana, Guacanagarí) and clear links to Spain’s presence.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of La Navidad without explaining its importance for Spain’s presence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Spanish contact with the Tainos in 1492 for relations between the two peoples.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Tainos’ small gold ornaments confirmed Columbus’s belief that wealth lay nearby, fixing the Spanish search for gold as the dominant Spanish demand on Indigenous communities.
• Initial Taino welcome — gifts, food, help during the wreck of the Santa María — let Columbus underestimate the resistance Spanish behaviour would generate within months.
• The Spanish trade of European trinkets (beads, hawk’s bells) for gold ornaments distorted both economies and made the Tainos appear ‘easy’ to deal with from a Spanish perspective.
• The Spanish framing of the Tainos as ‘gentle’ and naked ‘naturally’ suited for conversion shaped later imperial policy — including the encomienda labour system.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on contact without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Spanish labelling of the Caribs as ‘cannibals’ for the Spanish treatment of Indigenous peoples.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the ‘cannibal’ label, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The label originated with Columbus’s garbled spelling of ‘Carib’ and rapidly became a standard Spanish description for any Indigenous group resisting them.
• Spanish law eventually permitted the enslavement of Indigenous peoples judged anthropophagous, hostile or rebellious — the ‘cannibal’ label provided the legal opening.
• It allowed Spanish slavers to argue that captives from raids on the Lesser Antilles were lawful spoils, not protected subjects of the Crown.
• It distorted later European understandings of Indigenous peoples for centuries, casting Indigenous resistance as savagery rather than legitimate defence.
• Edexcel students should treat the ‘cannibal’ description as a feature of Spanish source perspective, not a neutral fact — this is exactly the kind of source-critical move the exam rewards.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the label to multiple consequences for Indigenous peoples, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the label without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the wrecking of the Santa María on Christmas Eve 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• The cacique Guacanagarí sent canoes to help unload the cargo — an early demonstration that the Spanish were dependent on Indigenous goodwill for survival.
• Columbus used the timbers to build a wooden fort, La Navidad, the first European settlement in the Americas.
• The wreck reduced Columbus’s fleet from three ships to two, forcing him to leave 39 men behind and sail home in the smaller Niña and Pinta.
• Columbus interpreted the wreck as providential — that God had wanted him to settle — reinforcing the religious framing of his voyage when he reported back to Isabella.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the wreck without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the events of October 1492–January 1493 led from Columbus’s landfall to a permanent Spanish foothold in the Americas. You may use the following in your answer: contact with the Tainos (October 1492), the wreck of the Santa María (December 1492). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
