Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Landfall at Guanahani on 12 October 1492 brought Columbus into contact with Tainos whose small gold ornaments convinced him to keep sailing south in search of larger sources of gold.
• This in turn took him to the north coast of Hispaniola, which Spanish observers found richer than the Bahamas — making Hispaniola the natural site for any settlement.
• The wreck of the Santa María on Christmas Eve 1492 was a disaster but, with the help of the cacique Guacanagarí, became the means of building La Navidad — a settlement that depended on Taino goodwill from the start.
• Without that wreck, Columbus would probably have returned home empty-handed; with it, he could claim a permanent foothold and leave 39 men behind under Diego de Arana.
• His departure on 4 January 1493 carried this evidence back to Spain — the foundation for the seventeen-ship second voyage later that year.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis — events linked with phrases like ‘this in turn enabled’, ‘because of this’. Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the cacique Guacanagarí’s help for the survival of Columbus’s first expedition.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Guacanagarí’s help, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Without Guacanagarí’s canoes the cargo of the Santa María would have been lost — depriving Columbus of the supplies and tools needed to build any kind of fort.
• Guacanagarí’s alliance gave the 39 men of La Navidad a local protector once Columbus sailed for Spain on 4 January 1493.
• It established the pattern Cortes and Pizarro would later use on a much larger scale: Spanish expeditions surviving and prospering through Indigenous alliances against Indigenous rivals.
• The episode shows that the Spaniards were utterly dependent on Indigenous goodwill at the start — an analytical move that breaks the ‘genius conquistador’ myth from Lesson 1 onwards.
• The collapse of that goodwill within twelve months — when the garrison turned on Guacanagarí’s rivals and was wiped out — underlines how fragile such alliances were if Spaniards behaved badly.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Guacanagarí’s actions without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English crusading army that left for the Holy Land in 1190.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Cross-section of Angevin society — tenants-in-chief brought their household knights; bishops such as Baldwin of Forde led contingents from their dioceses.
• Mounted sergeants and foot soldiers — men-at-arms without full knightly kit, plus shire foot, archers and crossbowmen, made up the bulk of the fighting strength.
• A seaborne contingent — about a hundred ships from the Cinque Ports, London and East Anglia, which sailed separately from the king and met him in Sicily.
• Bishops and clergy — senior churchmen led contingents and provided spiritual oversight (Baldwin of Forde, the Archbishop of Canterbury, died at Acre in 1190).
• Mixed motivations — the indulgence promised by Pope Gregory VIII, hopes of land or booty, and feudal obligation to a lord who had taken the Cross.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the immediate causes of the Third Crusade.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Indicative content: • The Battle of Hattin (4 July 1187) — Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and captured the True Cross. • Saladin’s capture of Jerusalem on 2 October 1187 — the Holy City was lost to the Muslims for the first time in 88 years. • Pope Gregory VIII’s bull Audita tremendi — framed Hattin as a punishment for Christian sin and called rulers to take the Cross. • Henry II and Philip II taking the Cross at Gisors (21 January 1188) — committed the kings of England and France to a joint expedition. • The Saladin Tithe — a 10% tax on moveables and revenue introduced in 1188 to finance the crusade in England and France. Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names. Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail. Developing: Two features but detail vague or partially inaccurate. Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard’s army was able to win the Battle of Arsuf in September 1191.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the discipline of the marching column
• the Hospitaller counter-charge
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Marching discipline — Richard kept his army in three solid blocks (van, centre, rear), refusing to let knights break ranks despite Saladin’s mounted archers harassing the column for days.
• Coastal march and naval support — the fleet shadowed the army on the seaward flank, supplying food and water and protecting one whole side from attack.
• Crossbowmen within the column — the army returned fire on Saladin’s mounted archers from inside the marching block, slowing their harassment.
• The Hospitaller counter-charge — the rear of the column held until breaking-point, then launched the decisive charge that broke the Muslim attack at the wood of Arsuf.
• Coordinated line charge — once the Hospitallers committed, the rest of the line followed almost simultaneously, multiplying the impact.
• Quality of crusader heavy cavalry — western lance-armed knights at full charge could break Saladin’s lighter mounted units once contact was made.
• Saladin’s mistake — he committed his army to an attempted breaking of the rear, exposing his troops to the counter-charge instead of continuing the harassment that had worked so well on the march.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why people in England were willing to take the Cross for the Third Crusade.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the fall of Jerusalem in 1187
• the indulgence offered by the Pope
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band. Indicative content: • The fall of Jerusalem in 1187 — Saladin’s capture of the Holy City on 2 October 1187 was a religious shock that preachers across England turned into a call to action. • The papal indulgence — Pope Gregory VIII’s bull Audita tremendi promised remission of the punishment for sins to those who took the Cross, a powerful spiritual reward in an age of acute fear of purgatory. • Crusading culture — a century of stories from the First Crusade, sermons, Templar and Hospitaller houses, and pilgrim badges from Jerusalem made the East feel familiar and the cause holy. • Royal example — Henry II, Philip II and then Richard all took the Cross publicly, encouraging tenants-in-chief and barons to follow them. • Feudal duty — men were summoned by lords who had taken the Cross; the obligation of knight service drew them in. • Hopes of land or booty — especially for younger sons with no inheritance, the East offered the chance of fiefs in the crusader states. • Legal protection — crusaders’ lands and debts were placed under royal and ecclesiastical protection while they were away, lowering the personal cost of going. Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated. Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points. Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive. Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Acre fell to the crusaders in July 1191.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the arrival of Philip II and Richard
• siege engines and mining
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Arrival of Philip II and Richard — Philip’s contingent reached Acre in spring 1191 and Richard’s in June, transforming a small siege into a full-scale operation with two royal armies.
• Siege engines and mining — trebuchets such as Richard’s ‘Bad Neighbour’, mantlets and undermining of towers steadily reduced the city walls.
• The two-year exhaustion of the garrison — King Guy of Lusignan had besieged Acre since 1189; the defenders had been short of food and reinforcements long before the kings arrived.
• Saladin’s inability to break the siege — his field army shadowed the crusaders but could not force them off Acre’s perimeter, especially after the kings arrived with fresh men.
• Naval blockade — the crusader fleet cut Acre off from supply by sea, while Saladin had no fleet of his own able to break in.
• Negotiated terms — the garrison surrendered on 12 July 1191 on terms (return of the True Cross, release of 1,500 prisoners, ransom of 200,000 dinars), accepting that further resistance was hopeless.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text: ‘Religious motives were the most important reason English crusaders went on the Third Crusade.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. You may use the following in your answer: • the bull Audita tremendi • feudal duty to a lord who had taken the Cross You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Arguments supporting the statement: • Pope Gregory VIII’s bull Audita tremendi framed Hattin as a punishment for Christian sin and called the laity to armed pilgrimage; the indulgence offered remission of the punishment for sins. • A century of crusading sermons, relics, pilgrim badges and Templar/Hospitaller houses had soaked English Christianity in the idea of the Holy Land as the holiest cause a layman could fight for. • Crusading was breathtakingly expensive (armour, multiple horses, supplies for years); the financial logic alone could not have produced 8,000 fighting men — spiritual reward must have been doing significant work. • Many crusaders, including the Archbishop of Canterbury Baldwin of Forde, died of disease in the East with no material gain. Arguments for alternative explanations: • Feudal duty — men were summoned by lords (and ultimately by Henry II and Richard) who had taken the Cross; the obligation of knight service drew them in regardless of personal piety. • Royal example — the public taking of the Cross at Gisors in 1188 made participation a matter of political and social honour as well as faith. • Hopes of land — younger sons with no inheritance had a chance of fiefs in the crusader states (the kingdom of Cyprus, conquered in 1191, was promptly distributed). • Legal and financial protection — crusaders’ lands and debts were protected while they were away; for the indebted this was a way to suspend pursuit by creditors. • Adventure and chivalric culture — the prestige of fighting alongside the Lionheart was its own draw for the warrior elite. Overall judgement: Religious motives were the engine that started the movement and gave it its scale, but feudal duty, royal example and material incentives multiplied its reach. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly — for example arguing that without Audita tremendi the crusade would not have happened, but without feudal obligation it could not have been raised in the numbers that fought at Acre and Arsuf — and reach a justified conclusion. Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout. Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven. Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement. Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the influence of the Church on crime and punishment in the period c1000–c1500 was different from its influence in the period c1500–c1700.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• In the Middle Ages the Church sheltered the accused: its courts could not impose death, Benefit of Clergy moved a claimant out of the king's courts, and sanctuary gave forty days' refuge.
• In the early modern period the Church's protection shrank while religion created new capital crimes: heresy sent about 280 Protestants to the stake under Mary I, and from 1488 claimants of Benefit of Clergy were branded so they could not use it twice.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the medieval Church mattered so much in crime and punishment in England.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Church courts
• sanctuary.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• It ran a parallel legal system through Church courts that could not impose the death penalty, so the Church effectively decided whether some accused people lived or died.
• Benefit of Clergy gave clergymen — and, in practice, anyone who could recite the neck verse — a route out of the king's courts.
• Sanctuary protected fugitives for up to forty days inside consecrated buildings, after which they could leave the kingdom by abjuring the realm.
• The Church controlled trial by ordeal: priests blessed the iron and the water, and their participation was what made the result count as God's judgement.
• When in 1215 Pope Innocent III's Fourth Lateran Council forbade clerical involvement in ordeals, the practice collapsed and royal trial by jury filled the gap — showing the Church's power to remake the system.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Church's activities without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 led to such important changes in English criminal justice.

You may use the following in your answer:
• trial by ordeal
• trial by jury.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Council, called by Pope Innocent III, forbade clergymen from participating in trial by ordeal — without priests to bless the water or iron, the ordeal could no longer claim divine judgement.
• Trial by ordeal collapsed across England within a generation, leaving a gap in how serious cases were decided.
• Royal courts filled the gap by extending trial by jury to serious cases — a shift from divine signs to human evidence.
• Decisions made by an international Church council could override an entrenched English legal practice — the impulse came from Rome, not Westminster.
• It was a turning point in the long history of English justice, marking the moment when twelve local men replaced God as the judge of fact.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Innocent III, Fourth Lateran Council, collapse of ordeals, rise of jury trial) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of 1215 without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Church was the most important factor in shaping crime and punishment in medieval England.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Sanctuary and Benefit of Clergy
• the role of local communities (tithings, hue and cry).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments supporting the Church as the most important factor:
• Church courts handled clergy and moral offences with their own punishments, and could not impose the death penalty.
• Benefit of Clergy and sanctuary protected accused people from the king's harshest punishments.
• The Church controlled trial by ordeal: when Pope Innocent III's Fourth Lateran Council banned clerical participation in 1215, the entire system of ordeal collapsed.
• Trial by jury extended to fill the gap, transforming the basis of English criminal justice — a change driven by a Church decision.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors):
• Day-to-day law enforcement still depended on local communities — tithings, the hue and cry, parish constables and oath-helpers.
• The Crown shaped serious crime: William I's Forest Laws and Murdrum fine were defined and enforced by royal officers, not the Church.
• Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) strengthened royal courts independently of Church reform.
• The Church's reach was uneven — many petty offences never went near a Church court.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Church influence against at least one other factor (community policing or royal authority), uses accurate period detail, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way guilt was decided in the period c1000–c1500 was different from the way it was decided in the period c1700–c1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Medieval courts asked God when human evidence ran out: the ordeals of hot iron, cold water and hot water were blessed by priests and read as divine judgement.
• By the nineteenth century guilt rested on evidence gathered by professionals: a paid police force from 1829, a Detective Branch from 1842 and CID from 1878 collected statements and exhibits for a jury.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why trial by ordeal ended in early thirteenth-century England.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Fourth Lateran Council
• the royal courts.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• In 1215 Pope Innocent III's Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergymen from participating in trial by ordeal — the decisive institutional decision.
• Without clerical involvement, the result of the ordeal could no longer be read as God's judgement, so it lost its religious authority.
• Royal authorities had a workable alternative: trial by jury was already used for lighter cases and could be extended to fill the gap.
• Some unease about the rationality and reliability of ordeals had been growing among educated clergy and lawyers; the 1215 ruling reflected as well as accelerated this shift.
• In 1219 Henry III's government told the royal judges that ordeals were no longer to be used, which pushed serious cases towards the jury.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Innocent III, Fourth Lateran Council, the rise of jury trial) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of ordeals without explaining their end.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Atlantic trade triangle for the development of British North America in the early eighteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with specific detail. For example: the triangle led to the entrenchment of enslaved labour on Chesapeake tobacco plantations because returning ships needed bulk cargo; and it led to the rise of New England port cities such as Newport because their distilleries and ships serviced the African leg of the trade. Equal attention to both with explicit causal language.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to plantations, ports or enslaved labour.
Emerging: Restates the existence of trade without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the shift from indentured servitude to chattel slavery for colonial society in the years 1713–41.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: importance lay in locking race into the colonial labour system, so that bondage was inherited and slavery could not be ended by the passage of time; and in widening the gap between free white labour and enslaved Black labour, which would shape the political economy of the southern colonies for the next century. Specific evidence (Bacon’s Rebellion 1676, post-1700 slave codes) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Notes the shift but does not explain why it mattered.
Emerging: Confuses indentured servitude and slavery, or describes one without the other.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the Atlantic slave trade became central to the British colonial economy in the early eighteenth century. You may use the following information in your answer: 
• The asiento (1713) 
• Tobacco plantations in the Chesapeake 
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections using causation and consequence. For example: the asiento gave British traders Spanish-American markets, expanding shipping capacity; tobacco plantations needed cheap, lifelong labour, drawing on this expanded shipping; rice plantations in the Carolinas reinforced demand; New England port cities profited from supplying ships and rum; the result was an Atlantic economy in which slavery was the structural pillar, not a side feature.
Secure: Clear narrative with several analytical links between trade and plantation development.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of why one event led to another.
Emerging: Lists facts about slavery without explaining how the system became central.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the rice economy of South Carolina for the population of that colony by the 1740s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the demand for rice-growing skills led Carolina planters to seek enslaved Africans from Senegambia and Sierra Leone, shaping the cultural composition of the enslaved population; and the heavy labour demands of rice cultivation led to enslaved Africans becoming the majority of the colony’s population by mid-century, the only mainland colony where this was the case. Causal language used.
Secure: Two consequences identified with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific demographic detail.
Emerging: Notes that rice was grown without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Middle Passage for the operation of the Atlantic slave trade.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to specific developments. For example: the Middle Passage mattered because the conditions of the crossing produced the high mortality and physical breaking that made resistance harder on arrival; and because it was the most profitable leg of the triangular trade, with returns that financed the manufactured goods sent on the next outward voyage. Specific evidence (around one in seven died, six to ten week voyages, around 12.5 million transported between 1500 and 1800s) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Describes the Middle Passage without explaining its importance.
Emerging: Mentions the Middle Passage without specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of plantation agriculture for the economic role of enslaved Africans in British North America before 1741.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: plantation agriculture mattered because the labour rhythm of tobacco and rice required a workforce that could be held for life, which entrenched chattel slavery; and because plantation profits sustained the colonial gentry whose political and cultural power dominated the South. Specific evidence (gang vs task systems, 150,000 enslaved Africans across the thirteen colonies by 1740, rice as the staple of South Carolina) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General comments on plantations without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Describes plantations without explaining their economic role.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the reasons migrants were drawn to York in the Viking period were similar to the reasons migrants were drawn to Liverpool in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were ports tied into long-distance trade: Jorvik reached Dublin, Bergen and the Baltic, while Liverpool handled a large share of Britain's overseas trade by 1850.
• Both offered work to newcomers without land or capital, in Jorvik's craft workshops and on Liverpool's docks.
• In both, trade growth and population growth fed each other, so arrivals attracted further arrivals.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why so much is known about everyday life in Viking York.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Coppergate excavation
• the city's trade goods.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The waterlogged ground at Coppergate preserved timber buildings, leather shoes, textiles and tools that would normally rot away.
• The excavation of 1976-81 by the York Archaeological Trust covered a whole block of workshops and yards, not a single building, so it shows a working street rather than one household.
• Imported goods survive alongside local ones: silver dirhams, Baltic amber, cowrie shells and Mediterranean silk all date and place the city's trade.
• Place and street names, including Coppergate itself from the Old Norse for cup-makers, preserve the language of the inhabitants.
• Written records for this period say almost nothing about ordinary craftsmen, so the archaeology carries most of the evidence.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which trade in Viking York was different from trade in the medieval London Steelyard.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Jorvik's traders were also its settlers and rulers, minting their own coin; the Steelyard's Hanseatic merchants were foreign residents under the legal status of alien.
• Jorvik produced as well as traded, with workshops in amber, leather, bone and iron; the Steelyard was mainly a warehouse and shipping base.
• Jorvik's trade grew out of Scandinavian settlement; the Steelyard's rested on privileges granted by English kings and could be taken away, as Elizabeth I did in 1598.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The economic impact of Viking York was more important than its political impact.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Coppergate excavation
• the kings of the Viking kingdom of York.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for the economic impact:
• The Coppergate workshops in amber, leather, bone and iron show a sophisticated urban craft economy.
• Trade reached the Caliphate (silver dirhams) and the Indian Ocean (cowrie shells), making Jorvik one of the wealthiest towns in early medieval Britain.
• By 1086 York held around 9,000 people, second only to London - an economic transformation.

Indicative content - support for the political impact:
• Jorvik was the capital of the Viking kingdom of York from 866, with its own kings, courts and coinage.
• Political control came first and made the trading boom possible: the kingdom was founded twelve years before the agreement of 878, and York lay outside its terms.
• Cultural fusion - Anglo-Scandinavian crosses, mixed personal names, Norse street names - followed from that political settlement.
• The end of the kingdom in 954, with Eric Bloodaxe's death at Stainmore, was a major turning point for northern England.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (Jorvik, Danelaw, Anglo-Scandinavian, entrepot).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why a mixed Anglo-Scandinavian culture developed in York by the eleventh century.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Church in York
• intermarriage and personal names.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Norse settlers converted to Christianity, and York's archbishops, including Wulfstan II in the early eleventh century, served congregations of Norse descent.
• Christian stone crosses in and around York were carved in Norse decorative styles such as the ring-chain pattern, mixing the two traditions in one object.
• Norse and English personal names appear side by side in church records, which points to intermarriage rather than separate communities.
• Old English and Old Norse were closely related, so speakers could understand one another and the languages mingled.
• Two centuries of shared town life, trade and local government in Jorvik gave the two populations the same daily interests.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why York grew rapidly under Viking rule.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the rivers Ouse and Foss
• the kingdom of York.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Jorvik was the political capital of the Viking kingdom of York from 866, which drew officials, merchants and settlers from across the Danelaw and Scandinavia.
• The city sat where the Ouse and the Foss meet, giving it river access to the North Sea and to Dublin, Bergen and the Baltic.
• Workshops on streets such as Coppergate made amber jewellery, leather, ironwork and bone combs, pulling in skilled craftsmen.
• Its silver coinage made it a regional financial centre as well as a market.
• Roman walls, Roman roads and an existing archbishopric gave the newcomers infrastructure to build on rather than start from nothing.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Puritan challenge to the religious settlement in the years 1558–88.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise detail. For example: (1) The 1566 Vestments Controversy — Puritan clergy refused to wear surplices and copes, calling them ‘rags of popery’; Archbishop Parker’s ‘Book of Advertisements’ led to the suspension of around 37 London ministers. (2) Calls for Presbyterian Church government — Thomas Cartwright argued in 1570 for replacing bishops with elders, on the model of Calvin’s Geneva.

Secure: Two features identified with one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why English Catholics found it difficult to accept the religious settlement.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Act of Uniformity
• the 1570 papal bull
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own. Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: the loss of the Latin Mass and traditional sacraments under the Act of Uniformity; recusancy fines of 12 pence per week from 1559 (raised to £20 per month from 1581); the Pope’s 1570 bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth and creating a clash between Catholic and English loyalty; the influence of the Counter-Reformation and the Council of Trent (1545–63) hardening Catholic identity. Reasons should be linked, not listed. Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained. Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the role of the Pope and foreign powers made the Catholic challenge more serious than the Puritan challenge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of three or more interconnected reasons. Should cover: Pope Pius V’s 1570 bull Regnans in Excelsis, which excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved her Catholic subjects of allegiance, turning quiet recusancy into potential treason; the existence of Mary, Queen of Scots as a Catholic alternative claimant from 1568; backing from King Philip II of Spain, with the resources of the Spanish Empire and the Netherlands; the missionary activity of Jesuits and Douai-trained priests after 1577. By contrast, Puritans accepted Elizabeth’s right to rule and challenged only the form of worship, with no foreign backers. Reasons must be linked into a clear analytical line. Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained, or several reasons identified without development. Emerging: One reason, or general assertions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Catholic challenge to the religious settlement in the years 1558–88.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed. For example: (1) The role of the Catholic nobility — the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland kept Catholic worship alive on their northern estates and were already estranged from Elizabeth’s reformist court before 1569. (2) Foreign Catholic backing — Pope Pius V issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis in 1570 excommunicating Elizabeth, encouraging Catholic powers like Spain to support Catholic claimants such as Mary, Queen of Scots. Secure: Two features identified with one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature. Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed. Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Catholic challenge to the religious settlement was much more serious than the Puritan challenge in the years 1558–88.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the role of the Pope and foreign powers
• the Vestments Controversy of 1566
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained, analytical answer using BOTH stimulus points and adding at least one factor of the candidate’s own (e.g. the role of the northern Catholic nobility, recusancy laws of 1571 and 1581, the limited reach of Puritan demands, the threat of foreign invasion via Mary, Queen of Scots). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that Catholic resistance was the more serious threat because it was backed by foreign powers and a papal bull, while Puritan dissent stayed within loyal Protestant boundaries. Period-specific terminology used accurately throughout (recusancy, vestments, Counter-Reformation, Presbyterian, Regnans in Excelsis). Secure: Both stimulus points used and one own point added; clear judgement with some support. Developing: Stimulus points used but limited additional content; judgement asserted rather than substantiated. Emerging: Limited engagement with stimulus; description rather than analysis; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabeth’s government tightened laws against Catholics in the 1570s and 1580s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1570 papal bull
• the Catholic plots
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own. Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: the 1570 bull Regnans in Excelsis turning recusancy from a private decision into potential treason; the 1571 Ridolfi plot and other Catholic conspiracies showing that English Catholics could be involved in attempts on Elizabeth’s life or throne; the arrival of seminary priests trained at Douai (from 1577) and Jesuit missionaries (from 1580) reviving English Catholicism; the war footing against Spain after 1585. Each reason should be supported by a specific fact (1571 Treasons Act; recusancy fines raised to £20 per month in 1581). Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained. Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the recruitment of soldiers was different in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the fourteenth century most men served because they owed service (1). The feudal levy called lords, knights and tenants to about 40 days a year in return for land (1). In the seventeenth century men were recruited by pay and by force (1). The New Model Army of 1645 paid regular wages, while trained bands, commissions of array and impressment supplied the rest (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the way English armies were recruited changed in the period c1250–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the feudal levy
• indentures.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Feudal service lasted only about 40 days a year, which was far too short for campaigns in France during the Hundred Years War.
• Indentures let a king contract a lord to bring a set number of men-at-arms and archers for a set time at a set daily rate.
• Paid, contracted soldiers were more experienced and stayed together, so they fought better than reluctant levies.
• The longbow needed mass training, so Edward III made Sunday practice a legal duty and banned 'wasteful' games by statute in 1363.
• Plunder from the chevauchée drew men who fought for what they could take rather than for feudal loyalty.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the training of soldiers was different in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Fourteenth-century training happened in the village, not in the army (1). Edward III made Sunday longbow practice compulsory so that trained archers were ready when the king called (1). Seventeenth-century training happened inside the regiment (1). New Model Army foot regiments drilled loading, firing and wheeling together until the movements were almost automatic under fire (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the demands that war made on civilians changed in the period c1250–c1500.

You may use the following in your answer:
• purveyance
• the chevauchée.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Bigger and longer campaigns needed more supplies, so purveyance took grain, livestock and carts at fixed prices, often leaving only a promise to pay.
• Armies marching to Scotland or the Channel ports were billeted on households along the route; towns such as Berwick and Dover lived with this almost permanently.
• The chevauchée made destruction a deliberate weapon, so French villagers lost farms and animals while English soldiers took plunder home.
• Taxation grew with the wars, so civilians paid for armies in money as well as in goods.
• Duties under the Assize of Arms and the Statute of Winchester (1285) meant ordinary freemen had to keep weapons and turn out at the muster.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the impact of war on civilians was similar in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both centuries soldiers took food and lodging from ordinary households (1). Medieval purveyance let royal officers seize grain, animals and carts at fixed prices, leaving promises to pay later (1). During the Civil War both sides used free quarter, eating at the householder's table and leaving a paper promise instead of money (1). In both periods civilians had no real way to refuse (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘Recruitment in the medieval period was based mainly on duty rather than pay.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the feudal levy
• indentures.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments for duty:
• The feudal levy summoned lords, knights and tenants in return for land — service, not wages.
• The Assize of Arms required freemen to keep weapons; the Statute of Winchester (1285) tied them to the village muster.
• Edward III's compulsory longbow practice forced training onto every village, regardless of pay.
• Foreign mercenary service was distrusted; English society in this period was structured around obligation, not employment.

Indicative content — arguments for pay:
• From the fourteenth century, indentures contracted lords to bring fixed numbers of men for fixed daily rates of pay — the start of paid soldiering on a large scale.
• Henry V's Agincourt army was raised this way through about 25 great captains.
• Plunder from the chevauchée was effectively informal pay; many soldiers fought for what they could take, not for feudal duty.
• The 40-day limit of feudal service was useless for long foreign wars, so cash had to play a role.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs duty against pay across the period, uses accurate period detail (feudal levy, Assize of Arms, indenture, chevauchée) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about how the People's Republic was governed in its first years. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. references to party committees, mass campaigns, danwei work units, Soviet advisers). Inferences go beyond the source — e.g. that the new state fused party and government, or that it relied on Soviet expertise. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the People's Republic of China entered the Korean War in October 1950.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Sino-Soviet Treaty (February 1950)
• United Nations forces near the Chinese border
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. strategic threat of US troops on the Yalu River, the new Sino-Soviet alliance and Stalin’s pressure, Mao’s ambition to lead world communism, the chance to prove the PLA, the use of the war as domestic propaganda. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Confident period vocabulary. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained with detail; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; reliance on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: General narrative of the Korean War without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the reasons for Mao's dominant position in the CCP after 1949.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation explains Mao’s dominance through ideology and the ‘mass line’; the other stresses the personality cult and the suppression of rivals). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about Mao's leadership of the CCP.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. one historian writes from inside the PRC tradition (Mobo Gao defending the Mao era) while the other writes from a revisionist Western tradition (e.g. Frank Dikötter), or they were written before/after access to PRC archives in the 1990s. Reason linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the role of Soviet support in establishing communist rule in China?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty terms ($300 million credit, c.10,000 advisers), Soviet help with industrial planning, but also the limits (loans not gifts, Mao’s irritation with Stalin, Soviet refusal to fight directly in Korea). Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: General essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Korean War strengthened Mao's position in China?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the 'Resist America, Aid Korea' campaign, the parallel campaign against counter-revolutionaries (700,000–2 million executed), Soviet war debt, the prestige of fighting the United States to a stalemate, the 180,000–400,000 Chinese dead. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (Politburo, Sino-Soviet Treaty, Chinese People’s Volunteers, danwei). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about Lenin’s role in the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, Lenin’s return in disguise on 10 October, the 10–2 vote at the Bolshevik Central Committee, his demand to act before the Second Congress of Soviets, his reading of the Decree on Peace). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that Lenin provided the decisive political push but did not plan the operational details. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Bolsheviks succeeded in seizing power in October 1917.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Lenin’s April Theses
• the role of Trotsky
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. Provisional Government collapse, Lenin’s political programme, Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee, the rearming of the Bolsheviks during the Kornilov Affair, the Bolshevik majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — April Theses, MRC, Sovnarkom, Soviet. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the rising without explaining why it succeeded. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about whether the October Revolution was a popular revolution or a Bolshevik coup.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents October as a small, conspiratorial coup carried out by perhaps 15,000–20,000 Red Guards while most of Petrograd carried on as normal; the other stresses that Bolshevik majorities in the soviets and factory committees by September gave the seizure genuine popular legitimacy). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the role of Trotsky in October 1917.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (Soviet-era textbooks that wrote Trotsky out after his exile in 1929, versus post-1991 archival biographies that restored his organisational role); they wrote at different times (Stalinist orthodoxy versus revisionist Western scholarship); or they had different purposes (defending Stalin’s claim to be Lenin’s heir versus reconstructing the operational record). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Lenin’s personal leadership in the success of the October Revolution?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of October 1917 — the April Theses, Lenin’s return on 10 October, the 10–2 Central Committee vote, Trotsky’s MRC, the role of the Aurora, the Decree on Peace — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the October Revolution was a small, planned coup rather than a popular revolution?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the c.15,000–20,000 active fighters, the role of the MRC, the Bolshevik majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets by September, the Kornilov Affair’s rearming of the party, the Second Congress of Soviets — to weigh the ‘coup’ reading against the ‘popular revolution’ reading. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Sovnarkom, Soviet, MRC, April Theses). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the first Fort Laramie Treaty (1851) for relations between the United States and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the 1851 Treaty, supported by accurate detail and links to subsequent events.

Indicative content:
• It was one of the largest inter-tribal councils held with the US, gathering around 10,000 representatives of the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Shoshone and others.
• It marked a shift from separation (the Permanent Indian Frontier) to concentration policy — recognising defined territories for individual nations rather than a single ‘Indian country’.
• It promised safe passage on the Oregon Trail in return for annuities of $50,000 a year for fifty years.
• Because Congress quickly reduced the annuity term to ten years and payments were late or short, the Treaty was experienced by Plains leaders as another broken promise.
• This early loss of trust shaped every later confrontation, from Little Crow’s War (1862) to Red Cloud’s War (1866–68).

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. policy shift AND loss of trust) with specific period detail (1851, $50,000, Conquering Bear, Fitzpatrick).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Treaty without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1851 Indian Appropriations Act for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identification; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Act funded the creation of reservations — specific areas of land set aside for individual nations, marking the legal beginning of the reservation system.
• It introduced annual annuities of money and goods from the US Government in return for territorial concessions.
• It signalled the federal shift from separation to concentration policy — putting Indigenous nations on patches of land rather than keeping them apart from settlers.
• Late or short annuity payments quickly undermined Indigenous trust in federal agreements, contributing to later conflicts.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the failure of the Permanent Indian Frontier for US policy by 1851.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The line set out under the 1830 Indian Removal Act was crossed every summer by Oregon Trail emigrants from 1836 onwards.
• The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the United States California and the South-West, putting US territory on the far side of the ‘permanent’ line.
• The 1849 Gold Rush sent 300,000 people across the Plains in five years, making safe passage a federal priority.
• Because separation was no longer realistic, the federal government turned to concentration: the 1851 Indian Appropriations Act and the first Fort Laramie Treaty.
• The failure also forced Washington to negotiate directly with Plains nations, embedding the annuity diplomacy that defined US-Indigenous relations for the next thirty years.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the breakdown of the Frontier to specific policy consequences with period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo for US policy on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• It added California and the South-West to the United States, placing federal territory on the far side of the Permanent Indian Frontier.
• It made safe overland passage across Plains territory a federal priority, since the new states needed to be linked to the East.
• It contributed to the 1849 Gold Rush by opening California to American claims and triggering further migration.
• It helped persuade Washington to fund reservations and annuities through the 1851 Indian Appropriations Act, replacing separation with concentration policy.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of annuity payments for relations between the US Government and the Plains nations after 1851.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Annuities were the core mechanism of the 1851 Indian Appropriations Act and Fort Laramie Treaty — annual payments of money and goods promised in return for territorial concessions.
• They were intended to support Indigenous nations confined to specific territories who could no longer rely on the same access to buffalo and trails.
• When Congress cut the fifty-year term to ten years, the Treaty was already weakened in Indigenous eyes.
• Late or spoiled goods reinforced the sense that federal promises could not be relied on, undermining further negotiations.
• Over the next decade, broken annuity diplomacy contributed directly to flashpoints such as Little Crow’s War in 1862, where unpaid annuities helped spark Dakota resistance.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands (mechanism AND failure) with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of annuities without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of broken annuity payments for trust between the Plains nations and the US Government.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Plains nations experienced the cuts and delays as evidence that federal promises could not be relied on, weakening every later negotiation.
• Reduced or spoiled supplies left some Indigenous communities dependent on hunting on disputed land, increasing clashes with settlers.
• It contributed directly to flashpoints such as Little Crow’s War in 1862, where unpaid annuities helped trigger Dakota resistance.
• It shaped the harder-edged stance taken by Plains leaders such as Red Cloud in later treaty negotiations.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Mary, Queen of Scots’ claim to the English throne.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise detail. For example: (1) Mary was descended from Margaret Tudor, eldest daughter of Henry VII, who married James IV of Scotland — making Mary great-granddaughter of Henry VII through a legitimate Tudor line. (2) Mary was Catholic, and to Catholic Europe Elizabeth was illegitimate (Parliament had declared her so after Anne Boleyn’s execution in 1536), so Mary was widely seen as the rightful queen.

Secure: Two features identified with one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots fled to England in 1568.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Lord Darnley
• Mary’s marriage to Bothwell
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own.

Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: the murder of David Rizzio in March 1566, by lords led by her husband Darnley, which broke trust between Mary and many of her nobles; Darnley’s own murder in February 1567 and Mary’s subsequent marriage to Bothwell, the prime suspect, which alienated Scottish opinion; her forced abdication in July 1567 and imprisonment; her escape in May 1568, defeat at the Battle of Langside, and lack of alternative refuge close at hand. Reasons should be linked into a clear causal chain.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained.

Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabeth chose to keep Mary, Queen of Scots in protective custody in England rather than restore her or send her abroad.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of three or more interconnected reasons. Should cover: the danger of an English army restoring Mary in Scotland alarming the Protestant Scottish lords governing for her infant son; the threat of Mary returning to France, where her Guise relatives could provide armies and ships to support a Catholic claim against Elizabeth; the unacceptable risk of Mary going to Spain and Philip II; the political usefulness of holding Mary in England without verdict, as established by the ‘not proven’ outcome of the York and Westminster conferences; and the sense among Cecil and the Privy Council that custody was the cheapest way to neutralise a permanent threat. Reasons must be linked, not listed.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained, or several reasons identified without development.

Emerging: One reason, or general assertions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of relations between Elizabeth and Mary, Queen of Scots in the years 1568–69.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise detail. For example: (1) Elizabeth refused to meet Mary in person, even after Mary fled to England in May 1568, fearing it would imply formal recognition; she instead held Mary in protective custody at a series of country houses. (2) Elizabeth’s government held the York and Westminster conferences in October 1568 to investigate Darnley’s murder, with the Earl of Moray producing the Casket Letters as evidence; the case was declared ‘not proven’, allowing Mary to be kept in England without formal conviction.

Secure: Two features identified with one piece of accurate supporting detail per feature.

Developing: Two features given with general support, or only one developed.

Emerging: One feature, or two without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The arrival of Mary, Queen of Scots in England in 1568 was the most dangerous moment of Elizabeth’s reign so far.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Mary’s claim to the English throne
• the proposed Norfolk marriage of 1569
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, analytical answer using BOTH stimulus points and adding at least one factor of the candidate’s own (e.g. Mary’s status as a focus for Catholic plots, the role of foreign powers, the Pope’s later excommunication of Elizabeth in 1570, the way Mary’s arrival contributed to the Northern Rebellion). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that Mary’s arrival was uniquely dangerous because it gave English Catholics an alternative queen on English soil, but its full danger was only realised through later plots. Period-specific terminology used accurately throughout (Casket Letters, recusancy, Privy Council, Northern Rebellion, Counter-Reformation).

Secure: Both stimulus points used and one own point added; clear judgement with some support.

Developing: Stimulus points used but limited additional content; judgement asserted rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Limited engagement with stimulus; description rather than analysis; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the proposed marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk in 1569 worried Elizabeth and William Cecil.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the power of the Duke of Norfolk
• Mary’s claim to the English throne
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band answers use both stimulus points and add information of their own.

Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: the Duke of Norfolk was the only duke in England, with vast lands and Catholic sympathies, so the marriage would create a powerful rival court inside England; the marriage gave Mary’s Catholic claim a credible English partner and an heir-producing future; it threatened to revive the influence of the older nobility, weakening Cecil and his reformist faction; and it offered the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland a focus for Catholic action that would lead directly into the 1569 Northern Rebellion. Reasons must be linked, not listed.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained.

Emerging: One reason, or general comment without specific support.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the papal bull Inter caetera (1493) for Spanish claims in the New World.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Inter caetera, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Issued by Pope Alexander VI — a Spanish-born pope, Rodrigo Borgia — in May 1493, drawing a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands and reserving everything west for Spain.
• It gave Ferdinand and Isabella a religiously underwritten title to half the unknown world before they had any clear idea what was in it.
• It framed Spanish exploration as a duty to spread Christianity, allowing the Crown to present seizure of land as a religious mission rather than naked conquest.
• It was the legal foundation for the Requerimiento (drafted 1513), the document Spanish commanders read to Indigenous peoples before attack.
• It set the diplomatic problem that the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) had to solve, because Portugal would not accept the original line.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. religious framing AND legal foundation for later policy) with specific period detail (Borgia, Cape Verde, Requerimiento).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the bull without explaining its importance for Spanish claims.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) for Portuguese empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The line was moved 270 leagues further west, giving Portugal sea-room across the southern Atlantic that the original Inter caetera bull had denied.
• In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral made landfall in Brazil, east of the new line — giving Portugal an unexpected claim on a continental American territory.
• Portugal kept its papal monopoly on the African route, allowing Vasco da Gama to reach India in 1498 unchallenged by Spain.
• The treaty effectively divided the non-European world between Lisbon and the Spanish crown, allowing Portugal to build a global empire (Brazil, Angola, India, Macao) without Spanish interference.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the treaty without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of King John II of Portugal’s objection to Inter caetera for the development of Spanish empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of John II’s objection, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• John II refused the original 100-league line and demanded direct negotiation, forcing Spain to compromise rather than rely on a papal pronouncement alone.
