• His objection produced the Treaty of Tordesillas, which moved the line to 370 leagues west and gave Portugal sea-room that allowed Cabral’s 1500 landing on Brazil.
• The peaceful renegotiation prevented an Iberian war that would have crippled Spain’s ability to back further voyages and stalled the conquest era before it began.
• It set the precedent that Spanish overseas claims required diplomatic agreement with other Catholic powers, not just papal grants — a precedent later cited in disputes over the Pacific (Magellan’s voyage 1519–22).
• It demonstrated that Portuguese maritime knowledge was, in some respects, ahead of Castilian — pushing Spain to invest in its own navigation infrastructure (the Casa de Contratación, founded 1503).

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking John II’s objection to multiple consequences for Spain, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of John II’s objection without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) for Indigenous peoples of the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Indigenous peoples were not consulted on the division of their own lands; the treaty assumed European Christian title without their consent.
• The treaty embedded the religious framing that justified Spanish conquest as a Christianising mission — later expressed in the 1513 Requerimiento read in Spanish before attacks.
• It gave Spanish encomenderos and conquistadors a Catholic legal basis for seizing land, used in awards of encomienda and viceroyalty grants throughout the period.
• The line itself shaped which Indigenous nations encountered which European empire — the Mexica, Inca and Taino fell under Spain; the peoples of Brazil under Portugal — affecting language, religion and labour systems for centuries.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the treaty without a specific consequence for Indigenous peoples.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the events of 1493–1500 turned a diplomatic crisis between Spain and Portugal into a divided New World. You may use the following in your answer: the papal bull Inter caetera (1493), Cabral’s landing in Brazil (1500). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Columbus’s return through Lisbon in March 1493 alarmed King John II, because the Castilian westward route threatened Portugal’s carefully built African network.
• Ferdinand and Isabella secured the papal bull Inter caetera in May 1493 from Pope Alexander VI — a Spanish-born pope — drawing a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands and giving Spain everything west.
• This in turn provoked John II to demand renegotiation, because the original line cut too close to Portuguese knowledge of land in the south Atlantic.
• The Treaty of Tordesillas (7 June 1494) moved the line to 370 leagues west — an apparent Spanish concession that quietly opened the south Atlantic to Portuguese voyages.
• Six years later, Pedro Álvares Cabral made landfall in 1500 on Brazil, east of the new line — meaning the diplomatic compromise had handed Portugal a continental American claim it would otherwise not have had.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis — events linked with phrases like ‘this in turn enabled’, ‘because of this’. Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of papal authority for the Spanish empire in the 1490s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of papal authority, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Pope Alexander VI’s bull Inter caetera (1493) gave Spain a Catholic legal title to half the New World — without it, the Spanish claim was nothing more than a Castilian flag-planting.
• The pope’s 1494 title of Reyes Católicos for Ferdinand and Isabella confirmed the religious framing of their reign and underwrote Spanish presentation of conquest as Christianising mission.
• Papal authority allowed Spain to require missionary work in conquered territories, embedding the Dominican and Franciscan friars in the colonial administration from the start.
• The 1506 papal ratification of the Tordesillas line gave the renegotiated boundary the same religious force as the original bull, making it harder for either crown to repudiate later.
• The use of papal authority in the 1513 Requerimiento connected the diplomatic decisions of the 1490s directly to the violence of the conquest period that followed.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of papal authority without explaining its importance for the Spanish empire.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Spain’s decision to protect runaway enslaved Africans in Florida for the Carolinas in the 1730s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences each developed with detail. For example: Spain’s policy led to a steady flow of enslaved people escaping south from the Carolinas, weakening the plantation labour force and undermining owners’ control; and it pushed Carolina planters to lobby for tighter slave codes and more aggressive patrols, which intensified the violence of the slave system in response. Causal language used.
Secure: Two consequences identified with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the Carolinas.
Emerging: Mentions Spanish Florida without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Stono Rebellion (1739) for slavery in the Carolinas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: Stono mattered because it produced the Negro Act of 1740, which banned enslaved gatherings, writing lessons and self-provisioning — a fundamental tightening of the slave system; and because it sharpened Anglo-Spanish tensions on the colonial frontier weeks before Britain declared war on Spain. Specific evidence (date, around 100 rebels, march towards Florida, around 20 settlers killed, militia at the Edisto River) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Describes the rebellion without explaining why it mattered.
Emerging: Names Stono without specific detail.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how resistance shaped the slave system in British North America in the years 1730–41. You may use the following information in your answer: 
• Spain’s offer of freedom to runaways in Florida 
• The Stono Rebellion (1739) 
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses connections using causation and consequence. For example: Spain’s Florida policy created an escape route that drew enslaved Africans south; rumours of that route fed into rising tension in the Carolinas, contributing to the timing of Stono; Stono in turn produced the Negro Act of 1740, the harshest slave code yet; meanwhile in the north, anxieties about urban enslaved populations produced the New York trials of 1741. The narrative explains why a wave of resistance produced an even tighter slave system. Secure: Clear narrative with several analytical links between resistance and reaction. Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of why resistance changed the slave system. Emerging: Lists revolts without showing how they reshaped colonial slavery.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the New York Conspiracy trials of 1741 for the city.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the trials led to around 30 executions and the transportation of around 70 enslaved people out of the colony, sharply reducing the size of the enslaved population in New York City; and they hardened white New Yorkers’ sense of vulnerability towards enslaved Africans in their midst, encouraging tighter restrictions on enslaved movement and assembly. Causal language used.
Secure: Two consequences identified with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to executions, transportation or restrictions.
Emerging: Notes that there were trials without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of everyday acts of resistance for the development of slave codes in the colonies before 1741.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: importance lay in the way that constant low-level resistance — sabotage, work slowdowns, running away — pushed colonial assemblies to pass increasingly harsh slave codes regulating literacy, movement and assembly; and in shaping a self-image among colonial elites that justified those codes as ‘protective’ rather than oppressive. Specific evidence (newspaper runaway advertisements, slave codes’ expanding restrictions, post-Stono Negro Act 1740) anchors the response.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Lists everyday acts of resistance without showing why they mattered.
Emerging: Notes that enslaved people resisted without explaining the consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the New York Conspiracy of 1741 for understanding slavery across the British colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Conspiracy mattered because it forced contemporaries (and historians) to confront the reality that slavery was not confined to the South — New York City had a large urban enslaved population alongside Newport and Boston; and because the trials show how panic and judicial process could combine to produce mass executions in a colonial setting. Specific evidence (Mary Burton’s testimony, around 180 arrests, around 30 executions, urban context of New York) anchors the response. The contested historiography is acknowledged.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: Describes the events without explaining their importance.
Emerging: Confuses Stono and the New York Conspiracy.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the methods used during a struggle session in early 1950s China. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. crowd denunciations, forced confessions, placards, beatings). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that struggle sessions were stage-managed by cadres, or that the goal was public lesson rather than private investigation. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957–58 followed the Hundred Flowers Campaign.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Mao's reaction to the volume of criticism
• the Hungarian uprising of 1956
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. the volume and content of criticism (calls to end one-party rule, posters by Lin Xiling), Mao’s reaction (alarm and the ‘snakes from their holes’ reframe), the Hungarian and Polish unrest of 1956, the need to clear opposition before the Great Leap Forward, factional dynamics within the CCP. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the campaigns without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about Mao's reasons for launching the Hundred Flowers campaign.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation reads the Hundred Flowers as a deliberate trap from the start; the other reads it as a genuine reform that turned into repression once the criticism alarmed Mao). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Hundred Flowers campaign.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP orthodox vs revisionist Western, Frank Dikötter or Jonathan Spence), used different evidence (CCP-published material vs post-archival research), or had different purposes (defending Mao vs critical re-examination). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the Three Antis and Five Antis campaigns in consolidating CCP rule?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the c.4.5 million officials investigated in the Three Antis, the destruction of the urban capitalist class through the Five Antis (state-private enterprises by 1956), the use of struggle sessions, the link to the parallel terror against counter-revolutionaries, and how these campaigns prepared the ground for the First Five-Year Plan. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Hundred Flowers Campaign was always intended as a trap by Mao?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — Khrushchev’s Secret Speech (1956), the Hungarian and Polish unrest, Mao’s February 1957 'Correct Handling of Contradictions' speech, the volume and content of criticism (Lin Xiling, Hu Feng, posters demanding end to one-party rule), Mao’s ‘snakes from their holes’ reframing, and the c.500,000 labelled rightists in 1957–58. Acknowledges the genuine historiographical disagreement (Dikötter and Spence vs the CCP narrative) and reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (struggle session, big-character poster, laogai, Anti-Rightist, danwei). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. A report of Mamie Till Bradley’s decision to hold an open-casket funeral for her son, September 1955.

‘She had insisted on an open casket. “I wanted the world to see what they did to my baby,” she said. The body had been mutilated almost beyond recognition. As mourners filed past the glass-topped coffin, women wept and men removed their hats. Many had travelled from Mississippi, Tennessee, Detroit and as far as Los Angeles. The murder of a Chicago boy in a Delta cotton field had become a story for the whole country.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the impact of Emmett Till’s murder.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘Mamie Till deliberately used the open casket to make Southern violence visible to a national audience’ supported by ‘I wanted the world to see what they did to my baby’ AND ‘The case had reached communities far beyond Mississippi’ supported by ‘Many had travelled from Mississippi, Tennessee, Detroit and as far as Los Angeles.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why opposition to desegregation in the South was so effective in the years 1954-60.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Ku Klux Klan
• the White Citizens’ Councils

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. Dixiecrat obstruction in Congress, the Southern Manifesto, the closure of Little Rock’s and Prince Edward County’s schools, the limited federal enforcement of Brown II) and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (massive resistance, lynching, Executive Order 10730, Dixiecrat, Citizens’ Council). Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated. Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit. Emerging: Description of resistance without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. Melba Pattillo Beals, one of the Little Rock Nine, on her first weeks at Central High School in September 1957.

‘The soldiers told us to keep our eyes ahead and not respond. The crowd was screaming things I had never heard people scream before. Inside the school, the soldiers walked us to every class. We were never alone in a corridor. At lunch a girl pushed me down a flight of stairs; my paratrooper, Danny, picked me up and said, “Put on your warrior face.” I learned what he meant. The nine of us decided that if we cried, the year was lost.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the integration of Central High School.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Federal troops were necessary inside the school as well as outside it’ supported by ‘Inside the school, the soldiers walked us to every class’ AND ‘The Nine showed deliberate emotional discipline as a strategy to sustain integration’ supported by ‘The nine of us decided that if we cried, the year was lost.’)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1985 textbook on the Eisenhower years):
‘Little Rock was a triumph for federal authority. The 101st Airborne Division’s arrival at Central High School demonstrated that the United States government would, if necessary, use military force to defend the Constitution against state defiance. After Little Rock, no Southern governor doubted the price of open resistance.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 study of massive resistance):
‘Little Rock was a costly draw. Eisenhower was forced into action only by Faubus’s flagrant defiance, and as soon as the troops left Faubus closed Little Rock’s high schools entirely. Across the South, school districts learned that determined resistance could still delay desegregation by years — sometimes a decade. The Constitution had been defended; integration had not.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the significance of Little Rock? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 reads Little Rock as a victory for federal authority; Interpretation 2 reads it as a costly draw that did not stop later resistance) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘a triumph for federal authority’ vs ‘a costly draw’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the significance of Little Rock.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1985 textbook focused on the Eisenhower presidency and the constitutional clash with Faubus, whereas Interpretation 2 is from a 2010 study of massive resistance that uses long-run evidence about Southern desegregation rates. The two interpretations have different focuses (federal authority vs school enrolment) and use different evidence (executive action vs district-by-district records).
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the significance of Little Rock?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context. (You may include any SPaG mark separately.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge (Faubus and the Arkansas National Guard, Eisenhower’s Executive Order 10730 and the 101st Airborne, Faubus’s closure of Little Rock’s high schools 1958-59, Prince Edward County’s five-year closure, the role of the White Citizens’ Councils and Dixiecrat obstruction), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently and accurately throughout.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; judgement offered but less fully substantiated. Vocabulary mostly precise.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit. Some period terminology used.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 2. Vocabulary general. [16 marks for argument plus 4 marks for SPaG and use of specialist terminology — 20 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the developments in Israel in the years 1949–54.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the creation of the IDF
• the Law of Return (1950)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. IDF creation and conscription, Law of Return and mass immigration, refugee policy/UNRWA, the Qibya reprisal). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing relations between Israel and Egypt in the years 1949–55.
You may use the following in your answer:
• fedayeen cross-border raids
• the Israeli Gaza raid (February 1955)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent analytical narrative addressing at least three aspects of Egypt-Israel relations (e.g. armistice without peace treaty, refugee camps in Gaza supplying fedayeen, Israeli reprisals, Nasser’s rise and Czech arms deal). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material. Causal links explicit. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects. [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little analysis. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Law of Return (1950) for the new state of Israel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) around 700,000 Jewish immigrants arrived between 1948 and 1951, roughly doubling the population and turning Israel into a state with a clear Jewish majority; (ii) the absorption costs (rationing, ma’abarot, the Ashkenazi-Mizrahi divide) shaped Israeli social politics for decades. Pairs an immediate and a longer-term consequence. [7–8] Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6] Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4] Emerging: A single point or restatement of the law without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the creation of the Israeli Defence Forces (1948) for the new state of Israel.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. unifying the Yishuv’s rival armed groups (with the Altalena clash forcibly absorbing the Irgun); compulsory conscription making the IDF the single most important national institution; the IDF’s reprisal doctrine shaping the border war and pushing Egypt towards Soviet rearmament. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the IDF without showing why its creation mattered for the state. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the refugee status of Palestinian Arabs after 1949 for the future of the conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the establishment of UNRWA in 1949 and the spread of camps across Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria; Israel’s refusal to allow return setting the ‘right of return’ as a permanent obstacle to peace; the role of refugee camps as recruiting grounds for fedayeen raiders and later the PLO from 1964. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term consequences. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the refugees without showing why their status shaped future conflict. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Israeli reprisal raid on Gaza (February 1955) for the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the death of 38 Egyptian soldiers humiliated Nasser soon after he took power in Egypt and undermined his authority in the Arab world; (ii) Nasser responded by negotiating a major arms purchase from Czechoslovakia in September 1955, breaking the Western monopoly on arming the Middle East and feeding directly into the Suez Crisis the following year. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates what happened in the raid without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Norman migration to England after 1066 was different from Viking migration in the period c800-c1066.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Norman migration was elite migration by perhaps 200 barons who held around 95% of English land by 1086; Viking migration was mass settlement by farming families across the Danelaw.
• Normans replaced the existing landowning class and the language of law and government; Vikings settled alongside the existing population and their language mingled with English.
• Normans arrived as a single conquering force in a few years; Viking settlement built up over two centuries of raiding, treaty and farming.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Jewish migrants were encouraged to settle in England after 1066.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Christian teaching on lending money
• royal castle-building.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Christian teaching in this period barred Christians from lending to other Christians at interest, while the crown urgently needed credit for castles and armies, so Jewish lenders filled the gap.
• Norman government ran on cash: the Domesday survey of 1086 shows how far royal taxation and record-keeping had grown, and that created sustained demand for finance.
• Jewish communities had already played this role in Normandy, so William drew on an arrangement he knew.
• Aaron of Lincoln lent to the crown, to great barons and to Cistercian monasteries, and became one of the wealthiest men in England - evidence of the scale of the need.
• Royal protection cut both ways: because Jewish subjects belonged directly to the king, he could tax them at will through tallage.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the experience of Hanseatic merchants in medieval England was similar to the experience of Flemish and Walloon weavers in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were tolerated because they were useful: Hanseatic merchants brought northern European trade to the Steelyard, and Flemish weavers brought the new draperies to Sandwich and Canterbury.
• Both lived under a special legal position that kept them apart, whether the status of alien or the self-governing stranger church.
• Both faced resentment from English competitors while town authorities defended them for the tax and customs revenue they generated.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Royal institutions were the most important factor shaping migration to medieval England between c1066 and c1500.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the role of William the Conqueror
• the 1290 expulsion of England’s Jewish population.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for royal institutions:
• William the Conqueror's decisions shaped both Norman elite migration, recorded in Domesday, and the arrival of Jewish moneylenders.
• Tallage on Jewish communities was a direct royal lever used throughout the period.
• Edward I's Edict of Expulsion in 1290 ended Jewish settlement in England by decree alone.
• Royal grants made the Steelyard possible, and royal action closed it in 1598.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Religion created the demand for Jewish lenders in the first place, and religious hostility drove the massacre at York in March 1190, in which about 150 people died.
• Economic influences pulled Flemish weavers into English towns after the Black Death of 1348-49, when labour was scarce and wages were rising.
• Attitudes in society could overrun royal protection, as at York in 1190, while elsewhere local trade ties let alien merchants prosper for centuries.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (tallage, alien, Hanseatic, Steelyard, Domesday).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Jewish communities in medieval England were both protected and vulnerable.

You may use the following in your answer:
• tallage
• the massacre at York (1190).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Jewish subjects belonged directly to the king, which gave them royal protection no other migrant group had.
• The same status made them a royal asset to be taxed: tallage could be raised at will, and rates rose sharply from the late twelfth century.
• Protection depended on the crown being present and willing. At York in March 1190 it was neither, and about 150 people died at Clifford's Tower.
• Christian hostility to lending at interest made the community both necessary and resented.
• When Edward I could no longer profit from Jewish lending, the same royal power that had invited the community expelled it in 1290.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the experiences of Norman, Jewish and Hanseatic migrants in medieval England were so different.

You may use the following in your answer:
• landownership after 1066
• the legal status of 'alien'.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Normans arrived as conquerors, not petitioners: they took the land and replaced the English ruling class, holding around 95% of it by 1086.
• Jewish migrants came as economic specialists invited by the king, held the unique status of belonging to him, were taxed through tallage and were finally expelled in 1290.
• Hanseatic merchants came as traders under the status of alien: they could prosper in their own enclave but could not own land freely or join English society on equal terms.
• Religion divided them: Norman and Hanseatic newcomers were Christian and part of Christendom, while Jewish communities faced sustained religious hostility.
• Each group filled a different need - military rule, royal credit and long-distance trade - and was treated accordingly.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of Jaffa of September 1192.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Jerusalem retained by the Muslims — Saladin kept control of the Holy City, the central aim of the crusade not achieved.
• Coastal strip retained by the Christians — the Latin Kingdom kept Acre, Jaffa and a strip of coast as a base for any future crusade.
• Pilgrim access — unarmed Christian pilgrims were guaranteed safe passage to visit the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
• Three-year truce — the agreement was set for an initial period of three years and eight months.
• Negotiated end to the campaign — the truce was concluded between Richard and Saladin without Philip II, who had already left, ending Richard’s share of the Third Crusade.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how Richard’s ransom of 1193–94 was raised in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Quarter tax on income and moveables — one of the most aggressive medieval taxes, levied at 25% of income and goods.
• Cistercian wool clip — the entire annual fleece of the Cistercian and Gilbertine monasteries was taken to fund the ransom.
• Church plate — gold and silver vessels were seized from cathedrals and monasteries to be melted down.
• Tallages on Jewish moneylenders — the archae were used to extract extraordinary sums from the Jewish community.
• Scutage on knight service — tenants-in-chief who would not serve in person paid heavy cash sums in lieu.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard I was captured on his journey home from the Holy Land.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Richard’s quarrel with Duke Leopold of Austria
• the closure of safer routes home
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Quarrel with Duke Leopold of Austria — Richard had thrown Leopold’s banner into the moat at Acre in 1191; Leopold sought a personal revenge that fed directly into Richard’s capture.
• Closure of safer routes — Philip II controlled the southern French coast and would have arrested him; Spanish coasts were closed by political agreements; Italy was unsafe because of the dispute with Henry VI.
• Forced choice of the Adriatic route — with western routes shut, Richard sailed north and tried to slip overland through the lands of his enemies.
• Storm and shipwreck — his ship was wrecked in the Adriatic in December 1192, leaving him to travel overland in disguise through hostile territory.
• Recognition near Vienna — the disguise failed; Richard was identified and seized in Erdberg near Vienna.
• Hostility of Henry VI — the Holy Roman Emperor was at odds with Richard over his alliance with the Welf duke Henry the Lion (Richard’s brother-in-law) and over Sicily, and was happy to receive Richard from Leopold for ransom.
• Political vulnerability of an absentee crusader — Richard’s army had largely dispersed after the Treaty of Jaffa; he was travelling with a small retinue easy to ambush.
• Sheer profitability — the prospect of an enormous ransom from a king at war with France made Richard worth more alive than free.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard I failed to recapture Jerusalem during the Third Crusade.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the supply lines from the coast
• the departure of Philip II
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Supply lines — Jerusalem lay forty miles inland in arid hill country; even if captured, it would have had to be supplied by mule trains through Muslim-controlled territory after the western armies left.
• Philip II’s departure — the French king sailed home in August 1191, removing a substantial part of the army and unleashing political pressure on Richard’s lands in France.
• The threat from John and Philip — rumours that Richard’s brother and the French king were carving up the Angevin Empire forced him to plan an early return.
• Saladin’s scorched-earth strategy — he destroyed wells, cisterns and walls along the route to Jerusalem, denying water and shelter to the crusaders.
• Internal Christian division — the dispute between Conrad of Montferrat and Guy of Lusignan over the throne of Jerusalem split the high command; Pisans, Genoese, Templars and Hospitallers had rival agendas.
• The advice of the local barons of the Latin Kingdom — they argued any captured Jerusalem could not be held after the western army went home; Richard accepted their advice and turned back at Beit Nuba.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard’s ransom of 1193–94 placed such a heavy burden on England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the size of the ransom
• existing taxation since 1188
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Sheer size — 150,000 marks of silver was equal to two or three years of total Crown revenue and had to be raised in months, not over a normal taxation cycle.
• Existing taxation — the Saladin Tithe of 1188 and the sale of offices at Richard’s coronation in 1189 had already drained reserves of cash and goodwill before the ransom was demanded.
• Aggressive levies — the quarter tax on income and moveables, the seizure of the Cistercian wool clip and church plate, the heavy scutage on tenants-in-chief, and tallages on the Jewish community fell on every part of society.
• Concentrated impact on the Church — whole monastic orders lost their main income source and cathedrals lost their plate, breeding lasting resentment.
• Damage to the wool trade — seizing the Cistercian fleece in one year disrupted England’s most valuable export trade.
• Lasting precedent — the ransom legitimised aggressive Crown taxation, a habit John inherited and pushed to breaking point.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘The departure of Philip II in 1191 was the main reason Richard could not retake Jerusalem.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the threat from John in England
• Saladin’s strategy of denying water
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Philip’s August 1191 departure removed a substantial fraction of the army.
• Once back in France, Philip plotted with John to seize Richard’s lands; the threat to Normandy created an unrelenting clock that drove Richard to compromise.
• Without Philip’s authority the joint legitimacy of the crusade was diminished, weakening Christian command at exactly the moment unified leadership was needed for an inland march on Jerusalem.
• The political pressure from France caused Richard to accept the Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192 rather than press on with another inland push.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Logistics — Jerusalem lay forty miles inland in waterless hill country; even Philip’s troops could not have solved the problem of supplying the city after capture.
• Saladin’s scorched-earth strategy — destruction of wells, cisterns and walls along the route denied the crusaders both water and bases.
• Internal Christian division — the Conrad of Montferrat / Guy of Lusignan dispute split the command; the Pisans, Genoese, Templars and Hospitallers all pulled in different directions.
• Advice of local barons — the Latin Kingdom barons told Richard a captured Jerusalem could not be held after the western armies left; their advice mattered as much as Philip’s absence.
• Length of campaign — the crusade had been on the road for over two years; supplies, horses and morale were running out regardless of French numbers.

Overall judgement: Philip’s departure created the political clock that forced compromise, but the strategic obstacles — logistics, Saladin’s denial of water, and the impossibility of holding a captured city — would have stopped the crusaders even if Philip had stayed. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion using precise period vocabulary (Beit Nuba, Treaty of Jaffa, Latin Kingdom, scutage).

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the weapons carried by English foot soldiers were different in the fifteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Fifteenth-century foot soldiers relied on the longbow (1). It was cheap, silent and fast, and a trained archer could shoot ten or twelve arrows a minute (1). Seventeenth-century foot soldiers carried the matchlock musket and the pike (1). A musket took about a minute to reload and could punch through plate armour, so pikemen with 16 to 18 foot pikes had to guard the musketeers while they reloaded (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why a standing army developed in England in the period c1500–c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the New Model Army
• the Restoration of 1660.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Pike-and-shot fighting needed long, repeated drill, so armies raised for a single campaign could not learn it in a few weeks.
• Wars lasted years rather than the 40 days of feudal service, so soldiers had to be paid and kept together.
• The New Model Army of 1645 proved the point: 22,000 men, paid, drilled and supplied from London, destroyed the Royalist field army at Naseby.
• After the Restoration in 1660 Charles II kept household regiments in pay, so a small permanent force never went away.
• Fortifications, warships and artillery cost so much that only a permanent administration could pay for and maintain them.
• Parliament still distrusted a standing army, so from 1689 it kept control by passing an annual Mutiny Act.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way soldiers were paid was different in the fourteenth century and the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the fourteenth century most men served for land or for plunder, not wages (1). Feudal duty gave the king about 40 days of unpaid service, and soldiers on a chevauchée took what they could carry (1). In the seventeenth century soldiers expected regular wages (1). The New Model Army was paid through a national administration in London, and Parliament had to raise taxes to keep the money flowing (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the composition of English armies changed in the period c1500–c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the musketeer and the pikeman
• the decline of the longbow.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Matchlock firearms could pierce plate armour, so the armoured horseman lost the protection that had made him the main striking arm.
• Because a musket was slow to reload, armies needed pikemen beside the musketeers, and the two together became the core of the infantry.
• A musket could be learned faster than a longbow, so kings no longer depended on a lifetime of village archery practice.
• Cavalry changed rather than vanished: troopers in back-and-breast armour with sword and pistols replaced the lance-and-plate knight.
• Dragoons were added as mounted infantry, riding to the fight and then dismounting to use a musket.
• Field artillery became reliable enough to bring on campaign, so gunners became a permanent part of an army.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why war continued to press hard on civilians in the period c1250–c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• purveyance
• free quarter.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Armies had no supply system of their own, so in every period they took food, animals and carts from the people they marched past.
• Medieval purveyance let royal officers buy at fixed, below-market prices and leave a promise to pay; in a bad harvest this could starve a village.
• During the Civil War both sides used free quarter, eating and sleeping in private houses and leaving paper promises that often went unpaid.
• Recruitment took men away from farms and trades, by feudal summons in the medieval period and by commissions of array and militia ordinances in the 1640s.
• Towns on campaign routes suffered most: Berwick and Dover in the medieval wars, and much of the West Country and Yorkshire in the 1640s.
• What changed was the scale and the paperwork, not the basic demand: war was still paid for by the people it passed through.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
‘The role of Oliver Cromwell was the main reason for the Parliamentary victory at Naseby in 1645.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Ironsides
• the New Model Army.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks.

Indicative content — arguments for Cromwell's role:
• Cromwell drilled the Ironsides specifically to rally after a charge and re-engage in formation, which was the decisive move at Naseby.
• His command of the Parliamentary right wing turned the cavalry battle into a flank attack on the Royalist infantry.
• His insistence on choosing officers by ability (the Self-Denying Ordinance) shaped the New Model Army that fought the battle.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Sir Thomas Fairfax was Lord General and overall commander; the army's organisation and choice of ground were his work.
• The New Model Army itself — paid, drilled, nationally administered, larger than the Royalist field army — gave Parliament a structural advantage that no individual commander created alone.
• Royalist failure: Prince Rupert's horse rode off the field to plunder, leaving the Royalist infantry exposed; this was a Royalist mistake as much as a Parliamentary success.
• Numbers: Fairfax and Cromwell fielded around 14,000 men against Charles I's 7,500.
• Pay and supply: regular Parliamentary pay produced steady morale that the Royalists could not match.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Cromwell against Fairfax, the New Model as a system and Royalist failures, uses accurate period detail (Ironsides, Self-Denying Ordinance, Rupert, named numbers) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the definition of crime in the period c1500–c1700 was different from the definition of crime in the period c1000–c1500.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Early modern law created crimes out of religion and poverty: heresy after the break with Rome in 1534, vagabondage under the 1547 Vagrancy Act and witchcraft under the 1542 Act.
• Medieval law had created its new crimes out of conquest and land: the Forest Laws criminalised hunting and wood-gathering, and the Murdrum fine protected Norman settlers.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why witchcraft prosecutions increased in England between c1542 and c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Witchcraft Acts
• the printing press.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• The 1542 Witchcraft Act made witchcraft a capital felony tried in the king's courts; later Acts in 1563 and 1604 increased the penalties — the legal framework expanded prosecutions.
• Religious upheaval after the Reformation created anxiety about supernatural power, with Protestants and Catholics each suspicious of the other.
• Economic stress (population growth, enclosure, bad harvests) produced scapegoats — typically poor, elderly women on the margins of village life.
• The printing press spread sensational pamphlets about witches who killed cattle, raised storms or harmed children, fuelling popular fear.
• Royal interest mattered: James I's Daemonologie (1597) treated witchcraft as a real danger and lent royal authority to the hunts.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (1542 Act, James I, printing press, religious change) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of witchcraft fears without explaining why prosecutions rose.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Tudor governments passed the 1547 Vagrancy Act and the 1601 Poor Law.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the dissolution of the monasteries
• enclosure.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Population growth and stagnant wages had increased the number of homeless, jobless people on the roads, alarming towns and parishes.
• The dissolution of the monasteries (1536–41) closed England's largest providers of poor relief almost overnight, leaving no organised system to handle vulnerable people.
• Enclosure of common land for sheep farming pushed peasants off ancestral plots, swelling the wandering population further.
• Authorities feared social disorder — they associated wandering with theft, begging and unrest — and reached for the criminal law to manage it (1547 Vagrancy Act).
• By 1601 it was clear that punishing all wanderers alike was unjust and ineffective; the Poor Law refined the approach by separating the 'impotent poor' (deserving parish relief) from 'sturdy beggars' (still punished as vagabonds).

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (population growth, dissolution of monasteries, enclosure, deserving/undeserving distinction) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of poverty without explaining why the laws were passed.

practice_questions.text:
‘Religious change was the most important factor in creating new crimes between c1500 and c1700.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• heresy and treason under Mary I and Elizabeth I
• the 1547 Vagrancy Act.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting religious change as the most important factor:
• Henry VIII's break with Rome and the Religious Settlement of 1559 redefined heresy and made loyalty to the Pope a treasonable offence.
• Mary I burnt around 280 Protestants for heresy; Elizabeth I executed Catholic priests as traitors.
• Religious anxiety after the Reformation helped fuel the witch-hunts — both sides feared the other's supernatural power.
• Decisions taken in church and state about doctrine directly created new capital offences.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors):
• Economic change was the principal driver of vagrancy laws — population growth, enclosure and the dissolution of the monasteries created the wanderers; the law followed the economy, not religion.
• The printing press spread sensational pamphlets that helped drive witchcraft prosecutions independently of doctrine.
• Monarchs' personal priorities mattered: James I's Daemonologie (1597) shaped policy, but his interest was not solely religious.
• Continuity from the medieval system (tithings, hue and cry, parish constables) shows that the day-to-day machinery of crime control changed less than the menu of crimes.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs religious change against at least one other factor (economic upheaval, technology/printing, royal personality), uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (e.g. heresy, treason, vagabondage, sturdy beggars, impotent poor, Witchcraft Act, Religious Settlement).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the treatment of witchcraft in the period c1500–c1700 was different from its treatment in the period c1700–c1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Between 1542 and 1700 witchcraft was a capital felony tried in the king's courts, and the East Anglian hunts of 1645–47 alone ended in roughly 100 hangings.
• The Witchcraft Act of 1736 repealed the old law and redefined the offence as fraud: it was now a crime to claim magical powers, and nobody was executed as a witch again.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why heresy and treason became so closely linked in Tudor England.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the break with Rome in 1534
• the Religious Settlement of 1559.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Henry VIII's break with Rome (1534) made the king the Supreme Head of the Church, so refusing his religious authority was both a spiritual offence (heresy) and a political one (treason).
• Mary I's revival of heresy laws and Elizabeth I's later treatment of Catholic priests as traitors meant the same religious dispute could now be punished under either label depending on the regime.
• Catholic priests under Elizabeth I owed loyalty to the Pope, who was now seen as a foreign political power; their presence in England was framed as treason rather than purely religious belief.
• The Religious Settlement of 1559 fixed an officially Protestant Church of England, so dissent from it was treated as a threat to political stability.
• Religious belief and political loyalty were not seen as separate questions in the sixteenth century; the monarch was head of both Church and state.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (1534 break with Rome, 1559 Religious Settlement, Mary I's burnings, Elizabeth's treatment of priests) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of religious change without explaining the link between heresy and treason.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of London (1518).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Signed in London in October 1518.
• A non-aggression pact between more than twenty European powers including France, the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, the papacy and the Italian states.
• Originated in Pope Leo X’s call for a crusade against the Ottoman Turks but was redirected by Wolsey into a wider European peace.
• Made Henry VIII the public guarantor of European peace, with Wolsey as broker.
• Lasted only until c.1521–22 when Habsburg-Valois war resumed.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Held between 7 and 24 June 1520 in a valley near Calais.
• A summit between Henry VIII and Francis I, attended by around 6,000 English and 6,000 French courtiers.
• Featured jousting, wrestling, banquets, music and Mass under cloth-of-gold tents and a temporary palace.
• Cost England approximately £15,000 — about a fifth of annual royal revenue.
• Followed almost immediately by Henry’s meeting with Charles V at Gravelines, undercutting the appearance of Anglo-French amity.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey arranged the Treaty of London in 1518.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Ottoman threat to Europe
• Wolsey’s ambition for England’s European role
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Ottoman threat — Pope Leo X had called for a Christian truce to prepare a crusade as the Ottomans pressed into the Balkans; Wolsey adopted and enlarged the idea.
• England as broker — Wolsey wanted to make a kingdom of 2.5 million people the deciding weight between the larger French and Habsburg powers, by being the host and guarantor of peace.
• Henry’s prestige — making Henry the public guarantor satisfied the king’s desire for European stature without the cost of war.
• Wolsey’s personal ambition — success would burnish his diplomatic reputation and might one day support a papal candidacy (he stood in 1521 and 1523).
• Avoiding bankruptcy — military glory was expensive; brokered peace gave Henry stature without exhausting the Treasury.

Mastering: Three or more reasons explained with precise detail; both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Mostly description without focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
‘Wolsey’s foreign policy ran into difficulty in the 1520s because of events he could not control.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor (1519)
• the Battle of Pavia (1525)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs structural change in Europe against Wolsey’s own decisions and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments that the events were outside his control:
• Charles V’s election as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519 created a Habsburg power France could not accept, and war returned by 1521.
• The death of Maximilian in 1519 removed the balance on which the Treaty of London had rested.
• At Pavia in 1525 Charles V captured Francis I and then refused to share the spoils with Henry.
• The Sack of Rome in 1527 left Pope Clement VII in imperial hands and closed the route to the annulment.
• England’s resources were small: a kingdom of about two and a half million people could not steer the rivalry of France and the Habsburgs.

Arguments that his own choices mattered:
• He committed England to Henry’s expensive wars instead of holding to the peace he had brokered in 1518.
• The 1522–23 invasion under Suffolk reached Montdidier but collapsed for want of supply.
• Reversing alliances after 1525 — the Treaty of the More, then support for the League of Cognac — made England look unreliable.
• He tied English policy to a papacy he could not protect, which left him without options in 1527.

Overall judgement: structural change in Europe was decisive, but Wolsey’s willingness to chase Henry’s wars turned difficulty into failure. Top-band answers weigh these factors and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520) is regarded by some historians as more spectacle than substance.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Henry’s meeting with Charles V at Gravelines
• the cost of the summit
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Gravelines meeting — days after the Cloth of Gold, Henry met Charles V to renew the imperial alliance, undercutting the appearance of Anglo-French amity.
• Cost — the summit cost England roughly £15,000, about a fifth of annual royal revenue, with no lasting diplomatic outcome.
• No treaty — the meeting produced ceremonial declarations but no binding diplomatic instruments comparable to the Treaty of London.
• Outbreak of war by 1521 — within two years Henry was at war with France again, demonstrating the summit had not altered underlying Habsburg-Valois rivalry.
• Wrestling match — the famous incident in which Francis threw Henry on his back captured the personal rivalry the summit was supposed to defuse.
• Personal vanity — both kings used the event to display wealth and chivalric prestige; political substance was secondary.
• Renaissance theatre — the summit fits a sixteenth-century pattern of court display rather than diplomatic settlement.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise detail; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘Wolsey was more successful as a peacemaker than as a war leader between 1515 and 1529.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Treaty of London (1518)
• the 1522–23 invasion of France
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs Wolsey’s peacemaking against his war record and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement (peacemaker):
• Treaty of London (1518) — brought together more than twenty European powers in a non-aggression pact, making Henry the public guarantor of European peace.
• Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520) — even as theatre, projected an image of Anglo-French amity that lasted at the diplomatic level.
• Treaty of the More (1525) and League of Cognac (1526) — restored Anglo-French cooperation and helped restrain Habsburg dominance after Pavia.
• Wolsey’s preference for diplomacy over war — consistently sought to maximise English influence without the cost of full-scale conflict, recognising the Treasury could not sustain prolonged war.

Arguments against (war leader more successful or peace overrated):
• 1513 French campaign — Wolsey organised the supply of an army of 30,000, captured Thérouanne and Tournai, and delivered the Battle of the Spurs.
• 1522–23 invasion under Suffolk reached Montdidier, only fifty miles from Paris — an impressive logistical achievement before supply collapsed.
• 1518 peace was short-lived — broken by 1521–22, suggesting the peacemaker reputation was overstated.
• 1527 Sack of Rome and the failure of the annulment proceedings exposed the limits of diplomacy when Henry actually needed it.
• Lack of a male heir — the strategic outcome Henry most wanted was not delivered by either war or peace.

Overall judgement: Wolsey was demonstrably more successful as a peacemaker than as a war leader — the Treaty of London is his lasting achievement — but the line between the two is blurred, since his peacemaking served Henry’s search for glory and his wars were managed as carefully as his treaties. Top-band answers will weigh both sides explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple criteria weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Suez Crisis (1956) for Egypt’s leadership of the Arab world.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Nasser’s personal prestige soared because he kept the Canal and survived two colonial powers; Voice of the Arabs gave Cairo a region-wide platform that no other Arab capital could match; the formation of the United Arab Republic in February 1958 turned that prestige into a political union with Syria; Arab states deferred to Cairo on Israel policy in the run-up to 1967. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation slips into description of the war itself. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the crisis without showing why it shaped Egyptian leadership of the Arab world. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Czech arms deal (1955) for relations between Israel and Egypt.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the deal broke the Western monopoly on arming the Middle East and brought Soviet bloc weapons into Egypt for the first time; it persuaded Israel that Egyptian rearmament had to be pre-empted before Soviet equipment was absorbed; it deepened US-Egyptian distrust and triggered the withdrawal of Aswan Dam funding, which in turn triggered nationalisation of the Suez Canal. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the deal without showing why it mattered for Israel-Egypt relations. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the formation of the United Arab Republic (1958) for the Arab world.
practice_questions.marks:
