Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the UAR was treated as the first concrete step towards pan-Arab unity and gave Nasser a political base larger than Egypt alone; it inspired short-lived imitations such as the Arab Federation between Iraq and Jordan; tensions between Egyptian officials and Syrian elites caused the union to collapse in 1961, exposing the limits of pan-Arabism in practice but leaving Nasser as its symbolic leader. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the UAR without showing why it mattered for the Arab world. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Nasser’s nationalisation of the Suez Canal (July 1956).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) it triggered the secret Sèvres Protocol between Britain, France and Israel and the military intervention that followed in October–November 1956; (ii) it confirmed Nasser’s standing as the leading Arab nationalist, feeding directly into the formation of the United Arab Republic with Syria in February 1958. Pairs an immediate and a longer-term consequence. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that the canal was nationalised without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of US opposition to the Anglo-French intervention at Suez (1956).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) US Treasury pressure on the pound sterling and a refusal to support an IMF loan forced Anthony Eden to call a ceasefire on 7 November 1956 and accept withdrawal; (ii) it confirmed that Britain and France could no longer act militarily east of Suez without American agreement, ending the era of independent Anglo-French power in the Middle East and contributing to Eden’s resignation in January 1957. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that the US was opposed without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the Suez Crisis in the years 1955–58.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Czech arms deal (1955)
• the Sèvres Protocol (October 1956)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the Czech arms deal and Aswan funding withdrawal, nationalisation and the Sèvres Protocol, the war and US/Soviet pressure, the formation of the UAR). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the Bolshevik attitude to the Constituent Assembly in January 1918. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, the SR victory in the November elections, the Bolsheviks demanding Sovnarkom’s decrees be ratified, Lenin’s walk-out, Sverdlov’s dissolution declaration the next morning, Red Guards locking the doors of the Tauride Palace). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the Bolsheviks treated the Assembly as a rival authority to be neutralised rather than a legitimate parliament. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Bolsheviks dispersed the Constituent Assembly in January 1918.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the November 1917 election results
• the Decree on Land
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. the SR plurality and the Bolshevik minority, the Assembly’s refusal to ratify Sovnarkom’s decrees, Lenin’s ‘higher form of democracy’ argument that the soviets superseded a bourgeois parliament, the wider clamp-down on the Kadets and rival parties already underway). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Sovnarkom, Constituent Assembly, Tauride Palace, Sverdlov, Chernov. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the dispersal without explaining why it happened. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the Bolshevik regime in the months after October 1917.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues the early Bolshevik regime was responsive to genuine popular demand, with the Land and Workers’ Control decrees ratifying changes that workers and peasants were already imposing from below; the other argues that closing the Constituent Assembly, banning the Kadets and shooting the Romanovs without trial show that the regime was authoritarian from the start). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the early Bolshevik decrees.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (Sovnarkom decree texts and committee minutes versus survivor testimony from Ekaterinburg and the Tauride Palace), they wrote at different times (early Soviet historiography emphasising legitimacy versus post-1991 archival biographies stressing coercion), or they had different purposes (defending the legitimacy of the soviet state versus reconstructing the closure of opposition). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that the early Bolshevik decrees of 1917 mostly ratified popular demands rather than imposed Bolshevik policy from above?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the early decrees — the SR origin of the Land Decree, the existing peasant seizures, the popularity of Workers’ Control in the cities, but also Sovnarkom’s sabotage-busting Red Guards, the December bank nationalisation and the closure of the Constituent Assembly — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the closure of the Constituent Assembly and the execution of the Romanovs show that the Bolshevik regime was authoritarian from the start?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the November 1917 SR victory, the demand to ratify Sovnarkom’s decrees, Sverdlov’s dissolution declaration, the secret transfer of the Romanovs to Ekaterinburg, the basement shootings of 16–17 July 1918, the parallel banning of the Kadets — to weigh the ‘authoritarian from the start’ reading against the ‘wartime emergency’ reading. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Sovnarkom, Constituent Assembly, Ipatiev House, Sverdlov). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the San Francisco Vigilance Committee of 1851 for law and order in the early West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• It established the model of citizen-organised ‘vigilance’ justice that was copied in other Western towns and territories, including the larger 1856 San Francisco committee and the Montana Vigilantes of 1863–65.
• It exposed the weakness of corrupt or absent official authority — pressuring municipal and territorial governments to professionalise courts and policing in the years that followed.
• It hardened ethnic divisions in the city, since vigilance trials disproportionately targeted Chinese, Hispanic and Irish migrants.
• It strengthened the political position of merchants and reformers like William T. Coleman who saw themselves as the West’s respectable class.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail (Coleman, 1851/1856, Montana, named groups).
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on lawlessness without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the key events of lawlessness and attempts to tackle it in the early West in the years c1849–1856.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the California Gold Rush mining camps
• the San Francisco Vigilance Committees

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• The 1849 Gold Rush brought around 300,000 people into California within a few years, creating mining camps with no recognised courts, jails or property lines — conditions in which claim-jumping, racial attacks and saloon violence flourished.
• Because federal authority sat thousands of miles away and territorial government was skeletal, miners improvised — running their own ‘miners’ courts’ on the spot.
• In 1851 in San Francisco, after a wave of arson and robberies and a corrupt city government, the merchant William T. Coleman organised the first Vigilance Committee, which made arrests, ran trials and hanged four accused inside three months.
• Because corruption persisted, a much larger Vigilance Committee was formed in 1856 following the murder of the reforming newspaper editor James King of William; around 6,000 members ran the city for nearly three months, hanged four more accused and forced corrupt officials out before disbanding.
• The model spread: Montana copied it, hanging Sheriff Henry Plummer in 1864 as the alleged leader of an outlaw band — suggesting that vigilance was a stage in the long story of law and order, not a final answer.

Mastering: Sustained narrative that explicitly links events using causal language (because, this led to, with the result that), stays within the dates, and uses specialist vocabulary (claim-jumping, vigilance committee, US marshal).
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage; period detail mostly accurate.
Developing: Some chronological coverage but linkage is weak; events listed rather than connected.
Emerging: Thin description of one or two events with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the absence of jails and federal courts in early mining camps.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Miners and townspeople improvised their own justice through ‘miners’ courts’ and vigilance committees, normalising hangings without appeal — as in San Francisco in 1851.
• Disputes over claims escalated into violence (claim-jumping), since there was no surveyor, court or written deed to settle them.
• Racial minorities — Chinese, Hispanic and Irish migrants — were targeted with little recourse, since informal courts reflected the prejudices of the camp majority.
• Outlaws moved freely between camps and territories, knowing that pursuit beyond a town’s edge usually stopped.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on lawlessness without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how lawlessness and attempts to tackle it changed in the West in the years c1849–1865.

You may use the following in your answer:
• mining camps and claim-jumping
• vigilance committees

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• From 1849 the gold camps of California created the first concentrated frontier population without recognised courts, jails or surveyed claims, producing endemic claim-jumping and saloon violence.
• Because the camps were transient and federal authority was distant, miners ran rough ‘miners’ courts’ on the spot — an improvised, unappealable form of justice.
• In 1851 the first San Francisco Vigilance Committee under William T. Coleman extended this pattern to a city, running trials and hanging four accused; in 1856 a second, much larger committee took over the city for almost three months in response to political corruption and the murder of James King of William.
• Because the model worked in the short term but offered no appeal, it was copied unevenly across the West — the Montana Vigilantes of 1863–65 hanging Sheriff Henry Plummer himself as the alleged leader of an outlaw band.
• Alongside vigilance, town marshals and elected county sheriffs began to appear, paid poorly and often drawn from the same gunmen they policed — the first thin layer of formal law that would thicken in the railroad era.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (Coleman, King of William, Plummer), and specialist vocabulary.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Chronological coverage but linkage is weak.
Emerging: Thin description of one or two events with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Foreign Miners’ Tax (1850) and racial harassment in the California mining camps.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Chinese and Hispanic miners were pushed off the richest claims and forced into lower-paid service work, even though Chinese migrants made up perhaps a quarter of California’s mining population.
• Patterns of racial violence were tolerated by improvised justice systems — vigilance committees and miners’ courts shared the prejudices of the camp majority.
• Hispanic Californios who had lived in the region before 1848 saw their pre-existing claims and rights eroded under American rule.
• The pattern set the template for later anti-Chinese legislation as the migrant population grew through the 1850s and 1860s.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on tensions without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the key events that made cow towns and mining camps difficult to police in the years c1849–1870.

You may use the following in your answer:
• mining camps from 1849
• cow towns from the late 1860s

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1849 the discovery of gold pulled around 300,000 migrants into California within a few years, producing mining camps with no recognised courts, jails or property lines — conditions in which claim-jumping and racial attacks flourished.
• Because the population was transient and almost entirely young men paid in cash, normal social restraints were absent — trouble was structural, not personal.
• From the late 1860s a second pattern emerged: cow towns at railheads such as Abilene, where drovers arrived with months’ wages, congregated in saloons and brothels, and carried revolvers as standard equipment of the trade.
• Because the violence was seasonal, town marshals were paid poorly or only on commission, often hired from the same gunmen they policed and rarely lasting more than a season.
• These conditions led directly to citizens’ vigilance committees (San Francisco 1851 and 1856; Montana 1863–65) and to the slow professionalisation of marshals and sheriffs that would shape the next decades.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, dates respected, specialist vocabulary used, both contexts (mining and cattle) covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both contexts and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one context, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the reception of Flemish and Walloon refugees in the sixteenth century was similar to the reception of Huguenot refugees after 1685.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were welcomed as fellow Protestants fleeing Catholic persecution, which shaped how the state and the Church treated them.
• Both were valued for skills England wanted: the new draperies at Sandwich and Canterbury from 1561, and silk weaving in Spitalfields after 1685.
• Both were given a legal and religious framework of their own - stranger churches, and grants of denization - that let them keep their identity while trading freely.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why religion shaped migration to England between c1500 and c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the stranger churches
• the revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• England's emergence as a Protestant nation after Henry VIII's break with Rome in 1534 made it a refuge for Protestants persecuted under Catholic rulers.
• In the 1560s Protestant Flemings and Walloons fled Spanish persecution in the Low Countries; Sandwich was authorised in 1561 to take twenty-five master weavers and their families, and they founded their own stranger church.
• The revocation of the Edict of Nantes in October 1685 drove around 50,000 Huguenots to England, the largest single religious migration of the period.
• The crown had already prepared the ground: Charles II offered denization to French Protestants by proclamation in 1681, and after 1685 James II authorised a church collection for the destitute.
• Religion also limited who was welcome. Catholic migrants received none of these proclamations or church collections.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the impact of Huguenot migrants on England after 1685 was different from the impact of Jewish migrants on medieval England.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Huguenots reshaped whole industries and were absorbed within two generations; medieval Jewish communities were confined to finance and were expelled in 1290.
• Huguenot influence reached banking, the army, silk weaving and skilled trades, with Huguenot families among the founders of the Bank of England in 1694; Jewish influence ran almost entirely through royal credit.
• Huguenots could hold property and trade through denization; medieval Jewish migrants belonged to the king and had no comparable legal route into English society.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Economic factors were the most important reason for migration to England between c1500 and c1700.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the cloth industry
• the Edict of Nantes (1685).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for economic factors:
• The cloth industry pulled Flemish and Walloon weavers into Sandwich and Canterbury from 1561, where the new draperies transformed exports.
• Demand for skilled silk weaving drew Huguenots to Spitalfields, where they built the tall-windowed houses their work required.
• Global trading companies and privateering tied English ports to Africa and the Atlantic, bringing African mariners such as Diego into English records.
• Town authorities defended the strangers' right to trade because of the customs revenue and taxes they generated.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Religion was decisive: the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in October 1685 triggered the largest single migration of the period, and Sandwich's 1561 charter framed the Flemings as religious refugees.
• Royal institutions chose who was welcome: Charles II's denization proclamation of 1681 and the church collection authorised under James II after 1685 applied to Protestants alone.
• Attitudes in society were uneven - English merchants were beginning to profit from transatlantic slavery while parish registers recorded Africans as members of their communities.
• The factors worked together: economic need created the demand, but religion decided who counted as a welcome migrant.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (denization, stranger churches, new draperies, Spitalfields, privateering).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Africans were present in Tudor and Stuart England.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the royal court
• global trade and privateering.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Tudor court employed African servants and entertainers: John Blanke was a royal trumpeter to Henry VII and Henry VIII, recorded in payment rolls between 1507 and 1512 and in the Westminster Tournament Roll of 1511.
• English voyaging and privateering brought African mariners into English crews, among them Diego, who sailed with Francis Drake on the circumnavigation of 1577-80.
• Wealthy households employed Africans as servants and household members, which is why they appear in parish registers, wills and inventories.
• More than 360 Africans have been identified in English records between 1500 and 1640, including Cattelena of Almondsbury, who owned her own cow in 1625.
• English law gave no clear sanction for slavery on home soil, which left room for some Africans to live and work independently even as English merchants profited from the Atlantic slave trade abroad.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why patterns of migration to England changed between the medieval period and c1500-c1700.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the English Reformation
• the cloth industry.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• England became a Protestant nation after 1534, which created a new category of welcome migrant: the Protestant refugee from a Catholic state.
• Economic growth in cloth, especially the new draperies and later silk weaving, pulled in skilled Flemish, Walloon and Huguenot workers in numbers far larger than medieval craft migration.
• Global trade and privateering tied English ports to Africa and the Atlantic for the first time, bringing Africans such as John Blanke and Diego into English records.
• Stranger churches and grants of denization were new institutional forms that gave refugees a legal and religious identity their medieval predecessors never had.
• Continuity matters too: the label of alien survived, the south-east remained the main entry route, and royal authority still decided who was welcome.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the firearms carried by British infantry were different in the seventeenth century and the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Seventeenth-century muskets were smoothbore and slow (1). A matchlock took about a minute to reload and was only useful in massed volleys at short range, so pikemen had to protect the musketeers (1). Nineteenth-century rifles were accurate at long range (1). The Pattern 1853 Enfield used rifling and the Minié ball to hit a target at around 600 yards, so soldiers no longer had to stand shoulder to shoulder (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why infantry tactics changed in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Minié ball
• smokeless powder.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Rifling and the Minié ball pushed accurate fire from about 75 yards to around 600, so the close-order line became a target rather than a strength.
• Rifled artillery firing explosive shells swept open ground, so troops had to spread out and use cover.
• Smokeless powder from the 1880s hid the firer, producing the 'empty battlefield' in which soldiers could not see who was shooting at them.
• Magazine rifles such as the Lee-Metford raised the rate of fire, so a small force in cover could stop a much larger attack.
• Mass production at Enfield Lock and by firms such as Armstrong and Vickers meant both sides had the same lethal reach.
• The Boer War showed the result in practice: British columns had to break up into open order against entrenched riflemen.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the supply of British armies on campaign changed in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• steam railways
• the Crimean War (1854–56).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Steamships could move a whole army and its stores overseas to a timetable; a British army was shipped to the Black Sea coast in 1854.
• Railways moved shells, food and men far faster than horses: a line was built from Balaclava harbour up to the siege works at Sevastopol.
• Industrial weapons needed industrial quantities of ammunition, so armies could no longer live off what they carried or seized.
• Mass-produced brass cartridges, tinned and refrigerated food and standard uniforms all had to be delivered from factories to a railhead.
• The telegraph travelled with the railway, so orders from London reached a general in hours rather than weeks.
• In the Boer War the rail network became a target in itself, and Boer commandos attacked it to cut British supply.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the cavalry declined in importance in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• rifled weapons
• the Battle of Balaclava (1854).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Rifled small arms could hit horses and riders at around 600 yards, so a charge had to cross a long killing zone before it reached the enemy.
• Field artillery firing shrapnel over open ground made the approach even more costly.
• Balaclava in 1854 showed the price: the Light Brigade rode more than a mile with Russian guns on three sides and lost roughly 40 per cent of its men.
• Smokeless powder hid the riflemen, so cavalry could not even see the line they were charging.
• Barbed wire, entrenchments and prepared positions gave defenders ground that horses could not cross.
• By the Boer War cavalry survived mainly as mounted infantry, riding to the fight and then dismounting to use rifles.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the making of weapons was different in the sixteenth century and the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Sixteenth-century weapons were made by hand, one at a time (1). Bowyers, fletchers, armourers and gunfounders worked in small workshops, so no two weapons were quite alike and parts were not interchangeable (1). Nineteenth-century weapons were mass-produced in factories (1). The Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield Lock used steam-driven machine tools and interchangeable parts, and firms such as Armstrong and Vickers turned out guns and shells in huge numbers (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘The decisive change in nineteenth-century warfare was the development of new weapons.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• rifling and the Minié ball
• steam-powered transport.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for weapons as decisive:
• Rifling and the Minié ball pushed accurate small-arms fire from 75 to 600 yards, ending the close-order line.
• Breech-loading rifled field artillery threw shells for miles, saturating open ground.
• Smokeless powder produced the ‘empty battlefield’, forcing dispersion and cover.
• These weapons made the heavy cavalry charge suicidal — demonstrated at Balaclava (1854).

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Steam railways and steamships allowed industrial-scale supply — the Crimean War saw an army shipped overseas and a railway built from Balaclava harbour to the Sevastopol siege lines.
• The telegraph collapsed political distance — orders from London to a field commander now travelled in hours.
• Mass production at Enfield Lock and Armstrong meant both sides had the same industrial reach — production capacity, not battlefield daring, became the deciding factor.
• Tactical doctrine had to catch up — open order, cover and dispersion were the human responses to industrial weapons; without these the weapons alone would have produced even higher casualties.
• Continuity argument: trench-style earthworks already existed (Torres Vedras 1810, Petersburg 1864–65); the nineteenth century industrialised existing techniques rather than inventing them outright.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs weapons against transport, production and tactical adaptation across the period c1700–c1900, uses accurate period detail (Minié ball, Enfield, breech-loading, Balaclava railway, Torres Vedras) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One factor dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It was led by Catholic nobles — specifically the Earls of Northumberland (Thomas Percy) and Westmorland (Charles Neville), with around 4,600 tenants raised in November 1569.
• It included a deliberate religious act — the rebels restored the Catholic Mass at Durham Cathedral on 14 November 1569 and tore up the English Bible and prayer book.
• Its target was Mary, Queen of Scots — the rebels marched south to free her from Tutbury, but Elizabeth had already moved her to Coventry.
• It collapsed without a major battle — the rebels disbanded in December 1569 once the Earl of Sussex raised 14,000 royal troops.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Revolt of the Northern Earls broke out in 1569.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of noble power
• Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Loss of noble power — the Earls had been stripped of Crown lands, mining rights and influence on the Council of the North, replaced by ‘new men’ such as William Cecil; rebellion was a way to reclaim status.
• Religious grievance — the 1559 settlement had outlawed the Catholic Mass, and the Earls’ tenants and households remained loyal to Catholicism; restoring the Mass at Durham was central to the rising.
• Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England (May 1568) — placed a Catholic alternative on English soil within reach at Tutbury, making rebellion appear winnable for the first time.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme — the Duke of Norfolk’s plan to marry Mary suggested even southern Protestants might accept her; Norfolk’s arrest in October 1569 forced the Earls to act before they were summoned.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise period detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification of a cause without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Revolt of the Northern Earls (1569–70) was significant for Elizabeth’s reign.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1570 papal bull (Regnans in Excelsis)
• the Council of the North
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons (using both stimulus points AND at least one of own knowledge) with clear causal links between them.

Indicative content:
• 1570 papal bull (stimulus) — Pius V’s Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved Catholics of allegiance, officially linking Catholicism to treason and shaping every later plot.
• Council of the North (stimulus) — reorganised under loyal Protestant control after the revolt, ending the old independent power of the Percy and Neville families and centralising Tudor authority in the north.
• 1571 Treasons Act and harsher recusancy fines — Parliament responded by making it a capital offence to deny Elizabeth’s right to rule and increased pressure on Catholics who refused Anglican services.
• Shift in the form of Catholic resistance — the failure of open rebellion pushed Catholic opposition underground into the Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586) plots, requiring Walsingham’s spy network.
• Mary, Queen of Scots became the focus of every later threat — she had been the rebels’ goal, and remained the gravitational centre of plots until her execution in 1587.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections between factors.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description of events without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason the Revolt of the Northern Earls broke out in 1569 was Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of noble power
• the 1559 religious settlement
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Mary’s arrival as main cause):
• Mary fled to England in May 1568; before then the Earls had grievances but had not rebelled. Her presence at Tutbury made the rebellion’s plan possible.
• Without a Catholic figurehead within striking distance, freeing her could not have been the rebels’ immediate aim; she gave the rising its goal.
• Every later plot (Ridolfi, Throckmorton, Babington) also pivoted on Mary — she was the gravitational centre of Catholic resistance from 1568 onwards.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Loss of noble power (stimulus) — both Earls had been stripped of lands, mines and influence on the Council of the North; rebellion was about reclaiming status, with religion as a unifying banner.
• 1559 religious settlement (stimulus) — making Catholic worship illegal created a decade of grievance among northern tenants and gave the rising its symbolic act at Durham; without religion the Earls could not have raised 4,600 men.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme (own knowledge) — Norfolk’s arrest in October 1569 was the immediate trigger; the Earls had to act before they were summoned. Mary’s presence enabled the plan, but Norfolk’s arrest forced the timing.

Justified judgement: Mary’s arrival was the trigger that turned long-standing grievances into action, but the underlying causes — lost noble power and the 1559 settlement — were the deeper drivers. A strong response weighs Mary as catalyst against these long-term factors and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed, judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors; judgement asserted rather than supported.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth’s response to the Revolt of the Northern Earls.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Mass executions across the north — around 450 rebels, mostly poorer tenants chosen by lottery, were hanged so every northern village saw retribution.
• Confiscation of rebel lands — Crown seized estates from the Percy and Neville families, breaking their long-term regional wealth.
• Reorganisation of the Council of the North — placed under loyal Protestant control to end the Earls’ old dominance.
• Pursuit of fugitive leaders — Northumberland was eventually returned by the Scots and beheaded at York in 1572.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots became central to the threat against Elizabeth after 1568.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Mary’s claim to the English throne
• the 1570 papal bull
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Her dynastic claim — as Henry VII’s great-granddaughter and a Catholic, Mary had a strong claim to the English throne if Elizabeth could be removed; this made her a natural figurehead.
• Her physical presence in England — from May 1568 she was held in English custody (Tutbury, then later Sheffield), within reach of any rising or rescue plot rather than safely abroad.
• The 1570 papal bull — once Pius V had excommunicated Elizabeth, killing or deposing her became a Catholic duty, and Mary was the only credible Catholic replacement.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme of 1569 — suggested even powerful English nobles would back a Mary-led succession, encouraging Catholic plotters to keep trying.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise period detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which law enforcement in early modern towns was similar to law enforcement in Anglo-Saxon villages.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Both depended on unpaid local people rather than professionals: Anglo-Saxon villagers served in tithings and answered the hue and cry, while early modern towns relied on part-time watchmen and parish constables.
• In both periods the public was still expected to join the chase; the state neither funded nor trained a force to do it for them.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why early modern punishment relied so heavily on public spectacle.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the absence of a police force
• public hangings at Tyburn.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail from the period. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• There was no professional police force; the state could not deter crime by promising to catch every offender, so it relied on the threat of frightening punishments to deter others.
• Public hangings at Tyburn drew large crowds; the visibility of the punishment was the point — passers-by were meant to fear committing the same crime.
• Treason punishments such as hanging, drawing and quartering were deliberately staged as political theatre to defend the king's authority and the divine right of kings.
• Bodies and body parts were displayed at city gates and on London Bridge as a permanent warning.
• Most ordinary people were illiterate; spectacle communicated the law more effectively than written statutes.

Mastering: At least two developed reasons, supported by specific detail (Tyburn, treason punishment, illiteracy etc.) and explicit links to deterrence.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of public punishment without explaining its purpose.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why transportation to the American colonies became an important punishment in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the colonies' need for labour
• the Bloody Code.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Transportation, used from around 1615 as an act of royal mercy, gave courts a serious alternative to hanging; the Transportation Act of 1718 then made it a normal sentence in its own right.
• It removed offenders permanently from England, since few transported convicts ever returned, addressing fears of repeat offending.
• It supplied cheap indentured labour to the American colonies, linking criminal policy to imperial expansion.
• It allowed judges and juries to soften the harshness of the Bloody Code in practice while keeping the threat of death on the books.
• It set the precedent for later large-scale transportation to Australia after American independence (1783).

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific period detail (date, Atlantic colonies, indentured labour) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of transportation without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the use of the death penalty in the eighteenth century was different from its use in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Under the Bloody Code more than 200 offences carried death by the 1810s, most of them against property, and hangings were staged in public at sites such as Tyburn.
• By the twentieth century hanging was reserved for murder and treason, carried out behind prison walls after 1868, and abolished for murder in 1965.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main purpose of the punishment of the Gunpowder Plotters in 1606 was to deter others from rebellion.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the use of hanging, drawing and quartering
• the public display of body parts on London Bridge.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks. The strongest answers reach a substantiated overall judgement.

Indicative content — arguments supporting deterrence as the main purpose:
• The punishment was deliberately staged in public; the plotters were dragged on hurdles to the place of execution to maximise the audience.
• The four-stage process — hanged until almost dead, disembowelled, then quartered — was designed to terrify any would-be rebels.
• Body parts displayed at city gates and on London Bridge created a permanent warning, especially against Catholic conspirators in the years following.
• James I and Robert Cecil deliberately publicised the plot, including through Parliament's annual thanksgiving sermon, to deter further Catholic plotting.

Indicative content — arguments against (other purposes):
• Retribution was central: treason was understood as an attack on the divinely appointed king; the punishment had to match the crime in its severity.
• Reinforcing the divine right of kings — the elaborate punishment was a public reassertion of royal authority and of the political order.
• Strengthening anti-Catholic feeling: the spectacle helped secure public support for tighter laws against Catholics, beyond simply deterring rebellion.
• Ordinary capital crime was punished by hanging; the elaborate treason punishment was reserved for offences against the monarch — suggesting that defending the king's person was as central as deterrence in general.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs deterrence against at least one other purpose, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the punishment of those who threatened the government in the seventeenth century was different from their punishment in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• In 1606 the Gunpowder Plotters were hanged, drawn and quartered and their body parts displayed at city gates and on London Bridge, because treason was treated as an attack on a king who ruled by divine right.
• In the twentieth century those who defied the state over war service faced tribunals: conscientious objectors were given non-combatant duty, alternative civilian work or prison, and none was executed in Britain.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Henry VIII’s case for an annulment from Catherine of Aragon.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Cited Leviticus 20:21 — that a man who married his brother’s widow would be childless.
• Argued that Pope Julius II’s 1503 dispensation had been beyond papal power because it contradicted divine law.
• Pointed to the lack of a surviving male heir as evidence of divine judgement on the marriage.
• Insisted Catherine’s first marriage to Prince Arthur in 1501 had been consummated, which created the barrier of affinity that Leviticus forbade.
• Maintained the matter must be resolved by the Pope through a formal annulment, not a divorce.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Blackfriars legatine court of 1529.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Held in London from May to July 1529 and presided over by two cardinals — Wolsey and Campeggio — acting as papal legates.
• Catherine of Aragon attended on 21 June, knelt at Henry’s feet, declared herself a true wife and a virgin at her marriage, then walked out and never returned.
• Campeggio’s instructions from Rome were to delay rather than decide; he had been told not to issue a final judgement.
• Adjourned by Campeggio on 23 July for the Roman summer recess, just as Wolsey expected to deliver verdict.
• Pope Clement VII subsequently revoked the case to Rome, ensuring it would never resume in England.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate names or detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Pope Clement VII refused to grant Henry VIII an annulment from Catherine of Aragon.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Sack of Rome (1527)
• Charles V
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• The 1527 Sack of Rome — Charles V’s troops stormed the city and the Pope fled to the Castel Sant’Angelo, leaving Clement effectively the emperor’s prisoner.
• Charles V was Catherine’s nephew — granting the annulment meant publicly humiliating his aunt while Charles’s soldiers held papal territory.
• The 1503 dispensation by Julius II — reversing it would imply a previous Pope had erred, undermining papal authority.
• Catherine’s public refusal — she would not retire to a convent, so any ruling against her would have to be made over her open resistance.
• Cardinal Campeggio’s instructions — sent to England with secret orders to delay, not decide; he tried to persuade Catherine to take the veil for months before opening the case.
• Clement’s personal caution — an indecisive Pope who hoped to outlast the crisis rather than confront a major Catholic monarch.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description of events without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Henry VIII wanted to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon mainly because he needed a male heir.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the succession
• Anne Boleyn
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the succession against other motives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Only Princess Mary, born in 1516, survived; Catherine had not been pregnant since 1518 and was in her early forties.
• The Tudor line was only two generations old, and Henry feared a female successor would invite the kind of civil war fought in the previous century.
• Henry read the lack of a son as God’s judgement, citing Leviticus on marrying a brother’s widow.
• He asked for an annulment rather than a divorce because he wanted a son whose legitimacy could not be questioned.

Arguments for other motives:
• Anne Boleyn refused to become his mistress and held out for marriage, which gave Henry a personal reason to act by 1527.
• Henry’s view of his own sovereignty made it intolerable that a foreign pope should decide the fate of his marriage.
• The Boleyn faction at court encouraged him to believe an annulment was both necessary and obtainable.
• Catherine’s nephew was Charles V, so ending the marriage also loosened a Habsburg tie that had brought England little return.

Overall judgement: the want of a son made the annulment necessary, but Anne Boleyn and Henry’s view of kingship explain why he pursued it so hard from 1527. Top-band answers weigh these factors and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey fell from power in 1529.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the failure of the divorce proceedings in London
• the influence of the Boleyns
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons. Indicative content: • Failure of the Blackfriars court — Campeggio’s adjournment in July 1529 and Clement’s revocation of the case to Rome left Wolsey unable to deliver the one thing Henry now demanded. • The Boleyn faction — Anne Boleyn, her father Thomas and her uncle the Duke of Norfolk had been working against Wolsey at court for at least two years; Anne believed (with some justice) that he had stalled her cause to favour a French marriage. • Charge of praemunire in October 1529 — using foreign papal authority without royal consent; legally watertight against a man who had been papal legate for fifteen years. • Loss of the chancellorship and his palaces — Hampton Court and York Place forfeited to the king; Sir Thomas More appointed Lord Chancellor in his place. • Long-running unpopularity — the Amicable Grant of 1525, his ostentation, and his monopoly of patronage had built up enemies who now closed in. • Henry’s own willingness to drop him — the king had publicly disowned the Amicable Grant in 1525 and used the same tactic in 1529; once Wolsey ceased to be useful, he had no protection. Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout. Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation. Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The failure of the divorce proceedings was the most important reason for Wolsey’s fall from power in 1529.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Cardinal Campeggio
• Anne Boleyn
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Reward sustained argument that weighs the failure of the annulment against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Arguments for ‘most important’: • The annulment was the only matter Henry cared about by 1529; failure on it stripped Wolsey of his usefulness. • Campeggio’s adjournment of Blackfriars and Clement’s revocation of the case happened weeks before the praemunire charge. • The legal mechanism that removed Wolsey (praemunire, his papal legateship) only had teeth because the papal route had failed. • The annulment crisis brought the Boleyn faction directly into Henry’s confidence and cut Wolsey off. • Henry’s personal anger over Blackfriars is well documented in contemporary letters. Arguments for alternative explanations: • Influence of the Boleyns — Anne, Thomas Boleyn and the Duke of Norfolk had worked against Wolsey since 1526–27, undermining him long before Blackfriars. • Long-standing unpopularity — the Amicable Grant of 1525, ostentation (Hampton Court), pluralism, and monopoly of patronage had built broad opposition. • Henry’s personal style — he had publicly disowned Wolsey over the Amicable Grant in 1525, signalling that the cardinal was always expendable. • Charles V’s control of the papacy — structural; no English minister could have delivered an annulment under those conditions, so Wolsey’s fall was inevitable. • Foreign policy failure — the post-Pavia diplomatic isolation in 1525–27 weakened Wolsey before the annulment ever began. Overall judgement: the failed annulment was the immediate trigger, but it was decisive only because the Boleyn faction, the king’s readiness to disown ministers, and Wolsey’s broader unpopularity made him impossible to defend. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion. Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout. Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached. Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of John’s character as king of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features must be given.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Administrative energy — John toured England in person, hearing pleas and checking accounts; the pipe rolls grew thicker every year of his reign.
• Suspicion of his barons — he demanded hostages, including the sons and wives of leading nobles, as a guarantee of good behaviour.
• Vindictiveness — he starved Matilda de Braose and her son to death at Windsor in 1210.
• Cleverness combined with arbitrariness — he experimented with new taxes (the 1207 thirteenth) and creative justice but applied them inconsistently.
• Personal repulsiveness to chroniclers — Roger of Wendover called him ‘cruel to all men’; Matthew Paris said hell was made fouler by his presence.
• Lack of military reputation — the nickname ‘Softsword’ followed his peace at Le Goulet.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of John’s claim to the English throne in 1199.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Proximity of blood — as Henry II’s youngest surviving son, John was the closest adult male relative of the dead Richard I.
• Adult kingship argument — supporters such as William Marshal and Hubert Walter argued that the realm needed an adult ruler rather than a 12-year-old boy.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine’s backing — the queen-mother used her authority to swing England, Normandy and her own duchy of Aquitaine behind John.
• Coronation at Westminster — John was anointed and crowned by the Archbishop of Canterbury on 27 May 1199, broadcasting legitimacy.
• Treaty of Le Goulet (May 1200) — Philip II of France formally recognised John as Richard’s heir on the Continent in return for a 20,000-mark relief and territorial concessions.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the murder of Arthur of Brittany was so damaging to John’s position in France.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the customs of noble captivity
• Brittany and Poitou
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Breach of noble captivity — medieval custom held that captured nobles were ransomed or honourably imprisoned, never killed; John’s probable murder of his own nephew at Rouen in 1203 broke that code openly.
• Breton blood feud — Arthur was the natural lord of Brittany; his murder turned the duchy from a wavering territory into a sworn enemy of John, opening Normandy’s western flank to attack.
• Poitevin defection — the leading Poitevin and Norman barons concluded that an oath to John was not binding for him, so it need not be binding for them; many switched to Philip II.
• Loss of moral authority — chroniclers spread the story across Europe, blackening John’s reputation at the very moment he needed allies.
• Philip II’s legal cover — Philip used the murder to maintain that John was an unworthy vassal whose fiefs could justly be confiscated.
• Symbolic loss — capturing Arthur at Mirebeau in August 1202 had been John’s greatest victory; throwing away that goodwill made the murder politically as well as morally a disaster.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John’s succession in 1199 was contested.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Arthur of Brittany
• Philip II of France
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Two rival rules of inheritance — proximity of blood favoured John as adult brother of the dead king; representation favoured Arthur as the son of John’s elder brother Geoffrey.
• Arthur’s age and location — the 12-year-old was being raised at the French court, giving Philip II direct control over a rival claimant.
• French royal interest — Philip II had everything to gain from a contested Angevin succession; he could weaken whichever side won.
• Regional loyalties split — Anjou, Maine and Touraine declared for Arthur on the basis of representation; England, Normandy and Aquitaine took John on adult-king grounds.
• Arthur’s personal claim through Brittany — he was already Duke of Brittany in his own right, giving him a power base.
• The need to buy Philip’s recognition — the Treaty of Le Goulet of May 1200 cost John 20,000 marks and territory in the Vexin, showing how unsettled the claim was even after coronation.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John was able to capture Arthur of Brittany at Mirebeau in 1202.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the speed of John’s march
• Eleanor of Aquitaine
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Speed of march — John covered roughly 130 km in 48 hours from Le Mans to Mirebeau, far faster than Arthur’s besieging force expected.
• Element of surprise — the attack came at dawn on 1 August 1202, catching the besiegers eating breakfast outside the castle and the knights still unarmed.
• Arthur’s tactical error — the 15-year-old had besieged his own grandmother Eleanor of Aquitaine in Mirebeau, drawing John south as a personal as well as a political duty.
• Quality of John’s force — experienced English and Norman household knights, guided by William des Roches, the seneschal of Anjou.
• Eleanor of Aquitaine’s coordination — the queen-mother had sent for help and pinned the besiegers in place with a vigorous defence.
• Lusignan misjudgement — Hugh and Geoffrey de Lusignan thought they had time to take the castle before relief arrived, and were captured along with Arthur.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; precise period detail.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘John’s personal character was the main reason his French vassals turned against him after 1199.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Arthur
• Philip II of France
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• The murder of Arthur in 1203 broke the customs of noble captivity and turned Brittany into a blood feud against the king.
• The starvation of the de Braose family at Windsor in 1210 was the most extreme example of a wider pattern of vindictiveness that frightened all great barons.
• John’s habit of demanding hostages from leading nobles and flirting with their wives and daughters destroyed personal trust.
• Chroniclers from Roger of Wendover to Matthew Paris record near-universal disgust with his personal manner.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Philip II of France was a determined and skilful enemy; he had been working to break up the Angevin Empire since the 1180s and would have looked for any pretext.
• Structural Angevin weakness — the empire stretched from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, was held together only by personal loyalty, and was financially exhausted by Richard’s ransom.
• The Lusignan affair — John’s seizure of Isabella of Angoulême from her Lusignan betrothed gave Philip a legitimate legal pretext to summon and condemn John.
• The fall of Château Gaillard in March 1204 was a question of military and engineering circumstances as much as character.
• Loss of revenue — even a popular king would have struggled to defend Normandy without the Angevin treasury Richard had drained.

Overall judgement: John’s personal character was the spark, but only because his strategic position was already vulnerable. Philip II would have moved in any case; structural Angevin weaknesses made any war hard to win; but the murder of Arthur and the king’s general untrustworthiness turned a difficult position into a hopeless one. A balanced judgement weighs character as the trigger against structural and external factors as the underlying conditions.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (proximity of blood, representation, relief, Lusignan, Mirebeau).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of salutary neglect for British rule in the colonies before 1740.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example, salutary neglect mattered because it allowed colonial assemblies to expand their financial powers without challenge from London, and because it normalised smuggling, so that later attempts after 1763 to enforce the Navigation Acts felt to colonists like a sudden attack on settled liberties. Specific anchors (Walpole, Molasses Act 1733, Sugar Act 1764) developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim that the policy was important without sustained focus on why; limited use of specific developments.
Emerging: Describes the policy without explaining its importance for what followed.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of widespread smuggling in the colonies before 1740.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: smuggling meant Britain collected very little revenue from American trade, leaving the customs service running at a loss; it also entrenched a culture in which colonial juries refused to convict their neighbours, making later imperial enforcement after 1763 far harder. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference; or one developed and one underdeveloped.
Emerging: Restates that smuggling existed without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Molasses Act of 1733 for relations between Britain and the colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example, the Molasses Act mattered because the gap between law and enforcement — a sixpence-per-gallon duty almost universally evaded by New England distillers — trained colonial merchants to treat imperial trade rules as optional, which shaped responses to the Sugar Act in 1764. A second development could be its role in damaging the credibility of the customs service. Specific examples developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Names the Act and gives a general consequence without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Mentions the Act without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of French competition in the fur trade for British authority on the colonial frontier.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development.
