For example: French traders offered better goods and closer alliances, which weakened British influence over Indigenous nations such as the Lenape and Shawnee; British licensing of fur traders was widely ignored along contested rivers, exposing how thinly imperial authority reached west of the Appalachians. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to fur trade or Indigenous nations.
Emerging: Mentions the rivalry without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how lax British governance shaped the colonial economy in the years 1713–40. You may use the following information in your answer:
• The Navigation Acts
• The Molasses Act of 1733
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why colonial trade grew the way it did rather than narrating a sequence. Links the Navigation Acts to a culture of evasion enabled by the long coastline and weak customs service; links the Molasses Act of 1733 to the entrenchment of New England’s rum and West Indies trade despite the duty; brings in own knowledge such as the role of Walpole or the strength of colonial assemblies. Reaches an analytical judgement about how authority and enterprise interacted.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists features of the period without explaining how lax governance shaped the economy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the long Atlantic coastline for the failure of British trade enforcement in the colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example, the geography mattered because around 1,500 miles of coast with countless inlets meant a small customs fleet could never patrol it, leaving the rules unenforceable; it also mattered because remote landings allowed European luxury goods to flow inland untaxed, distorting markets and undermining customs revenue. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Notes the long coastline without showing why it mattered for enforcement.
Emerging: Describes the geography without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the founding of Santo Domingo in 1496 for Spain’s presence in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Santo Domingo, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Santo Domingo was the first permanent European city in the Americas and the capital of Spanish operations in the New World for around thirty years — replacing the failed wooden fort of La Navidad with a planned colonial city.
• It became the launching pad for the next wave of Spanish expansion: the conquest of Cuba (1511–15), Balboa’s expedition that reached the Pacific (1513), and Cortes’s Mexican voyage (1519) all drew on Hispaniola for men, ships and supplies.
• It was the site of the first stone cathedral, the first university, and the first audiencia (royal court) in the Americas — signalling the transition from frontier outpost to bureaucratic colony.
• It anchored the gold-tribute and forced-labour economy that would be exported to the rest of the Caribbean and the mainland — a model first tested on the Tainos of Hispaniola.
• It established the precedent for siting Spanish capitals near sheltered harbours and gold-bearing rivers, which Mexico City and Lima would later follow.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. springboard for later conquest AND template for colonial government) with specific period detail (Hispaniola, audiencia, the launching of Cuba and Mexico expeditions). Clear links to Spain’s presence.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Santo Domingo without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Columbus’s rule as governor of Hispaniola (1494–1500).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The gold-tribute system imposed on the Tainos — with mutilation as punishment for failing to deliver — broke up Taino communities and contributed to the collapse of the Hispaniola population.
• Settler revolts on Hispaniola showed that even the Spanish colonists found Columbus’s rule intolerable — pushing the Crown to intervene through royal commissioners.
• Francisco de Bobadilla’s 1500 mission led to Columbus’s arrest in chains and the loss of his governorship — transferring control of Hispaniola from Columbus’s family to Crown-appointed officials.
• The pattern of brutality and collapse on Hispaniola became the warning case that later reformers like Las Casas would use to argue against the encomienda system.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Columbus’s rule without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the arrival of smallpox on Hispaniola in 1518.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Mortality of 50–90% in some districts of Hispaniola completed the demographic collapse of the Tainos as an independent people, with very few surviving as a distinct community by 1540.
• The shrinking Indigenous workforce on Hispaniola pushed the Crown to authorise the licensed shipment of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean from 1518 onwards — the start of the transatlantic slave trade.
• Smallpox spread from Hispaniola ahead of Spanish expeditions, reaching Mexico in 1520 and Peru even earlier than the conquistadors, weakening Indigenous resistance to later conquest.
• The catastrophe entrenched the Spanish view that Indigenous labour was abundant but disposable — shaping the encomienda system as a labour regime to be exported to the mainland.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on smallpox without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spanish actions on Hispaniola between 1494 and 1519 led to the collapse of the Taino population. You may use the following in your answer: the gold-tribute system imposed by Columbus (from 1494), the arrival of smallpox (1518). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Columbus’s gold-tribute system from 1494 forced every Taino over fourteen in gold-bearing districts to deliver gold dust every three months on pain of mutilation — pulling labour off the fields and breaking up communities.
• This in turn caused starvation and family breakdown, while sexual violence, mass enslavement and the killing of resisters reduced the Taino population from hundreds of thousands in 1492 to around 30,000 by 1514 — BEFORE smallpox even arrived.
• The shrinking workforce was concentrated in unhealthy conditions in encomienda labour gangs, leaving communities malnourished and exhausted.
• Because of this, when smallpox arrived in 1518 it found populations already weakened — mortality of 50–90% in some districts completed what Spanish rule had begun.
• By 1540 the Tainos of Hispaniola were essentially extinct as an independent people — a collapse that was both human-made and biological, not one or the other.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis — events linked with phrases like ‘this in turn weakened’, ‘because of this’. Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (settler revolts, sexual violence, the 1514 census, the link to African enslavement). Reaches a substantiated overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Francisco de Bobadilla’s mission of 1500 for Spanish rule in the Caribbean.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Bobadilla’s mission, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Bobadilla’s arrest of Columbus and his brothers in 1500 ended the Columbus family’s personal control of Hispaniola and transferred authority to Crown-appointed officials.
• It established the principle that the Indies were a Crown colony, not the private inheritance of an explorer — a precedent that the Casa de Contratacion (1503) and later the Council of the Indies would build on.
• It opened the door to royal investigation of conquistador conduct — the same kind of intervention that would later see Cortes lose New Spain’s governorship and the New Laws of 1542 sent to Peru.
• It signalled to Indigenous communities, briefly, that the Crown might restrain colonist abuses — though in practice the gold-tribute system continued.
• It created the political template for Spanish imperial government: a powerful local commander watched and removable by a more powerful royal commissioner.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the 1500 arrest, the audiencia, the link forward to the Casa de Contratacion).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Bobadilla’s mission without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of disease in the Spanish settlement of the Caribbean.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of disease, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• European diseases — smallpox in 1518, but also measles and influenza — killed Indigenous peoples in numbers that no Spanish weapon could match, with mortality of 50–90% in some districts.
• Disease completed a demographic collapse already underway because of forced labour, sexual violence and dispossession — meaning students should treat it as part of conquest, not as a separate natural disaster.
• The shrinking Indigenous workforce on Hispaniola directly drove the Crown’s decision to license the first shipments of enslaved Africans in 1518 — beginning the transatlantic slave trade.
• Smallpox spread ahead of Spanish expeditions to the mainland, weakening Aztec leadership in Tenochtitlan in 1520 and Inca leadership in Peru before 1532 — helping make the great mainland conquests possible.
• Disease shaped Spanish ideology: it allowed conquistadors to claim that God favoured them, while the actual mechanism of victory was a virus they did not know they were carrying.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail; clear analytical move that disease is part of conquest, not separate.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of disease without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. A leaflet briefing volunteers for the CORE Freedom Rides, spring 1961.

‘The buses leave Washington on 4 May. We will travel through Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi and into New Orleans. Black riders will use white waiting rooms; white riders will use Black ones. The Supreme Court has ruled this is our right. The state authorities will not protect us. Riders should expect arrest, beating and possibly worse. Anyone unwilling to remain nonviolent under any provocation should not come.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Freedom Riders.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘The Freedom Riders deliberately exposed themselves to violence to test the law’ supported by ‘Riders should expect arrest, beating and possibly worse’ AND ‘The riders relied on a Supreme Court ruling rather than state co-operation’ supported by ‘The Supreme Court has ruled this is our right. The state authorities will not protect us’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the civil rights movement adopted new methods of protest between 1960 and 1962.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Greensboro sit-ins
• the Freedom Riders

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the example of the Montgomery Bus Boycott; Ella Baker’s argument for student-led organising and the founding of SNCC; the failure of Southern states to enforce Brown and Boynton; the strategic use of television coverage of white violence; the reluctance of the Kennedy administration to act without provocation), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (sit-in, SNCC, Freedom Riders, Anniston, Boynton v. Virginia). Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated. Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit. Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 2005 textbook on the civil rights movement):
‘The Freedom Rides of 1961 succeeded because the activists won the moral argument. Photographs of the Anniston firebombing turned American and world opinion against segregation, shamed the Kennedy administration, and made federal enforcement of interstate desegregation politically unavoidable.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2018 study of the Kennedy administration and civil rights):
‘The Freedom Rides forced federal action only because the violence in Alabama threatened to wreck John Kennedy’s foreign policy. Robert Kennedy wanted the rides cancelled; he sent marshals only when the embarrassment of the Anniston and Birmingham attacks risked overshadowing the president’s Vienna summit with Khrushchev.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the Freedom Rides? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 credits the moral force of the activists’ campaign and public opinion; Interpretation 2 credits Cold War foreign-policy embarrassment as the trigger for federal action) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the activists won the moral argument’ vs ‘the violence in Alabama threatened to wreck John Kennedy’s foreign policy’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the Freedom Rides.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is taken from a 2005 movement-focused textbook that uses activist memoirs and press coverage as its main evidence base, whereas Interpretation 2 is taken from a 2018 study of the Kennedy administration that draws on State Department records, White House memoranda and Robert Kennedy’s files. The two have different focuses and use different bodies of evidence.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the Freedom Rides?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge (the planning of the rides by CORE; the Boynton v. Virginia ruling; the Anniston firebombing and Birmingham beatings; Bull Connor’s collusion with the Klan; the second wave of SNCC riders from Nashville; Robert Kennedy’s reluctance and the Vienna summit; the deployment of 600 federal marshals; the November 1961 ICC desegregation order), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. James Meredith appealing for federal help during his attempt to enrol at the University of Mississippi in 1962.

‘I have applied to the university three times. Each time the registrar has invented a new technical reason why I cannot register. The Governor of Mississippi has personally blocked the door on my last attempt. I am asking the federal government to enforce the order of the federal court. Without that enforcement no Black citizen of this state will ever attend this university, regardless of how many rulings the courts hand down.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the integration of the University of Mississippi.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘The university actively obstructed Meredith despite a federal court order’ supported by ‘Each time the registrar has invented a new technical reason why I cannot register’ AND ‘Federal court rulings alone were not enough to integrate Mississippi institutions’ supported by ‘Without that enforcement no Black citizen of this state will ever attend this university’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about how landlords were treated during the 1950–52 land reform in China. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. crowd denunciations, public trials, beatings, executions, confiscation of property). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that the violence was organised by CCP cadres rather than spontaneous, or that the goal was to bind peasants to the party through shared guilt as well as shared gain. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the CCP moved from voluntary cooperation to enforced collectivisation between 1952 and 1956.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the demands of the First Five-Year Plan
• Mao’s ‘Socialist High Tide’ speech of July 1955
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. Mao’s belief that cooperatives would deliver more grain to feed the First Five-Year Plan, his fear of a revival of rich-peasant power, the political defeat of cautious figures (Liu Shaoqi, Deng Zihui) at and after the July 1955 speech, the example of Soviet collectivisation, and cadre quotas pushing the timetable on the ground. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the campaigns without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the impact of the 1950 Agrarian Reform Law on the Chinese countryside.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation reads the 1950 law as a genuine liberation that gave peasants land and dignity; the other reads it as a violent class war that delivered only a brief, illusory ownership before the cooperatives took the land back). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the 1950 Agrarian Reform Law.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP orthodox vs revisionist Western such as Dikötter or Spence; or sympathetic such as Mobo Gao), used different evidence (CCP-published material vs post-archival research and survivor testimony), or had different purposes (defending the early Mao era vs critical re-examination). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Mao’s personal leadership in accelerating collectivisation between 1955 and 1956?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the July 1955 ‘Socialist High Tide’ speech, Mao’s defeat of cautious figures (Deng Zihui, Liu Shaoqi), the rewriting of the central plan to make higher-stage cooperatives universal by 1957, the role of cadre quotas at village level, and the contribution of broader factors such as the demands of the First Five-Year Plan and the Soviet model. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the move to higher-stage cooperatives by 1956 was driven mainly by force rather than peasant enthusiasm?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the genuine popularity of Mutual Aid Teams (c.40% of households by end of 1952), the relative caution of lower-stage cooperatives, Mao’s July 1955 speech as the turning point, the political defeat of Deng Zihui, the 96% figure for higher-stage cooperatives by end of 1956, cadre quotas, and the speak-bitterness model carried over from 1950. Acknowledges the genuine historiographical disagreement (Dikötter and Spence vs Mobo Gao) and reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (mutual aid team, higher-stage cooperative, speak bitterness, Socialist High Tide). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the railroad network for the growth of the cattle industry in the years 1867–1885.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the railroad network, supported by specific period detail.

Indicative content:
• In 1867 Joseph McCoy built stockyards beside the new Kansas Pacific line at Abilene, Kansas, allowing Texas longhorns walked up the Chisholm Trail to be shipped east to Chicago slaughterhouses.
• Because rail shipping was much cheaper and faster than walking cattle to eastern markets, ranching could be run as big business rather than as a frontier sideline — producing the cattle boom of the 1870s.
• Refrigerated cars from around 1880 allowed beef rather than live cattle to be shipped, lowering the price of meat in eastern cities and expanding the market further.
• The Northern Pacific (1883) and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe opened new shipping points across the Plains, multiplying the cow towns the trade depended on.
• Together these effects made ranching profitable enough to attract eastern and European investment by the mid-1880s — the conditions for the open-range boom that ended in the ‘Big Die-Up’ of 1886–87.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the railroad to specific cattle-industry consequences, with named places (Abilene, Chicago) and dates (1867, 1880, 1883).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of railroad without explaining importance for the cattle industry.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the key events in the building and impact of the First Transcontinental Railroad in the years 1862–1869.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Pacific Railroad Act (1862)
• Promontory Point (1869)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1862, with Southern senators absent from a Congress at war, the Pacific Railroad Act chartered the Union Pacific to build west from Omaha and the Central Pacific to build east from Sacramento, backed by federal bonds of $16,000–$48,000 per mile and roughly twenty alternating sections of land per mile.
• Because the Sierra Nevada blocked the Central Pacific almost immediately, around 15,000 Chinese workers were recruited to drill, blast and tunnel through granite at lower wages and higher risk than white labourers.
• Because the Union Pacific’s route across the Plains crossed Indigenous hunting grounds, survey parties needed army escorts, and the line accelerated the destruction of the buffalo as hide hunters could now ship at industrial scale.
• Both companies competed for federal payments per mile, pushing each other to lay 1–10 miles a day — the Central Pacific laying ten miles in twelve hours in April 1869 to win a bet.
• On 10 May 1869 a ceremonial golden spike at Promontory Point, Utah, joined the two lines and the telegraph carried the word ‘done’ to the nation, cutting the New York-to-San Francisco journey from six months to about eight days.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1862, 1869, $16,000–$48,000, Chinese labour), specialist vocabulary (Promontory Point, land-grant railroad).
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Chronological coverage but linkage is weak.
Emerging: Thin description of one or two events with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Pacific Railroad Act (1862) for the development of settlement in the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Act chartered two private companies (Union Pacific and Central Pacific) to build a continental line and gave them federal bonds plus land grants — making private capital in the West financially possible.
• The land grants made the railroads the largest private landlords in the West: by selling 160-acre and 320-acre plots advertised across Europe, they shaped who settled where for the next three decades.
• Once completed in 1869, the line allowed settlers, supplies and machinery to reach the Plains in days rather than months, accelerating homesteader migration after the 1862 Homestead Act.
• The Act’s subsidy structure was repeated for the Northern Pacific, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe, and other lines, producing a 93,000-mile network by 1880 that turned the Plains into a national agricultural region.
• Because the railroads chose where towns rose and fell, frontier settlement followed the rails — Abilene, Dodge City, Cheyenne and dozens of others were railroad creations.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1862, 1880, 93,000 miles).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how the spread of the railroad network changed the West in the years 1869–1885.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Abilene and the cattle industry
• the destruction of the buffalo

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• From 1867 the new Kansas Pacific line reached Abilene, where Joseph McCoy had built stockyards; Texas longhorns walked the Chisholm Trail north and were shipped east to Chicago slaughterhouses, turning ranching into big business through the 1870s.
• Because the railroads needed paying customers, hide hunters such as William ‘Buffalo Bill’ Cody were contracted to feed crews and to ship hides east in bulk; General Philip Sheridan endorsed buffalo extermination as a deliberate strategy against Plains nations because it destroyed their food source.
• Because federal troops could now be moved to flashpoints by rail in hours, the army responded faster to Plains conflicts — reshaping the balance of force after the Sand Creek and Little Bighorn period.
• The network kept spreading: the Northern Pacific opened its Minnesota-to-Pacific line in 1883 and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe pushed across the Southwest the same year, multiplying cow towns and shipping points.
• Refrigerated cars from around 1880 allowed beef rather than live cattle to be shipped east, expanding the eastern market and producing the over-stocked open ranges that would collapse in the ‘Big Die-Up’ of 1886–87.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail, specialist vocabulary, both contexts (cattle and buffalo) covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one context, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of land-grant railroads for the pattern of settlement on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Federal land grants made the railroads the largest private landlords in the West, with roughly twenty alternating sections of land per mile of track (later forty).
• Because the railroads sold this land in 160-acre and 320-acre plots advertised across Europe, they shaped who settled where for three decades after 1862.
• Towns rose where the rails decided to stop — Abilene, Cheyenne, Dodge City and many others were railroad creations.
• Land-grant pricing affected the success of homesteaders, since cheap rail land directly competed with the supposedly free 160 acres of the Homestead Act.
• The pattern shaped the demographic make-up of the Plains, with concentrated communities of German, Scandinavian and Russian Mennonite settlers arriving via railroad agents in Europe.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (twenty/forty sections per mile, 160/320 acres, named towns).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how the railroad changed the relationship between the federal government and the West in the years 1862–1880.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1862 Pacific Railroad Act
• the spread of the network

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1862, in the middle of the Civil War, a Republican Congress without Southern senators passed the Pacific Railroad Act, chartering two private companies and backing them with federal bonds and land grants — an unprecedented intervention in Western development.
• Because the federal government paid per mile of track and granted alternating sections of public land, the railroads became the largest private landlords in the West, deciding where towns rose and which migrants reached the Plains.
• Because the lines crossed Indigenous territories, federal troops were committed to escorting survey parties; once track was laid, troops could be redeployed within hours rather than weeks, hardening federal authority on the Plains.
• The 1869 completion at Promontory Point joined the coasts and accelerated the federal land-policy programme: the Homestead Act, the Timber Culture Act and later the Dawes Act all worked in the railroad-shaped landscape.
• By 1880 the 93,000-mile network had embedded the federal government, the railroads and the army in a single web of authority across the West — a far thicker layer than the thin marshal-and-sheriff system of the 1850s.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail, specialist vocabulary, both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Great Awakening for colonial society in the 1730s and 1740s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: the Awakening mattered because Whitefield’s tours bound the thirteen colonies into a single religious public for the first time; it also mattered because the Old Lights/New Lights split taught believers to choose between rival clergy, undermining deference to inherited authority. Specific anchors (Whitefield, Edwards, Princeton 1746) developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus; limited use of specific developments.
Emerging: Describes the Awakening without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of George Whitefield’s preaching tours of the colonies after 1739.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: Whitefield’s open-air sermons drew crowds of up to 30,000 and exposed colonists to a shared revivalist message that crossed colonial borders; his style helped split established Protestant churches into Old Lights and New Lights, fracturing local religious authority. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to Whitefield’s tours.
Emerging: Restates that Whitefield preached without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Benjamin Franklin for the development of the colonial Enlightenment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: Franklin mattered because his Pennsylvania Gazette and ‘Poor Richard’s Almanack’ carried Enlightenment ideas to readers far beyond the gentry; he also mattered because his Library Company of Philadelphia (1731) and American Philosophical Society (1743) created lasting institutions for shared learning. Specific examples developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Names Franklin and gives general consequences without sustained focus on importance.
Emerging: Mentions Franklin without explaining his significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the spread of newspapers and public libraries in the colonies before 1760.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the growth from one weekly in 1704 to about two dozen newspapers by the mid-1760s meant political and religious argument could travel quickly between colonies; the founding of subscription libraries gave artisans and shopkeepers access to books once limited to the gentry, broadening political literacy. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to newspapers or libraries.
Emerging: Mentions the existence of these without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how cultural change shaped colonial society in the years 1730–55. You may use the following information in your answer:
• The preaching of George Whitefield
• The work of Benjamin Franklin
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why colonial society changed rather than narrating in sequence. Links Whitefield’s tours to a colonies-wide religious public and to fractures in established churches; links Franklin’s newspapers and library to a wider, more confident reading public; brings in own knowledge such as Edwards’s sermon, the founding of Princeton (1746) or new colleges. Reaches an analytical judgement about how revival and reason combined.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists figures or events without explaining how they reshaped colonial society.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of religious revivalism for relations between colonists and traditional clergy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: revivalism mattered because the Old Lights/New Lights split forced congregations to choose between rival ministers, undermining the assumption that the parish-appointed clergyman should be obeyed; it also mattered because new colleges like Princeton (1746) trained an alternative supply of New Light ministers, embedding the split institutionally. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Notes that revivalism caused tension without showing why it mattered.
Emerging: Describes revivalist preaching without explaining significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the part played by individuals in law enforcement in the seventeenth century was different from the part they played in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Matthew Hopkins acted as a private contractor with no appointment from king or Parliament, hired and paid by individual towns, sometimes more than £20 a visit.
• Robert Peel acted as a minister of the Crown: as Home Secretary he carried the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act, creating a salaried public force answerable to commissioners and to Parliament.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the witch-hunts of 1645–47 happened in East Anglia.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Civil War
• Puritan belief.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Civil War (1642–46) had disrupted local government in East Anglia; some Justices of the Peace had been removed and central oversight of trials had weakened, allowing Hopkins to operate.
• East Anglia was a Puritan stronghold; the strict Protestant focus on personal sin and the active power of the Devil made witchcraft accusations more credible to local communities.
• Matthew Hopkins, a Suffolk minister’s son, took advantage of these conditions and offered his services as a paid private witch-finder, with John Stearne, from spring 1645.
• Cheap printed pamphlets spread sensational stories of witches; villagers had a ready-made template for accusations.
• Economic stress and bad harvests in the 1640s heightened resentment of poor neighbours and made scapegoats — especially older, poorer women — easier to find.

Mastering: At least two reasons sustained with specific detail (Civil War, Puritan belief, Hopkins as private contractor, printing press) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the witch-hunts without explaining why they happened in this region.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the East Anglian witch-hunts collapsed within three years of starting.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Matthew Hopkins
• the cost of the trials.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own, and reasons must be linked to each other rather than listed.

Indicative content:
• 1645: Hopkins and Stearne, taking advantage of Civil War disruption and East Anglia’s Puritan culture, begin offering paid witch-finding services to towns and Justices of the Peace.
• Their methods (watching, pricking, the swimming test) extract confessions; sensational pamphlets spread reports across the region; magistrates accept their evidence.
• 1646: minister John Gaule of Great Staughton begins preaching publicly against Hopkins’s methods, denouncing them as unreliable and printing his sermons.
• Towns begin questioning the costs Hopkins runs up; central legal authority strengthens as the war ends.
• 1647: Hopkins falls ill and dies, probably of tuberculosis, soon after publishing The Discovery of Witches; the hunts collapse.
• After 1647: prosecutions decline sharply; judges refuse to convict on Hopkins-style evidence; the law is finally repealed in 1736.

Mastering: At least two reasons sustained with specific detail (Gaule's sermons, costs, Hopkins's death, the return of normal judicial oversight) and explicit links between them.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the end of the hunts without explaining causes.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the methods used to prove guilt in the 1640s were similar to the methods used in the Middle Ages.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Hopkins's swimming test read a physical result as proof: a floating suspect was guilty because the water had rejected her.
• The medieval ordeal of cold water worked the same way, with a priest blessing the pool and sinking taken as innocence; both treated a bodily sign, not evidence, as the verdict.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Civil War was the most important reason why the witch-hunts of 1645–47 took place.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• weakened local government during the Civil War
• the role of Matthew Hopkins.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting the Civil War as the main reason:
• The war (1642–46) disrupted local government in the eastern counties; Justices of the Peace had been removed and judicial oversight was at a low point precisely when Hopkins began operating.
• Armies marching, requisitioning food and pressing men into service produced economic stress and broken communities — the conditions in which scapegoats are most easily found.
• Hopkins’s ability to claim large fees from each town reflects the weakness of central oversight, which would normally have questioned such expenses.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors):
• East Anglia’s Puritan culture predated the war and provided the religious framework that made witchcraft credible — especially James I’s Demonologie (1597).
• Matthew Hopkins as a determined private witch-finder was the proximate cause; without his energy and willingness to travel, the legal framework would have lain unused.
• The printing press distributed pamphlets that gave villagers a ready-made template for accusations — a long-running cause, not a wartime one.
• Economic stress and bad harvests in the 1640s produced resentment of poor neighbours and made older, poorer women particularly vulnerable to accusation.
• The end of the hunts in 1647 followed the death of Hopkins, the spread of legal scepticism (Gaule’s sermons) and rising costs — not the end of the war alone — suggesting Hopkins himself mattered as much as the war.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs the Civil War against at least one other factor, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (witchfinder, Puritan, pamphlet, swimming test, pricking, watching, Demonologie).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the witch-hunts of 1645–47 came to an end.

You may use the following in your answer:
• John Gaule
• the death of Matthew Hopkins.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Cost — towns started to balk at the fees Hopkins charged for trials, food and lodging.
• Growing scepticism: the minister John Gaule of Great Staughton publicly denounced Hopkins’s methods in 1646, arguing in print that watching, pricking and swimming proved nothing.
• The personal collapse of Matthew Hopkins, who was ill and died in 1647 (probably of tuberculosis); without his energy, the hunts had no driving organiser.
• The end of the Civil War restored normal judicial oversight; central courts began to reject the kind of evidence Hopkins had produced.
• Trial outcomes themselves were beginning to embarrass magistrates as some accusations were exposed as false.

Mastering: At least two reasons sustained with specific detail (Gaule’s sermons, Hopkins’s death, costs) and explicit links to why the hunts ended.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the end of the hunts without explaining causes.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on the Bolshevik leadership in 1918. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, Trotsky’s ‘no war, no peace’ strategy, the German advance in February 1918, the Left Communists’ protest, the Left SR walk-out from Sovnarkom, Lenin overruling Bukharin in the Central Committee). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the treaty exposed serious divisions inside Bolshevism over the meaning of revolution. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Reds won the Civil War of 1918–21.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the role of Trotsky
• foreign intervention
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. interior lines and the central railway hub, the unified Bolshevik political leadership of Sovnarkom, Trotsky’s 5-million-strong Red Army with ex-Tsarist officers and political commissars, Bolshevik propaganda, the failure of foreign intervention to commit serious force, and the structural weaknesses of the Whites — geographically scattered fronts, monarchist symbols and the return of land to gentry). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Brest-Litovsk, Czech Legion, Komuch, Volunteer Army, political commissar. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the war without explaining why the Reds won. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the importance of foreign intervention in the Russian Civil War.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues foreign intervention was a serious attempt to overthrow Bolshevism that prolonged the war and forced the Reds onto the defensive; the other argues that intervention was small, half-hearted and politically helped the Reds by allowing them to claim the patriotic mantle as defenders of Russia against foreign invaders). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about why the Reds won the Civil War.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (Soviet-era textbooks crediting Lenin’s leadership and Trotsky’s Red Army versus post-1991 archival biographies that stress White structural weaknesses and geography); they wrote at different times (Cold War narratives that emphasised Bolshevik ruthlessness versus revisionist Western scholarship); or they had different purposes (defending Communist legitimacy versus reconstructing the operational record). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Trotsky in the Red victory in the Civil War?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the Civil War — Trotsky’s armoured train, the conscription of 50,000 ex-Tsarist officers under political commissars, the death penalty for desertion, the 5-million-strong force by 1920 — but also Lenin’s political grip, the Cheka’s rear-area terror, the central railway hub, and the Whites’ structural weaknesses. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Whites lost the Civil War mainly because of their own divisions and weaknesses, rather than because of Red strengths?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — Denikin in the south, Kolchak in Siberia, Yudenich in the Baltic, Wrangel’s November 1920 evacuation of Crimea, the Whites’ reliance on monarchist symbols and their return of land to the gentry, the fragmented fronts — weighed against Red strengths in interior lines, unified Sovnarkom leadership, Trotsky’s Red Army and Bolshevik propaganda. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Sovnarkom, Brest-Litovsk, Volunteer Army, political commissar, Czech Legion). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Château Gaillard.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features are required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Three concentric wards — an outer, middle and inner enclosure, each commanding the next, designed so attackers had to fight their way through three sieges.
• A great cylindrical keep with sloping walls — designed so that medieval miners could not easily undermine it and stones dropped from the battlements would skid down the slope at attackers.
• A deep dry moat cut from the rock — protecting the inner ward and making approach difficult.
• A position on a chalk bluff above the Seine at Les Andelys — controlling the river approach to Rouen.
• Cost — around £11,500, more than every other English royal castle of Richard’s reign combined.
• Speed of construction — completed in barely two years, 1196–98.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Philip II’s siege of Château Gaillard.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Stockade across the Seine — Philip cut the river with a chain of boats so that supplies could not reach the castle from downstream.
• Methodical reduction over winter 1203–04 — the French worked through each ward in turn rather than risking a costly assault.
• Expulsion of civilians — refugees from Les Andelys were forced out into no-man’s-land between the lines and many died of cold and starvation.
• Sapping of the outer ward — French miners fired the outer tower on 22 February 1204, collapsing it.
• Entry through the latrine chute — an enterprising soldier crawled in through a chute on the middle ward, opening it from inside.
• Length — from September 1203 to March 1204, around six months.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Château Gaillard fell to Philip II in 1204.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the length of the siege
• lack of relief from John
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Length of the siege — from September 1203 to March 1204 the garrison ran short of food, fuel and replacement weapons; even the strongest castle eventually starves.
• Lack of relief from John — the king refused to commit personally to lifting the siege and crossed back to England in December 1203, leaving the garrison isolated.
• River blockade — Philip II’s stockade of boats across the Seine cut off resupply by water.
• Methodical French sapping — the outer ward fell to fire on 22 February 1204; the middle ward fell when soldiers entered through a latrine chute.
• Numerical superiority — Philip kept a large force in the field while John could not concentrate enough men to challenge it.
• Garrison exhaustion — Roger de Lacy’s 200 men had no rotation or reinforcement during a six-month siege.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John lost Normandy in 1204.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Arthur of Brittany
• the fall of Château Gaillard
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• The murder of Arthur of Brittany in 1203 turned Brittany and Poitou into open enemies and shattered baronial trust in Normandy.
• The Lusignan affair gave Philip II a legal pretext to declare John’s French fiefs forfeit in 1202.
• Strategic indecision — John failed to bring Philip to battle in 1203 and abandoned Normandy in December.
• The fall of Château Gaillard on 6 March 1204 opened Rouen to French capture in June.
• Angevin financial exhaustion after Richard’s crusade and ransom; John could not outspend Philip in the field.
• Defection of Norman barons whose lands lay close to the French frontier and who could not see John as a likely winner.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Richard I built Château Gaillard.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the river Seine
• defence of Rouen
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Defence of Rouen — the castle stood twenty-five miles upstream of the Norman capital and was meant to block any French force advancing along the Seine.
• Control of the Seine — the river was the main route for both armies and supplies in upper Normandy; whoever held the bluff at Les Andelys controlled access to Rouen.
• Loss of the Vexin — in Richard’s absence Philip had taken much of the Norman Vexin; Château Gaillard was meant to make any further French gain impossible.
• Statement of military prestige — Richard reportedly said he could hold it ‘were its walls of butter’; the castle was a deliberate symbol of Angevin recovery.
• Cutting-edge engineering — the design (concentric wards, sloping cylindrical keep) was meant to defeat the latest siege techniques and stand for generations.
• Personal motivation — Richard’s defence of his French heartlands was the central goal of his post-crusade reign.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The loss of Normandy in 1204 was the result of John’s personal failures rather than wider Angevin weaknesses.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Arthur
• Château Gaillard
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• The murder of Arthur in April 1203 broke the customs of noble captivity and dissolved baronial loyalty in Normandy, Brittany and Poitou.
• John’s strategic indecision in 1203 — refusing to bring Philip to battle and refusing to relieve Château Gaillard — was a personal failing.
• His treatment of the Lusignans (over Isabella of Angoulême) handed Philip the legal pretext for war.
• His abandonment of Normandy in December 1203 demoralised remaining loyalists.
• His character — vindictive, suspicious, untrustworthy — meant the great barons would not commit to a doubtful war.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Philip II of France had been working to break up the Angevin Empire since the 1180s and was a very capable opponent; he would have moved at any opportunity.
• Angevin finances were exhausted by Richard’s crusade taxes, the 150,000-mark ransom and the cost of Château Gaillard itself; even a popular king would have struggled to outspend Philip.
• Structural weakness — the empire stretched from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, was held together only by personal loyalty, and depended on Norman barons whose lands straddled the frontier.
• Once Château Gaillard fell on 6 March 1204 after a six-month siege, no medieval defensive system could have held Rouen long against a determined enemy.
• Even Richard, the warrior king, had been forced to spend most of his reign campaigning in France just to hold the empire together.

Overall judgement: John’s personal failings — the murder of Arthur, the strategic indecision, the alienation of the barons — were the trigger for collapse in 1203–04, but they pulled at lines that were already strained by Angevin financial exhaustion, structural overstretch and Philip II’s long campaign. A balanced judgement weighs personal failure as the proximate cause against structural weakness as the underlying condition; both were necessary for the loss.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (fief, forfeit, relief, scutage, demesne, sap).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Thomas Cromwell’s career before he entered royal service.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Born around 1485 in Putney, the son of Walter Cromwell, a Putney blacksmith and brewer of low social standing.
• Spent time on the continent as a soldier in Italy, a clerk in a Florentine bank and a cloth merchant in the Low Countries.
• Built a legal practice in London on his return, working as an attorney and adviser to merchants.
• Entered Wolsey’s service in the early 1520s and worked on dissolving smaller monasteries to fund the cardinal’s colleges at Oxford and Ipswich.
• Had no university degree and no clerical career — unusual for a Tudor minister.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Cromwell’s position by the end of 1534.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Held the office of Principal Secretary from April 1534, transforming it into the central coordinating role of government.
• Was a sworn member of the Royal Council and Master of the King’s Jewels.
• Had drafted the major statutes of the break with Rome, including the Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) and the Act of Supremacy (1534).
• Worked closely with Archbishop Cranmer on the annulment and the early Reformation.
• Would shortly be appointed Vicegerent in Spirituals (1535), giving him authority over every bishop in England.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate names or detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell survived Wolsey’s fall in 1529.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Reformation Parliament
• loyalty to Wolsey
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained, supported reasons. Indicative content: • Public loyalty to Wolsey — Cromwell stayed at his master’s side and organised the legal defence; Henry took this as evidence of future loyalty rather than treason. • Election to the Reformation Parliament — secured a seat at Taunton in November 1529, giving him a public platform during the political crisis. • Legal expertise — he had drafted bills, valued church property and managed commissioners for Wolsey; these skills were now in short supply. • No clerical status — unlike Wolsey, More or the bishops, he was not exposed to praemunire or church-faction politics. • Personal connections — he had built a network of London lawyers, merchants and gentry that survived Wolsey’s disgrace. • The king’s need — Henry needed someone who could think his way out of the annulment crisis; Cromwell offered a route the bishops would not. Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed. Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation. Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin. Emerging: Description of events without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Cromwell’s mastery of parliamentary statute was the main reason he became Henry VIII’s chief minister by 1534.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Reformation Parliament
• the king’s annulment
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs Cromwell’s use of statute against other reasons for his rise and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• He built his reputation in the Reformation Parliament from November 1529, drafting bills and marshalling votes as no other royal servant could.
• The parliamentary route to the annulment was the one solution the bishops and the lawyers had not offered.
• He drafted the Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533, which declared England an empire and closed the appeal to Rome.
• Statute gave the break with Rome permanence, which made him indispensable rather than merely useful.

Arguments for other reasons:
• Staying loyal to Wolsey in 1529 won Henry’s respect before Cromwell had drafted anything for the king.
• Service to Wolsey had taught him how to value church property and manage commissioners, experience no other layman held.
• Membership of the Royal Council by late 1530 gave him the personal access on which everything else depended.
• The Boleyn faction backed him because he could deliver the marriage they wanted.
• Henry’s desperation after Blackfriars made him willing to try a solution he would have rejected in 1527.

Overall judgement: statute was the tool, but loyalty, access and the king’s desperation put the tool in his hands. Top-band answers weigh these factors and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell rose to such a powerful position between 1529 and 1534.
You may use the following in your answer:
• service to Wolsey
• the Royal Council
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Service to Wolsey — gave Cromwell experience of monastic dissolution, parliamentary drafting and administering commissioners that no other layman possessed.
• Loyalty in 1529 — staying with Wolsey through the disgrace was a calculated gamble that earned Henry’s respect.
• The Reformation Parliament — election as MP for Taunton in November 1529 gave him the platform to demonstrate parliamentary skill.
• Membership of the Royal Council — sworn in by late 1530, attending royal business and earning Henry’s confidence in person.
• The annulment crisis — offered Henry a parliamentary route to break with Rome, succeeding where Wolsey, More and the bishops had failed.
• Statutory genius — turned Parliament into the engine of state; the Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) and Act of Supremacy (1534) were his drafts.
• Office accumulation — Master of the Jewels (1532), Chancellor of the Exchequer (1533), Principal Secretary (1534), then Vicegerent in Spirituals (1535) coordinated finance, government and church reform from one desk.
• Boleyn alliance — Anne and her family backed him because he delivered the marriage; the alliance gave him cover at court.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important reason for Cromwell’s rise to power between 1529 and 1534 was his ability to deliver the King’s annulment.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Thomas Cranmer
• the Reformation Parliament
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the annulment against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The annulment was Henry’s overriding goal in 1532–33; Cromwell’s parliamentary route succeeded where Wolsey’s legatine route had failed.
• Cranmer’s elevation to Canterbury in 1533, secured on Cromwell’s advice, delivered the annulment in May 1533.
• The Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) was drafted by Cromwell specifically to make the annulment legally binding without papal consent.
• Henry’s gratitude rewarded Cromwell with rapid promotions: Master of the Jewels, Chancellor of the Exchequer, Principal Secretary.
• Without the annulment, Cromwell would never have moved beyond mid-rank office.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Mastery of parliamentary statute — Cromwell’s rise depended on technical skill no rival possessed; this was structural, not occasional.
• Loyalty to Wolsey in 1529 — the gamble that won Henry’s confidence preceded any service on the annulment.
• Membership of the Royal Council from 1530 — gave him the access required to do anything else.
• Boleyn alliance — Anne and Thomas Boleyn championed him; without the faction, the annulment alone would not have secured his promotion.
• Religious conviction — MacCulloch argues Cromwell’s evangelicalism gave him an independent agenda that fitted Henry’s emerging religious policy.
• Office innovation — the Vicegerent in Spirituals (1535) reflected a structural reorganisation, not just a reward for the annulment.

Overall judgement: the annulment was the decisive opportunity, but Cromwell’s rise rested on a unique combination of legal skill, political loyalty and faction alliance that turned that opportunity into permanent office. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Babington Plot, 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It involved a plan to assassinate Elizabeth — Anthony Babington, a wealthy young Catholic gentleman, wrote to Mary in July 1586 setting out plans to kill the Queen and welcome a Spanish-backed invasion.
• It was uncovered through intercepted ciphered letters — Walsingham’s chief cryptanalyst Thomas Phelippes deciphered the correspondence and added a forged postscript asking Babington to name his fellow plotters.
• It directly implicated Mary, Queen of Scots — her reply on 17 July 1586 explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination, providing the written evidence used to convict her.
• It led to mass executions — Babington and six co-conspirators were hanged, drawn and quartered in September 1586; Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Walsingham’s spy network was effective at catching Catholic plotters.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Walsingham’s agents
• the breaking of ciphers
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Scale and reach — around 50 agents in England and Europe, partly funded by Walsingham himself, allowed continuous surveillance of suspected Catholics, foreign embassies and ports of entry.
