• Cipher-breaking — Thomas Phelippes could decipher almost any contemporary code; intercepted letters were copied and resealed so plotters never knew they had been read.
• Use of stings and false channels — the Chartley beer-barrel route was a controlled channel that let Mary believe her letters were secret while every word was being read by the Privy Council.
• Authority and tools — the Privy Council could authorise torture of suspects (e.g. Throckmorton) and Walsingham had direct access to Elizabeth and Cecil, so intelligence translated quickly into arrests.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots was executed in 1587.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Babington Plot
• the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• Babington Plot (stimulus) — Mary’s letter of 17 July 1586 explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination; Walsingham and Phelippes had ensured the correspondence was preserved as written evidence.
• 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (stimulus) — passed after Throckmorton, this law allowed anyone in whose name a plot was made to be tried and executed; it gave the Privy Council a legal route to Mary they had previously lacked.
• Pressure from the Privy Council (own knowledge) — William Cecil (Burghley), Walsingham and Parliament had pressed for Mary’s execution since 1572; once Babington gave them proof, they pushed Elizabeth to act.
• Foreign threat from Spain (own knowledge) — Philip II was already preparing the Armada; killing Mary removed the legitimate Catholic alternative monarch he could install if his invasion succeeded.
• Pattern of plots since 1571 — Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington showed Mary would remain a magnet for conspiracies as long as she lived; only her death would end the cycle.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason Mary, Queen of Scots was executed in 1587 was the strength of evidence from the Babington Plot.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Walsingham’s spy network
• Spanish invasion plans
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Babington evidence as main reason):
• Mary’s 17 July 1586 letter explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination — this was direct written treason in her own hand, which Ridolfi and Throckmorton had never produced.
• Without that proof, Elizabeth would have lacked political cover to execute an anointed queen and royal cousin; previous plots had not led to her death.
• The trial at Fotheringhay in October 1586 used the letter as the central piece of evidence under the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Walsingham’s spy network (stimulus) — the evidence only existed because Walsingham deliberately ran the Chartley sting and Phelippes deciphered the letters; without the network there would be no Babington case to use.
• Spanish invasion plans (stimulus) — by 1586 Philip II was actively preparing the Armada; killing Mary now removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative ruler before any invasion landed, making her execution a strategic decision as much as a legal one.
• Privy Council pressure (own knowledge) — Cecil and Walsingham had pushed for Mary’s execution since 1572; the Babington letter unlocked years of pent-up political demand, not just the 1586 case.
• 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (own knowledge) — without that legal framework, the Babington evidence alone would not have made trial of an anointed queen possible.

Justified judgement: The Babington evidence was the immediate trigger, but it only existed because of Walsingham’s sting; only a legal route because of the 1585 Act; and only acted on because of Privy Council pressure and the Spanish threat. A strong response weighs the trigger against these enabling factors and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Walsingham’s methods for catching Catholic plotters.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Use of cipher-breaking — Thomas Phelippes deciphered intercepted letters and even forged postscripts (e.g. asking Babington to name his fellow plotters).
• Network of agents at home and abroad — around 50 spies in England and Europe tracked Catholic priests, courier routes, and foreign embassies including the Spanish ambassador.
• Stings and controlled channels — at Chartley Hall in 1585 Walsingham let Mary believe her letters were being smuggled in beer barrels while every letter was being read.
• Authorised interrogation — suspects such as Francis Throckmorton were arrested and tortured under Privy Council authority until they confessed.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Catholic plots of 1571–87 led to harsher treatment of English Catholics.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1570 papal bull
• the Throckmorton Plot
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Each plot produced new legislation — the 1571 Treasons Act (after Ridolfi) made denying Elizabeth’s right to rule treason; the 1581 Act increased recusancy fines to £20 a month; the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (after Throckmorton) targeted plotters and their patrons.
• Catholicism became politically associated with foreign invasion — Ridolfi was Spanish-backed, Throckmorton French- and Spanish-backed, Babington again Spanish-backed; the Privy Council framed every English Catholic as a potential fifth column.
• Priests became automatic suspects — the 1585 Act made it treason for a Catholic priest trained abroad to enter England; Walsingham’s network tracked them from arrival.
• The papal bull of 1570 (Regnans in Excelsis) had told Catholics they owed Elizabeth no allegiance, so plots seemed to confirm Catholicism itself was a security threat.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. Advice to President Kennedy on the political effect of the Birmingham campaign, May 1963.

‘The photographs from Birmingham yesterday have changed the public mood overnight. Calls and telegrams to the White House are running ten to one in favour of federal action. Republican congressmen who voted against earlier civil rights measures are now telling reporters that something must be done. The Department of Justice estimates that without a public message from the President within the week, the situation in the South will deteriorate further. The political costs of action are now lower than the political costs of inaction.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the impact of the Birmingham campaign.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘Television and press images of Birmingham shifted Northern white public opinion sharply’ supported by ‘The photographs from Birmingham yesterday have changed the public mood overnight’ AND ‘Birmingham forced even Republican opponents of earlier civil rights measures to support action’ supported by ‘Republican congressmen who voted against earlier civil rights measures are now telling reporters that something must be done’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was passed.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Birmingham campaign
• the March on Washington

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. Lyndon Johnson’s legislative skill in breaking the Senate filibuster; the moral leverage of Kennedy’s assassination; the role of A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin in building the march’s coalition; television coverage of fire hoses and police dogs; the role of the Letter from Birmingham Jail), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (Children’s Crusade, Letter from Birmingham Jail, March on Washington, filibuster).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1995 biography of Lyndon Johnson):
‘The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was Lyndon Johnson’s achievement. Twenty years in the Senate had taught him every lever in the building. He used Kennedy’s assassination, the longest filibuster in Senate history, and pressure on Republican leader Everett Dirksen to pass a bill that no other president of the era could have moved.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 movement-focused history of civil rights):
‘The 1964 Act was forced on Washington by the movement. Without the Children’s Crusade in Birmingham, the photographs of fire hoses and dogs, and the 250,000 marchers in Washington, no president would have proposed federal civil rights legislation. Johnson signed a bill the streets had written.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the Civil Rights Act of 1964? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 credits Johnson’s legislative skill and Senate experience; Interpretation 2 credits the movement’s direct-action campaigns and the pressure of public opinion) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was Lyndon Johnson’s achievement’ vs ‘Johnson signed a bill the streets had written’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is taken from a 1995 biography of Lyndon Johnson and uses White House recordings, congressional voting records and Johnson’s own papers as evidence, whereas Interpretation 2 is taken from a 2010 movement-focused history that draws on activist memoirs, SNCC and SCLC records and oral histories. The two have different focuses and different bodies of evidence.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the Civil Rights Act of 1964?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge (the Birmingham campaign and Bull Connor’s fire hoses; the Children’s Crusade; the Letter from Birmingham Jail; Kennedy’s 11 June 1963 television address; the March on Washington and the ‘I Have a Dream’ speech; A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin; Kennedy’s assassination; Johnson’s pressure on Senator Dirksen and the 60-day filibuster; the murders of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 2. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. A civil rights organisation’s statement of 22 June 1964, the day after three Freedom Summer volunteers were reported missing in Mississippi.

‘James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner are missing in Neshoba County, Mississippi. The Mississippi authorities will not search for them. We have called the FBI in Washington and we have called the White House. The country’s attention is on these three because two of them are white. Last week the body of a Black Mississippian, beaten and dumped in a river, was reported on a single inside page of the Jackson newspaper. Tomorrow, when the search begins, the country will see what has been happening to Black Mississippians for a hundred years.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about Freedom Summer.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Freedom Summer’s organisers expected to need federal protection because Mississippi authorities would not act’ supported by ‘The Mississippi authorities will not search for them’ AND ‘The choice of white volunteers was strategic because violence against Black activists alone had been ignored’ supported by ‘The country’s attention is on these three because two of them are white’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the tactics of English or British infantry were different at the Battle of Agincourt (1415) and the Battle of Waterloo (1815).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: At Agincourt the infantry stood still and shot (1). Archers behind sharpened stakes, with dismounted men-at-arms between them, killed the French before contact (1). At Waterloo the infantry formed squares and fired volleys (1). Wellington kept his men behind the crest of the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge, then formed four-deep squares with bayonets outwards to stop repeated French cavalry charges (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the role of cavalry in battle changed in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of Waterloo (1815)
• the Battle of Balaclava (1854).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• In 1815 cavalry could still decide a battle, but even then disciplined squares at Waterloo held them off with bayonets and volleys.
• Rifling and the Minié ball let infantry hit horses and riders at around 600 yards, so a charge had to cross a long killing zone.
• Massed artillery could sweep the open ground a charge needs; at Balaclava in 1854 the Light Brigade rode more than a mile with guns on three sides.
• Command failures were punished far more heavily than before: Raglan's vague order and Nolan's gesture cost roughly 40 per cent of the brigade in about twenty minutes.
• Newspaper reporting made those losses a public scandal, which changed what commanders were willing to risk.
• By the Boer War cavalry had become mounted infantry, riding to the fight and dismounting to shoot.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why public attitudes in Britain towards the army changed in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• newspaper reporting
• photography.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• The electric telegraph carried William Howard Russell's reports from the Crimea to The Times within days, so readers followed a war while it was still being fought.
• Russell exposed cholera, missing boots and supply failure, and described the Light Brigade charge as a blunder; the army could no longer control its own story.
• Roger Fenton's government-sponsored photographs of 1855 were turned into engravings for newspapers, giving readers a picture of the campaign for the first time.
• Rising literacy and cheap mass-circulation papers (the Daily Mail from 1896) put military failure in front of millions of voters.
• Public anger produced action: Florence Nightingale's nursing mission, parliamentary debate during the war, and pressure that fed into Cardwell's reforms.
• By the Boer War the pattern was fixed, and concentration-camp policy in South Africa became a national scandal.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of the commander was similar at the Battle of Agincourt (1415) and the Battle of Waterloo (1815).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both battles the commander chose the ground and stayed with his men (1). Henry V picked a narrow, muddy funnel between two woods so the larger French army could not spread out, and fought on foot with his line (1). Wellington chose the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge, fortified Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte, and rode along the line under fire (1). In both cases the commander's presence steadied the troops and let him change the plan during the fighting (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the reporting of war was different in the seventeenth century and the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the seventeenth century war news travelled slowly and came from the army itself (1). Printed pamphlets and newsbooks carried reports written weeks later, usually by one side, so most people learned about a battle long after it ended (1). In the nineteenth century a paid correspondent reported by telegraph (1). William Howard Russell filed to The Times from the Crimea within days, and Roger Fenton's photographs were printed as engravings, so the public followed the war as it happened (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘Leadership was the most important reason for the different outcomes of Waterloo (1815) and Balaclava (1854).’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Wellington at Waterloo
• Lord Raglan at Balaclava.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for leadership as decisive:
• Wellington wrote precise orders, used reverse-slope tactics on the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge and was personally present along the line.
• Raglan’s order at Balaclava was ambiguous; from his hilltop he saw a different battlefield from his cavalry; Captain Nolan’s gesture compounded the error.
• Wellington committed reserves at the right moment (against the Imperial Guard); Raglan failed to recall the Light Brigade in time.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Position of the guns: the Light Brigade rode more than a mile down a valley with Russian batteries on three sides, which would have destroyed any cavalry unit in any period.
• Terrain: Wellington chose his ground and fortified Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte, while the Light Brigade was sent into ground the enemy had chosen.
• Allied support: the Prussians arrived at Waterloo and tipped the battle; at Balaclava no equivalent reinforcement existed.
• Communications: in 1815 a commander’s eye and his aide-de-camp were everything; by 1854 the telegraph and the press meant blunders became national news within days, which sharpened the political consequences of poor leadership.
• Wider supply: the Crimean army was hungry, ill-supplied and stricken with cholera, and Russell exposed it; these were structural problems that no single commander could have erased.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs leadership against weapons, terrain, allies and supply across both battles, uses accurate period detail (Mont-Saint-Jean, squares, Hougoumont, Nolan’s gesture, the North Valley) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One battle dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Casa de Contratacion (1503) for Spain’s government of the Indies.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Casa de Contratacion, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The Casa licensed every Spanish ship, sailor, cargo and passenger crossing the Atlantic — making it the world’s first imperial bureaucracy and the model for later colonial agencies like the Council of the Indies (1524).
• It captured the royal fifth (quinto real) of all bullion returning from the Indies, turning American gold and silver directly into Crown income for European wars.
• By restricting all American trade to Seville, it kept Castilian merchants in control of the wealth and shut Aragonese, Portuguese, French and English shipping out of the Atlantic.
• It made smuggling, contraband and piracy chronically profitable for the next two centuries — the very monopoly that protected Crown income created the conditions for foreign attacks on Spanish shipping.
• It made the domestic Spanish economy structurally dependent on a single trade route — a long-term weakness when bullion shipments were disrupted.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. Crown revenue AND keeping rivals out) with specific period detail (Seville, the quinto real, the model for later bureaucracies).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Casa de Contratacion without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the encomienda system on Hispaniola.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Tainos ‘entrusted’ in batches to encomenderos were forced into gold-panning gangs and worked until exhaustion or death — a major contributor to the population fall to around 30,000 by 1514.
• The shrinking Indigenous workforce drove the Crown’s decision to license the first shipments of enslaved Africans to the Indies in 1518 — beginning the transatlantic slave trade.
• The brutality of encomienda on Hispaniola triggered Antonio de Montesinos’s 1511 sermon — the first public Spanish protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples and the start of the long argument that would lead to the New Laws of 1542.
• Encomenderos became a colonial aristocracy with strong vested interests — later resistant to Crown reform, as shown in the 1546 rebellion against the New Laws in Peru.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on encomienda without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the licensing of the first shipments of enslaved Africans to the Spanish Indies in 1518.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• It marked the formal beginning of the transatlantic slave trade — a system that would carry an estimated 12 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic over the following three centuries.
• It allowed Spanish settlers to keep operating gold and (later) silver mines and Caribbean plantations as the Indigenous workforce collapsed — sustaining the colonial economy past the demographic catastrophe of Hispaniola.
• The asiento system that grew out of it became a hugely valuable Crown monopoly, contracted out to Genoese, Portuguese and later British merchants.
• It entrenched the colonial assumption that forced labour was the basis of New World wealth — shaping Spanish (and later European) colonial economies until the abolitions of the nineteenth century.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on African enslavement without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spain built an imperial system in the Caribbean between 1503 and 1518. You may use the following in your answer: the founding of the Casa de Contratacion (1503), the formalising of the encomienda system (1503). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• The 1503 founding of the Casa de Contratacion in Seville created a single royal agency to license every ship, sailor and cargo crossing the Atlantic — capturing the royal fifth and shutting out non-Castilian rivals.
• In the same year the encomienda system was formalised, ‘entrusting’ Indigenous workers to settlers in exchange for tribute and Christian instruction — this was the labour mechanism the Casa’s wealth depended on.
• The brutality of encomienda on Hispaniola provoked the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos’s 1511 sermon — the first public protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples and a sign of an internal Spanish debate growing alongside the empire.
• In 1513 the Requerimiento gave Spanish violence a legal veneer — conquistadors could read it aloud, often unintelligibly, before attacking and then claim a ‘just war’.
• The collapse of the Taino workforce on Hispaniola pushed the Crown to license the first shipments of enslaved Africans to the Indies in 1518 — beginning the transatlantic slave trade and completing the four-pillared system (monopoly, encomienda, missionary, Requerimiento) that Spain would carry to Mexico and Peru.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with clear linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Montesinos, Requerimiento, asiento). Reaches an analytical overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Antonio de Montesinos’s 1511 sermon for Spanish imperial policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Montesinos’s sermon, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• It was the first public Spanish protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples in the Americas — demolishing the convenient idea that ‘everyone thought it was acceptable’.
• The sermon scandalised the Hispaniola colonists but reached the Crown — pushing Ferdinand to convene the meetings that produced the Laws of Burgos (1512), the first attempt to regulate encomienda.
• It influenced the young encomendero Bartolome de las Casas, who would become the most determined campaigner for Indigenous rights and a central figure in the New Laws of 1542.
• It set the precedent that Catholic mission and imperial extraction were in tension — a tension that would run through the whole period and produce the Las Casas–Sepulveda debate of 1550–51.
• It established that the moral case for Spanish empire could be challenged from within the Spanish Church itself — not from outside, by Protestants, but from inside, by Dominicans.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the date 1511, the Laws of Burgos 1512, the influence on Las Casas).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the sermon without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Requerimiento (from 1513) for Spanish conduct in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Requerimiento, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Requerimiento gave Spanish violence a legal veneer — if Indigenous peoples did not accept the Pope and the Spanish king, war could be declared a ‘just war’ under Spanish law.
• It allowed conquistadors to argue that captives from war were lawful enslaved spoils, not protected royal subjects — with direct consequences for the slave trade in Indigenous prisoners.
• It was often read in Spanish at dawn, sometimes from offshore — making the legal ‘requirement’ impossible to fulfil and exposing the document as a fig leaf.
• It shaped the conduct of Cortes’s and Pizarro’s expeditions a few years later — both leaders went through the formal motion of reading it before attacking, even when the audience could not understand a word.
• It became a target for critics like Las Casas, who said he did not know whether to laugh at it or weep — using the Requerimiento itself as evidence that Spanish empire needed reform.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the 1513 drafting, the legal ‘just war’ doctrine, the link forward to Cortes/Pizarro and Las Casas’s critique).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Requerimiento without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Irish migration to Britain in the nineteenth century was different from Huguenot migration in the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Irish migrants were pushed out by famine and arrived destitute; Huguenots were pushed out by religious persecution and many arrived with trades and capital.
• Huguenots were welcomed as fellow Protestants and given denization and church collections; Irish Catholics met sustained anti-Catholic hostility and 'No Irish need apply' notices.
• Huguenot arrivals were counted in tens of thousands and concentrated in Spitalfields; around one million Irish left during 1845-52 and settled across every industrial city.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Industrial Revolution shaped migration to Britain between c1700 and c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• factory cities
• the docks.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Factory cities created huge demand for labour: Manchester grew from around 25,000 people in 1772 to a city of hundreds of thousands by 1851, drawing rural Irish, German and Italian migrants.
• Liverpool's docks, tied to Atlantic trade, became the entry point for Irish famine migrants from 1845.
• Particular trades pulled in particular specialists - German pork butchers, Italian craftsmen making mosaics and statues for Victorian churches and town halls.
• Empire shipping employed lascars from Bengal and Yemen, who made up around a quarter of the British merchant marine by 1855, on lower wages than white British sailors.
• Industrial wages were a pull factor, but they collided with hostility whenever competition pinched, and the popular press amplified the resentment from the 1850s.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the experience of lascars in nineteenth-century Britain was similar to the experience of Caribbean workers after 1948.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were recruited from the Empire or Commonwealth to do work Britain needed, at sea in the nineteenth century and in transport and the NHS after 1948.
• Both were paid less or given the least attractive jobs: lascars earned below the rate for white British sailors, and Caribbean workers met a colour bar in employment.
• Both clustered in the districts that would take them, in dockside boarding houses in Cardiff and South Shields, and in Notting Hill and other inner-city areas after 1948.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Economic factors were the most important reason for migration to Britain between c1700 and c1900.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Industrial Revolution
• the Great Famine of 1845–52.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for economic factors:
• Industrial demand for skilled and unskilled labour pulled in Irish navvies, Italian craftsmen and German pork butchers.
• Liverpool's port economy made it the natural entry point for Irish famine migrants who took dock and factory work.
• Empire shipping employed lascars at lower wages than British sailors - a straightforward economic logic.
• European migrants found trade niches, from clockmaking to mosaic work, that paid better than the alternatives at home.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Famine was a push factor, not a wage calculation: around one million people left Ireland between 1845 and 1852 and another million died.
• Religion shaped reception: anti-Catholic prejudice against the Irish, and antisemitic suspicion of Eastern European Jews from the 1880s, were not products of the labour market.
• The Empire was a political structure that drew lascars, ayahs and African mariners into Britain whatever the wage differential.
• Civil liberties made Britain a refuge for political exiles such as Karl Marx, in London from 1849, and for formerly enslaved campaigners such as Olaudah Equiano and Mary Prince.
• Attitudes decided what was possible: the press from the 1850s framed migrants as a threat to wages and public health, and blame for the Liverpool cholera epidemic of 1849 fell on Irish migrants.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (lascars, ayahs, abolitionism, urbanisation, civil liberties).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why formerly enslaved Africans became influential in Britain between c1700 and c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• published life stories
• the abolitionist movement.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Olaudah Equiano's autobiography of 1789 sold widely and gave the abolitionist campaign a first-hand account that readers could not dismiss.
• Mary Prince's narrative of 1831 was the first account of a Black woman's life published in Britain, and it helped build pressure for the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.
• The abolitionist movement gave Black writers a platform, a publisher and an audience of subscribers across British cities.
• The Somerset judgment of 1772 gave campaigners a legal foothold, even though it limited removal from England rather than abolishing slavery.
• Britain's tradition of civil liberties, however uneven, allowed campaigners to lecture, publish and petition in ways that were impossible in the colonies.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why hostility towards migrants varied between different groups in nineteenth-century Britain.

You may use the following in your answer:
• anti-Catholic prejudice
• the role of the press.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Religion was central: Irish Catholics met sustained anti-Catholic hostility, including 'No Irish need apply' notices and hostile press cartoons, where the Protestant descendants of Huguenots did not.
• Economic competition sharpened hostility wherever migrants were seen to undercut local wages, especially in the poorest districts of industrial cities.
• The popular press magnified panic about disease, blaming Irish migrants for the Liverpool cholera epidemic of 1849, and from the 1880s campaigned against 'pauper aliens'.
• Empire migrants such as lascars and ayahs faced a different hostility, rooted in racial hierarchy and in their weak legal position on British soil.
• The abolitionist tradition gave high-profile Black writers such as Equiano and Prince a more welcoming reception than poor migrant labourers received.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the role of Soviet aid during China’s First Five-Year Plan. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. presence of Soviet engineers, blueprints, machinery, ‘gift’ projects, Russian-language manuals). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that Chinese industry was technically dependent on Moscow, or that Soviet aid was treated as a political alliance as well as economic exchange. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why China launched the First Five-Year Plan in 1953.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Korean War
• the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. the defence lessons of Korea, the prestige of catching up with the imperial powers, ideological commitment to the Soviet model, the practical opportunity created by the 1950 Treaty (advisers, gift projects, credit), and the need to consolidate CCP rule by delivering visible results. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the Plan without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the success of the First Five-Year Plan in China.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation reads the Plan as a clear success that built a lasting industrial base; the other reads it as a Soviet-shaped success on paper that disguised a serious squeeze on agriculture and a politically unstable dependence on Moscow). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the First Five-Year Plan.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP orthodox accounts of the 1950s vs revisionist Western works after the Sino-Soviet split), used different evidence (state-published industrial figures vs post-archival research and Chinese factory records), or had different purposes (defending the early PRC vs comparing China unfavourably with capitalist development). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Soviet aid in the success of the First Five-Year Plan?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the c.156 ‘gift’ projects, c.10,000 advisers, blueprints for Anshan, Wuhan and Baotou, training of Chinese students in Russia, and the contribution of internal factors such as Liu Shaoqi’s and Zhou Enlai’s management, peasant grain procurement, and CCP mass mobilisation. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the First Five-Year Plan was more a political success than an economic one?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the c.118% rise in industrial output, the new steel cities, c.58% of state investment going to heavy industry, the squeeze on agriculture and consumer goods, the political consolidation of CCP rule through the danwei system, the strain caused by Khrushchev’s Secret Speech of 1956, and Mao’s growing discomfort with Soviet-style planning. Acknowledges the genuine historiographical disagreement (Dikötter and Spence vs Mobo Gao) and reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (gift project, danwei, heavy industry, Sino-Soviet). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Nasser’s closure of the Straits of Tiran (May 1967).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) Israel treated the closure as a casus belli and its cabinet voted within two weeks for the pre-emptive strike that opened the Six Day War on 5 June 1967; (ii) closure escalated Arab confidence and helped pull King Hussein of Jordan into the Egyptian-led mutual defence pact of 30 May, turning the West Bank into a battlefield. Pairs an immediate and a longer-term consequence. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that the Straits were closed without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Israeli reprisal raid on Samu (November 1966).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) it humiliated King Hussein in front of the Palestinian population on the West Bank, forcing him to align Jordan with the Arab front-line states he had previously kept his distance from; (ii) it gave radical voices in Cairo and Damascus political ammunition to demand that Egypt confront Israel directly rather than hide behind UNEF, accelerating the spiral that led to May 1967. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the raid without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Soviet misinformation in May 1967 about Israeli troop movements on the Syrian border.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) it persuaded Nasser to move Egyptian troops into Sinai on 14 May and demand the withdrawal of UNEF on 18 May, removing the buffer that had kept the peace since 1956; (ii) it embarrassed the Soviet Union when Israel offered observers to verify there were no troops, exposing the limits of Moscow’s control over its Arab allies and shaping its more cautious posture during the war itself. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the misinformation without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the road to the Six Day War in the years 1964–67.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Cairo Conference (1964)
• the closure of the Straits of Tiran (May 1967)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the Cairo Conference and PLO/Fatah split; Fatah raids and the Samu reprisal; the air battle of 7 April 1967; Soviet misinformation and the closure of the Straits of Tiran; the Egyptian-Jordanian mutual defence pact). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the founding of the PLO (1964) for the future of the conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the PLO became the internationally recognised body claiming to represent the Palestinians, displacing Jordan as the spokesman for the West Bank; tension between the Egyptian-sponsored PLO leadership and Arafat’s Fatah determined who would dominate the cause after 1967; the PLO’s founding gave the Palestinian national movement a permanent institution outside any single Arab state. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the PLO without showing why its founding mattered for the future of the conflict. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Egyptian-Jordanian mutual defence pact (30 May 1967) for the Six Day War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the pact placed Jordanian forces under Egyptian command, turning a two-front problem (Sinai and Golan) into a three-front war that Israel had to plan to fight at the same time; it brought the West Bank and East Jerusalem within combat range and so made their occupation in June 1967 possible; for King Hussein it tied his throne to Nasser’s prestige, which collapsed when Egypt was defeated. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the pact without showing why it mattered for the war. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Homestead Act (1862) for the settlement of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Around 1.6 million families eventually filed homestead claims on roughly 270 million acres of public land — a demographic transformation of the Plains within a generation.
• Because the 160-acre limit was too small for the dry High Plains, a majority of original claims failed within five years; abandoned land funnelled to neighbours and bigger buyers, concentrating ownership in some districts.
• The Act broadened eligibility to women heads of households and (after 1865) freed Black families — the legal basis for the 1879 Exoduster movement to Kansas.
• It pulled European migrants onto the Plains, including the Russian Mennonite community that brought Turkey Red wheat in 1874 — an unintended agricultural consequence.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail (1862, 1.6 million, 270 million, 160 acres, 1879).
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the Act without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the key events in the federal government’s attempts to support homesteaders in the years 1862–1873.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Homestead Act (1862)
• the Timber Culture Act (1873)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In May 1862, with Southern senators absent from Congress, the Homestead Act offered 160 acres of public land for an $18 fee after five years’ continuous residence, deliberately broadening eligibility to women, migrants and (after 1865) freed Black families.
• Because 160 acres on the dry Plains was rarely enough for a viable farm, a majority of original claims failed within five years — a problem visible to Congress within a decade.
• Because settlers also lacked timber for houses, fences and fuel, and because some agronomists believed (wrongly) that ‘rain follows the plough’, Congress passed the Timber Culture Act in 1873 offering an extra 160 acres for planting 40 acres of trees within ten years.
• Because the 40-acre requirement proved unrealistic, the rule was reduced to 10 acres in 1878, and many homesteaders gamed the system by planting token groves they let die.
• These linked Acts produced a settled Plains by the 1890s, but with a mixed legacy — mass settlement alongside heavy claim failure and concentration of land in the hands of railroads, banks and bigger buyers.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1862, 1873, 1878, 160 acres, 40/10 acres), and specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, Timber Culture Act).
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Chronological coverage but linkage is weak.
Emerging: Thin description of one or two events with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the failure of many homestead claims on the High Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Abandoned 160-acre claims were sold cheaply to neighbouring families and to bigger buyers, concentrating land ownership in some districts within a generation of 1862.
• It exposed the limits of the Homestead Act’s eastern-farming assumptions, prompting Congress to pass the Timber Culture Act in 1873 to add 160 acres on top of an existing claim.
• It pushed surviving homesteaders towards new technology — the steel plough, windmills, Turkey Red wheat, dry-farming methods — which reshaped Plains agriculture by the 1880s.
• Because the railroads were also selling cheap land, claim failure pushed families into renting or buying from rail companies, deepening railroad influence over settlement patterns.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on hardship without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how new technology and methods helped homesteaders to succeed on the Plains in the years 1862–1885.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the steel plough
• Turkey Red wheat

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• From the 1862 Homestead Act, families could claim 160 acres of public land, but the matted root system of Plains sod broke iron and wooden ploughs — the practical obstacle to using the land at all.
• Because John Deere’s polished steel plough (developed from 1837) could cut through the sod cleanly, families could finally turn over the prairie and plant crops; this made homesteading physically possible.
• Because deep wells were essential and labour was scarce, wind-pumped windmills (refined commercially through the 1870s) replaced bucket-and-rope wells, giving steady water for stock and families.
• Because eastern wheat varieties failed in Plains droughts, Russian Mennonite migrants from around 1874 introduced Turkey Red wheat, a hardy winter wheat that became the dominant crop of the southern and central Plains within a generation.
• Because rainfall was the limiting factor, dry-farming methods pioneered by Hardy Webster Campbell from the 1880s — deep ploughing, harrowing the surface to seal in moisture, fallow rotation — squeezed more out of every inch of rain. Together these methods turned the Plains into a settled agricultural region by the late 1880s.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1862, 1874, 1880s), specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, Turkey Red wheat, dry farming), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Chronological coverage but linkage is weak.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Timber Culture Act (1873) for homesteading on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• It allowed serious homesteaders to double a 160-acre claim to 320 acres, closer to the size the dry Plains actually required.
• It was widely abused: many claimants planted token groves, let them die and bought up the land cheaply when the tree-planting requirement could not be met — concentrating land in fewer hands.
• Because the 40-acre planting target was unrealistic, the rule was reduced to 10 acres in 1878, signalling that Congress was learning the limits of its earlier policy.
• The Act was based partly on the mistaken ‘rain follows the plough’ theory; its repeal in 1891 marked the end of the open-frontier land-policy era.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific period detail (1873, 1878, 1891, 40/10 acres).
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the Act without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how the Plains were transformed for homesteaders by federal land policy and new technology in the years 1862–1885.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Homestead Act (1862)
• new methods and technology

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1862 the Homestead Act offered 160 acres of public land for an $18 fee, deliberately broadening eligibility to women, migrants and (after 1865) freed Black families — the legal frame for the great Plains migration.
• Because the 160-acre allotment was too small for the dry High Plains, a majority of early claims failed; Congress responded with the Timber Culture Act in 1873, offering an extra 160 acres for planting 40 acres of trees.
• Because Plains sod broke iron and wooden ploughs, John Deere’s steel plough became the indispensable tool, while wind-pumped windmills made deep-well water possible without endless labour.
• Because eastern wheat failed in drought, Russian Mennonite migrants brought Turkey Red wheat from around 1874, and dry-farming methods pioneered by Hardy Webster Campbell taught families to retain soil moisture.
• These linked changes — legal access to land, supplementary acreage, mechanical and biological technology, and disciplined methods — together turned the Plains into a settled agricultural region by the mid-1880s, even as the Acts also produced widespread claim failure and concentration of ownership.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail across both Acts and the technologies, specialist vocabulary, both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the recruitment of soldiers was different in the seventeenth century and the late nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Seventeenth-century recruitment was local, sudden and often forced (1). Trained bands, commissions of array and impressment supplied men for a particular war, and vagrants and debtors could be swept up (1). Late nineteenth-century recruitment was permanent and organised (1). From 1870 short service offered six years with the regulars and six in the reserve, and recruits joined through a permanent depot in their own county district (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the British army became more professional in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Crimean War (1854–56)
• Cardwell's reforms.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Industrial weapons demanded trained, drilled soldiers who could use rifles in open order rather than massed amateurs.
• Crimean failures — cholera, missing supplies and elderly commanders who had bought their ranks — were reported by telegraph and made reform a political necessity.
• The abolition of purchase in 1871 meant promotion by seniority and merit, so ability rather than money decided who commanded.
• The 1870 Army Enlistment Act created short service, six years with the colours and six in the reserve, giving Britain a trained pool of former soldiers.
• The 1872 Localisation Act paired battalions and tied each regiment to a county district with a permanent depot, so training and recruitment were continuous.
• The Childers reforms of 1881 and the Haldane reforms of 1906–12 continued the process, adding county titles, a General Staff and the Territorial Force.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way army officers were chosen was different in the medieval period and the late nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the medieval period command followed landholding (1). The king led the great lords, the lords led their knights and the knights led tenants from their own estates, so rank in the army copied rank in society (1). In the late nineteenth century command was supposed to follow merit (1). Purchase of commissions was abolished in 1871, after which promotion went by seniority and ability, and middle-class men could become officers (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the position of the ordinary British soldier changed in the period c1700–c1900.

You may use the following in your answer:
• war reporting
• short service.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• In the eighteenth century the ranks were filled by recruiting parties offering shillings and beer, and the soldier had a poor reputation in respectable society.
• Russell's Crimean reporting made the suffering of ordinary soldiers a national issue, so the public began to see them as men to be looked after.
• Short service from 1870 replaced a term of many years, so a man could leave the army with a working life still ahead of him.
• County regiments and permanent depots gave recruits a local identity and a visible place in their community.
• Barracks were standardised, pay improved a little and basic literacy classes ran in many depots.
• The nickname 'Tommy Atkins', spread by newspapers and by Kipling's verse, shows how the regular soldier became a recognised national figure.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the social background of ordinary soldiers was similar in the seventeenth century and the late nineteenth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both periods the ranks were filled by the poor (1). Seventeenth-century regiments took labourers, apprentices and the unemployed, with impressment used to gather vagrants and debtors when volunteers ran short (1). Late nineteenth-century recruits came overwhelmingly from the urban poor, because pay was low and the work hard (1). In both periods men enlisted mainly because they had few other options (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘Edward Cardwell was the most important figure in modernising the Victorian British army.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• abolition of the purchase of commissions
• short service.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for Cardwell as most important:
• 1871 abolition of purchase of commissions opened the officer corps to merit and seniority, addressing the central post-Crimean criticism.
• The 1870 Army Enlistment Act introduced short service (six and six), creating a trained reserve.
• The 1872 Localisation Act paired battalions in regimental districts and gave the army a permanent local presence.
• Recruitment depots replaced ad-hoc recruiting parties with visible local institutions.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• William Howard Russell’s Crimean reporting (1854–56) and the photographs of Roger Fenton created the political climate without which Cardwell could not have acted.
• The Childers reforms of 1881 finished the regimental reorganisation, giving regiments their county titles and consolidating Cardwell’s structure.
• Industrialisation produced the rifled weapons, telegraph, railways and mass press that made an old-style army impossible — reform was driven by technology as much as by individuals.
• The Haldane reforms of 1906–12 added the Territorial Force, the modern General Staff and the British Expeditionary Force; Cardwell laid foundations but Haldane finished the modern army.
• Public opinion: by the 1890s mass-circulation papers (Daily Mail from 1896) made any return to Crimean conditions politically impossible — the press, not Cardwell alone, locked in reform.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Cardwell against the press, technology and later reformers (Childers, Haldane), uses accurate period detail (purchase of commissions, short service, linked battalions, royal warrant, Childers, Haldane) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One factor dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Act of Supremacy of 1534.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Declared Henry VIII ‘the only Supreme Head on earth of the Church of England’.
• Ended papal jurisdiction in England, transferring authority over doctrine, appointments and revenues to the crown.
• Was passed by Parliament in November 1534, drafted under Cromwell’s direction.
• Built on the 1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals, which had already declared England an ‘empire’.
• Worked alongside the Act of Succession and Treason Act to make denial of the new order a capital offence.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Declared in its preamble that ‘this realm of England is an empire’ with no superior on earth.
• Made it illegal to appeal any English legal case to Rome — including Catherine of Aragon’s defence of her marriage.
• Drafted personally by Thomas Cromwell.
• Passed by the Reformation Parliament in April 1533.
• Cleared the legal path for Cranmer to annul Henry’s marriage to Catherine in May 1533.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Henry VIII broke with Rome between 1529 and 1534.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the King’s annulment
• royal supremacy
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained, supported reasons. Indicative content: • The annulment — Pope Clement VII would not grant it under Charles V’s influence; Henry needed an English answer. • Royal supremacy — the doctrine of imperium, gathered in the Collectanea satis copiosa, argued the king of England answered to no foreign prince. • Church wealth — the English Church held a fifth of the country’s landed wealth and paid annual fees to Rome. • Evangelical influence — Cromwell, Cranmer and Anne Boleyn promoted reformist ideas at court. • Failure of conciliar diplomacy — the Sack of Rome in 1527 and the imperial-papal alliance left Henry with no Roman route. • Personal anger — Clement’s revocation of the case to Rome in 1529 humiliated Henry publicly. Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed. Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation. Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin. Emerging: Description of events without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Act of Supremacy of 1534 was the most important of the Reformation statutes.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• royal supremacy
• the Act in Restraint of Appeals
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the Act of Supremacy against the other statutes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• It declared Henry the only Supreme Head on earth of the Church of England, ending papal authority outright.
• It gave the crown power over doctrine, appointments and church revenues.
• Because it was statute, it could only be undone by Parliament, which made the break durable.
• It underpinned the vicegerency through which Cromwell governed every English bishop from 1535.

Arguments for the other statutes:
• The Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533 declared this realm an empire and stopped Catherine appealing to Rome, so it delivered the annulment the whole crisis was about.
• The Submission of the Clergy in 1532 had already forced the Church to accept royal assent for canon law.
• The Act in Conditional Restraint of Annates of 1532 cut the money flowing from English bishops to Rome.
• The Act of Succession of March 1534 created the oath, and the Treason Act of December 1534 made refusing it a capital offence.

Overall judgement: the Act of Supremacy stated the principle, but it worked only because earlier statutes had cleared the ground and later ones supplied the punishment. Top-band answers weigh these statutes and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell was able to enforce the break with Rome between 1534 and 1540.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the oath of supremacy
• the treason laws
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• The oath of supremacy — required of all adult subjects under the Act of Succession; refusal was treason. Cromwell ordered systematic administration of the oath through bishops and royal commissioners.
• Treason laws — the 1534 Treason Act made denial of the supremacy in word or writing a capital offence, allowing prosecution of dissenters such as More, Fisher and the Carthusian priors.
