• Statutory authority — Cromwell ran enforcement through Acts of Parliament, giving the system legal permanence and Parliamentary cover.
• Vicegerency in Spirituals — from 1535 Cromwell held the king’s deputised spiritual authority over every bishop, allowing him to coordinate the church.
• Royal injunctions — 1536 injunctions ordered parishes to preach against papal authority and use the Lord’s Prayer, Creed and Commandments in English.
• Information network — Cromwell built up reports from bishops, JPs and informers, allowing rapid identification of dissent.
• High-profile executions — the deaths of More and Fisher in 1535 demonstrated that even senior figures faced consequences.
• Cranmer’s alliance — the Archbishop of Canterbury cooperated fully, giving the regime ecclesiastical legitimacy.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important reason for the break with Rome between 1529 and 1534 was Henry VIII’s desire for an annulment.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• royal supremacy
• Cromwell’s influence
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Reward sustained argument that weighs the annulment against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Arguments for ‘most important’: • The annulment was the immediate trigger: every major statute from 1532–34 was driven by Henry’s need to settle his marriage and secure the succession. • The Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) was drafted specifically to prevent Catherine appealing to Rome. • Cranmer’s elevation in 1533 served the annulment first, the Reformation second. • Without the failure of the annulment in 1529, Henry would have had no public motive to challenge papal authority. • Anne Boleyn’s influence at court depended on the annulment proceeding; the Boleyn faction kept the religious agenda moving. Arguments for alternative explanations: • Royal supremacy — the doctrine of imperium, set out in the Collectanea satis copiosa, would have remained an academic argument without political will, but it provided the constitutional framework Henry actually wanted long-term. • Cromwell’s influence — he turned a personal crisis into a statutory revolution, drafting the laws and running their enforcement; without him the break could have remained ad hoc. • Church wealth — fiscal opportunity gave Henry a powerful long-term incentive that survived the annulment crisis (and would shape the dissolution of the monasteries). • Evangelical reformist current — Cranmer, Cromwell and Anne Boleyn shaped the religious direction, not just the political break. • Continental context — Lutheran Germany had already shown that breaking with Rome was thinkable; the wider European Reformation legitimised English moves. Overall judgement: the annulment was the indispensable trigger but not the sufficient cause. The break with Rome happened on the scale it did because Cromwell, Cranmer and Henry himself shared an interest in royal supremacy and were prepared to use parliamentary statute to entrench it. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion. Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout. Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached. Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of the sheriff under King John.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features are required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Collecting royal revenue — the sheriff gathered the ‘county farm’, demesne rents, fines, dues and customs and paid them in twice a year at the Exchequer at Westminster.
• Presiding over the shire court — the sheriff held the regular court for the shire, hearing local cases that did not go to the king’s justices.
• Buying his office — sheriffs typically paid the Crown for their appointment and recouped the cost from the shire over their term, sometimes by harsh exactions.
• Leading the county levy in arms — in time of war the sheriff raised and led the men of his shire for the king’s service.
• Accountability to John in person — John’s constant tours meant sheriffs could be questioned and replaced more often than under previous reigns.
• Arresting royal criminals — sheriffs answered for those accused of pleas of the Crown.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1207 tax on income and moveables.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Rate — one-thirteenth of every free man’s income and the value of his moveable goods.
• Tax base — assessed on income and moveable goods rather than on land or feudal status; the first such tax raised for the king’s own war rather than for a crusade or a ransom.
• Conciliar approval — John summoned a great council to win formal consent for the levy.
• Yield — raised approximately £57,000, more than two ordinary years of royal revenue at a single stroke.
• Purpose — intended to fund a campaign to recover Normandy lost in 1204.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John’s use of feudal incidents caused such resentment among the barons.
You may use the following in your answer:
• reliefs
• wardships and marriages
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Reliefs — the inheritance fee paid by an heir to a deceased baron rose from a customary £100 to thousands of marks — 7,000 marks from John de Lacy and 10,000 from William fitz Alan — making baronial inheritance a punitive tax.
• Wardships — John kept the lands of underage heirs and milked their revenues for the duration of the wardship, often selling guardianship to favourites who exploited estates.
• Marriages of heiresses — John sold off the marriages of widows and heiresses for huge sums (Geoffrey de Mandeville paid 20,000 marks for Isabel of Gloucester in 1214), forcing women into chosen matches.
• Arbitrary application — the same incident was charged at different rates for different barons, depending on the king’s favour or vendetta.
• Lack of consent — feudal incidents were imposed by the king’s personal authority and did not require the great barons to be consulted, undermining the Curia Regis tradition.
• Cumulative weight — combined with eleven scutages and the 1207 thirteenth, the financial pressure on the baronial class became unsustainable.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John raised so much money from England between 1199 and 1215.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of Normandy
• scutage
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Loss of Normandy — recovering the duchy required an army, fleet and Continental allies, all of which had to be paid for in cash.
• Scutage — John levied eleven scutages in seventeen years at rising rates, raising large sums while leaving the great barons at home.
• The 1207 thirteenth — an unprecedented one-thirteenth tax on income and moveables, raising around £57,000.
• Feudal incidents — reliefs, wardships and marriages charged at multiples of customary rates produced very large windfall sums.
• Tallages on the Anglo-Jewish community — the 1210 Bristol Tallage alone was set at 66,000 marks.
• Sheriff and demesne management — the sale and rotation of sheriffdoms, plus tighter control of demesne manors and royal forests, squeezed extra revenue from existing sources.
• Hubert Walter’s administrative inheritance — the Exchequer, pipe rolls and itinerant eyre meant John already had a sophisticated machine to assess and collect.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation; both stimulus points developed and own information added.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John’s constant personal presence in England changed how the kingdom was governed.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of Normandy in 1204
• the role of the sheriffs
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Speed of justice — pleas could be heard within days of arriving at the king’s court rather than waiting weeks for a chance hearing.
• Closer supervision of sheriffs — sheriffs could be questioned and replaced in person, with John selling and unselling sheriffdoms more often than under his predecessors.
• Greater reach of royal authority — with the king moving constantly, his power was felt in places that had previously been distant from royal scrutiny.
• More arbitrary rulings — without the buffer of distance, baronial disputes were settled by personal royal will, sometimes inconsistently.
• Pipe-roll record-keeping — the personal supervision of the Exchequer thickened the rolls and tightened the audit of every shire.
• Loss of safety valve — after 1204 there was nowhere else for the king to be, and his personal scrutiny became inescapable.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The 1207 tax on income and moveables was the main reason for baronial resentment of King John by 1212.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• scutage
• feudal incidents
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• The 1207 thirteenth raised around £57,000 in a single year, an unprecedented assault on personal wealth.
• It set a precedent for taxing free men by personal wealth rather than feudal obligation, alarming the political class.
• It financed John’s preparations for the recovery of Normandy, which the great barons increasingly saw as a doomed enterprise.
• It came on top of, not instead of, the older sources of royal income.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Scutage — eleven levies in seventeen years at rising rates, including levies in years without an active campaign, were a more visible and constant grievance than a single 1207 thirteenth.
• Feudal incidents — reliefs of 7,000 and 10,000 marks, exorbitant marriage fines and abusive wardships hit named individuals personally and produced a long list of specific grievances later catalogued in Magna Carta.
• John’s personal style — demands for hostages, the starvation of the de Braose family, vindictive justice — alienated the barons in ways finance alone could not explain.
• Loss of Normandy in 1204 — the underlying cause of all the financial demand and the loss of confidence in royal leadership.
• The Interdict 1208–14 — spiritual and political crisis on top of finance.
• Misuse of patronage — sale and rotation of sheriffdoms among foreign mercenaries provoked specific grievance among the ‘Northerners’.

Overall judgement: The 1207 thirteenth was a striking innovation, but resentment by 1212 was cumulative. Scutage and feudal incidents were the more constant grievance because they hit barons personally, repeatedly and at the king’s arbitrary discretion. The 1207 thirteenth crystallised the problem; it did not create it. A balanced judgement weighs the 1207 tax as a key new pressure against scutage, feudal incidents and personal style as the underlying drivers.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (scutage, demesne, relief, wardship, escheat, tallage).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Wolfe’s victory at Quebec in 1759 for British North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: Wolfe’s victory led to the fall of Montreal in 1760 and the British conquest of Canada, removing France as a continental rival; it also led to a vast new frontier reaching to the Mississippi that Britain could not afford to police, setting up the policy disputes after 1763. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to Quebec or what followed.
Emerging: Notes the victory without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Treaty of Paris (1763) for relations between Britain and the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: the treaty mattered because Britain’s acquisition of Canada and territory east of the Mississippi removed the French threat that had bound the colonies to imperial protection; it also mattered because the cost of the war and the new western territory drove the post-1763 reforms (Proclamation Act, Sugar Act) that colonists came to resent. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus; limited use of specific developments.
Emerging: Describes the treaty without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Proclamation Act of 1763 for the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the Act forbade settlement west of the Appalachians, which angered settlers and land speculators (including George Washington) who had expected new lands as a reward for service in the war; it also strained colonial relations with Britain by suggesting London prioritised Indigenous diplomacy over colonial economic interests, contributing to a sense of betrayal after 1763. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the Act’s provisions.
Emerging: Mentions the Act without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of relations with Indigenous peoples for the course of the French and Indian War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: most western Indigenous nations preferred French traders to British settlers, so they fought alongside France in early campaigns such as the destruction of Braddock’s force in 1755; the Haudenosaunee’s mostly British alignment helped stabilise the New York frontier and freed regular troops for the Quebec campaign. Specific examples of nations and battles developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions Indigenous involvement without showing why it shaped the war.
Emerging: General references to Indigenous peoples without specific examples.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how Britain came to dominate North America in the years 1754–63. You may use the following information in your answer:
• The French and Indian War
• The role of Wolfe in Canada
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why Britain won rather than narrating in sequence. Links the early defeats (Braddock 1755) to weak frontier alliances; links Pitt’s 1757 strategy and naval blockade to the recapture of Louisbourg (1758) and the campaign against Quebec; brings in own knowledge such as the Plains of Abraham (1759), the fall of Montreal (1760) and the Treaty of Paris (1763). Reaches an analytical judgement about how Britain’s resources and Indigenous diplomacy combined.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists events without explaining how Britain came to dominate.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of King George’s War (1744–48) for relations between Britain and the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the war mattered because the New England capture of Louisbourg in 1745 raised colonial confidence in their own military capacity; the return of Louisbourg to France in 1748 meanwhile bred resentment that imperial decisions ignored colonial sacrifice, foreshadowing later disagreements after 1763. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Notes the war happened without showing why it mattered for relations.
Emerging: Describes campaigns without explaining significance.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. John Lewis, SNCC chairman, recalling Bloody Sunday two months later in 1965.

‘We were marching in pairs along the road. Hosea Williams and I were at the front. We crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge and saw the line of state troopers and Sheriff Clark’s posse blocking the highway. The major gave us two minutes to disperse. We were saying our prayers when, after ninety seconds, the troopers came at us with billy clubs and horses. I felt my skull crack. The last thing I remember thinking was: this is how I will die, on the road outside Selma, for the right to register to vote.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about Bloody Sunday in Selma.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘The state troopers attacked before the dispersal deadline they themselves had given’ supported by ‘The major gave us two minutes to disperse … after ninety seconds, the troopers came at us with billy clubs and horses’ AND ‘Marchers expected severe and potentially fatal violence in pursuit of voting rights’ supported by ‘this is how I will die, on the road outside Selma, for the right to register to vote’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was passed.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Bloody Sunday at Selma
• President Johnson’s ‘We Shall Overcome’ speech

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. SNCC’s prior voter-registration groundwork in Selma since 1963; the killing of Jimmie Lee Jackson in Marion; the gap left by the 1964 Civil Rights Act on voting; the death of James Reeb after the ‘turnaround’ march; the legal protection of the third Selma-to-Montgomery march by federal troops; Johnson’s legislative skill in winning over Republican leader Everett Dirksen), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (Edmund Pettus Bridge, federal registrars, Section 5 pre-clearance).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1998 history of the Selma campaign):
‘Selma succeeded because the SCLC and SNCC built carefully on years of local organising. Black Selmans had been trying to register since 1963; the SCLC’s arrival in 1965 brought national attention to a movement that already existed. Without the courage of the marchers on the bridge there would have been no Voting Rights Act.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2014 study of Lyndon Johnson):
‘The Voting Rights Act was the work of a Texan president. Johnson had been moving the votes in Congress for the bill since the autumn of 1964. Bloody Sunday gave him the public moment he needed for his “We Shall Overcome” address, but the bill had been months in preparation in the White House before the bridge.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the passing of the Voting Rights Act? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 credits the movement’s prior local organising and the marchers’ courage; Interpretation 2 credits Johnson’s prior legislative groundwork and his ability to use Bloody Sunday as the moment to push a bill that was already in preparation) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘Without the courage of the marchers on the bridge there would have been no Voting Rights Act’ vs ‘the bill had been months in preparation in the White House before the bridge’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the passing of the Voting Rights Act.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is taken from a 1998 movement-focused history of the Selma campaign and uses oral histories from local Black activists, SNCC field reports and accounts of the marches as its main evidence base, whereas Interpretation 2 is taken from a 2014 presidential study that draws on Johnson’s phone recordings, White House memos and congressional voting records. The two have different focuses and different bodies of evidence.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the passing of the Voting Rights Act?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge (SNCC’s 1963 organising in Selma; the death of Jimmie Lee Jackson; the 7 March attack on the Edmund Pettus Bridge; ABC’s broadcast to 48 million viewers; the death of James Reeb; the federalisation of the Alabama National Guard for the third march; Johnson’s ‘We Shall Overcome’ address; Johnson’s pressure on Republican leader Dirksen; the suspension of literacy tests; federal registrars; Section 5 pre-clearance), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. A survey of the immediate effect of the Voting Rights Act in the Deep South, late 1965.

‘In the five months since the Act was signed, federal examiners have enrolled more than 80,000 Black voters in counties where local registrars had previously refused them. Across the Deep South a further 170,000 Black citizens have been registered by their local boards, who now know that their decisions will be reviewed in Washington. The literacy test, which has been the principal device of exclusion since 1890, has been suspended in 26 of the 27 counties of Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina where less than half the eligible adults voted in 1964.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the impact of the Voting Rights Act.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘The Act’s federal-registrar mechanism worked because half of new voters were enrolled directly by Washington, bypassing local registrars’ supported by ‘federal examiners have enrolled more than 80,000 Black voters in counties where local registrars had previously refused them’ AND ‘The threat of federal pre-clearance changed the behaviour of local registrars even where examiners had not been sent’ supported by ‘a further 170,000 Black citizens have been registered by their local boards, who now know that their decisions will be reviewed in Washington’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about how the people’s communes affected daily life in rural China during the Great Leap Forward. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. mass mess halls, communal childcare, abolition of private plots, women working alongside men, militia drill). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that family life was reorganised around collective production rather than the household, or that the commune absorbed roles previously held by women in the home. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mao launched the Great Leap Forward in 1958.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Mao’s reaction to the Soviet model of industrialisation
• the slogan ‘catch up with Britain in 15 years’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. Mao’s ideological discomfort with Soviet bureaucracy after Khrushchev’s 1956 Secret Speech, the political opportunity created by the 1957 Anti-Rightist purge, the structural readiness of higher-stage cooperatives by end of 1956, Mao’s wish to reassert authority over Liu Shaoqi and the planners, and the practical aim of squeezing more grain from the countryside. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the Leap without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the importance of the Lushan Conference of 1959.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation reads Lushan as the moment Mao recognised the Leap was failing and quietly began to ease it; the other reads it as the moment Mao deliberately doubled down by purging Peng Dehuai and prolonging the disaster). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the causes of the Great Leap Forward.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP orthodox 1981 Resolution vs revisionist Western such as Dikötter, MacFarquhar or Yang Jisheng), used different evidence (state-published material vs PRC archives opened after 1990), or had different purposes (defending Mao’s record vs holding him personally responsible). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Lysenkoism and backyard steel in causing the failure of the Great Leap Forward?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — close planting and deep ploughing, the c.60 million peasants diverted from harvest to backyard furnaces, the ‘tofu-dreg’ quality of the steel produced, the contribution of communal mess halls to grain depletion, inflated reporting from below, and the alternative explanation of forced procurement quotas after Lushan. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that Mao’s personal decisions at the Lushan Conference were the most important reason the Great Leap Forward continued after 1959?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — Peng Dehuai’s private letter, Mao’s decision to circulate it as an attack, Peng’s removal as Defence Minister and replacement by Lin Biao, the silencing effect on other CCP leaders, the continuation of inflated quotas into 1960, and the alternative explanation of structural commune problems and provincial cadre fanaticism (MacFarquhar, Yang Jisheng) versus top-down personal command (Dikötter). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (commune, Lushan, Lysenkoism, mess hall, Great Leap). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the Cheka’s role in Bolshevik Russia between 1917 and 1922. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, Dzerzhinsky’s ‘organised terror’ admission, the September 1918 Decree on the Red Terror, the 250,000 staff and informants by 1921, the Petrograd hostage shootings, the operation outside the courts). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the Cheka was designed as a class-war instrument rather than a normal police force. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Bolsheviks crushed the Kronstadt Mutiny in March 1921.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Petropavlovsk resolution
• the Tenth Party Congress
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. the political danger of demands like ‘Soviets without Bolsheviks’ and free socialist parties from a base that had carried October 1917, the proximity of the rising to Petrograd, the spread of strikes and peasant revolt elsewhere, the Tenth Party Congress’s simultaneous ban on factions, and the regime’s willingness to combine military force with the parallel NEP concession). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Cheka, Politburo, Petropavlovsk, Tenth Party Congress. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the rising without explaining why it was crushed. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the nature of the Bolshevik regime by 1921.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues that by 1921 the Bolshevik regime had become a one-party police state, with the Cheka, the Politburo, the ban on factions and the suppression of Kronstadt all pointing the same way; the other argues that the regime was still a contested revolutionary government forced into hard choices by Civil War and famine, illustrated by the simultaneous NEP retreat). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Red Terror.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (Cheka archives and Sovnarkom decree texts versus survivor and exile testimony from former Petrograd hostages); they wrote at different times (Soviet-era surveys that justified the Terror as wartime emergency versus post-1991 archival biographies that emphasise its scale and class targeting); or they had different purposes (defending the legitimacy of the Bolshevik state versus reconstructing victim experience). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the Cheka in keeping the Bolsheviks in power between 1918 and 1921?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the Cheka and the Red Terror — the September 1918 Decree, Dzerzhinsky’s ‘organised terror’, the 250,000 staff by 1921, the Petrograd hostage shootings — alongside other survival factors (Trotsky’s Red Army, the central railway hub, Sovnarkom’s political grip, the propaganda framing of the Whites). Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Kronstadt Mutiny showed the Bolshevik regime was losing the support of its own revolutionary base?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the ‘pride and glory of October’ status of the Kronstadt sailors, Petrichenko’s 28 February resolution, the ‘Soviets without Bolsheviks’ slogan, the Petropavlovsk demands for free socialist parties and an end to grain requisitioning, Tukhachevsky’s ice assault on 17 March, the parallel Tambov peasant revolt and the simultaneous NEP — weighed against the alternative reading that the mutiny was a wartime aberration suppressed by a still-popular regime. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Cheka, Politburo, Petropavlovsk, Tenth Party Congress). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of UN Resolution 242 (1967) for relations between Israel and the Arab world.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. it set out land for peace as the basis for ending the conflict and so framed every later negotiation, including Camp David in 1978 and Oslo in 1993; its ambiguity over ‘territories’ vs ‘the territories’ meant both sides could read it differently and so deferred resolution rather than producing it; the Khartoum ‘three nos’ immediately blocked implementation but kept 242 as the long-term reference. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Resolution 242 without showing why it mattered for relations between Israel and the Arab world. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Six Day War (1967) for Palestinian refugees.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. between 280,000 and 325,000 Palestinians fled the West Bank into Jordan, many for the second time after 1948, and the new refugee camps in the East Bank produced the militant generation that drove the 1970 Black September crisis; the Palestinians who remained on the West Bank came under Israeli military rule for the first time, beginning the occupation that has continued; the war forced Palestinian leaders to assume that Arab states would not recover the land for them and so to act independently through Fatah and the PLO. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the refugees without showing why the war mattered for them. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Israeli occupation of East Jerusalem (1967) for the future of the conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. East Jerusalem was annexed by Israel within weeks of the ceasefire and declared part of an ‘eternal undivided capital’, an action no Arab state and no major UN member recognised; the status of Jerusalem became the most intractable single issue in every later peace process, including Camp David and Oslo; the visible presence of Israeli authority over Muslim and Christian holy places gave the conflict a religious dimension that pan-Arab nationalism had previously played down. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions East Jerusalem without showing why its occupation mattered for the future of the conflict. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Israeli pre-emptive air strike on 5 June 1967.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the destruction of about 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground in three hours gave Israel air supremacy on every front, making the rapid ground victories of the next five days possible; (ii) it confirmed in the Arab world that Egypt’s decisive moves of May 1967 had been a bluff Nasser could not back up, ending his role as the unchallenged leader of pan-Arabism and shifting Palestinian leadership towards independent groups such as Fatah. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Israel struck first without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Khartoum Resolution (September 1967).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the ‘three nos’ closed off any quick implementation of UN Resolution 242 and committed Arab states to a long confrontation with Israel rather than negotiation; (ii) Saudi Arabia and Kuwait agreed at Khartoum to subsidise Egypt and Jordan, allowing both states to rebuild militarily and politically without compromising in negotiations — a policy choice that helped make the 1973 Yom Kippur War possible. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the ‘three nos’ without analysing their effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the Six Day War and its diplomatic aftermath in 1967.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Israeli pre-emptive air strike (5 June 1967)
• UN Resolution 242 (November 1967)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the pre-emptive air strike and ground campaign; the four Occupied Territories and the second wave of Palestinian refugees; UN Resolution 242 and its land for peace principle; the Khartoum ‘three nos’ and the closed Suez Canal). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Balboa’s 1513 expedition for the later Spanish empire in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Balboa’s expedition, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Balboa was the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas, on 25 September 1513 — turning the Pacific from a rumour into a Spanish ocean.
• His claim of the ‘South Sea’ for Spain opened the door to a westward push that would reach Mexico, Peru and the Philippines, anchoring the long-term shape of the empire.
• The Indigenous intelligence Balboa gathered about a southern empire of gold became official Spanish knowledge at court — planting the seed Pizarro acted on in 1532 when he sailed for Peru.
• The new Spanish foothold in Panama, including Panama City founded in 1519, became the bridgehead from which Pizarro’s expedition was launched.
• Balboa’s 1519 execution by Pedrarias Davila showed how political the conquistador era was — a forerunner of the rivalries between Cortes and Velazquez and Pizarro and Almagro.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. opening the Pacific AND seeding Pizarro’s Peruvian expedition) with specific period detail (the date 1513, Pedrarias Davila, the link forward to Pizarro 1532).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Balboa’s expedition without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the conquest of Cuba (1511–15).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Cuba became Spain’s next Caribbean base after Hispaniola — with Santiago and Havana as ports for ships, men, horses and supplies for further expeditions.
• Hernan Cortes’s 1519 expedition to Mexico was launched from Santiago de Cuba — defying Velazquez but using his island, his ships and his men.
• The encomienda system was carried over from Hispaniola, and the Cuban Taino population collapsed under it within a generation.
• The execution of the Taino cacique Hatuey in 1512 became one of the most quoted indictments of conquest in Las Casas’s writings — influencing the long argument over Indigenous rights.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the conquest of Cuba without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Magellan’s voyage (1519–22) for Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Spain gained a foothold in the Philippines, which it would hold until 1898, and a westward route to the spice trade that did not infringe Portugal’s eastward route under the Treaty of Tordesillas.
• The first circumnavigation under Elcano in 1522 demonstrated that the Pacific could be crossed, integrating the new Spanish empire into a single global commercial system.
• The voyage created the geographic conditions for the later Manila Galleon, which carried American silver to Asia and Asian silk and porcelain back through Mexican ports.
• The huge cost — only one ship and 18 of around 270 men returned — underlined how dangerous Pacific crossings were and shaped how Spain regulated transatlantic and trans-Pacific shipping.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Magellan’s voyage without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spain built a launching pad for the conquest of the mainland between 1511 and 1522. You may use the following in your answer: Balboa reaching the Pacific (1513), the conquest of Cuba (1511–15). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Diego Velazquez conquered Cuba between 1511 and 1515, founding Santiago and Havana — ports that turned the island into a staging post for further expeditions, and a place to recruit men, breed horses and build ships.
• While the Cuban conquest was underway, Balboa crossed the isthmus of Panama in September 1513 and saw the Pacific — opening a strategic question (how to cross it?) and gathering Indigenous intelligence about a southern empire of gold.
• This in turn drove Spanish thinking westward: rumours of a Pacific empire of gold became official intelligence at court, planting the seed for Pizarro’s Peruvian expedition in 1532.
• In 1519–22 Magellan’s expedition (under Elcano after Magellan’s death) crossed the Pacific and answered the strategic question Balboa had opened — proving the Pacific could be sailed and giving Spain a claim to the Philippines.
• Because of all this, when Hernan Cortes left Santiago de Cuba in February 1519, he was launching from the platform Cuba had built, on the Pacific-facing strategic frontier Balboa had opened — and into a continent that Magellan’s voyage was about to turn into part of a global Spanish commercial system.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with clear linkage (‘this in turn made possible’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Magellan, Pedrarias Davila, the link forward to Cortes and Pizarro). Reaches an analytical overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Cuba as a Spanish base in the period 1515–19.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Cuba, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Cuba supplied the men, horses, ships and provisions that supported every Spanish expedition into the western Caribbean and onto the mainland in this period.
• Santiago de Cuba was the port from which Hernan Cortes launched his expedition to Mexico in February 1519 — without Cuba, there is no Mexico in 1519.
• As governor of Cuba, Diego Velazquez tried to control which expeditions left from his island and to recall those that defied him — making Cuba a stage for conquistador rivalry as well as conquest.
• Cuban Taino communities, devastated by encomienda and disease within a generation, were the workforce that fed and supported the Spanish forces preparing for mainland war.
• The conquest of Cuba also produced figures like the friar Bartolome de las Casas, who began as a young encomendero on the island and would later become the most determined Spanish critic of conquest.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (Velazquez, Cortes’s 1519 expedition, the Taino population collapse).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Cuba without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Spanish claim to the Philippines after Magellan’s voyage.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Spanish claim to the Philippines, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Spanish claim, founded on Magellan’s voyage of 1519–22, gave Spain a claim in Asia that it made good from 1565 and held until 1898 — the only major European Asian colony reached from the Americas.
• The Philippines became the western terminus of the later Manila Galleon trade, which carried American silver to Asia and Asian silk and porcelain back through Mexican ports.
• Combined with Balboa’s 1513 Pacific claim, the Philippines turned the Pacific into a Spanish ocean and made the empire genuinely global.
• The voyage demonstrated that Tordesillas-compliant westward routes existed — Spain could reach the spice trade without infringing Portugal’s African and Indian Ocean monopoly.
• It made the Spanish silver economy of the Andes (after 1545) part of a single Pacific commercial system — the world’s first global currency was Spanish silver shipped through Manila.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the 1521 landing, the link to Tordesillas, the connection to silver and the Manila Galleon).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Philippines claim without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Drake’s raid on Cadiz in 1587.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It was a pre-emptive English naval attack — Drake led 23 ships into Cadiz harbour on 19 April 1587 to disrupt Philip II’s invasion fleet before it could sail.
• It destroyed Spanish shipping — around 30 warships and supply vessels were destroyed over two days, alongside Drake’s subsequent attacks on Sagres and shipping along the Iberian coast.
• It targeted Spanish supplies, not just ships — the destruction of barrels of seasoned wood for water casks meant the Armada in 1588 had to rely on unseasoned casks that leaked.
• Drake described it himself as ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’, signalling its intended humiliation as much as material damage.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why English privateering damaged relations with Spain.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Treaty of Tordesillas
• Drake’s knighthood in 1581
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• It violated Spanish trading monopolies — Spain claimed exclusive rights to trade with its American colonies under the Treaty of Tordesillas; Drake’s raids on the Spanish Main and his circumnavigation were direct breaches.
• It was royally sanctioned — Elizabeth invested in voyages, took a share of Drake’s £400,000 in plunder, and knighted him at Deptford in 1581; Philip II read this as the Crown endorsing piracy.
• It cost Spain enormous sums — Drake’s circumnavigation alone returned roughly a year of Crown revenue; cumulative privateering losses tied up Spanish convoys and Treasury planning.
• It humiliated Spain on the global stage — raids on silver convoys at Nombre de Dios and ports along the Pacific coast made Philip’s claim to global Catholic primacy look brittle.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why relations between England and Spain deteriorated between 1569 and 1587.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Drake and privateering
• English involvement in the Netherlands
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• Privateering (stimulus) — Drake’s raids on Spanish ports and silver convoys, his 1577–80 circumnavigation and royal knighthood in 1581 were read in Madrid as Crown-backed piracy attacking Spain’s American monopoly.
• Netherlands (stimulus) — the Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committed 7,400 English troops under Leicester to support Protestant Dutch rebels against Philip; Spain treated the treaty as a formal declaration of war.
• Religion (own knowledge) — the 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis recast Elizabeth as illegitimate in Catholic eyes; the Counter-Reformation framed England’s Protestantism as something Philip had a duty to overturn.
• Plots and Mary, Queen of Scots (own knowledge) — Spanish backing for the Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots, and Mary’s execution in February 1587, removed Philip’s diplomatic restraint and gave him a Catholic martyr.
• Cadiz raid (own knowledge) — Drake’s April 1587 attack destroyed around 30 Spanish ships and seasoned timber for casks, delaying the Armada by a year and demanding a military response.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important reason England and Spain went to war by 1588 was English involvement in the Netherlands.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• religious differences
• Drake’s raid on Cadiz (1587)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Netherlands as main reason):
• The Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) sent Leicester with 7,400 men to fight Spanish forces; Philip treated it as an open declaration of war.
• A Spanish-controlled Netherlands sat directly across the Channel from Kent — military intervention there was an existential strategic clash, not just a diplomatic dispute.
• Leicester’s loss of Sluys and Deventer (1587) and the parallel Spanish reconquest under Parma kept the conflict active and visible.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Religious differences (stimulus) — the 1570 papal bull and Counter-Reformation framed Protestant England as a target Philip had a religious duty to overturn; without that framing the Netherlands quarrel might have stayed limited.
• Cadiz raid (stimulus) — April 1587 destroyed around 30 ships and seasoned timber, delayed the Armada by a year and forced Philip into a public response; it was the open military trigger.
• Privateering and Drake (own knowledge) — from the early 1570s English raids on Spanish silver convoys, Drake’s circumnavigation (1577–80) and the 1581 knighthood made the commercial relationship irrecoverable long before 1585.
• Mary’s execution (own knowledge) — February 1587 removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative monarch; Philip’s decision to launch the Armada is hard to read without it.

Justified judgement: The Netherlands intervention was the formal break, but it sat on top of religion (the long-term cause), privateering (the running grievance) and Mary’s execution and Cadiz (the short-term triggers). A strong response weighs Nonsuch as the legal trigger against the deeper religious and commercial causes and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Leicester’s expedition to the Netherlands, 1585–87.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It was authorised by treaty — the Treaty of Nonsuch (August 1585) committed England to send 7,400 men to support Protestant Dutch rebels against Spain.
• It was politically embarrassing — Leicester accepted the title of Governor-General without Elizabeth’s permission and was publicly repudiated by the queen.
• It lost strategic towns — Sluys was lost to Spain, and Deventer was handed over by an English Catholic deserter.
• It produced few military successes — the most famous engagement, Zutphen in September 1586, was a small skirmish remembered chiefly for the death of Sir Philip Sidney.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe (1577–80) was significant for relations with Spain.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the capture of Spanish treasure
• Drake’s knighthood in 1581
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links. Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own): • Direct breach of Spain’s monopoly — Drake plundered Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America, territory Spain considered closed under the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. • Enormous financial damage — he returned with around £400,000 of Spanish treasure, roughly a year’s Crown revenue for England; the loss to Spain was strategic, not just financial. • Royal endorsement of piracy — Elizabeth knighted Drake on board the Golden Hind at Deptford in 1581, taking the queen’s share publicly; Philip II read this as official approval. • Symbolic blow to Spanish primacy — circumnavigation was the second in history (after Magellan’s expedition) and the first by an English commander; it punctured the image of Catholic Spain as ruler of the seas. Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links. Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation. Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the Irish who came to Liverpool during the Famine were different from the Huguenots who came to England after 1685.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Famine migrants arrived destitute and dependent on poor relief; Huguenots arrived with trades, capital and, for many, grants of denization.
• Huguenots were welcomed as fellow Protestants; Irish Catholics met anti-Catholic hostility, sectarian rioting and 'No Irish Need Apply' notices.
• Around one million Irish left during 1845-52, with almost 300,000 landing at Liverpool in 1847 alone; the Huguenot wave was around 50,000 across several years.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Liverpool became the main entry point for Irish migration in the nineteenth century.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the sea crossing from Ireland
• the docks.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The short crossing from Dublin or Cork made Liverpool the cheapest entry point, at a fraction of the cost of a transatlantic fare.
• By 1850 Liverpool handled a very large share of Britain's overseas trade, and its dock economy needed unskilled labour at exactly the moment Famine migrants needed work.
• An established Catholic infrastructure of parishes, priests and mutual aid drew Irish Catholics towards a town where their community already had a foothold.
• Regular packet ships to North America meant Liverpool also worked as a transit port; some migrants stopped only because they could not afford the onward fare.
• Father Nugent's refuges, ragged schools and emigrant aid gave the poorest arrivals a reason to stay that other British cities could not match.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the living conditions of Irish migrants in Liverpool in the 1840s were similar to the living conditions of Caribbean migrants in Notting Hill in the 1950s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were crowded into the worst housing available: cellars and courts in Liverpool, and houses of multiple occupation around Powis Square in Notting Hill.
• In both, overcrowding was blamed on the migrants themselves rather than on the landlords and the shortage of housing.
• In both, migrants had little choice of where to live - poverty in one case, the colour bar in the other - and paid a high price for the little that was on offer.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Anti-Catholic prejudice was the most important reason for hostility towards Irish migrants in 19th-century Liverpool.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1849 cholera epidemic
• the role of the Orange Order.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for anti-Catholic prejudice:
• Liverpool had a strong Orange Order tradition, and sectarian rioting flared at Orange parades and on St Patrick's Day.
• Mid-Victorian Britain was deeply anti-Catholic, so Irish newcomers were religious as well as ethnic outsiders.
• 'No Irish Need Apply' notices and stereotyped press cartoons drew on a Protestant British identity defined against Catholicism.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Public-health panic was decisive: the cholera epidemic of 1849 killed more than 5,000 people and the press blamed Irish migrants, five years before John Snow's Soho study proved cholera was waterborne.
• Economic competition mattered: overcrowding in courts and cellars fuelled fears that Irish labour would undercut local wages.
• The press multiplied prejudice, with Punch and local Liverpool papers depicting Irish migrants in dehumanising terms through the 1850s and 1860s.
• The sheer pace of arrival was a factor in itself: almost 300,000 destitute migrants landed in 1847 alone, which overwhelmed local relief whatever their religion.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (entrepot, Select Vestry, court housing, Orange Order).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Catholic Church mattered so much to Irish migrants in nineteenth-century Liverpool.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Catholic schools
• Father Nugent.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The diocese built churches, schools and convents faster than anywhere else in industrial Britain, because the Catholic population grew so fast.
• Father Nugent founded refuges, ragged schools and emigrant aid schemes that reached thousands of the Irish poor.
• Catholic schools educated the children of migrants and gave the second generation literacy and a route into skilled work.
• Catholic friendly societies provided sickness, funeral and unemployment relief when state provision was almost non-existent.
• The Church became a political base as well as a religious one: the Liverpool Scotland seat returned the Irish Nationalist T. P. O'Connor from 1885 until 1929.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Irish migrants in Liverpool were more integrated by 1900 than they had been in 1850.

You may use the following in your answer:
• trade unions
• the dock economy.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Catholic Church, friendly societies and trade unions gave migrants welfare, education and a way into civic life.
• The dock economy created a stable working community: by 1900 more than 60% of Liverpool dock workers were of Irish descent.
• Father Nugent's charitable networks helped turn the children of the poorest Famine arrivals into settled workers and voters.
• Political representation followed: the Liverpool Scotland seat returned the Irish Nationalist T. P. O'Connor from 1885 until his death in 1929.
• Continued migration from Ireland into the early 1900s kept the culture alive even as integration deepened, so identity was renewed rather than lost.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which crimes against property in the eighteenth century were different from crimes against property in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Eighteenth-century property crime was physical and local: armed riders stopped coaches on unlit roads, and gangs landed smuggled tea and brandy on Cornish, Sussex and Kent beaches.
• Twentieth-century property crime moved onto networks: phishing, identity theft and online fraud used the internet, and the Computer Misuse Act 1990 had to create the offence of unauthorised access.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why highway robbery declined in the nineteenth century.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the railways
• banking reform.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Turnpike trusts produced better-maintained, busier and better-lit roads, increasing the chance that a highwayman would be seen.
• Banking reform meant travellers increasingly carried bank notes and cheques rather than gold — less worth stealing.
• The Bow Street Runners’ mounted patrols, set up by the Fielding brothers from the late eighteenth century, swept the main routes out of London.
• From the 1830s railways allowed long-distance travellers to move at speed and entirely off the road network.
• Higher conviction rates as policing strengthened in the early nineteenth century made the crime higher-risk for the offender.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (turnpikes, banks, Bow Street Runners, railways) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the change without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the case of the Tolpuddle Martyrs in 1834 changed attitudes to organised labour in Britain.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Unlawful Oaths Act of 1797
• the national protest campaign.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• It exposed the use of an obscure 1797 Unlawful Oaths Act to prosecute farm labourers for forming a friendly society, when trade unions had been legal since 1824 — revealing how government could repurpose old laws to target organised labour.
• It triggered a major national protest: a London demonstration of around 100,000 in April 1834 and a petition of around 800,000 signatures.
• It led directly to the free pardon in 1836 and the Martyrs’ return by 1838 — an early example of mass campaigning forcing the government to overturn a court sentence.
• It legitimised the labour movement, making trade-union activity more publicly respectable in Victorian Britain.
• It illustrates the wider point that definitions of crime change as politics changes — what was prosecuted in 1834 was politically unthinkable a generation later.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (1797 Act, 800,000 petition, 1836 pardon) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the case without explaining importance.
