practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which smuggling in the eighteenth century was similar to poaching under the Norman Forest Laws.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Both were social crimes: smuggled tea and brandy were welcomed in Cornish and Kentish villages, and medieval villagers sheltered poachers rather than informing on them.
• Both were created by government decisions rather than by any change in behaviour — high customs duties in one case, the royal forest boundary in the other.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Changes in technology were the main reason for the changing definitions of crime in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Britain.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the spread of railways from the 1830s
• the Tolpuddle Martyrs.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks. The strongest answers reach a substantiated overall judgement.

Indicative content — arguments for technology as the main reason:
• Railways from the 1830s undercut highway robbery by moving long-distance travellers off the roads entirely.
• Banking technology — bank notes and cheques — meant travellers carried less gold; the target of highway robbery shrank.
• Turnpike roads, themselves a transport innovation, lit and policed key routes more effectively than older parish roads.
• Cheap printing made it cheaper to publish trial reports, exposing harsh sentences to a national audience and changing public attitudes.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors more important):
• Free-trade reforms in the 1840s, not technology, removed the profit margin from smuggling and effectively killed the trade.
• The decriminalisation of witchcraft in 1736 reflected a change in elite legal opinion, not technology.
• The Tolpuddle Martyrs case turned on a political decision to revive an old oath law and on a national protest campaign — political and social factors, not technological ones.
• Industrial Britain’s redefinition of trade-union activity as legitimate followed broader political change (1832 Reform Act, working-class organisation) rather than any single technology.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs technology against at least one other factor, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the treatment of protest in the nineteenth century was different from its treatment in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• In 1834 six Dorset labourers were prosecuted under an obscure 1797 oath law and sentenced to seven years' transportation for forming a friendly society.
• By the twentieth century trade unions were respectable and legal, and those who defied the state over conscription were dealt with by tribunals rather than transportation.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Tlaxcalan alliance for the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Tlaxcalan alliance, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The Tlaxcalans, an independent Nahua state who had resisted Aztec domination for generations, supplied tens of thousands of warriors who did the bulk of the fighting in the campaigns of 1519–21.
• They gave Cortes local intelligence on Aztec politics, geography and tribute structures — intelligence the small Spanish force could not have gathered for itself.
• Tlaxcalan territory provided refuge after La Noche Triste in June 1520 and the workforce that helped build the thirteen brigantines used in the siege of Tenochtitlan.
• The alliance reframes the conquest as a coalition victory rather than a Spanish solo achievement — which is exactly the analytical move historians like Matthew Restall reward.
• The Tlaxcalans negotiated favourable terms after the conquest — their city kept its autonomy under New Spain — demonstrating that they were genuine allies, not subjects.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. military numbers AND political/strategic intelligence) with specific period detail (Tlaxcala’s independence, the brigantines, La Noche Triste). Clear analytical framing that the conquest was a coalition.
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Tlaxcalans without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of La Noche Triste (30 June 1520).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Spanish lost over half their force, most of their treasure and much of their artillery as they were driven out of Tenochtitlan along the causeways.
• The death of Montezuma during the uprising removed the Spaniards’ political route to ruling through a hostage emperor.
• Cortes was forced to retreat into Tlaxcalan territory and rebuild from scratch, depending heavily on his Indigenous allies for survival.
• The setback delayed the conquest by almost a year, giving smallpox time to arrive in Tenochtitlan in autumn 1520 — a delay that may, paradoxically, have helped the Spanish coalition by gutting Aztec leadership.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the Sad Night without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the smallpox epidemic in Tenochtitlan in autumn 1520.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• The new Aztec emperor Cuitlahuac, who had led the resistance on La Noche Triste, died of smallpox after only 80 days on the throne — depriving the Aztecs of an experienced military leader before the final siege.
• The disease devastated Tenochtitlan’s leadership, military commanders, priests and population, weakening the city before the Spanish coalition returned in 1521.
• It changed the demographic balance of the war — the Tlaxcalans and other allies were less affected because the disease had not yet reached their populations in the same numbers.
• It made it possible for the Spanish to claim divine favour, since they did not understand that they had unwittingly carried the disease to the city.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the smallpox epidemic without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the events of 1519–21 led to the fall of Tenochtitlan. You may use the following in your answer: the Tlaxcalan alliance (1519), the smallpox epidemic in Tenochtitlan (autumn 1520). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Cortes’s landing at Vera Cruz in April 1519, defying his governor Velazquez, was followed by a brief war with the independent Nahua state of Tlaxcala, which then accepted alliance with him — turning a small Spanish force into a coalition army of tens of thousands.
• Because of this alliance, Cortes could march on Tenochtitlan and meet Montezuma in November 1519 — seizing the emperor as a hostage and ruling through him for several months.
• The massacre at the festival of Toxcatl by Pedro de Alvarado in May 1520 provoked a full Aztec uprising; on La Noche Triste (30 June 1520) the Spanish were driven out, Montezuma killed, and Cortes lost more than half his men.
• This in turn forced Cortes back into Tlaxcalan territory to rebuild — and gave smallpox, which arrived in Tenochtitlan in autumn 1520, time to gut the Aztec leadership and kill the new emperor Cuitlahuac after only 80 days on the throne.
• Because of all this, when Cortes returned in 1521 with thirteen brigantines and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan warriors, he faced a city already weakened by epidemic, without experienced commanders, and isolated from its tribute peoples — and Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with clear linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Toxcatl massacre, Cuauhtemoc, the brigantines). Reaches an analytical overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of La Malinche (Dona Marina) for the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of La Malinche, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• La Malinche spoke both Nahuatl and a Mayan language, giving Cortes a translation chain (through Geronimo de Aguilar) into Aztec politics that no Spanish-only force could have achieved.
• She brokered the alliance with Tlaxcala — without translators, the brief war could not have been ended in negotiation, and the coalition that won the conquest could not have been built.
• She read political signals at the meeting with Montezuma in November 1519 and is credited with detecting an ambush at Cholula that allowed the Spanish to strike first.
• Indigenous sources show her as a recognised political actor in her own right — not as a passive interpreter — making the conquest a story of named Indigenous agency rather than Spanish solo action.
• Modern historians like Camilla Townsend cite her as evidence that the conquest was a coalition project — the analytical framing top-band answers reward.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (Aguilar, Tlaxcala, Cholula, Townsend’s framing).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of La Malinche without explaining her importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 for the Spanish empire in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the fall of Tenochtitlan, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• It ended the Mexica imperial state — the largest political organisation Europeans had ever fought against in the Americas — and replaced it with New Spain, the first Spanish mainland colony.
• The destruction of Tenochtitlan and the founding of Mexico City on its ruins gave Spain a continental capital from which the rest of Mesoamerica could be subdued.
• The vast tribute system the Mexica had built was inherited by the Spanish — encomiendas were granted to conquistadors over Indigenous communities that had paid tribute to Tenochtitlan, an instant labour and revenue base.
• The conquest gave the conquistadors a model that Pizarro would copy in Peru — coalition with disaffected subject peoples, exploitation of internal divisions, capture of a capital city.
• It opened the door to the silver mines of New Spain (and, after 1545, Potosi in Peru) and to the long-term shape of Spanish America: Catholic, Spanish-speaking, ruled from a former Indigenous capital.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (Mexico City, encomienda, the link forward to Peru and Potosi).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the fall of Tenochtitlan without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. Malcolm X on his changed views in February 1965, a week before his assassination.

‘The point I want to make is that since I have been back from Mecca, since I have seen the brotherhood that exists in the religion of Islam, I have changed. I no longer believe that all white people are devils. The system in this country that produces racism — that I will fight, by any means necessary. But I will work with anyone, of whatever colour, who is genuinely interested in attacking that system. The Nation of Islam taught me one thing. The Hajj taught me another.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about Malcolm X’s views in February 1965.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘Malcolm had abandoned the Nation of Islam’s teaching that all white people were evil’ supported by ‘I no longer believe that all white people are devils’ AND ‘Malcolm now distinguished individual white people from a racist system, which he intended to keep fighting’ supported by ‘The system in this country that produces racism — that I will fight, by any means necessary’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1992 popular biography of Martin Luther King):
‘Malcolm X was the opposite of King in everything that mattered. King wanted integration; Malcolm wanted separation. King preached love of the enemy; Malcolm preached self-defence by any means necessary. King appealed to the conscience of white America; Malcolm dismissed that conscience as a fiction. They were two roads, and the country had to choose one.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2011 history of Malcolm X drawing on his last year):
‘The static contrast between Malcolm and King fails after April 1964. Malcolm’s Hajj convinced him that race could be remade across colour lines. He founded the OAAU as an internationalist civil-rights organisation, travelled to Selma in support of the SCLC, and met SNCC organisers in Harlem. By February 1965 the two men were closer than at any earlier point.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about Malcolm X’s relationship to Martin Luther King? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees Malcolm and King as static opposites whose visions could not be reconciled; Interpretation 2 sees a convergence after April 1964 in which Malcolm’s Hajj, the founding of the OAAU and his contact with the Selma campaign brought him closer to the SCLC) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘Malcolm X was the opposite of King in everything that mattered’ vs ‘By February 1965 the two men were closer than at any earlier point’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about Malcolm X.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is taken from a 1992 biography of Martin Luther King and naturally focuses on Malcolm’s public Nation-of-Islam years that contrasted most sharply with King, drawing largely on King’s papers and Malcolm’s pre-1964 speeches; Interpretation 2 is taken from a 2011 study of Malcolm’s last year that uses OAAU records, his Hajj letters, FBI surveillance files of his African travels and accounts of his Selma visit. The two have different focuses (the Nation period vs the post-Hajj period) and different bodies of evidence.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about Malcolm X’s relationship to Martin Luther King?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context. Marks will be awarded for the quality of your written communication, including spelling, punctuation, grammar and your use of specialist terms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across Malcolm’s Nation years and his post-Hajj year (membership of the Nation of Islam from prison; the doctrine of separatism and ‘blue-eyed devils’; growth of the Nation from 400 to around 50,000 between 1952 and 1959; rejection of the 1963 March on Washington as ‘the Farce on Washington’; the ‘chickens coming home to roost’ remark of December 1963; Elijah Muhammad’s suspension; Malcolm’s personal break with the Nation; the April 1964 Hajj and the name el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz; the founding of the OAAU; the Capitol meeting with King on 26 March 1964; the Selma visit of February 1965; the assassination at the Audubon Ballroom on 21 February 1965; the post-1966 Black Power movement’s claim of his legacy), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently. SPaG is consistently accurate, with sophisticated use of subject-specific terminology.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated. SPaG is generally accurate with appropriate subject-specific terminology.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit. SPaG is reasonable with some subject-specific terminology.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. SPaG is uneven; subject-specific terminology limited. [16 marks for content + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Malcolm X broke with the Nation of Islam in 1963-64.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the ‘chickens coming home to roost’ remark
• the Hajj of 1964

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. Malcolm’s discovery of Elijah Muhammad’s sexual relationships with Nation secretaries which contradicted the Nation’s teaching of strict discipline; the ninety-day suspension after the Kennedy comment; Malcolm’s growing political ambition for an organisation that could engage with the wider civil rights movement and African independence; the experience of Sunni Islam at Mecca contradicting the Nation’s race theology), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (Nation of Islam, Hajj, OAAU, el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From a 1964 letter Malcolm X wrote home from Mecca during his Hajj, later quoted in his Autobiography (1965).

‘Never have I witnessed such sincere hospitality and overwhelming spirit of true brotherhood as is practiced by people of all colors and races here in this Ancient Holy Land. We were truly all the same — brothers — because their belief in one God had removed the “white” from their minds, the “white” from their behavior, and the “white” from their attitude. I have eaten from the same plate, drunk from the same glass, and slept on the same rug — while praying to the same God — with fellow Muslims, whose eyes were the bluest of blue, whose hair was the blondest of blond, and whose skin was the whitest of white.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the Hajj’s effect on Malcolm X.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘The Hajj convinced Malcolm that the Nation of Islam’s teaching about white people was wrong’ supported by ‘fellow Muslims, whose eyes were the bluest of blue, whose hair was the blondest of blond, and whose skin was the whitest of white’ AND ‘Malcolm experienced lived multi-ethnic religious community for the first time in his life’ supported by ‘I have eaten from the same plate, drunk from the same glass, and slept on the same rug’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of War Communism on Russian society between 1918 and 1921. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, the fall in Petrograd’s population from 2.4 million to 750,000, the 20 per cent of 1913 industrial output, the grain requisitioning detachments, the part-cash part-rations wages, peasants ceasing to sow a surplus). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that War Communism produced a withdrawal of the cities and a peasant strike against the regime. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Lenin replaced War Communism with the New Economic Policy in March 1921.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Kronstadt Mutiny
• the 1921 famine
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. Kronstadt and the Tambov rising as a peasant strike against requisitioning, the 1921 famine on the Volga, the strikes in Petrograd, the collapse of industrial output, Lenin’s judgement that peasant revolt was more dangerous than the Whites had been, and the political logic of buying peasant compliance with the tax in kind). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — War Communism, tax in kind, Tenth Party Congress, Nepmen. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of War Communism without explaining why it was abandoned. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about Bolshevik social policy on women and the family in the 1920s.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues that Bolshevik legislation on women, family law, abortion and education was genuinely transformative for Soviet women in the 1920s; the other argues that the radical laws were largely urban and that rural reality changed slowly, with most early gains rolled back under Stalin in the 1930s). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the success of the New Economic Policy.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (state grain output statistics versus party debate records and Trotsky’s critiques); they wrote at different times (1920s NEP-era surveys versus post-1991 archival studies); or they had different purposes (defending Lenin’s legacy versus reconstructing the Bolshevik factional debate around Bukharin and Trotsky). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the impact of Bolshevik policies on women between 1917 and 1924?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of Bolshevik social policy — the legalisation of abortion in 1920, the simplification of divorce, equal pay legislation, Kollontai’s reforms at the Commissariat for Social Welfare, Lunacharsky’s schools and the Likbez literacy drive — weighed against the slow rural take-up, the limited reach of communal kitchens and the eventual rollback of many reforms under Stalin. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the New Economic Policy was a temporary retreat rather than a return to capitalism?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the tax in kind on peasants, the legalisation of small workshops and trade, the Nepmen, the state retaining heavy industry, banks, transport and foreign trade, Lenin’s ‘state capitalism’ and ‘temporary tactical retreat’ framing, and Bukharin’s defence of the NEP as a road to socialism via the peasantry — weighed against the ‘return to capitalism’ reading pressed by the party’s hardliners. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Sovnarkom, NEP, tax in kind, Nepmen, Likbez). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Pontiac’s Rebellion (1763–64) for British policy in North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: the rebellion led directly to the Proclamation Act of October 1763, which closed land west of the Appalachians to colonial settlement to reduce frontier violence; it also led to a permanent garrison of British regulars in the new western territories, which colonists then resented and were taxed to support. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to British policy decisions.
Emerging: Notes that the rebellion happened without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Sugar Act (1764) for relations between Britain and the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: the Sugar Act mattered because it moved smuggling cases out of friendly colonial juries into vice-admiralty courts, ending the customary impunity of New England merchants; it also mattered because James Otis’s pamphlet attacking it argued that Parliament could not tax colonists who sent no members to it, an argument that framed the Stamp Act crisis the following year. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus; limited use of specific developments.
Emerging: Describes the Act without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Paxton Boys’ actions in 1763–64 for Pennsylvania politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the December 1763 massacre of the Conestoga undermined Pennsylvania’s reputation for Quaker peaceful relations with Indigenous peoples and exposed the assembly’s weak grip on the backcountry; the February 1764 march on Philadelphia forced Benjamin Franklin to negotiate a settlement, which gave western settlers louder voices in colonial debate without producing prosecutions for the killings. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the events.
Emerging: Mentions the Paxton Boys without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of post-war British debt for the development of policy towards the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the £130 million debt mattered because interest alone consumed half the annual budget, driving Grenville’s ministry to seek revenue from the colonies through the Sugar Act and later the Stamp Act; it also mattered because the cost of garrisoning the new western territories made an end to salutary neglect financially urgent. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Notes the debt without showing how it shaped policy.
Emerging: Describes the war without explaining the financial consequences.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how relations between Britain and the colonies deteriorated in the years 1763–64. You may use the following information in your answer:
• Pontiac’s Rebellion
• The Sugar Act of 1764
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why relations deteriorated rather than narrating in sequence. Links Pontiac’s Rebellion to the Proclamation Act and the resentment of land-hungry settlers; links the Sugar Act’s vice-admiralty courts to the protests of New England merchants and James Otis’s pamphlet; brings in own knowledge such as the standing army of 10,000 troops, the cost of the war, or the Paxton Boys massacre. Reaches an analytical judgement about how frontier and tax grievances reinforced each other.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists events without explaining how relations deteriorated.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of relations with Indigenous peoples for British policy after 1763.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the threat posed by Pontiac’s Rebellion mattered because it forced Britain to issue the Proclamation Act of 1763, which placed the western interior under imperial supervision and angered colonial speculators; the standing army needed to police those lands then mattered because it had to be paid for, and that drove the very tax measures the colonies came to resent. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions Indigenous peoples without showing how they shaped British policy.
Emerging: General references to the frontier without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the PFLP airplane hijacks (1970) for international attitudes towards the Palestine issue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the Dawson’s Field hijackings put the Palestinian cause on global front pages but shifted Western public sympathy away from the Palestinians as the tactic of mass-hostage-taking became the visible face of the movement; the same hijackings forced King Hussein to confront the PLO on his own soil, leading to Black September and the PLO’s expulsion from Jordan, which moved the Palestinian leadership’s base into Lebanon and changed the regional balance; Western governments introduced permanent passenger and luggage screening at airports, normalising counter-terrorism in everyday life. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the hijackings without showing why they mattered for international attitudes. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Yom Kippur War (1973) for the future of the conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Egyptian forces crossing the Suez Canal restored Arab honour and gave Sadat the political authority to negotiate from a position of equality, opening the diplomatic track to Camp David in 1978; UN Resolution 338 reactivated the ‘land for peace’ principle of Resolution 242 for the first time since Khartoum; US shuttle diplomacy led by Kissinger established the United States as the indispensable mediator and froze the Soviet Union out of the post-war settlement. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the war without showing why it mattered for the future of the conflict. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Black September (1970) for the PLO.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. expulsion from Jordan removed the PLO’s state-within-a-state base on Israel’s longest border and forced its leadership and fighters into Lebanon, where they would be drawn into the Lebanese Civil War from 1975; the loss of safe territory pushed PLO factions towards spectacular international terrorism in the early 1970s, including Munich; the militant group named after the expulsion carried the trauma of 1970 directly into the 1972 Munich attack. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Black September without showing why it mattered for the PLO. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Munich Olympics attack (September 1972).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the death of eleven Israeli athletes broadcast live to a worldwide audience hardened Western public opinion against terrorism as a Palestinian tactic and led Arafat to begin distancing the PLO from international attacks by 1974; (ii) Israel launched ‘Operation Wrath of God’, a years-long campaign of targeted killings of those it held responsible, normalising the use of cross-border assassination in Israeli security policy. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the attack without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Sadat’s expulsion of Soviet military advisers from Egypt (July 1972).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) it freed Sadat from the constraint of being treated as a Soviet client and made it possible for the United States to mediate after the Yom Kippur War without Cold War objections, paving the way for Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy; (ii) it persuaded Israeli intelligence that Egypt was militarily weakened and contributed to the Cabinet’s mistaken belief in October 1973 that Sadat would not actually launch an attack — the intelligence failure that opened the Yom Kippur War. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the expulsion without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing developments in the Arab-Israeli conflict in the years 1967–73.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the PFLP hijacks at Dawson’s Field (September 1970)
• the Yom Kippur War (October 1973)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the War of Attrition along the Suez Canal; the PFLP hijacks and Black September expulsion; the Munich Olympics attack and its effect on international opinion; Sadat’s expulsion of Soviet advisers in 1972; the Yom Kippur War and Resolution 338). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material from the student’s own knowledge. Connects events through causation rather than just sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence; little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Interdict’s impact on everyday life in England 1208–14.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features are required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Suspension of public Mass — church doors were locked, bells silenced, and the central act of medieval worship withdrawn from ordinary parishes.
• Burial outside consecrated ground — the bodies of the dead could not be buried in churchyards; corpses were placed in unconsecrated pits or roadside ditches.
• Marriages unblessed — couples could not have a church wedding; many lived as husband and wife without legal religious status.
• Exile of bishops — many of England’s senior clergy fled abroad rather than continue under royal pressure, leaving dioceses leaderless.
• Continued baptism and last rites — baptism for infants and confession for the dying were usually still permitted, so the most basic life-cycle rites continued.
• Royal seizure of Church lands — the king took over the temporalities of fugitive bishops, draining them for revenue and altering the local economy.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the dispute between John and Innocent III over the see of Canterbury.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Rival candidates — the Canterbury monks elected Reginald in secret in 1205; John forced them to elect his nominee John de Gray; both appealed to Rome.
• Innocent III’s choice of Stephen Langton — in 1207 the Pope rejected both candidates and imposed an English-born theologian teaching in Paris.
• John’s seizure of Canterbury lands — the king confiscated the cathedral chapter’s estates and drove the monks into exile.
• Innocent III’s response of interdict — in March 1208 the Pope placed England under interdict to compel acceptance.
• Personal excommunication of John — in November 1209 Innocent excommunicated the king himself.
• Threat of deposition — in 1212 the Pope declared John deposed and authorised Philip II to enforce the sentence by invasion.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John quarrelled with Pope Innocent III between 1205 and 1208.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Canterbury monks
• Stephen Langton
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• The Canterbury monks — in 1205 they secretly elected one of their own, Reginald, before John could impose his candidate, opening a contested election.
• John’s nominee — he forced through the election of John de Gray, Bishop of Norwich, an experienced royal administrator, and refused to accept any rival candidate.
• Stephen Langton’s appointment — in 1207 Innocent III rejected both nominees and imposed Langton, an Englishman teaching in Paris and a leading theologian.
• The principle of royal nomination — John insisted that the king had the customary right to nominate the Archbishop of Canterbury and treated Langton’s elevation as a frontal challenge.
• Innocent III’s ambition — the Pope had already imposed his will on Philip II of France and on German rulers and intended to demonstrate papal authority over royal nomination in England as well.
• Money — vacant sees and confiscated chapter lands generated huge royal revenue, and John was reluctant to surrender that windfall.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John submitted to Pope Innocent III in 1213.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the threat of French invasion
• the plot of 1212
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Threat of French invasion — in 1213 Philip II had assembled a fleet to enforce John’s deposition; submission turned a French invasion into an attack on a papal fief.
• Papal deposition of 1212 — Innocent III had declared John deposed; only submission could reverse the sentence.
• The 1212 baronial plot — the discovery of FitzWalter and de Vesci’s assassination plot showed how thin John’s domestic support had become.
• Domestic religious damage — six years of Interdict had eroded the king’s standing; reconciliation restored normal religious life and royal legitimacy.
• Need to focus on Normandy — John was preparing the campaign that ended at Bouvines in 1214; he could not fight Pope, France and barons at once.
• Tactical brilliance of resigning England as a papal fief — turning Innocent III from John’s greatest enemy into his protector at the cost of a 1,000-mark annual tribute.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Interdict had a serious impact on the people of England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• burial in consecrated ground
• the length of the Interdict
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Centrality of the Mass — the celebration of the Eucharist was the heart of medieval worship; its suspension cut the rhythm of every Sunday and feast day.
• Burial in consecrated ground — the dead could no longer be buried in churchyards; corpses were placed in unconsecrated pits, distressing relatives and disturbing communities.
• Marriage and life-cycle rites — church weddings were forbidden, leaving couples in legal limbo and the Church’s social role weakened.
• Length of the punishment — six years from March 1208 to July 1214, long enough that a generation of children grew up without normal Christian community life.
• Exile of clergy — many bishops fled abroad, leaving dioceses without leadership and royal officials taking over Church estates.
• Royal extortion — John used the Interdict to seize Church lands and intensify tallages, especially on the Anglo-Jewish community in 1210, redistributing pain across society.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The reconciliation between John and Innocent III in 1213 was the most significant event of John’s reign.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the threat of French invasion
• the annulment of Magna Carta
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Threat of French invasion — submission converted Philip II’s 1213 fleet from a deposing army into the unwelcome aggressor against a papal fief.
• Annulment of Magna Carta — Innocent III, now John’s overlord, annulled the charter within ten weeks of Runnymede in August 1215, prolonging the king’s reign and unleashing the First Barons’ War.
• Restoration of religious life — the Interdict was lifted in July 1214 and English Christianity resumed normal function, restoring the king’s legitimacy.
• The legal status of England as a papal fief survived John, binding successive English kings to a continental overlord and shaping later disputes.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• The loss of Normandy in 1204 was the underlying disaster of the reign — without the financial and political fallout of 1204, the rest of the crises would not have followed.
• Magna Carta of 1215 was the more famous outcome and the more lasting constitutional event.
• The 1207 thirteenth was a more original administrative innovation.
• The murder of Arthur of Brittany in 1203 had earlier and more permanent consequences for John’s standing in France.
• The defeat at Bouvines on 27 July 1214 ended any prospect of recovering Normandy and was the trigger for the baronial rebellion.
• Magna Carta itself, even after annulment, set out grievances that shaped English politics for centuries.

Overall judgement: The 1213 reconciliation was an extraordinary tactical reversal that bound papal authority to John’s defence and made possible the annulment of Magna Carta. But it cannot be called the most significant event of the reign. The loss of Normandy in 1204 created the financial pressure that drove the rest of the reign; Magna Carta crystallised the political legacy. The reconciliation was decisive in 1213–15 but secondary in long-term significance to the events of 1204 and 1215. A balanced judgement weighs the immediate brilliance of 1213 against the longer arc of loss and constitutional reform.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (interdict, excommunication, papal legate, fief, demesne, scutage).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Jewish migration to Britain after 1881 was similar to Huguenot migration after 1685.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both were driven out by religious persecution: the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, and the pogroms that followed the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881.
• Both settled in the same corner of east London and worked in the same kind of trade, silk weaving for the Huguenots and tailoring for Jewish migrants.
• Both built their own religious and welfare institutions, from stranger churches to synagogues and the Jewish Board of Guardians.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Eastern European Jewish migrants came to Britain between c1880 and 1914.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the pogroms
• the East End sweated trades.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Religious persecution was the main push: pogroms in the Russian Empire intensified after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in March 1881.
• The May Laws of 1882 restricted where Jews could live, work and study, which made emigration the only realistic future for many families.
• The East End sweated trades offered immediate piece-rate work in tailoring or cap-making without any English.
• An existing Anglo-Jewish community meant synagogues, the Jewish Board of Guardians and mutual-aid societies could absorb new arrivals.
• America was more expensive to reach; many families meant to travel on and settled in the East End instead.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of the press in shaping attitudes to migrants before 1914 was similar to its role after 1945.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• In both periods the press framed migrants as a threat to housing, wages and public health, from 'destitute aliens' in the 1890s to coverage of Commonwealth and EU migration after 1945.
• In both, mass-circulation papers reached a new and larger audience, the Daily Mail from 1896 and the post-war tabloids.
• In both, press campaigns fed directly into legislation: the Aliens Act of 1905, and the Commonwealth Immigrants Acts of 1962 and 1968.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The role of the media was the most important reason for the passing of the 1905 Aliens Act.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the British Brothers’ League
• the East End sweated trades.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for the role of the media:
• Newspapers framed Jewish migration as an alien invasion through the 1880s and 1890s, and the Daily Mail from 1896 carried that message to a mass readership.
• Press coverage of the Royal Commission on Alien Immigration of 1902-03 amplified hostile testimony and kept the issue in front of the public.
• Stereotyped and often antisemitic cartoons made the argument in a form that reached readers who followed no politics.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• The British Brothers' League, founded in the East End in May 1901 by William Stanley Shaw and championed in Parliament by Major William Evans-Gordon, MP for Stepney, organised the local campaign.
• Economic competition in the sweated trades fuelled fears that cheap labour would undercut local wages.
• The Conservative government under Arthur Balfour saw electoral advantage in restriction; the Act was a political calculation, not only a response to the press.
• Antisemitic prejudice predated the press campaign and shaped how the stories were received.
• The cumulative arrival of around 150,000 migrants over two decades created a felt pressure in the East End that no single factor explains.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (pogrom, sweated trades, alien, denization, restriction).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Aliens Act was passed in 1905.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the British Brothers' League
• the role of the press.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Around 150,000 Jewish migrants had arrived between 1881 and 1914, and the concentration in a few East End streets made the change highly visible.
• The British Brothers' League, founded in the East End in May 1901 by William Stanley Shaw, held mass rallies demanding restriction and found a champion in Major William Evans-Gordon, MP for Stepney.
• Newspapers, including the Daily Mail from 1896, ran sustained scare stories about 'destitute aliens' undermining British wages and housing.
• The Royal Commission on Alien Immigration of 1902-03 gave the campaign an official platform and its findings a public airing.
• The Conservative government under Arthur Balfour saw an electoral advantage in acting, and the Act's exemptions for cabin-class passengers show the target was poor Jewish migrants specifically.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the East End of London became the focus of Jewish settlement in this period.

You may use the following in your answer:
• cheap tenement housing
• the existing Anglo-Jewish community.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• An existing Anglo-Jewish community provided synagogues, the Jewish Board of Guardians and welfare societies that could absorb arrivals.
• The sweated trades of tailoring, cap-making and boot-making offered piece-rate work that needed no English.
• Cheap tenement housing in Whitechapel, Spitalfields and Stepney was within reach of destitute newcomers.
• Yiddish newspapers, theatres and religious schools reinforced the area's identity as a Jewish neighbourhood.
• Trade-union organisation, including the Hebrew Cabinet Makers' Association and the Jewish tailors' unions, gave migrant workers a stake in the wider labour movement.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the case of Elizabeth Barton, the Nun of Kent.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Was a Benedictine nun who began receiving visions in 1525 and had previously been respected by Archbishop Warham and Henry VIII himself.
• After 1532 prophesied that Henry would die within a month if he married Anne Boleyn.
• Was arrested by Cromwell in November 1533 and forced to confess at Paul’s Cross that her visions were fabricated.
• Was condemned by Act of Attainder in early 1534 — without a formal trial.
• Was hanged at Tyburn on 20 April 1534, alongside five male supporters including her confessor Edward Bocking.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Thomas More’s opposition to the Reformation.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for each feature. Indicative content: • Resigned as Lord Chancellor in May 1532, the day after the Submission of the Clergy. • Refused to swear the preamble of the 1534 Oath of Succession because it denied papal authority — though he accepted the succession itself. • Took refuge in legal silence, arguing that silence implied no opinion (qui tacet consentire videtur). • Was held in the Tower of London for fifteen months from April 1534. • Was convicted of treason on 1 July 1535 on the disputed testimony of Sir Richard Rich, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535. Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail. Secure: Two features with relevant detail. Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate. Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why John Fisher was executed in 1535.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the oath of supremacy
• Pope Paul III
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Refusal of the oath — Fisher would not swear the 1534 Oath of Succession because its preamble denied papal authority.
• Defence of Catherine of Aragon — he had been her confessor and her most articulate public defender at Blackfriars in 1529.
• Cardinal’s hat — Pope Paul III made Fisher a cardinal in May 1535 while he was imprisoned in the Tower; the move infuriated Henry and made an execution politically symbolic.
• The 1534 Treason Act — made denial of the supremacy a capital offence; Fisher’s refusal therefore brought him within the law’s reach.
• Cromwell’s strategy — the regime needed an example of episcopal resistance crushed to deter other bishops; Fisher was the only one who openly resisted.
• Personal credibility — as a 65-year-old theologian of European reputation, Fisher could not be silenced by intimidation alone.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description of events without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Elizabeth Barton was a serious threat to Henry VIII’s government.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Anne Boleyn
• the Act of Attainder
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the threat Barton posed against her weaknesses and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments that she was a serious threat:
• Her prophecy that Henry would die within a month of marrying Anne Boleyn struck at the new queen and at the annulment itself.
• She had been taken seriously by Archbishop Warham and by Wolsey, and had spoken with the king in person.
• Her prophecies spread through London and into the houses of leading Catholics, giving opposition a popular voice.
• The regime thought a public confession and then an Act of Attainder were both necessary, which suggests it took her seriously.

Arguments that the threat was limited:
• She had no armed following and no political programme beyond her visions.
• The forced confession at Paul’s Cross destroyed her credibility before Parliament acted.
• Condemnation by attainder, without a contested trial, shows how easily the regime could dispose of her.
• Her execution provoked no rising; the first serious revolt came only with the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536.

Overall judgement: Barton mattered less for what she could do than for what she showed — that religious opposition could reach the political nation — which is why Cromwell made an example of her. Top-band answers weigh these points and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why opposition from Sir Thomas More was important between 1532 and 1535.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Oath of Succession
• Sir Richard Rich
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons. Indicative content: • Standing of the dissenter — More was a former Lord Chancellor and humanist of European reputation, lending opposition unmatched moral weight. • Resignation in 1532 — coming the day after the Submission of the Clergy, it signalled to Europe that the most senior layman in the kingdom regarded the new policy as incompatible with conscience. • Oath of Succession — More accepted the succession itself but refused the preamble denying papal authority; this distinction made the case about royal supremacy, not the marriage. • Legal sophistication — his appeal to silence (qui tacet consentire videtur) forced the regime to legislate against silent dissent in the 1534 Treason Act. • Sir Richard Rich’s testimony — the conviction depended on disputed reported speech, exposing the political nature of treason prosecutions. • European reaction — the deaths of More and Fisher became propaganda gifts to Catholic powers; Charles V used them in diplomatic correspondence. • Catholic memory — More’s reported last words, ‘the king’s good servant, but God’s first’, became a touchstone of English Catholic identity for centuries. • Demonstration effect — the execution warned everyone in the political nation that even the most sophisticated legal evasion would not protect a refuser. Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout. Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation. Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘Cromwell’s response to opposition between 1533 and 1535 succeeded mainly because of the use of new treason laws.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Elizabeth Barton
• Thomas Cranmer
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the treason laws against alternative explanations and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘mainly the treason laws’:
• The 1534 Treason Act made denial of the supremacy in word or writing a capital offence, giving Cromwell a legal weapon previous regimes had lacked.
• The Act made it possible to prosecute More on the basis of reported private conversation (Rich’s testimony).
• The Acts of Succession (1534) and Supremacy (1534) created the obligation that the Treason Act enforced; together they formed a system.
• The Act of Attainder against Barton allowed condemnation without contested trial, removing legal cover from prophetic dissent.
• High-profile executions of More, Fisher and the Carthusian priors deterred lesser-known potential dissenters.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Elizabeth Barton case — succeeded partly because Cromwell forced a public confession at Paul’s Cross, breaking her credibility before parliamentary action.
• Thomas Cranmer’s role — ecclesiastical legitimacy from the Archbishop of Canterbury was needed alongside legal coercion; the 1536 Ten Articles and royal injunctions reshaped parish life beyond the courts.
• Information networks — Cromwell built informer systems through bishops, JPs and royal commissioners that identified dissent before it became organised.
• Henry VIII’s personal will — G.W. Bernard argues the king himself drove the radicalism; the laws codified what Henry already wanted.
• Pope Paul III’s misjudgement — making Fisher a cardinal in 1535 effectively forced Henry’s hand and turned a deterrent prosecution into an international cause célèbre.
• Public order — the relative passivity of the wider population (until the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536) was as important as legal coercion in keeping the regime stable.

Overall judgement: the treason laws were necessary but not sufficient. Cromwell succeeded because legal coercion, ecclesiastical reform under Cranmer, parish-level injunctions, information networks and the king’s personal will all reinforced each other. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English fleet that fought the Spanish Armada in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Race-built galleons designed by John Hawkins — lower hulls, no high ‘castles’ at bow and stern, faster and more manoeuvrable than older galleons.
• Long-range gunnery — English guns could fire broadsides at greater distance, allowing the fleet to attack the Armada without grappling and boarding on Spanish terms.
• Experienced commanders under Lord Howard of Effingham — with Drake as vice-admiral and Hawkins and Frobisher leading squadrons.
• Use of fireships — eight unmanned ships filled with pitch and gunpowder were set adrift into the Spanish fleet at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the fireships at Calais were so important to the English victory.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Spanish crescent formation
• the planned meeting with Parma
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• They broke the Spanish formation — the disciplined crescent had survived a week of running battles in the Channel; the fireships forced Spanish captains to cut anchors and scatter.
• They prevented the Parma rendezvous — with the fleet broken and pushed away from Calais, there was no longer a coherent force to escort Parma’s barges across the Channel.
• They exposed the Armada to Gravelines — the next day Lord Howard’s fleet caught the disordered Spanish ships at close range and hammered them with broadsides for eight hours.
• They cost the Spanish their anchors — ships that had cut cables off Calais were unable to anchor again on the storm-bound coasts of Scotland and Ireland on the way home.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Spanish Armada failed in 1588.
You may use the following in your answer:
• English ship design
• the storms after the campaign
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• English ship design (stimulus) — Hawkins’s race-built galleons were faster, more manoeuvrable and carried longer-range guns, allowing English squadrons to attack from a safe distance and avoid the Spanish boarding tactics.
• Storms (stimulus) — September gales around Scotland and Ireland wrecked roughly two dozen ships and drowned thousands; the storms turned a defeat into a disaster.
• Fireships at Calais (own knowledge) — on the night of 7–8 August 1588, Lord Howard’s eight fireships broke the Spanish crescent formation, costing them their anchors and exposing them to Gravelines the next day.
• Failure of the Parma rendezvous (own knowledge) — there was no deep-water port for the Armada to wait in, the Dutch Sea Beggars were blockading the Flemish coast, and Parma’s barges were not ready.
• Spanish leadership and supply problems (own knowledge) — Medina Sidonia had no naval experience and admitted it in writing; Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid had destroyed seasoned wood for water casks, so supplies leaked and spoiled at sea.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important reason the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588 was the English fireships at Calais.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• English ship design and gunnery
• the storms after Gravelines
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (fireships as decisive):
• The fireships broke the Spanish crescent formation at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588 — the formation that had survived every Channel battle.
• They prevented any link-up with Parma’s 30,000 troops, removing the entire purpose of the campaign.
• They cost the Spanish their anchors and exposed them to the Gravelines bombardment the following day.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• English ship design and gunnery (stimulus) — Hawkins’s race-built galleons and long-range broadsides made the running Channel battles winnable; without that, the fireships would have followed a coherent Spanish victory rather than a stalemate.
• Storms after Gravelines (stimulus) — September gales around Scotland and Ireland turned defeat into catastrophe, but they hit a fleet already broken; arguably they magnified the result rather than caused it.
• Failure of the Parma rendezvous (own knowledge) — the absence of a deep-water Flemish port and the Dutch Sea Beggars’ blockade meant the rendezvous would have failed even without the fireships.
• Spanish supply and leadership failures (own knowledge) — Medina Sidonia’s inexperience and the leaking unseasoned casks (a legacy of Cadiz 1587) weakened the fleet across the whole campaign.

Justified judgement: The fireships were the tactical hinge — they turned a stalemate into a defeat. But they only succeeded because English race-built ships had kept the campaign alive long enough, because the Parma plan was already breaking down, and because Spanish supply was already failing. Strong answers argue the fireships were decisive because they exploited weaknesses the other factors had created — no single factor on its own would have been enough.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Spanish invasion plan for 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• A combined naval and land operation — 130 ships and around 30,000 men under Medina Sidonia would sail from Lisbon up the Channel to Calais.
• A planned rendezvous with the Duke of Parma — 30,000 veteran Spanish troops in the Netherlands would be escorted across the Channel in barges to land in Kent.
• Reliance on a Catholic rising in England — once Parma’s army landed, Philip expected English Catholics to support the invasion.
• Tight coordination required — the Armada had to arrive off Calais exactly when Parma’s barges were ready, with no deep-water port available for the great galleons to wait in.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Spanish failed to link up with the Duke of Parma in August 1588.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Dutch Sea Beggars
• the lack of a deep-water port
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.
