Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Parma’s barges were not ready on time — the assumption that Parma could appear at Calais on demand turned out to be unrealistic given the logistics of moving 30,000 men.
• The Dutch ‘Sea Beggars’ blockaded the Flemish coast — small Dutch warships made it impossible for Parma’s shallow barges to leave Dunkirk safely.
• There was no deep-water port for the Armada to shelter in — Medina Sidonia’s great galleons could not enter the shallows where Parma’s barges sat, leaving the fleet exposed at Calais.
• English fireships at Calais broke the Armada’s formation — on the night of 7–8 August the Spanish fleet cut its anchors and scattered, ending any chance of a coordinated meeting.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the use of field defences was similar in the seventeenth century and the First World War.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both periods soldiers dug in to survive enemy fire (1). At Naseby in 1645 the New Model Army fought from prepared ground and hid musketeers in a hollow road, and seventeenth-century sieges used layered ditches and earthworks (1). On the Western Front from 1914 both sides dug front, support and reserve trenches linked by communication trenches (1). The idea was the same in both centuries: use the ground for cover; what changed was the scale (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the nature of warfare on land changed in the period c1800–1918.

You may use the following in your answer:
• industrial weapons
• trench warfare.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Rifling, magazine rifles and smokeless powder pushed accurate fire out to 1,000 yards, so close-order attack became suicidal.
• Machine guns firing around 500 rounds a minute gave the defender an advantage no attacking formation could overcome by courage.
• Quick-firing artillery could drop shells for miles; on the Somme a seven-day bombardment fired well over a million rounds.
• Barbed wire and concrete dugouts let defenders survive bombardment and then meet the attackers with intact machine guns.
• Railways and mass production kept armies supplied at industrial rates, so wars became contests of attrition rather than single decisive battles.
• Fronts with no open flanks, from the North Sea to Switzerland, meant the only way forward was straight through prepared defences.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the effect of a new weapon on the battlefield was similar in the fifteenth century and the First World War.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In both periods a new weapon killed attackers before they could reach the enemy (1). At Agincourt in 1415 massed longbows stopped French cavalry and men-at-arms in the mud long before they closed with the English line (1). On the Western Front the machine gun did the same job from a trench, cutting down infantry crossing no man's land (1). In both cases attacking troops had to change their tactics or accept huge losses (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the composition of the British army changed in the period c1700–1918.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Cardwell's reforms
• conscription in 1916.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Industrial weapons made the cavalry charge useless, so mounted troops shrank while infantry and artillery grew.
• Cardwell's short service and regimental districts built a professional regular army with a trained reserve behind it.
• The small pre-war British Expeditionary Force could not fight a continental war, so Kitchener's volunteers and then conscripts filled the ranks.
• The Military Service Act of January 1916 brought in conscription for single men aged 18 to 41, widening the social base of the army.
• New technology created new units: logistics corps, signal companies, tunnelling units, gas companies and, from 1917, tank battalions.
• Aircraft became a service of their own when the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service merged into the Royal Air Force in 1918.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of the commander was different at the Battle of Waterloo (1815) and the Battle of the Somme (1916).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: At Waterloo the commander could see and control his battle (1). Wellington rode along the ridge, watched the French attacks and committed his reserves himself at the decisive moment (1). On the Somme the commander worked from a headquarters far behind the line (1). Haig planned a 25-mile attack, set the timetable and the bombardment in advance, and then depended on telephone and runner reports that arrived hours late (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for the heavy British casualties on the Somme was poor leadership by General Haig.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the artillery bombardment of 24 June–1 July 1916
• the role of General Haig.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for Haig as main cause:
• He authorised the seven-day bombardment that failed to cut the wire and destroy German dugouts on much of the front.
• He sustained the offensive for over four months despite mounting casualties; later phases at Pozières, Thiepval and the Ancre also produced very heavy losses for limited ground.
• He approved the early use of tanks at Flers-Courcelette in September 1916 before they were reliable, arguably wasting the surprise of a new weapon.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Strategic context: Britain was fighting a coalition war and the Somme was timed to take pressure off the French at Verdun, where the French army was close to collapse.
• Industrial firepower (machine guns, quick-firing artillery, barbed wire) gave the defender an inherent advantage on the Western Front; any 1916 attack would have been costly.
• Munitions quality: many British shells in early 1916 were duds, undermining the bombardment regardless of who commanded.
• The New Armies were inexperienced — the line-walking advance reflected their training level, not just headquarters orders.
• Operational learning curve: the BEF’s tactics and technology improved through the Somme and into 1917–18, contributing directly to the Hundred Days victories of August–November 1918.
• Revisionist historians (Sheffield, Philpott, Todman) argue Haig should be judged by 1918 as well as by 1 July 1916; the ‘lions led by donkeys’ line is a 1960s cultural verdict, not a verdict of the war itself.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Haig against industrial firepower, coalition strategy, munitions quality and the BEF learning curve, uses accurate period detail (creeping barrage, Flers-Courcelette, Verdun, Hundred Days) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One factor dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which policing in the eighteenth century was different from policing after 1829.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• The Bow Street Runners, founded by Henry Fielding in 1749, were never more than a few dozen men, paid partly by reward and working only out of central London.
• The Metropolitan Police created in 1829 was a salaried, uniformed force of thousands under a single command, walking fixed beats across the whole London area.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Robert Peel introduced the Metropolitan Police in 1829.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the growth of London
• the Peterloo Massacre of 1819.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• London’s population had passed a million by 1820 and old systems of unpaid parish constables and watchmen could no longer cope with urban crime.
• Recent disturbances — including the 1819 Peterloo Massacre, where the army had killed eighteen protestors — showed that using soldiers for crowd control was politically unacceptable.
• The Bow Street Runners had proved since 1749 that a paid, organised force could work, but they were small and confined to central London.
• Peel had already begun reforming the Bloody Code (1823–27); harsh laws were more enforceable when paired with proportionate punishment, which required a police force to catch the people who would now be punished by prison or transportation rather than execution.
• Public anxiety about French-style state policing had to be addressed by a force that was uniformed, civilian and unarmed — the design Peel produced.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (population, Peterloo, Bow Street, penal reform) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the new force without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Metropolitan Police Act of 1829 changed law enforcement in Britain.

You may use the following in your answer:
• beat policing
• the County and Borough Police Act 1856.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• It established the first uniformed, salaried, professional police force for the London area, with headquarters at Scotland Yard.
• It set the template — civilian uniform, unarmed beat patrol, focus on prevention — that the 1839 and 1856 County Police Acts spread across England and Wales.
• It made detective work possible at scale: the Detective Branch (1842) and the CID (1878) were direct successors of Peel’s force.
• It established the principle of policing by consent — an unarmed officer walking a known beat — that became central to British attitudes to the police.
• It allowed Peel’s parallel reforms of the Bloody Code to work, since proportionate punishment required reliable detection.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (Scotland Yard, beat policing, 1839 and 1856 Acts, CID) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Act without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the equipment and appearance of the police in 1829 were similar to those of the police in 2000.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Peel's constables were deliberately civilian: a blue coat and top hat rather than army red, and only a wooden truncheon and a rattle.
• British constables were still routinely unarmed at the end of the twentieth century; firearms were held back for Armed Response Vehicles, introduced in London in 1991.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Robert Peel was the most important reason for the development of professional policing in nineteenth-century Britain.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Metropolitan Police Act 1829
• the work of the Fielding brothers.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting Peel as the most important reason:
• Peel as Home Secretary delivered the 1829 Metropolitan Police Act, creating the first unified, salaried, uniformed force.
• Peel had already reformed the Bloody Code (1823–27), so a police force could be paired with proportionate punishment — the two reforms were a single project.
• Peel personally drafted the principles of consent and prevention, with Rowan and Mayne, that defined British policing.
• His name remained attached to the force (‘Peelers’, ‘bobbies’) and his model was adopted by every force created after him.

Indicative content — arguments against (other factors mattered as much or more):
• Henry and John Fielding had created the Bow Street Runners (1749) and the Horse Patrol (1763), proving that paid policing could work; without this eighty-year experience the Met would not have been politically possible.
• The growth of London’s population past a million, plus rapid industrialisation in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, made reform inevitable; Peel’s timing reflected demographic pressure as much as personal initiative.
• The Peterloo Massacre (1819) discredited the army for civilian policing and forced reform; the political climate, not Peel alone, drove the change.
• The 1839 and 1856 County Police Acts — passed under different governments — spread the model nationally; Peel did not personally extend the Met beyond London.
• CID (1878), the most important nineteenth-century development for serious crime, came thirty years after Peel’s death and was driven by scandal and necessity, not by his planning.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Peel against at least one other factor, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (parish constable, watchman, beat constable, peeler, bobby, Scotland Yard, Detective Branch, CID).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the detection of crime in the nineteenth century was different from its detection in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Victorian detectives worked from witness statements and sketches: the Detective Branch of 1842 and the CID of 1878 had no fingerprints, no forensic science and no national record of suspects.
• Twentieth-century detection rested on science and records: a fingerprint bureau from 1901, the Police National Computer from 1974 and DNA fingerprinting from 1984.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Pinkerton’s National Detective Agency for the establishment of law and order in the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Pinkerton agency, supported by specific period detail.

Indicative content:
• Founded in 1850 by Allan Pinkerton, the agency became the most important private police force in the country after the Civil War — reinforcing a thinly-staffed federal–territorial system.
• Because railroad companies hired Pinkerton agents to ride carriages and recover stolen mail and bullion, cross-jurisdiction policing became routine in a way US marshals alone could not have achieved.
• Banks hired Pinkertons to track gangs that crossed state lines — most famously the James-Younger gang in the 1870s — producing a national pattern of investigation rather than purely local pursuit.
• Federal authorities used Pinkerton information when prosecuting in territorial courts, blurring the line between private detective work and federal law enforcement.
• Their methods were sometimes brutal — the 1875 raid on the James farm killed Jesse James’s young half-brother — but they normalised cross-state policing and embedded private detective work as a permanent part of the Western law-and-order system.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the agency to specific consequences for law and order, with named clients (railroads, banks), named targets (James-Younger gang) and named dates (1850 founding, 1875 farm raid).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the agency without explaining importance for law and order.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the spread of railroads for law and order on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the railroads to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that train robbery and mail theft became federal-scale crimes prosecuted in territorial courts — Wells Fargo employed its own armed messengers and the Pinkertons were hired to chase gangs across state lines.
• Another consequence was that federal troops could now be moved to Plains flashpoints in hours rather than weeks, hardening federal authority once track had been laid.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named institution or feature.
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of statehood for the development of law and order in the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• A territory answered directly to Washington and was policed by appointed US marshals; a state had its own legislature, courts and police powers, shifting authority from federal appointees to elected officials.
• Because Nebraska (1867), Colorado (1876) and the Dakotas, Montana and Washington (all 1889) gained statehood across the period, the pattern of who held authority changed steadily westwards.
• State governments could raise their own taxes to pay for courts, jails and sheriffs, producing a more developed system than territorial budgets had allowed.
• The transition was not instant: the Johnson County War of 1892 in Wyoming — two years after statehood — showed that elected sheriffs could still be outgunned by hired cattle-baron gunmen.
• By the 1890s, the rough sequence federal → territorial → state had embedded a more settled, locally accountable system of law across most of the former frontier.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1867, 1876, 1889) and specialist vocabulary (territory, statehood, marshal, sheriff).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the development of law and order on the Plains in the years 1850–1876.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the founding of Pinkerton’s National Detective Agency (1850)
• the Montana Vigilantes (1863–65)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1850 Allan Pinkerton founded his detective agency in Chicago, creating the first national private police force at a moment when official law on the frontier was still thin and territory-based.
• Because the Civil War left the federal state much stronger by 1865, US marshals and territorial courts could now reach further west, but they remained understaffed across enormous territories such as Montana and Dakota.
• Because official law was thinly spread, in 1863–65 the Montana Vigilantes hanged at least 21 men, including the Bannack sheriff Henry Plummer in January 1864, whom they accused of secretly leading a road-agent ring — showing how quickly lynch law filled gaps in the system.
• Because the railroads built after 1862 carried federal mail, currency and inter-state shipments, train robbery and rustling became federal-scale crimes; railroads hired Pinkertons to ride their carriages and chase the James-Younger gang across state lines.
• By the time Colorado became a state in 1876, the layered system — federal marshals, county sheriffs, town marshals and private detectives — had begun to work together, even though vigilantism would continue to reappear wherever official law was still thin.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1850, 1863–65, 1864, 1876), specialist vocabulary (US marshal, vigilance committee, road-agent), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Montana Vigilantes (1863–65) for understanding law and order in the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Vigilantes operated in the gold-mining settlements of Bannack and Virginia City between 1863 and 1865, hanging at least 21 men — including the Bannack sheriff Henry Plummer in January 1864 — without trial.
• Because the territorial government in Montana was thinly staffed, the Vigilantes’ actions showed how quickly informal lynch law could replace court law where federal authority was weak.
• Their hanging of an elected sheriff exposed how blurred the line between ‘lawmen’ and ‘outlaws’ could be on the frontier — Plummer was both, depending on whose account was believed.
• The Vigilantes were celebrated by some Western newspapers as the only force willing to act, but worried others who feared lynch law would become permanent — a debate that ran through the rest of the period.
• The pattern repeated wherever official law was thin: California mining camps, range wars, the Johnson County War of 1892. The Montana Vigilantes set the template for what vigilantism in the West would look like.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1863–65, January 1864, 21 men, Bannack/Virginia City) and specialist vocabulary (vigilance committee, road-agent).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the founding of Pinkerton’s National Detective Agency in 1850.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the agency to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that railroad companies could hire Pinkerton agents to ride carriages and recover stolen shipments, producing routine cross-jurisdiction policing that US marshals alone could not have provided.
• Another consequence was that gangs operating across state lines — most famously the James-Younger gang in the 1870s — were now tracked by a national private force working alongside federal authorities, normalising the pursuit of crime beyond county or territorial borders.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named institution or event.
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the Great Famine on rural Chinese communities. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences, each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail from the source (e.g. abandoned villages, dispersed families, eating bark or roots, hidden grain, peasant deaths). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that survival depended on illegal private plots and black-market exchange, or that the famine destroyed traditional family and clan structures in the affected provinces. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Great Famine of 1958–62 caused such a high death toll.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the people’s communes
• the consequences of the Lushan Conference of 1959
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. the abolition of private farming under the communes, communal mess halls eating through reserves, Lysenkoist farming methods wrecking the 1959 harvest, inflated reporting and forced procurement after Lushan, the diversion of c.60 million peasants to backyard steel, the Soviet advisers’ withdrawal in 1960, and weather as a contributing factor. Uses the stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the famine without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the main cause of the Great Famine in China.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation reads the famine as a policy disaster — communes, procurement, Lysenkoism, Lushan — while the other treats weather and unavoidable shocks such as the Sino-Soviet split as the dominant cause). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the causes of the Great Famine.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP ‘three years of natural disasters’ framing vs revisionist Western works after PRC archives opened in the 1990s), used different evidence (state-published material vs provincial archives, Yang Jisheng’s journalist investigations), or had different purposes (defending Mao vs holding him personally responsible). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping in the recovery from the Great Famine?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the 7,000 Cadres Conference of January 1962, Liu’s ‘30% natural, 70% man-made’ verdict, the sanzi yibao package (private plots, free markets, sideline industries, household contracts), the role of Chen Yun in industrial rebalancing, and the alternative explanation that the recovery was set in motion by harvest reality, the closure of mess halls, and the easing of procurement, with Liu and Deng presiding rather than driving. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the recovery measures of 1962–65 amounted to a betrayal of socialist principles?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the sanzi yibao package, the survival of the commune as the basic unit, the recovery of grain and industrial output by 1965, the deliberate use of socialist language by Liu and Deng, Chen Yun’s industrial role, and Mao’s contemporary reading of the package as ‘capitalist road’ recovery that justified the Cultural Revolution. Acknowledges the genuine historiographical disagreement (Dikötter and Spence vs Mobo Gao) and reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (commune, sanzi yibao, 7,000 Cadres Conference, capitalist roaders). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of religious houses in local communities before 1535.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Landlords — religious houses owned roughly a fifth of the landed wealth of England and Wales, renting farms to tenants and employing servants on their estates.
• Almsgivers — monasteries distributed food and small charity at the gate to travellers and the local poor.
• Spiritual centres — Masses said in monastic churches were believed to relieve the souls of the dead in purgatory.
• Schools — many larger houses educated the sons of local gentry families.
• Hostels — abbeys provided lodging for travellers on long-distance roads.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Cromwell’s commissions of 1535.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Valor Ecclesiasticus — a county-by-county valuation of every ecclesiastical benefice and religious house, completed in months and producing the most thorough fiscal survey since Domesday.
• Visitors’ commission — Richard Layton and Thomas Legh inspected houses asking questions about sexual misconduct, superstition and disloyalty.
• Comperta reports — the visitors compiled records of alleged abuses that landed on Cromwell’s desk by early 1536.
• Speed — both surveys were nationwide and were completed within roughly a year, demonstrating Cromwell’s administrative reach.
• Use of gentry commissioners — the work was done by local landed laymen, binding the gentry into the early Reformation.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell ordered the dissolution of the monasteries between 1535 and 1540.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Valor Ecclesiasticus
• the Comperta reports
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Fiscal motive — the Valor Ecclesiasticus revealed annual monastic income of around £165,000, more than the crown’s ordinary revenue, providing an irresistible fiscal target.
• Justification through reform — the Comperta reports catalogued sexual and superstitious abuses, providing a moral cover for suppression.
• Religious conviction — Cromwell’s evangelicalism, supported by Cranmer, viewed monasticism as theologically outdated; the 1536 Ten Articles reduced the role of monastic intercession.
• Royal supremacy — monasteries owed their authority to the Pope and were structurally hard to control; their suppression completed the break with Rome.
• Political binding — selling monastic land to the gentry created a propertied class with a permanent stake in the Reformation.
• War finance — Henry needed to fund French and Scottish campaigns in the 1540s and could not raise such sums through ordinary taxation.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The gentry gained more from the dissolution of the monasteries than any other group.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• sales of monastic land
• monastic servants
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the gains of the gentry against those of other groups and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Around two thirds of monastic estates had been sold or granted away by the end of the 1540s, mostly to gentry, lawyers and merchant families.
• Buyers gained land that had been off the market for centuries, and with it local standing.
• Gentry commissioners were also employed to run the surveys and the surrenders.
• Every buyer then had a permanent reason to defend the Reformation, so a purchase became political influence.

Arguments that others gained more, or that gentry gains were limited:
• The crown took the immediate prize, with annual revenue rising by something like £130,000.
• Abbots and senior monks who surrendered quietly received pensions, and some moved into parish livings.
• The gentry paid for their land, so the gain was an investment rather than a gift.
• Lay servants of the houses generally received nothing, and the urban poor lost gate-alms, so the losses fell on those least able to bear them.

Overall judgement: the crown gained the money first, but the gentry gained the land, and the land is what lasted. Top-band answers weigh these groups against each other and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the dissolution of the monasteries had such a long-lasting impact on English society.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Court of Augmentations
• sales of monastic land
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Court of Augmentations — the new department channelled monastic income to the crown and managed sales, giving Tudor government a permanent fiscal arm and an institutional memory of the dissolution.
• Sales of monastic land — around two thirds of monastic estates were sold by the end of the 1540s, mostly to the gentry, creating a new landowning class with a stake in the Reformation surviving.
• Doubling of crown revenue — royal income rose by roughly £130,000 a year, transforming what the Tudor state could afford to do, particularly in war.
• Destruction of buildings — abbey churches were stripped of lead, towers pulled down and stone reused, permanently changing the English landscape.
• Loss of welfare provision — gate-alms and monastic schools disappeared, with no equivalent replacement until Elizabeth’s Poor Laws decades later.
• Religious change — the parish church absorbed many monastic functions; Cranmer’s 1536 Ten Articles reframed how Mass and intercession worked.
• Political alignment — gentry buyers had a personal interest in resisting any restoration of Catholicism, narrowing the Marian and Elizabethan options.
• Northern resentment — concentrated monastic landholding made the suppression more disruptive in the north and contributed to the Pilgrimage of Grace.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for the dissolution of the monasteries between 1535 and 1540 was the crown’s need for money.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Valor Ecclesiasticus
• Cromwell’s religious convictions
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the financial motive against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The Valor Ecclesiasticus of 1535 produced a precise fiscal target before any moral case had been built — the survey’s purpose was financial.
• The Court of Augmentations was created specifically to channel monastic income to the crown.
• Royal revenue roughly doubled, allowing Henry to fund the wars of the 1540s without ruinous taxation.
• Two thirds of monastic land was sold within a decade — the crown took the cash rather than holding the estates for ongoing reform.
• The smaller houses were dissolved first because they were the easier and less politically costly target, not because they were the most theologically problematic.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Religious conviction — Cromwell’s evangelicalism, Cranmer’s 1536 Ten Articles and the new royal injunctions show genuine Reformation purpose.
• The Comperta reports — whatever their reliability, they reflected real reformist concerns about monastic standards stretching back to Erasmus and Wolsey’s 1520s closures.
• Royal supremacy — monasteries owed their authority to the Pope; their existence was incompatible with the 1534 Act of Supremacy.
• Political binding — the deliberate sales of monastic land to gentry buyers created a propertied class invested in the Reformation surviving.
• Henry’s personality — G.W. Bernard argues Henry himself drove the appetite for the suppressions, not just Cromwell.

Overall judgement: financial considerations made the suppression worth doing on this scale; religious and political considerations made it possible to justify and to consolidate. A top-band answer weighs these motives explicitly and explains how they reinforced each other.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which Caribbean migration to Britain after 1948 was different from Irish migration in the 1840s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Caribbean migrants came as legal citizens under the British Nationality Act of 1948 and were often actively recruited; Irish migrants came as refugees from famine with no invitation at all.
• Caribbean migrants were recruited into named employers - the NHS, London Transport, British Rail - while Irish migrants took whatever casual dock and building work they could find.
• Irish migration was counted in hundreds of thousands within a few years; Caribbean migration built up steadily across the 1950s.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the British Nationality Act of 1948 led to large-scale Caribbean migration to Britain.

You may use the following in your answer:
• post-war labour shortages
• the Empire Windrush.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Act created a single status of Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies, which gave Caribbean people the legal right to live and work in Britain. Its purpose was to hold a common citizenship across the white Dominions, and Caribbean migration was an unintended consequence.
• Post-war Britain faced a severe labour shortage as cities rebuilt and the welfare state expanded; the NHS, London Transport and British Rail recruited directly in Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad.
• Many Caribbean men had served in the RAF or the merchant marine during the war and already saw Britain as the mother country.
• The arrival of the Empire Windrush on 22 June 1948, with more than a thousand passengers and heavy newsreel coverage, made the legal right visible and encouraged later arrivals.
• Opportunity was limited at home, and United States immigration restrictions from 1952 closed the alternative destination, which left Britain the obvious choice.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the treatment of refugees in Britain during the world wars was similar to the treatment of religious refugees before 1700.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• In both, refugees fleeing a hostile power were welcomed as victims of an enemy: around 250,000 Belgians in 1914, and Protestant Flemings and Huguenots fleeing Catholic states.
• In both, organised charity carried much of the relief - more than 2,500 local War Refugees Committee groups in 1914, and parish collections for Huguenots after 1685.
• In both, the state chose which refugees to help: the Polish Resettlement Act of 1947, like the denization proclamation of 1681, named the group it was designed for.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Legislation was the most important factor shaping migration to Britain between 1900 and the present.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the British Nationality Act 1948
• the Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for legislation:
• The British Nationality Act of 1948 created the citizenship that made Caribbean and South Asian migration legally possible.
• The Commonwealth Immigrants Acts of 1962 and 1968 and the Immigration Act of 1971 ended free Commonwealth migration in successive steps, each reacting to the migration the last had produced.
• The Polish Resettlement Act of 1947 and the patriality rule of 1971 show legislation actively choosing which groups Britain welcomed.
• Free movement from the EU ended on 31 December 2020, which shows legislation still setting the terms in the twenty-first century.

Indicative content - support for other factors:
• Economic pull did the work the law only permitted: post-war labour shortage drew Caribbean and South Asian workers into the NHS, transport and textiles.
• Wars created refugee streams whatever the law said: around 250,000 Belgians in 1914, around 70,000 European Jews between 1933 and 1939, and Polish service personnel after 1945.
• Decolonisation produced events the law had to react to: the Ugandan expulsion of 1972 brought around 28,000 East African Asians regardless of British intentions.
• Attitudes and the media shaped what laws were politically possible, from Powell's 1968 speech to coverage of EU migration after 2004.
• EU enlargement in 2004 was an institutional decision, but the scale of Polish migration - around one million by 2017 - was driven by the gap in wages.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (decolonisation, Commonwealth, patriality, asylum, free movement).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Commonwealth migration to Britain was restricted between 1962 and 1971.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the labour voucher system
• East African Asians.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• The Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 ended free movement and required most Commonwealth migrants to hold a Ministry of Labour voucher, allocated by job category.
• The second Commonwealth Immigrants Act, passed in three days in 1968, was designed to keep East African Asians with British passports out after Kenya's Africanisation policies.
• Enoch Powell's speech of 20 April 1968 made restriction respectable in mainstream politics and raised the political cost of doing nothing.
• The Immigration Act of 1971 tied entry to having a parent or grandparent born in Britain, which in practice favoured the descendants of white Dominions settlers.
• Restriction ran alongside protection: the Race Relations Acts of 1965, 1968 and 1976 outlawed discrimination inside Britain even as the border tightened.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why attitudes in society shaped migration legislation in Britain between 1962 and 1971.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the role of the media
• the 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Act.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• By the early 1960s Commonwealth migration had grown enough for restrictionist feeling to show in opinion polls and local elections, notably the Smethwick result of 1964.
• Tabloid coverage of Commonwealth migration echoed, on a larger scale, the press campaign against Eastern European Jewish migrants in the 1880s and 1890s, and made restriction electorally attractive.
• Enoch Powell's speech on 20 April 1968 gave those attitudes a mainstream political voice, and the 1968 Act was pushed through in three days in the same climate.
• Decolonisation created visible refugee movements - independence in Uganda in 1962 and Kenya in 1963 - that legislation reacted to.
• Anti-discrimination law developed in parallel in 1965, 1968 and 1976: legislators tried to cap entry while protecting those already settled, a contradiction the Windrush scandal of 2018 later exposed.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the position of Liu Shaoqi within the CCP between 1962 and 1965. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (e.g. Liu’s leadership of the four cleanups, his ‘30 per cent natural, 70 per cent man-made’ speech, his presidency of the PRC). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that Liu was the operational leader of the recovery, but his authority depended on Mao’s tolerance. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that reads more as paraphrase than inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mao was able to launch the Cultural Revolution in 1966 against his own party leadership.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Little Red Book
• the Socialist Education Movement
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. Lin Biao’s PLA cult of Mao, the Socialist Education Movement and its redirection upwards, the reform of education, the Wu Han affair, Mao’s personal authority surviving the Great Leap) and shows how they interacted. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists Mao’s actions without explaining why they enabled the Cultural Revolution; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about why Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents the Cultural Revolution as a genuine attempt to renew socialism; the other presents it as Mao’s personal counter-attack on rivals after the Great Leap). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about Mao’s motives in launching the Cultural Revolution.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (Cold War-era versus post-1990s archival access); they used different evidence (CCP-published material like the 1981 Resolution versus revisionist Western archival research, e.g. Roderick MacFarquhar); or they had different purposes (commemorative versus critical). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why; or names a reason without supporting it. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the role of Lin Biao in preparing the Cultural Revolution?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own knowledge — the 1964 publication of the Little Red Book, the ‘Learn from the PLA’ campaign, Lin replacing Peng Dehuai in 1959, the army’s loyalty to Mao personally — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on Lin Biao or the PLA and barely engages with the interpretations as views; or relies on the stimulus alone. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that the Socialist Education Movement of 1962–65 was the dress rehearsal for the Cultural Revolution?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the four cleanups, work teams, denunciation meetings, the upward redirection of targets to ‘capitalist roaders’, Liu’s role as campaign leader, the Wu Han affair, the May 16 Notification — to test how far the Socialist Education Movement explains the Cultural Revolution. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Socialist Education Movement, four cleanups, capitalist roaders, May 16 Notification). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning; limited subject vocabulary. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors or no period vocabulary. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Sadat’s visit to Israel (1977).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the visit broke the Arab taboo on direct dealings with Israel and triggered immediate retaliation — three Egyptian ministers resigned, Syria broke relations with Egypt and the Arab League moved towards suspending Egypt by 1979; (ii) it began a chain of negotiations — Begin’s reciprocal visit to Ismailia in December 1977, Carter’s Camp David summit in September 1978 and the Treaty of Washington in March 1979 — that produced the first Arab-Israeli peace treaty. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Sadat went to Israel without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the OAPEC oil embargo (1973–74).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the four-fold rise in world oil prices triggered recession across the West, with petrol queues in the United States and a three-day working week in Britain, demonstrating Western economic dependence on Arab oil; (ii) it persuaded the Nixon and Ford administrations to commit US prestige to a settlement, making Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy and the Sinai disengagement deals possible. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that prices rose without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Treaty of Washington (1979) for Egypt.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Egypt became the first Arab state to recognise Israel and recovered the whole of Sinai by 1982, including the oilfields and the canal frontage; Egypt was suspended from the Arab League and its headquarters moved to Tunis until 1989, leaving Cairo isolated for a decade; the treaty unlocked roughly $1.3 billion a year of US military aid and underwrote Mubarak’s long presidency after Sadat’s assassination in 1981. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the treaty without showing why it mattered for Egypt. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Camp David Accords (1978) for the Palestinian issue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the second Camp David framework on Palestinian ‘autonomy’ was negotiated without any Palestinian or Jordanian representative present and was duly rejected by the PLO and King Hussein, so produced no transfer of power; with Egypt locked into a separate peace, Israel was freer to settle the West Bank and to invade Lebanon in 1982 to pursue the PLO; the Camp David framework nevertheless became the diplomatic shape used at Madrid in 1991 and at Oslo in 1993, conditioning future peacemaking. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Camp David without showing why it mattered for the Palestinians. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy (1973–75) for relations between Israel and Egypt.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the Sinai Disengagement I and II agreements pulled the two armies apart, returned the western Sinai oilfields to Egypt and reopened the Suez Canal in June 1975, ending the front-line conditions of 1967–73; shuttle diplomacy locked the United States, not the Soviet Union, into the role of regional broker, fitting Sadat’s pivot away from Moscow; it produced the working confidence between Cairo and Washington on which Sadat’s 1977 trip to Jerusalem and the 1979 treaty were built. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Kissinger without showing why his diplomacy mattered for Israel-Egypt relations. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the road to the Treaty of Washington in the years 1973–79.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the OAPEC oil embargo (1973)
• Sadat’s visit to the Knesset (1977)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the oil embargo and Western recession; Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy and the Sinai disengagement deals; Sadat’s Knesset speech and Begin’s reciprocal visit; Camp David and the Treaty of Washington). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as the reopening of the Suez Canal in 1975 or Carter’s mediation. Connects events through causation rather than sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the recruitment of soldiers was different in the medieval period and the twentieth century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Medieval recruitment worked through the lord, not the state (1). The king summoned his lords, who brought knights and tenants under feudal duty for about 40 days a year (1). Twentieth-century recruitment worked through national law (1). The Military Service Act of January 1916 conscripted single men aged 18 to 41 directly, with tribunals to hear claims for exemption (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of women in Britain's armed forces was different in the nineteenth century and the Second World War.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: In the nineteenth century women had no place in the armed forces (1). Women such as Florence Nightingale's nurses worked alongside the army in hospitals, but they were not enlisted and held no rank (1). In the Second World War women were conscripted into uniformed services (1). From December 1941 single women aged 20 to 30 were called up, and ATS members crewed anti-aircraft batteries while WAAF women worked the radar screens (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the way Britain recruited soldiers changed in the period c1850–c1960.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Military Service Act 1916
• National Service.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Cardwell's short service and regimental districts built the volunteer machinery that carried Britain into 1914.
• Industrial war needed numbers no volunteer system could supply: Kitchener raised over two million men by the end of 1915, and it was still not enough.
• Casualties on the Western Front outran volunteering, so the Military Service Act of January 1916 conscripted single men aged 18 to 41, and married men from May.
• In 1939 the government did not wait for casualties: the Military Training Act came in May and the National Service (Armed Forces) Act on 3 September.
• Total war widened the pool: from December 1941 single women aged 20 to 30 were conscripted into the ATS, WAAF and WRNS.
• Cold War and imperial commitments kept peacetime National Service going from 1948 until the last conscript was called up in 1960.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Britain moved from a conscript army to an all-volunteer professional army in the period c1900–present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• National Service (1948–60)
• the professional army.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Conscription was always an emergency measure: it was introduced for the two world wars and then kept on for the Cold War and decolonisation.
• The 1957 Defence White Paper traded mass conventional forces for the nuclear deterrent, so huge numbers of conscripts were no longer needed.
• National Service was expensive and unpopular, and much of the training time was spent on men who would soon leave.
• Modern equipment needed long technical training, which suited a soldier who signed on for years rather than for two.
• The last conscript was called up in 1960 and the last left the regulars in 1963, since when the army has been all-volunteer.
• Recruitment now competes with civilian employers, so pay, conditions and skills training matter more than compulsion.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the recruitment of women into Britain's armed forces changed in the period c1900–present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Second World War
• combat roles.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• In the First World War women volunteered for support work through bodies such as the WAAC and the WRAF, mostly in clerical and domestic roles.
• Total war in 1939–45 needed every pair of hands, so women were placed in technical and operational jobs to release men for combat units.
• From December 1941 single women aged 20 to 30 were conscripted, the first time British women had been called up.
• ATS women crewed heavy anti-aircraft batteries and WAAF women worked radar screens, which blurred the line between support and front line.
• After 1945 attitudes shifted slowly, and the separate women's services were folded into the regular forces.
• All ground close-combat roles, including the infantry and the Royal Marines, were opened to women in 2018.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
‘Conscription was the most important change in British army recruitment in the modern era.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Military Service Act 1916
• the all-volunteer professional army.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for conscription as most important:
• The 1916 Military Service Act was the first mass national conscription of the modern era and supplied the manpower for the Western Front from 1916 to 1918.
• The 1939 National Service (Armed Forces) Act extended conscription to all men 18–41 on day one of the war, allowing rapid wartime mobilisation.
• The 1941 conscription of women into the ATS, WAAF and WRNS broke the principle that compulsion only applied to men.
• National Service (1948–60) sustained Britain’s Cold War and decolonisation commitments through compulsory peacetime service.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Voluntarism remains the bedrock principle: the all-volunteer professional army (1963–present) is the longest-running modern recruitment system, longer than conscription was in force.
• The Pals Battalions and Kitchener volunteers raised over two million men in 1914–15 before any conscription was imposed.
• The opening of all combat roles to women in 2018 changed who can be recruited more fundamentally than the 1916 Act, which only changed compulsion.
• Cardwell’s nineteenth-century reforms (short service, regimental districts) created the recruitment infrastructure on which both volunteer and conscription armies depended.
• Conscription was always temporary — ended in 1919, ended in 1960 — while professionalisation has been continuous.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs conscription against voluntarism, women’s integration and Cardwell-era infrastructure, uses accurate period detail (1916, 1939, 1941, 1948, 1960, 2018), and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One factor dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about why Trotsky failed to succeed Lenin in 1924–25. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, Trotsky’s absence from Lenin’s funeral, the Politburo’s fear of Bonapartism after the Civil War, his late conversion to Bolshevism in August 1917, his arrogant manner with the apparatus, or his focus on Permanent Revolution while Stalin built the party machine). Inferences go beyond surface description to explain why the detail mattered for the succession. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Stalin had emerged as the leader of the USSR by 1929.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Lenin’s Testament
• the role of General Secretary
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — e.g. Stalin’s control of the General Secretariat and the 1924 Lenin Enrolment of 240,000 new members; the suppression of Lenin’s Testament in May 1924 and Stalin’s use of the funeral and Lenin cult; Trotsky’s Bonapartism and arrogance; the Triumvirate’s defeat of the Left Opposition in 1925 over Permanent Revolution versus Socialism in One Country; the United Opposition’s defeat in 1926–27; and the destruction of Bukharin’s Right Opposition in 1928–29 over collectivisation. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Politburo, General Secretary, Triumvirate, Comintern. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists Stalin’s rivals without explaining how each was defeated. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the reasons for Stalin’s rise to power between 1924 and 1929.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation argues that Stalin’s rise was decided by his bureaucratic control of the General Secretariat and his ability to pack congresses through the Lenin Enrolment, while the other argues that ideological persuasion — Socialism in One Country versus Permanent Revolution — convinced the rank and file that Stalin’s programme was the realistic one). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about Stalin’s rise to power.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (Soviet party records and congress voting figures versus memoirs and the suppressed Testament); they wrote at different times (Cold War era surveys versus post-1991 archival biographies such as Khlevniuk and Kotkin); or they had different purposes (defending or rebutting the totalitarian-school reading of Stalin as a uniquely cunning operator). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
