How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Lenin’s Testament in Stalin’s rise to power?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the Testament and its postscript, the May 1924 Politburo decision to suppress it, Krupskaya’s role, Kamenev and Zinoviev’s motives, and the way the Lenin cult overrode the Testament’s critique — weighed against the broader machinery of Stalin’s rise (the General Secretariat, the Lenin Enrolment, Trotsky’s missed funeral, Socialism in One Country and the defeat of each Opposition in turn). Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that Stalin’s control of the party machinery was the most important reason for his victory over Trotsky?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the post of General Secretary from April 1922, the 1924 Lenin Enrolment of 240,000, the packing of congress delegations, the role of the Orgburo and the Secretariat — weighed against rival explanations: Trotsky’s Bonapartism, his missed funeral and late conversion to Bolshevism, the suppression of Lenin’s Testament, and the appeal of Socialism in One Country in a country exhausted by war and isolation. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Politburo, Sovnarkom, Comintern, Triumvirate, Lenin Enrolment). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of King John’s use of taxation between 1209 and 1214.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Repeated scutage — John levied scutage eleven times in his reign compared with three under Richard I; the 1214 scutage stood at three marks per knight’s fee, the highest rate of the reign.
• Punitive feudal ‘fines’ — reliefs and inheritance payments were set far above customary levels; William Fitz Alan was charged 10,000 marks and John de Lacy 7,000 marks for their inheritances.
• The 1207 thirteenth — an experimental tax on movables and income, the most ambitious assessment of personal wealth seen in England since the Conquest.
• Sale of wardships and marriages — orphaned heirs and heiresses were auctioned to the highest bidder, generating cash but breaking customary expectations.
• Tallage of the Anglo-Jewish community — the 1210 Bristol Tallage of 66,000 marks tied royal finance to violent extortion against a vulnerable community.
• Use of fines on widows — widows paid enormous sums not to be remarried against their will, turning a customary protection into a revenue stream.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the rebellion of 1215 before John reached Runnymede.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Renunciation of homage — the rebel barons formally renounced their oaths of homage at Northampton on 5 May 1215, a legal step that broke the feudal contract with the king.
• The siege of Northampton — the rebels attempted to take Northampton castle but failed, and instead moved north against Lincoln.
• The taking of Lincoln — the city of Lincoln fell into rebel hands, giving the rising a base in the East Midlands.
• The march on London — on 17 May 1215 the rebel army entered London with the support of sympathetic citizens, capturing the financial centre of the kingdom.
• Use of Henry I’s coronation charter — Stephen Langton supplied the rebels with a copy of Henry I’s charter as the model for their demands.
• Refusal of scutage — the Northern barons had refused the 1214 scutage on the ground that they were not obliged to serve overseas, providing the financial trigger for revolt.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or named places.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature, or features unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the failure of the 1214 Bouvines campaign turned baronial resentment into open rebellion.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the cost of the campaign
• the Northerners
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• The cost of the campaign — the 1214 scutage at three marks per knight’s fee, the loans from London moneylenders, and intensified tallages on the Jewish community had drained the kingdom for a war that produced nothing.
• The Northerners — the Yorkshire and Northumbrian barons had refused the scutage on the ground that they were not obliged to serve overseas; defeat at Bouvines vindicated their refusal and turned them into a coherent rebel coalition.
• Loss of strategic credibility — with Otto IV deposed and Flanders neutralised, John had no foreign allies left and could not threaten Philip II again; the basis of John’s government — recovery of Normandy — had collapsed.
• Mercenary government — throughout 1213–14 John had relied on captains such as Falkes de Bréauté and Engelard de Cigogné; without victory in France he could no longer pay them, but their presence intensified baronial fury.
• The 1212 precedent — the FitzWalter–de Vesci plot had already shown that rebellion was thinkable; their unpunished return after 1213 emboldened wider opposition.
• Stephen Langton’s mediation — the archbishop’s production of Henry I’s coronation charter from Canterbury archives gave the rebels a respectable legal framework to pursue grievances rather than personal revenge.
• Loss of London on 17 May 1215 — the surrender of the city stripped John of access to credit and meant rebellion could no longer be crushed by mercenary cash.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the plot of 1212 was a serious moment in King John’s reign.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Robert FitzWalter and Eustace de Vesci
• the Welsh campaign
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• The aim of the plot — FitzWalter and de Vesci planned either to murder John during the Welsh campaign or to abandon him to the Welsh and offer the throne to a rival, an open challenge to royal life and legitimacy.
• The status of the conspirators — both men were great tenants-in-chief, not marginal malcontents; their willingness to act revealed how thin John’s domestic support had become.
• The simultaneity of crises — in 1212 John faced the threat of French invasion authorised by the papal deposition, the Welsh war, and a baronial conspiracy at the same time; no English king had survived such a combination since 1066.
• Cancellation of the Welsh campaign — John had to abandon the Welsh expedition, take fresh hostages from baronial children and tighten his grip on royal castles, draining military momentum.
• Failure to punish the conspirators — FitzWalter and de Vesci escaped abroad and returned under the cover of the 1213 papal reconciliation; their survival emboldened wider opposition.
• FitzWalter’s later role — the same Robert FitzWalter became Marshal of the Army of God in 1215, leading the rebellion that produced Magna Carta; the leniency of 1212 had long-term consequences.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the rebel capture of London in May 1215 was a turning point in the rebellion against John.
You may use the following in your answer:
• royal credit and the Exchequer
• the support of the citizens
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Financial collapse — London was the seat of the Exchequer and the centre of royal credit; once the rebels held it, John could no longer raise loans to hire continental mercenaries.
• Symbolic victory — possession of the capital gave the rebellion legitimacy in the eyes of waverers and demonstrated that the king’s government had failed.
• Citizen support — Londoners admitted the rebel army on 17 May 1215, showing that opposition to John extended beyond the great barons and into the urban population.
• Loss of strategic mobility — the Thames and the road network around London were crucial for moving men and supplies; rebel control closed both.
• Pressure for negotiation — with London lost and Stephen Langton mediating, John could no longer respond by force; within weeks he was preparing to seal the charter at Runnymede.
• Continuity of legitimacy — possessing London allowed the rebels to claim they spoke for the ‘community of the realm’, an idea that ran through the 1215 settlement.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The defeat at Bouvines in 1214 was the main reason the barons rebelled against King John in 1215.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of Normandy in 1204
• John’s use of arbitrary power
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Bouvines made the recovery of Normandy impossible — it ended the strategy that had justified ten years of taxation, leaving the cost without reward.
• The crushing scutage of 1214 had been raised specifically for the campaign; once the campaign failed the Northerners could not be persuaded to pay another.
• Defeat removed John’s ability to hire continental mercenaries on credit, and so removed the threat that had kept some barons in line.
• The political shock of Bouvines turned doubters into rebels and persuaded waverers that John’s government had failed; within months the rebels were openly mustering.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• The loss of Normandy in 1204 was the deeper cause — it created the financial pressure that drove every later tax and so the resentment that fuelled rebellion.
• John’s use of arbitrary power — punitive reliefs on inheritances, fines on widows, hostages, and the use of mercenary captains such as Falkes de Bréauté — offended baronial expectations of customary government.
• The dispute with Innocent III and the Interdict 1208–14 had eroded John’s religious legitimacy and the morale of the kingdom for six years.
• The 1212 plot of FitzWalter and de Vesci showed that armed rebellion was already thinkable; their survival created a leadership cadre for 1215.
• The taking of London on 17 May 1215 was the immediate trigger that forced negotiation at Runnymede.
• Stephen Langton’s mediation and his use of Henry I’s coronation charter gave the revolt a programme it would otherwise have lacked.

Overall judgement: Bouvines was the catalyst that turned long-running grievances into open revolt — without the defeat the Northerners might have grumbled but not marched. But it cannot be called the main cause. The structural conditions of rebellion were laid by the loss of Normandy in 1204, by a decade of arbitrary taxation, and by John’s personal style of government. Bouvines lit a fire in dry timber the king had spent ten years stacking. A balanced judgement weighs the immediate trigger of 1214 against the longer arc of financial and political pressure since 1204.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (scutage, feudal incident, homage, demesne, mercenaries, Northerners).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Joseph McCoy for the growth of the cattle industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Joseph McCoy, supported by specific period detail.

Indicative content:
• In 1867 McCoy bought the small Kansas town of Abilene beside the Kansas Pacific line and built stockyards for 3,000 cattle, a hotel and loading pens — creating the first cow town.
• Because McCoy sent riders south to bring Texas drovers north, around 35,000 longhorns reached Abilene in 1867 and 700,000 by 1871, turning a Texas surplus into a national industry.
• Because Abilene worked, the cow-town model spread — Newton, Wichita, Ellsworth, Caldwell and from 1875 Dodge City — multiplying shipping points along the railroads.
• McCoy linked the Chisholm Trail to the eastern slaughterhouses, allowing Texas longhorns to reach Chicago by rail and producing the ‘beef bonanza’ of the 1870s.
• Without his railhead market, Texas longhorns would have remained a low-value local stock; McCoy made the price gap profitable on a national scale.

Mastering: Sustained explanation linking McCoy to specific consequences for the industry, with named places (Abilene, Chicago, Chisholm Trail) and dates (1867, 1871).
Secure: Two strands of importance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of McCoy without explaining importance for the industry.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the changes in the cattle industry in the years 1866–1885.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Goodnight–Loving Trail (1866)
• Abilene as the first cow town (1867)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1866 Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving drove 2,000 longhorns west and north into New Mexico and Colorado, supplying army posts and Denver mining camps along the new Goodnight–Loving Trail — opening a non-railroad market for Texas beef.
• Because Joseph McCoy built stockyards beside the Kansas Pacific line at Abilene in 1867, Texas longhorns could now also walk the Chisholm Trail north and be shipped east to Chicago slaughterhouses.
• Because the price gap between $3–$4 Texas cattle and $30–$40 northern beef was so wide, the ‘beef bonanza’ followed: by 1871 around 700,000 head reached Abilene in a single season.
• Because John Iliff and others demonstrated that cattle could be fattened on free northern grass, the open-range model spread across Wyoming, Montana and the Dakotas through the 1870s, attracting eastern and European investment.
• By 1885 refrigerated cars from around 1880 had made beef rather than live cattle the eastern shipment, lowering meat prices and turning ranching into a national industry — the conditions that would crash in the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1866, 1867, 1871, 1880), specialist vocabulary (long drive, open range, cow town, Chisholm Trail), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Goodnight–Loving Trail for the growth of the cattle industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• In 1866 Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving trailed 2,000 longhorns west and north out of Texas into New Mexico and Colorado, opening a route that did not depend on the Kansas railheads.
• Because the trail reached Fort Sumner and the Denver mining camps, it supplied the army garrisons running the Indian Wars and the reservations whose treaty annuities included beef rations.
• Because the army-and-mining market was profitable, Texas drovers had a second outlet alongside the Abilene route — making the industry less dependent on a single railhead.
• The trail also brought longhorns onto the northern grass that John Iliff would shortly turn into open-range ranching, seeding the model that spread across Wyoming and Montana.
• Goodnight’s later partnership with Iliff supplied army posts and reservations directly, blending trail-driving and Plains ranching into a single industry by the 1870s.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1866, 2,000 head, Fort Sumner, Denver) and specialist vocabulary (long drive, open range).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the development of open-range Plains ranching in the years 1866–1885.

You may use the following in your answer:
• John Iliff
• the long drive

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• From the late 1860s the Colorado rancher John Iliff realised that the unfenced grass north of the Arkansas River would fatten cattle for free, and by 1870 was running tens of thousands of head on the open range.
• Because Iliff supplied the army posts, the reservations and the Union Pacific construction crews, he showed that ranching ON the Plains was more profitable than simply trailing cattle through them.
• Because the long drive was the way Texas longhorns reached the Plains in the first place — 1,000–1,500 miles, two to three months, 10–12 cowboys per crew — the new northern ranches were stocked from the same Texas herds Goodnight, Loving and McCoy had been moving since 1866–67.
• Because eastern and European investors poured capital into Wyoming and Montana ranches in the late 1870s and early 1880s, the open range became a national industry — cowboys, foremen and absentee owners.
• By 1885 the open range was overstocked and over-leveraged; the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 would kill an estimated 60% of cattle in some Wyoming ranges, ending the open-range model and forcing the shift to fenced ranching covered in Lesson 12.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail, specialist vocabulary (open range, long drive), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the railroads for the growth of the cattle industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Because the Kansas Pacific reached Abilene by 1867, Joseph McCoy could build stockyards beside the line and ship Texas longhorns east to Chicago slaughterhouses, turning a $3–$4 Texas animal into a $30–$40 eastern carcase.
• Because the cow-town model could move — Newton, Wichita, Ellsworth, Caldwell, then Dodge City from 1875 — the trade kept pace with the spreading railhead network.
• Because refrigerated cars from around 1880 allowed beef rather than live cattle to be shipped, eastern meat prices fell and the eastern market grew, expanding ranching into a national industry.
• Because the Northern Pacific (1883) opened a Minnesota-to-Pacific line and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe pushed across the Southwest the same year, new shipping points multiplied across the Plains.
• Without the rail network, Texas longhorns and northern open-range cattle would have stayed local stock — the railroad turned the price gap into the ‘beef bonanza’ of the 1870s and 1880s.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1867, 1880, 1883) and specialist vocabulary.
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the long drive for the cowboy’s working life.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the long drive to a specific feature of cowboy work.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that work was strictly seasonal and badly paid — around $25–$40 a month, with three months on the trail, a few weeks of round-up either side and the winter laid off — producing a workforce of single, mobile young men rather than settled families.
• Another consequence was that the cowboy’s skills, equipment and vocabulary were inherited from the Mexican vaquero tradition — chaps, lariat, branding methods and around a third of cowboys themselves — making the cowboy a hybrid figure rather than a purely Anglo-American invention.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific period detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the purpose of punishment in the nineteenth century was different from its purpose in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Pentonville, opened in 1842, was built to reform: single cells, masked exercise, silent labour and chapel cubicles were meant to force the prisoner to face his conscience.
• Sixteenth-century punishment aimed at deterrence and retribution in public: flogging, branding, the pillory and hanging were staged so that onlookers would be frightened out of offending.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why public execution was abolished in 1868.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the crowds at public hangings
• the growth of prisons.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own. Indicative content: • Public hangings drew huge drunken crowds — up to 30,000 at major executions outside Newgate — that critics said brutalised onlookers rather than deterring crime. • Reformers had built a long campaign against the spectacle: Howard’s 1777 State of the Prisons, Fry’s Newgate visits from 1813 and Peel’s repeal of capital statutes (1823–27) had reframed punishment as moral reform, not public theatre. • The number of capital offences had already collapsed: from over 200 in 1815 to about a dozen by 1837, leaving public execution rare and increasingly anomalous. • Pentonville and the separate system showed that prisons could deliver punishment behind walls, removing the practical case for keeping the gallows public. • Parliamentary inquiries through the 1850s and 1860s repeatedly recommended that hangings be moved inside prison walls; the Capital Punishment Amendment Act 1868 enacted this change. Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (Bloody Code repeals, Howard, Fry, Pentonville, parliamentary inquiries) and explicit links to the question. Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail. Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail. Emerging: Description of the change without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the influence of individuals on punishment in the eighteenth century was similar to their influence in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• John Howard toured the gaols and published The State of the Prisons in 1777, turning evidence into a parliamentary campaign that produced the Health of Prisoners Act and the Penitentiary Act.
• Sydney Silverman used the same method of persistent parliamentary pressure, introducing four abolition Bills before the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act was passed in 1965.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the separate system at Pentonville came under criticism by the 1860s.

You may use the following in your answer:
• mental breakdown among prisoners
• the cost of single cells.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• Prison doctors reported alarming rates of mental breakdown: between 1842 and 1850 over twenty Pentonville inmates were certified insane and sent to Bedlam.
• Suicide and attempted suicide were common, and Charles Dickens, who visited prisons run on these lines, condemned prolonged solitary confinement as cruel.
• The masked exercise, single chapels and total silence were increasingly seen as cruel rather than reformative — a slower, quieter version of the punishment the Bloody Code had used noisily.
• The system was very expensive: each prisoner needed a single cell, individual chapel cubicle and dedicated work tools, making it difficult to scale to the rising prison population after transportation ended.
• Even contemporary reformers began to argue that human beings need company and conversation; prison historians such as Michael Ignatieff later argued the separate system was as cruel as the older code.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (insanity figures, cost, contemporary criticism, historiography) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the regime without explaining why it was criticised.

practice_questions.text:
‘Pentonville prison was the most important development in punishment in the period c1700–c1900.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the separate system
• the ending of transportation in 1868.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary. Indicative content — arguments supporting Pentonville as the most important development: • Pentonville (1842) was the flagship of the separate system, copied at 54 new prisons by the 1850s — it set the template for the British prison estate. • It enshrined the principle that punishment was prison-based, hidden behind walls, and reform-oriented (work, chapel, silent reflection). • It made it possible to abolish public execution (1868) and end transportation (1868) because there was now a credible domestic alternative. • Joshua Jebb’s radial design and individual cells became the architectural standard for the modern British prison. Indicative content — arguments against (other developments mattered as much or more): • Peel’s repeal of the Bloody Code (1823–27) and the Gaols Act 1823 came before Pentonville and shifted the legal baseline; without them Pentonville would have served the old capital code. • John Howard’s State of the Prisons (1777) and Elizabeth Fry’s Newgate work (from 1813) created the reform climate Pentonville expressed. • The ending of transportation (1868) and of public execution (1868) were the visible signs of the change; for ordinary Britons these endings mattered more than one prison’s design. • The separate system also caused serious harm — mental breakdown, suicide — and was relaxed by the 1860s; calling its showpiece ‘the most important development’ ignores its costs. • Later developments, especially the rise of probation and non-custodial alternatives in the twentieth century, arguably represent a bigger shift than Pentonville did. Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Pentonville against at least one other factor (Peel’s repeals, Howard and Fry, ending of public execution and transportation), uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended. Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (Bloody Code, transportation, separate system, silent system, Pentonville, oakum, treadwheel, Newgate).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the treatment of women in prison after 1823 was different from their treatment before 1813.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Before Elizabeth Fry's visits, about 300 women and their children were crammed into two Newgate wards, sleeping on straw with no work, no schooling and no prison clothes.
• After her campaign and the Gaols Act of 1823, women prisoners were to have female matrons, separate accommodation, religious instruction and useful work.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of grammar schools in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Curriculum focused on classical languages — pupils studied Latin grammar, rhetoric and classical authors such as Cicero, Virgil and Ovid, with some Greek.
• Long, disciplined school day — running from around 6am to 5pm in summer, with short breaks; corporal punishment such as birching was routinely used to enforce study.
• Concentrated in towns and funded by patrons — over 130 new grammar schools were founded under Elizabeth, often endowed by guilds, merchants or wealthy individuals.
• Pupils were almost exclusively boys — mainly the sons of gentry, clergy, merchants and prosperous yeomen, with a few free places for academically able poor boys.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabethan theatre in London by 1588.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks. Indicative content: • Purpose-built playhouses outside the city walls — James Burbage built The Theatre in Shoreditch in 1576, followed by The Curtain (1577) and The Rose (1587), beyond the reach of the Puritan London corporation. • Mixed audiences paying tiered prices — a penny stood you in the yard as a ‘groundling’, two pence got a gallery seat, three pence a seat on the stage, putting apprentices and gentry in the same building. • Companies required noble patronage — the Queen’s Men and the Lord Admiral’s Men were the leading troupes; without a patron a company was treated as vagabonds under the 1572 Act. • Plays mixed comedy, history and tragedy — Christopher Marlowe’s Tamburlaine drew crowds from 1587; performances were daytime, in partly open-air buildings. Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail. Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed. Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature. Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why education expanded in Elizabethan England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Royal Injunctions of 1559
• the growing ‘middling sort’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• The Royal Injunctions of 1559 required clergy to encourage Bible reading in English — this made basic literacy a religious duty for Protestant households and pushed parents to teach reading at home or send children to petty schools.
• Wealth from trade and farming created a ‘middling sort’ — merchants, prosperous yeomen and gentry could afford grammar school fees and saw schooling as the route into law, the Church and government service.
• Charitable foundation by guilds, towns and individuals — over 130 new grammar schools were founded under Elizabeth, often endowed in wills as a form of public-spirited philanthropy.
• Government concern with social order — an educated, Protestant elite was seen as a defence against Catholicism and rebellion; the same logic that funded universities funded grammar schools.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why theatre became popular in Elizabethan England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• noble patronage
• purpose-built playhouses
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links. Indicative content: • Noble patronage (stimulus) — companies such as the Queen’s Men and the Lord Admiral’s Men needed an aristocratic patron to perform legally; without it they could be punished as vagabonds under the 1572 Act. Patronage protected actors and gave their plays prestige. • Purpose-built playhouses (stimulus) — from 1576 (The Theatre), 1577 (The Curtain) and 1587 (The Rose), London had permanent venues capable of holding 2,000–3,000 spectators, replacing temporary inn-yard performances and creating a daily entertainment industry. • Tiered ticket pricing (own knowledge) — a penny got entry to the yard, two pence a gallery seat; this allowed apprentices, merchants and gentry to attend the same play, making theatre genuinely popular across classes. • Royal favour (own knowledge) — Elizabeth enjoyed plays at court and her licensing system shielded the theatres from the Puritan-leaning London corporation that wanted them closed. • Talented playwrights (own knowledge) — Christopher Marlowe’s Tamburlaine from 1587 brought blank verse and large historical themes to mass audiences, raising the artistic standing of theatre. Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections. Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge. Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone. Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why leisure activities differed between rich and poor Elizabethans.
You may use the following in your answer:
• cost and access
• free time
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Cost and access — hunting required deer parks, hawks, horses and trained falconers; real tennis required enclosed courts found only in noble houses or palaces; these pursuits were physically out of reach for the poor.
• Time available — labourers, apprentices and farm workers had limited free hours and most leisure happened on Sundays after church, leading to alehouse games (skittles, dice, cards) and parish football rather than long ritualised pursuits.
• Class identity and display — nobility and gentry used hawking, hunting and dancing the pavane to display refinement; gambling at chess and Primero showed wealth they could afford to lose. Leisure was a way of performing rank.
• Shared violent spectatorship — bear-baiting and cock-fighting drew all classes because they were cheap to attend and depended on betting; this is one area where rich and poor mingled despite the wider divide.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason new grammar schools were founded in Elizabethan England was the spread of Protestantism.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Royal Injunctions of 1559
• the growing ‘middling sort’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Protestantism as main reason):
• Royal Injunctions of 1559 (stimulus) required clergy to promote Bible reading in English, making literacy a Protestant duty and pushing parents toward formal schooling for their sons.
• Grammar school curriculum reinforced Protestant worship — pupils learned to read the Prayer Book, the Bible and the Ten Commandments alongside Latin classics.
• Many new schools were founded with explicitly Protestant aims by Anglican clergy, town corporations and reform-minded merchants.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• The growing ‘middling sort’ (stimulus) — merchants and prosperous yeomen could now afford grammar school fees and saw schooling as a ladder into law, the Church and government, fuelling demand regardless of religion.
• Charitable philanthropy (own knowledge) — guilds, livery companies and individuals endowed schools in their wills as public-spirited acts; this was a long Tudor tradition pre-dating Protestantism.
• Government concern with social order (own knowledge) — an educated Protestant elite was seen as a defence against Catholic recusancy and foreign threat, so political insecurity (especially after 1570 excommunication) drove foundations as much as religious zeal.
• Continuity from earlier reigns (own knowledge) — grammar schools had been founded throughout the Tudor period; the Elizabethan expansion accelerated an existing pattern rather than starting it.

Justified judgement: Protestantism gave moral and political weight to schooling and the Royal Injunctions made literacy a religious duty, but the practical drivers were the wealth and aspirations of the ‘middling sort’ and a charitable foundation tradition that pre-dated the Reformation. A strong response weighs religious motivation against social and economic causes and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. A press report of the Mexico City medal ceremony, 17 October 1968.

‘Tommie Smith and John Carlos, two Black American sprinters who finished first and third in the 200-metre dash, used the victory ceremony tonight to make a Black Power protest. As the United States national anthem began, the two athletes, standing shoeless on the rostrum, bowed their heads and each raised a black-gloved fist. Smith said afterwards that the gloves stood for “Black America”, the bowed heads for the lynched, and the bare feet for Black poverty. The crowd of 50,000 booed loudly as the runners left the stadium. Within hours, the United States Olympic Committee was meeting with International Olympic Committee president Avery Brundage to discuss expulsion.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Mexico Olympics salute.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘The salute had a planned set of meanings rather than being a spontaneous gesture’ supported by ‘the gloves stood for “Black America”, the bowed heads for the lynched, and the bare feet for Black poverty’ AND ‘The protest was met with hostility by the stadium crowd and the Olympic authorities’ supported by ‘The crowd of 50,000 booed loudly’ or ‘the United States Olympic Committee was meeting with International Olympic Committee president Avery Brundage to discuss expulsion’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 2006 history of the Black Panther Party that emphasises its grassroots welfare work):
‘The Panthers should be remembered as the most ambitious community programme to come out of the 1960s civil rights movement. By 1969 the Free Breakfast for Children programme was feeding about 20,000 children every weekday in nineteen cities. Free clinics, sickle-cell anaemia testing, escort services for pensioners and Liberation Schools served Black neighbourhoods abandoned by the federal government. The Panthers proved that a Black community could build its own welfare state from below.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2017 history of the FBI’s domestic counter-intelligence programme):
‘Whatever the Panthers’ programmes promised, by 1971 the Party had been broken. COINTELPRO had infiltrated the leadership with paid informants, manufactured feuds with rival groups through forged letters, and licensed police raids that killed Fred Hampton in his bed in Chicago in December 1969. The free breakfasts continued in a few chapters; the political organisation that ran them did not. The Panthers’ story by 1975 is mostly the story of how the federal state destroyed them.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the achievements of the Black Panther Party? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees the Panthers as a successful grassroots welfare organisation that built a community-led alternative to the federal welfare state; Interpretation 2 sees the Panthers as an organisation broken by federal repression by 1971, with the survival programmes outliving the political body that created them) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the most ambitious community programme to come out of the 1960s civil rights movement’ vs ‘by 1971 the Party had been broken’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the Black Panther Party.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 2006 history of the Panthers that draws on Party records, Free Breakfast Programme statistics and interviews with former members about their welfare work, and so foregrounds the survival programmes; Interpretation 2 is from a 2017 history of COINTELPRO that draws on FBI files released after the 1976 Church Committee, court records of police raids, and the killing of Fred Hampton in December 1969, and so foregrounds federal repression. The two have different focuses (community welfare vs federal counter-intelligence) and different bodies of evidence (Party records vs FBI files), and so reach different judgements on the Panthers’ achievements.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the achievements of the Black Panther Party?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context. Marks will be awarded for the quality of your written communication, including spelling, punctuation, grammar and your use of specialist terms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across the Panthers’ founding and decline (the founding by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland in October 1966; the Ten-Point Programme; the armed police-monitoring patrols and the May 1967 California state Capitol protest; the Free Breakfast for Children programme feeding around 20,000 children per day across nineteen cities by 1969; free clinics, sickle-cell testing and Liberation Schools; J. Edgar Hoover’s 1969 description of the Panthers as ‘the greatest threat to the internal security of the country’; the COINTELPRO infiltration and forged-letter operations; the killing of Fred Hampton in Chicago on 4 December 1969; the Party’s collapse in the mid-1970s under repression, internal feuds and criminal entanglements; Carmichael’s contribution of ‘institutional racism’ as an analytical category; the Smith-Carlos salute as the global symbol of Black Power), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently. SPaG is consistently accurate, with sophisticated use of subject-specific terminology.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated. SPaG is generally accurate with appropriate subject-specific terminology.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit. SPaG is reasonable with some subject-specific terminology.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. SPaG is uneven; subject-specific terminology limited. [16 marks for content + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Black Power emerged as a movement in 1966.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Meredith March Against Fear
• ghetto poverty in Northern cities

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. younger SNCC and CORE activists’ loss of patience with nonviolent direct action after the beatings of the Freedom Rides, the killings of Freedom Summer and the Selma assault; the failure of the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act to address Northern de facto segregation, racist policing or housing; the influence of Malcolm X’s critique of integrationism after his assassination in February 1965; the example of African independence movements and the OAU; rising urban unrest from Watts in 1965 to Detroit in 1967), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (Black Power, SNCC, SCLC, integrationism, self-defence).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From a Black Panther Party recruitment pamphlet, ‘What We Want, What We Believe’, distributed in Oakland from late 1966.

‘We want full employment for our people. We want decent housing fit for the shelter of human beings. We want education that teaches us our true history and our role in the present-day society. We want an end to the robbery by the capitalist of our Black community. We want an immediate end to police brutality and the murder of Black people. We want all Black men to be exempt from military service. We want freedom for all Black men held in federal, state, county and city prisons and jails. We want land, bread, housing, education, clothing, justice and peace.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the aims of the Black Panther Party.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘The Panthers wanted economic transformation as well as civil rights’ supported by ‘an end to the robbery by the capitalist of our Black community’ AND ‘The Panthers connected racism in the United States to the war in Vietnam’ supported by ‘We want all Black men to be exempt from military service’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Stamp Act (1765) for relations between Britain and the American colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: the Stamp Act led directly to the Stamp Act Congress in October 1765, the first inter-colonial meeting on a political grievance, which produced a coordinated petition to the king; it also led to the formation of the Sons of Liberty as a network of crowd action that forced every stamp distributor in the thirteen colonies to resign or flee by the end of 1765. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to colonial actions.
Emerging: Notes that the Stamp Act happened without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Sons of Liberty for the development of colonial opposition in 1765–73.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: the Sons of Liberty mattered because their crowd action against Andrew Oliver in Boston in August 1765 forced his resignation as stamp distributor and set a template copied in New York, Philadelphia and Charleston; they also mattered because they organised the non-importation boycotts that hurt London merchants enough to force repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766, teaching colonists that organised pressure could move Parliament. A third anchor might be the network’s role in the Tea Party of 1773, where 100 men in disguise destroyed 342 chests of tea. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus; limited use of specific developments.
Emerging: Describes the Sons of Liberty without explaining their significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Boston Massacre (1770) for the patriot movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the killings of 5 March 1770 mattered because Paul Revere’s engraving turned a confused street incident into an iconic image of British tyranny circulated through every colony, giving the patriot cause its first martyrs — including Crispus Attucks. They also mattered because the deaths fed Sam Adams’s Committees of Correspondence and gave Boston a moral authority that helped the town claim inter-colonial sympathy after the Port Act four years later. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Describes the Massacre without explaining its long-term significance.
Emerging: General references to British troops in Boston without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Boston Tea Party (December 1773) for British policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the destruction of 342 chests of East India Company tea led directly to the Boston Port Act of 1774, closing Boston harbour until the tea was paid for, which was meant to isolate Massachusetts from the other colonies; it also led to the Massachusetts Government Act stripping the colony’s charter and making the upper house Crown-appointed, which colonists read as a warning that any colony’s self-government could be suspended. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the Acts of 1774.
Emerging: Mentions the Tea Party without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how opposition to British policies grew in the years 1765–74. You may use the following information in your answer:
• The Stamp Act
• The Boston Tea Party
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why opposition grew rather than narrating in sequence. Links the Stamp Act crisis to the formation of the Sons of Liberty and the success of non-importation, which then conditioned the response to the Townshend duties of 1767 and the Boston Massacre of March 1770; links the Tea Act of 1773 to the Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts of 1774; uses own knowledge such as the Declaratory Act, Committees of Correspondence, or the Quebec Act. Reaches an analytical judgement about the rhythm of escalation, calm and renewed escalation rather than treating the road to revolution as a straight line.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis of connections.
Emerging: Lists events without explaining how opposition grew.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Intolerable Acts (1774) for inter-colonial cooperation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Boston Port Act mattered because closing the harbour of a town of 16,000 forced food, money and political support to flow in from other colonies, breaking the isolation London had hoped to achieve; the Massachusetts Government Act mattered because suspending an entire colonial charter signalled to the other twelve colonies that any of them could be next, producing the First Continental Congress at Philadelphia in September 1774. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions the Acts without showing how they drove inter-colonial cooperation.
Emerging: General references to British policy without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Cortes’s appointment as Governor and Captain-General of New Spain in 1523.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Cortes used his governorship to grant encomiendas to his soldiers, creating a new colonial aristocracy of conquistadors who controlled Indigenous labour and tribute — effectively recycling the old Aztec tribute system with new Spanish owners on top.
• Cortes ordered the rebuilding of Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, with the cathedral on the site of the Templo Mayor and the viceregal palace on Montezuma’s palace — cementing Spanish power on Aztec foundations.
• The appointment encouraged the arrival of Franciscan and Dominican missions, including the Twelve Apostles of Mexico in 1524 — beginning the systematic Christianisation of the Nahua population.
• It also planted the seed of Cortes’s downfall: it gave him a power base independent of the Crown that the crown would later move to dismantle by recalling him in 1528.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the appointment without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Spanish conquest for the Aztec people in the period 1521–c1555.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Demographic collapse: central Mexico’s population fell from an estimated 15–25 million in 1519 to perhaps 1–2 million by 1600 — smallpox in 1520, measles in 1531 and typhus in 1545 each killed a generation of people without immunity, made worse by forced labour and the loss of land.
• The destruction of the priesthood and the religious state: temples were pulled down, codices burned, and Catholic worship imposed. The cathedral was deliberately built on the Templo Mayor.
• Cultural survival: despite the catastrophe, Nahuatl was still widely spoken, codex-painting traditions adapted to Catholic subjects, and Indigenous town councils (cabildos) preserved a layer of self-government under Spanish rule.
• Economic dispossession: Aztec tribute structures were repurposed as Spanish encomiendas; the same maize, cotton and labour that had once gone to Tenochtitlan now went to Spanish encomenderos.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail across at least two timescales (immediate / medium-term / long-term).
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the conquest’s aftermath without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the foundation of Panama City (1519) for the development of Spanish power in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Panama City, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Panama City, founded in 1519 by Pedrarias Davila on the Pacific side of the isthmus, gave Spain a continental Pacific port for the first time — converting Balboa’s 1513 sighting of the Pacific into a permanent base.
• It provided the staging point for the expeditions of Pizarro, Almagro and Luque from 1524 onwards, leading directly to the 1530–32 voyage that would bring down the Inca empire.
• It allowed Spanish goods and treasure to cross the narrow isthmus by mule train, linking the Caribbean and Pacific economies and opening South America to Spanish trade and conquest.
• It illustrates the pattern of Spanish empire-building — a chain of coastal bases (Santo Domingo, Havana, Vera Cruz, Panama) from which the next conquest could be launched.
• Without Panama, the conquest of Peru and the silver economy of the second half of the 16th century could not have developed on the same timetable.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. strategic Pacific access AND launchpad for Peru) with specific period detail (Balboa 1513, Pedrarias Davila 1519, Pizarro’s expeditions, the mule trains).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Panama City without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the encomienda system in Cortes’s New Spain (1523–28).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the encomienda, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The encomienda gave Cortes a way to reward his soldiers without needing money — instead of cash, he granted them rights to the labour and tribute of named Indigenous communities, creating an instant settler aristocracy.
• It repurposed the existing Aztec tribute system: the same maize, cotton and labour that had flowed to Tenochtitlan now flowed to Spanish encomenderos. This continuity made the colony economically functional from day one.
• It tied the Christianisation programme to the labour system — encomenderos were nominally responsible for the religious instruction of their workers, which gave the Franciscans and Dominicans access from 1524.
• It became the central political problem of the Spanish empire. The encomenderos became hereditary, powerful and independent, prompting the New Laws of 1542 (the next big intervention by Charles V).
• It set the template for Peru, where the same encomienda model was applied after Pizarro’s conquest.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands with specific period detail (the recycling of Aztec tribute, the link forward to the New Laws, the missions).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the encomienda without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Cortes’s recall to Spain in 1528.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Cortes’s recall, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The recall established a key principle of Spanish imperial government: no conquistador, however successful, could be allowed to govern conquered territory indefinitely. The crown distrusted independent power.
• It led directly to the creation of the first audiencia of New Spain in 1528 — a royal court of judges answerable to the Crown — and from 1535 the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Bureaucratic, salaried royal officials replaced personal conquistador rule.
• It signalled to other conquistadors (notably Pizarro in Peru) that the Crown would not tolerate a kingdom-within-a-kingdom — a warning that would matter again at the 1546 conquistador rebellion against the New Laws.
• It softened, but did not erase, the personal power of Cortes — he was given the marquisate of the Valley of Oaxaca and substantial estates, but stripped of executive command.
• It illustrates Charles V’s broader policy of centralising royal authority over the Americas — the same logic that produced the Council of the Indies (1524) and the New Laws (1542).

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (audiencia 1528, viceroyalty 1535, marquisate of Oaxaca, link forward to Pizarro).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the recall without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spanish power was extended in the Americas in the years 1519–28. You may use the following in your answer: the foundation of Panama City (1519), the rebuilding of Mexico City (1521–22). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1519 Pedrarias Davila founded Panama City on the Pacific side of the isthmus, giving Spain a base from which expeditions could push south down the Pacific coast — the strategic platform that would later launch Pizarro.
• Meanwhile, Cortes’s coalition with the Tlaxcalans and the smallpox epidemic of 1520 made possible the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 — collapsing the largest Indigenous state Europeans had encountered.
• This in turn allowed the rebuilding of Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlan in 1521–22, with the cathedral built on the Templo Mayor — a continental Spanish capital with a tribute base inherited from the Mexica.
• Because of the new colony’s scale, in 1523 Charles V appointed Cortes Governor and Captain-General of New Spain, and Cortes granted encomiendas to his soldiers and welcomed the Franciscan missions of 1524.
• This in turn created the political problem that defined the rest of the period: the conquistadors had become powerful enough to alarm the Crown. By 1528 Cortes had been recalled and the audiencia installed. Spanish power was no longer in conquistador hands — it was being centralised under the crown.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Tlaxcalans, smallpox, encomienda, audiencia).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1572 Vagabonds Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Harsh punishment of able-bodied wanderers — first-offence vagabonds were to be whipped and bored through the right ear with a hot iron; a second offence could mean execution.
• Compulsory parish responsibility for the impotent poor — Justices of the Peace in every parish were required to keep a register of the deserving poor and levy a compulsory poor rate to support them.
• Restrictions on travelling performers — actors and minstrels without a noble patron could be treated as vagabonds, which is why companies needed the protection of a nobleman such as the Earl of Leicester.
• Use of Justices of the Peace as enforcers — JPs were given the legal authority to identify, register, punish and relieve the poor of their parish, professionalising local enforcement.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how Elizabethan parishes treated the ‘impotent poor’.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Registration by Justices of the Peace — from 1572 each parish kept a list of the deserving poor — the elderly, sick, orphaned and disabled.
• Funding through the compulsory poor rate — a local property tax was levied on the better-off parishioners and used to provide pensions, food and small payments.
• Voluntary almsgiving and town schemes — towns such as Norwich (1570 census of the poor) and Ipswich pioneered organised parish relief, ward by ward, alongside private charity.
• Use of almshouses — surviving and newly endowed almshouses provided shelter for the elderly and infirm in many parishes.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why poverty increased in Elizabethan England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• population growth
• enclosure
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• Population growth (stimulus) — England’s population rose from roughly 3 million in 1558 toward 4 million by 1600. Demand for food outstripped supply, pushing up prices and squeezing wage labourers whose wages did not keep pace.
• Enclosure (stimulus) — landowners hedged off arable common land for sheep because wool was profitable; one shepherd replaced many ploughmen, displacing rural labourers from their employment and from common rights.
• Price inflation (own knowledge) — food and goods prices rose sharply across the sixteenth century while wages lagged, pushing wage-earning households below subsistence even when in work.
• Dissolution of the monasteries (own knowledge) — Henry VIII’s 1530s dissolution had ended the monastic almshouses, hospitals and daily charity that had cushioned medieval poverty; the gap had still not been filled by Elizabeth’s reign.
• Bad harvests of 1586 and 1587 (own knowledge) — back-to-back failed harvests pushed fragile households into vagabondage; demobilised soldiers returning from the Netherlands and Ireland added to the wandering population.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabeth’s government changed its policies towards the poor between 1572 and 1576.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor
• demobilised soldiers
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Recognition that poverty had economic causes — demobilised soldiers and labourers displaced by enclosure made it visible that many able-bodied poor wanted work but could not find it, pushing the 1576 Act to provide raw materials for parish work.
• Influence of pioneering town schemes — Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor and Ipswich’s relief schemes had shown that distinguishing the genuinely unemployed from the wilfully idle worked better than punishment alone.
• Protestant religious thinking — clergy increasingly preached that the poor were Christ’s neighbours and a moral duty, not simply a public-order problem.
• Concern about social order — the Privy Council feared that mass vagabondage could lead to rebellion; constructive provision of work in the parish, backed up by Houses of Correction for those who refused, was seen as more effective than the 1572 punishments alone.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for changing attitudes towards the poor by 1588 was the failure of harsh punishment to solve the problem.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1572 Vagabonds Act
• Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (failure of harsh punishment as main reason):
• 1572 Vagabonds Act (stimulus) — whipping and burning through the ear did not stop people from moving in search of work; numbers of vagabonds remained high, showing punishment alone was not deterring those driven by genuine need.
• Visibility of demobilised soldiers and displaced labourers undermined the assumption that all wanderers were wilfully idle, forcing a rethink of the 1572 approach.
• The 1576 Poor Relief Act explicitly added work materials and Houses of Correction, recognising that punishment without provision of work was insufficient.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor (stimulus) — town schemes had already begun distinguishing impotent from sturdy poor before national punishment had clearly ‘failed’; pioneering local practice drove change as much as national failure did.
• Protestant religious thinking (own knowledge) — clergy preached the poor as a Christian duty, shaping attitudes among landowners and JPs and making compulsory poor rates politically possible.
• Economic reality of population growth, inflation and bad harvests (own knowledge) — the scale of the crisis (especially after 1586) made parish-level provision a practical necessity regardless of attitudes.
• Concern with social order (own knowledge) — the Privy Council saw constructive provision of work as a defence against rebellion, not just charity; political calculation drove change as much as moral failure of punishment.

Justified judgement: The harshness of 1572 did fail in its own terms — vagabondage continued — and that failure pushed the move toward provision of work in 1576. But the change of attitude rested equally on town pioneers like Norwich, on Protestant teaching, and on the sheer economic scale of the crisis. A strong response weighs the failure of punishment against these other drivers and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabethan authorities distinguished between the ‘impotent poor’ and the ‘sturdy beggars’.
You may use the following in your answer:
• religious teaching about charity
• fear of disorder
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Religious and moral framework — Tudor Christianity taught that helping the genuinely needy was a duty but encouraging the lazy was sinful; the distinction allowed authorities to be generous to the deserving while punishing the ‘wilfully idle’.
