• Public order concerns — able-bodied wanderers were feared as potential criminals and rebels (especially after the 1569 Northern Rebellion), so framing them as ‘sturdy beggars’ justified harsh deterrent punishments under the 1572 Act.
• Cost control — if every poor person counted equally, the parish poor rate would be unaffordable; restricting compulsory relief to the impotent kept the cost on the rate-payers manageable.
• Limits of medieval understanding — contemporaries lacked modern economic explanations and assumed that anyone who could work would find work; the moral binary made sense within that worldview, even though it disguised structural causes such as inflation, enclosure and bad harvests.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about peasant resistance to collectivisation between 1929 and 1932. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, the slaughter of livestock before joining the kolkhoz, the use of armed ‘25,000-ers’ to enforce collectivisation, the seizure of seed grain, the issuing of internal passports to stop peasant flight, or Stalin’s ‘Dizzy with Success’ retreat). Inferences go beyond surface description to explain what the detail reveals about peasant attitudes or regime methods. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Stalin introduced the policy of collectivisation in 1929.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the grain procurement crisis of 1927–28
• the First Five-Year Plan
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — e.g. the 1927–28 procurement crisis when peasants withheld grain at low state prices; the need to fund industrialisation by exporting grain; the political logic of breaking peasant independence after a decade of compromise under the NEP; ideological commitment to socialism in the countryside; and the defeat of Bukharin’s Right Opposition which removed the last party voice for the NEP. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — kolkhoz, dekulakisation, Sovnarkom. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Describes features of collectivisation without explaining why Stalin chose it. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the consequences of collectivisation in the Soviet countryside.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation stresses the success of collectivisation in giving the state direct control of grain supply and funding industrialisation, while the other stresses the demographic catastrophe — livestock losses, the Holodomor, dekulakisation and a generation of rural alienation). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Ukrainian famine of 1932–33.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (Politburo decrees and grain export data versus survivor testimony and Ukrainian Communist Party cadre records); they wrote at different times (Cold War-era studies such as Conquest’s ‘Harvest of Sorrow’ versus post-archival accounts such as Davies and Wheatcroft’s ‘Years of Hunger’); or they wrote with different purposes (arguing for genocide recognition versus reconstructing economic policy in conditions of indifference). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of dekulakisation in the success of collectivisation?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of dekulakisation — the three-category Politburo decree of January 1930, the ‘25,000-ers’, the deportation of around 1.8 million peasants, the role of Molotov and Kaganovich — weighed against rival explanations of collectivisation’s success (state quotas, Machine Tractor Stations, internal passports, the brief retreat of ‘Dizzy with Success’). Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Ukrainian famine of 1932–33 was the deliberate result of Stalin’s policies rather than an unavoidable accident?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the rising quotas in Ukraine, the August 1932 decree on theft of socialist property, the December 1932 internal-passport decree, the village blacklists, the continued export of grain in 1932–33, the simultaneous attack on Ukrainian language and cadres — weighed against the Davies and Wheatcroft reading of criminal indifference rather than directed genocide, and the Conquest/Applebaum argument for deliberate national targeting. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (kolkhoz, sovkhoz, Sovnarkom, Holodomor, dekulakisation). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For Paper 3 inference questions on collectivisation, look for sources that hint at the gap between regime claims and rural reality — the slaughtered livestock, the closed villages, the seized seed grain. One sharp inference about that gap will outscore a paragraph of paraphrase. For 12-mark causation essays on why Stalin abandoned the NEP, weigh the 1927–28 grain procurement crisis, the political logic of breaking the peasantry, the demand for grain exports to fund industry, and the ideological commitment to socialism in the countryside — reach a substantiated judgement, do not list. For 16- and 20-mark interpretation questions, examine BOTH interpretations as views, not as evidence to be cross-examined for bias. Avoid slipping into moral commentary (‘Stalin was evil’); examiners reward analysis of cause, consequence and significance. Use period vocabulary — kolkhoz, sovkhoz, Sovnarkom, dekulakisation, Holodomor — to lift SPaG and depth marks together.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the causes of the Pilgrimage of Grace.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Religious grievance — the dissolution of the smaller monasteries earlier in 1536 hit the north hardest, where monastic landholding and gate-alms were concentrated.
• Fiscal grievance — the 1534 Subsidy Act extended taxation into peacetime; the Statute of Uses (1536) threatened the gentry’s tax-saving land arrangements.
• Agrarian grievance — bad harvests in 1535 made high rents and enclosures harder to bear.
• Political grievance — northern lords like Lord Darcy resented Cromwell’s rise and the loss of the north’s influence at court.
• Rumours — commoners feared further taxes on weddings, baptismal fonts and parish church plate.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Robert Aske’s leadership of the Pilgrimage of Grace.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Naming — Aske reframed the rising as a ‘pilgrimage’, with the Five Wounds of Christ as its banner, allowing gentry and commoners to march together.
• Oath — he composed an oath of loyalty to king, commonwealth and church that disciplined the host and gave it a religious form.
• Capture of York — he took York without a fight on 16 October 1536, then Pontefract Castle on 21 October.
• Pontefract Articles — he led the drafting of the 24 articles in December 1536 calling for the restoration of monasteries, repeal of the Statute of Uses and dismissal of Cromwell.
• Negotiation — he persuaded the rebel host of around 30,000 to disperse on Norfolk’s promise of a pardon and a free Parliament at York.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Pilgrimage of Grace broke out in October 1536.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the dissolution of the monasteries
• the Statute of Uses
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• The dissolution of the smaller monasteries — threatened northern abbeys, cut off gate-alms, and was carried out by unfamiliar royal commissioners taking inventories.
• The Statute of Uses (1536) — closed the legal device by which gentry families avoided feudal dues on land, antagonising the very class needed to keep order.
• The 1534 Subsidy and 1535 collection — extended taxation into peacetime and bit hardest in a year of poor harvests.
• Rumours of further taxes — on weddings, baptismal fonts and parish church plate spread through Lincolnshire and Yorkshire in autumn 1536.
• Resentment of Cromwell — northern lords objected to a low-born minister directing royal policy and to the loss of the north’s influence at court.
• Loyalty to old religion — the Pope’s authority, traditional Mass and the cult of saints were still strong in northern parishes; the supremacy felt foreign.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Duke of Norfolk was the main reason the Pilgrimage of Grace failed.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the negotiations at Doncaster
• Robert Aske
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs Norfolk’s part against other reasons for the failure and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Outnumbered roughly four to one, Norfolk opened talks at Doncaster on 27 October 1536 rather than fight a battle he could not win.
• He offered a pardon and a free Parliament at York, promises he and the king knew were tactical.
• He returned north under martial law in February 1537 with orders to make examples, and around 216 people were executed.
• As a great northern magnate he was credible to the rebels in a way that an outsider would not have been.

Arguments for other reasons:
• Robert Aske was a lawyer who took oaths seriously; he trusted the king’s word and persuaded the host to disperse.
• Bigod’s rising in January 1537 gave Henry the pretext to declare the first pardon broken.
• The gentry leaders had won concessions and lost interest in further resistance.
• Once dispersed in winter, a host of that size could not be reassembled.
• The rebels insisted they were loyal to the king, so they had no way to press their advantage.

Overall judgement: Norfolk bought the time, but it was Aske’s trust in the pardon and the rebels’ own loyalty to the crown that made the rising collapse. Top-band answers weigh these factors and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Pilgrimage of Grace was the most serious challenge to Henry VIII’s rule.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the size of the rebel host
• the Pontefract Articles
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Size — around 30,000 men gathered under Aske, considerably more than the force Norfolk could deploy.
• Pontefract Articles — demanded the restoration of dissolved monasteries, repeal of the Statute of Uses, dismissal of Cromwell and Cranmer, recognition of Princess Mary, and a free Parliament held outside London.
• Geographical reach — covered Lincolnshire and the whole of Yorkshire, including the strategic strongholds of York, Pontefract Castle and Hull.
• Cross-class alliance — the ‘pilgrimage’ banner united commoners, parish clergy, gentry and senior nobles like Lord Darcy.
• Religious legitimacy — the Five Wounds of Christ banner and Aske’s oath gave the rising a moral force missing from earlier Tudor protests.
• Linkage of grievances — the rebels combined religious, fiscal, agrarian and political demands, threatening the entire programme of the Reformation Parliament.
• Inability to fight — Norfolk himself admitted he could not win a battle and had to negotiate.
• Risk of foreign intervention — the rising worried Charles V’s diplomats and risked giving Catholic powers a pretext to intervene.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536 was opposition to the dissolution of the monasteries.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Statute of Uses
• Robert Aske
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the religious motive against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The dissolution of the smaller monasteries earlier in 1536 was the most visible recent change, and the rebels marched under the religious Five Wounds banner.
• The Pontefract Articles led with the demand to restore the dissolved houses.
• Northern monasteries were heavily concentrated in Lincolnshire and Yorkshire — the regions that rose first and hardest.
• Aske framed the rising as a ‘pilgrimage’, signalling that religion was the rallying cause.
• The wider supremacy — royal headship of the church and the abolition of papal authority — fed the same religious anger.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Fiscal grievance — the 1534 Subsidy bit during a bad harvest in 1535; the Statute of Uses (1536) threatened gentry land arrangements directly.
• Political grievance — northern lords resented Cromwell’s rise and the loss of northern influence at court; the Pontefract Articles called for his dismissal.
• Agrarian grievance — rents, enclosures and a poor harvest in 1535 fed everyday economic anger that the religious banner gave a focus to.
• Rumours — threats of further taxes on weddings and church plate alarmed commoners independently of the dissolution.
• Cross-class mobilisation — gentry leaders like Lord Darcy and Aske combined a faction grievance against Cromwell with the commoners’ religious anger; without political grievance the gentry would not have led.
• Historiography — M.E. James and C.S.L. Davies argue the rising is best understood as multi-causal, with religion as the rallying language but not the only motive.

Overall judgement: opposition to the dissolution provided the slogan and the timing, but the size, geographical reach and cross-class character of the Pilgrimage required the alignment of fiscal, agrarian and political grievances. A top-band answer weighs the dissolution against these other factors and explains how the ‘pilgrimage’ banner held them together.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the First Continental Congress (1774) for relations between Britain and the colonies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: the Congress led directly to the Continental Association, a coordinated boycott of British imports enforced by local committees of inspection across twelve colonies, which extended patriot political control into towns and villages; it also led to an agreement to reconvene in May 1775 if grievances were unresolved, which produced the Second Congress and the Continental Army at the very moment war broke out at Lexington and Concord. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the Continental Association or the Second Congress.
Emerging: Notes that the Congress met without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Thomas Paine’s ‘Common Sense’ (1776) for the move to independence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: ‘Common Sense’ mattered because its 120,000 copies in three months — in a population of 2.5 million — reached a mass colonial audience that previous patriot writing had not, converting public opinion in colonies still hoping for reconciliation; it also mattered because it attacked monarchy itself, naming George III the ‘Royal Brute of Britain’, which made it intellectually impossible to argue that the conflict was just with bad ministers. A third anchor might be Paine’s reframing of independence as common sense for a continent rather than a province, which gave colonial assemblies the cover to authorise their delegates to vote for the Lee resolution. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus.
Emerging: Describes ‘Common Sense’ without explaining its impact.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Second Continental Congress (1775–76) for the conduct of the conflict with Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Second Congress mattered because on 15 June 1775 it appointed George Washington commander-in-chief of a Continental Army, transforming the Massachusetts siege of Boston into an inter-colonial war effort; it also mattered because the Olive Branch Petition of July 1775 was its last attempt at reconciliation — its rejection and the Prohibitory Act of December 1775 cleared the way for the Lee resolution and the Declaration. A third anchor might be its role as a wartime government raising loans and conducting diplomacy. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Describes the Congress without showing how it shaped the war.
Emerging: General references to delegates without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the king’s rejection of the Olive Branch Petition (1775) for the colonial cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the king’s refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition led to his August 1775 proclamation declaring the colonies in open rebellion, which placed even moderate colonists outside royal protection; it also led to the Prohibitory Act of December 1775, which cut off colonial trade and authorised the seizure of American ships, persuading colonial assemblies to authorise their delegates to vote for independence. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the Prohibitory Act or the rebellion proclamation.
Emerging: Mentions the petition without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the colonies moved from seeking reconciliation in 1774 to declaring independence in 1776. You may use the following information in your answer:
• The First Continental Congress
• Thomas Paine’s ‘Common Sense’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains why opinion shifted rather than narrating in sequence. Links the First Congress’s Continental Association to the political organisation of resistance at town level; links Lexington and Concord (April 1775) and the Second Congress’s creation of the Continental Army; brings in the Olive Branch Petition, the king’s rejection and the Prohibitory Act of December 1775; uses Paine’s 120,000-copy pamphlet to show how mass opinion was converted in early 1776; ends with the Lee resolution and Jefferson’s drafting of the Declaration. Reaches an analytical judgement about the contingency of independence rather than treating it as inevitable.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis.
Emerging: Lists events without explaining the shift in colonial opinion.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Thomas Jefferson’s role in the Declaration of Independence (July 1776).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: Jefferson’s authorship mattered because his draft framed independence in the language of natural rights — ‘all men are created equal’, ‘life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness’ — which gave the new republic an ideological foundation later used by abolitionists and civil rights movements; it also mattered because his concrete list of grievances against George III turned a philosophical case into a legal indictment of the king’s rule. A third anchor might be the Congress’s removal of his clause condemning the slave trade, which reveals the limits of the document’s reach. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Describes Jefferson without explaining the wider significance of his draft.
Emerging: General references to the Declaration without specific examples.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how settler pressures destroyed the Indigenous way of life on the Plains in the years 1865–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the destruction of the buffalo
• the 1874 Black Hills gold strike

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• After the First Transcontinental Railroad split the buffalo herd in two in 1869, hide hunters could ship bison hides east in bulk; rail companies contracted men such as William ‘Buffalo Bill’ Cody to feed crews, and General Philip Sheridan endorsed the slaughter as a strategy against Plains nations.
• Because the southern herd was destroyed by 1875 and the northern herd by 1883, Indigenous peoples lost food, clothing, shelter and the centre of their spiritual life — deepening dependence on unreliable federal rations.
• Because cattle ranches under John Iliff and others took the open range and the water that the buffalo had used, hunting territory was privately stocked with longhorns reservations could not access.
• Because in 1874 a US Army expedition under Custer confirmed gold in the Black Hills, around 15,000 prospectors poured into Lakota territory recognised by the 1868 second Fort Laramie Treaty just six years earlier — the treaty collapsed.
• The Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876) followed, but the long-term outcome was overwhelming US response, the Dawes Act (1887), and the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) — with the cumulative pressures, not any single event, doing the destructive work.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1869, 1874, 1876, 1890), specialist vocabulary (reservation, annuity, hide hunter, Bozeman Trail), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the destruction of the buffalo for Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• From an estimated 30 million bison in 1800, fewer than 1,000 wild animals remained by 1890 — with the southern herd destroyed by 1875 and the northern herd by 1883.
• Because the buffalo was the source of food, clothing, shelter and spiritual life, Plains nations lost the basis of their material and religious culture in a single generation.
• Because the slaughter was endorsed by General Philip Sheridan as a strategy against Plains nations — he wrote that exterminating the bison was “the only way to bring lasting peace” — the destruction was not an accidental side-effect but a deliberate weapon.
• Because hunting bands could no longer feed themselves on the open range, dependence on late, short or spoiled federal rations became the daily reality of reservation life.
• The collapse of the buffalo unlocked the next round of dispossession: empty grass for cattle ranching, weakened resistance to the Dawes Act (1887), and the spiritual desperation that fuelled the Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee in 1890.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (30 million in 1800, 1,000 by 1890; 1875, 1883), specialist vocabulary (hide hunter, reservation, annuity).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the 1874 Black Hills gold strike.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the strike to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that around 15,000 prospectors poured into territory recognised as Lakota under the 1868 second Fort Laramie Treaty, breaking a treaty that was only six years old and exposing how easily settler pressure overrode federal promises.
• Another consequence was that the Lakota and their Cheyenne allies prepared for war — with Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse rallying off-reservation bands — producing the conditions for the Battle of the Little Bighorn in June 1876.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named event or institution.
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how gold strikes broke treaty lines on the Plains in the years 1858–1876.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Pike’s Peak gold rush (1858–59)
• the Bozeman Trail

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In the summer of 1858 prospectors found gold near Pike’s Peak in present-day Colorado — on land guaranteed to the Cheyenne and Arapaho under the 1851 first Fort Laramie Treaty — and within a year roughly 100,000 prospectors had crossed those hunting grounds.
• Because the federal government rewrote the treaty in 1861 rather than enforce it, the pattern was set: settler pressure on a treaty line would be answered with a new, smaller treaty line.
• In 1862 John Bozeman blazed a trail north from the Oregon Trail to the new Montana goldfields, cutting through Lakota Powder River country — producing Red Cloud’s War (1866–68), the only Plains war the Lakota strategically won.
• Because the second Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 closed the Bozeman Trail and recognised the Black Hills as Lakota, federal authority appeared to have learned its limits — for six years.
• In 1874 Custer’s expedition confirmed gold in the Black Hills; 15,000 prospectors poured in, the treaty collapsed, and the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876) followed — with the cycle from gold strike to treaty collapse to war repeating itself.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail, specialist vocabulary, both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of US reservation policy for Indigenous peoples of the Plains in the years 1851–1887.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The 1851 first Fort Laramie Treaty established the principle of separate territories for named nations, but each subsequent treaty — 1861, 1868, the Black Hills agreement of 1877 — reduced the area further, training the federal government to expect cession.
• Because annuities arrived late, short or spoiled, dependence on rations became the daily reality of reservation life — with hunger driving bands off reservations to hunt and into conflict with the army.
• Because Indian agents were political appointees, often unsupervised, and frequently corrupt, supplies were skimmed before reaching the people they were meant to serve — Andrew Myrick’s 1862 ‘eat grass’ remark helped trigger Little Crow’s War.
• Because reservations were assumed to be the destination of all Plains peoples, the policy intensified the assault on Indigenous culture beyond mere territory — Carlisle School (1879) and the Dawes Act (1887) extended the logic to language, religion and family land.
• By 1887 the policy had failed on its own terms: the buffalo were gone, the open range was fenced, and the territory promised in 1851 had been reduced to a fraction of its original size.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1851, 1862, 1868, 1879, 1887), specialist vocabulary (reservation, annuity, Indian agent, Dawes Act).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the spread of railroads for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the railroads to a specific feature of Indigenous Plains life.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that the First Transcontinental Railroad (1869) physically split the great buffalo herd into northern and southern populations that never recombined — with hide hunters then shipping bison hides east in bulk and the southern herd destroyed by 1875.
• Another consequence was that federal troops could now be moved to Plains flashpoints in hours rather than weeks, hardening the army’s reach and giving the federal government a faster instrument with which to enforce reservation policy.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named event or feature.
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the death of Huayna Capac (c.1527).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Inca empire was left without a recognised emperor — Huayna Capac’s named heir died at the same time, probably also of smallpox — opening the way for rival sons to claim the throne.
• A civil war broke out between Huascar in Cuzco and Atahualpa in Quito (1529–32), splitting the empire’s armies and elite into two warring camps.
• The civil war ended just weeks before Pizarro’s force reached Cajamarca, leaving Atahualpa’s veteran army exhausted and his political authority untested.
• Smallpox — almost certainly the cause of Huayna Capac’s death — reached the Andes ahead of the Spaniards via Indigenous trade routes, suggesting that European disease was already a force in Andean politics before any Spaniard arrived.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Huayna Capac’s death without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Battle of Cajamarca (16 November 1532).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa, instantly seizing the empire’s only recognised authority — a tiny force of 168 Spaniards now controlled the political centre of an empire of millions.
• Thousands of Atahualpa’s unarmed retinue were killed in the plaza, removing the senior aristocracy and military command of the northern Inca army.
• Atahualpa offered an enormous gold and silver ransom — a room filled once with gold and twice with silver — producing a flow of bullion to Spain that previewed the silver economy of the next decade.
• Atahualpa was executed by garrotte on 26 July 1533. With both Inca emperors now dead (Huascar had been killed by Atahualpa’s forces earlier), the empire was leaderless and the Spaniards could install Manco Inca as a puppet.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Cajamarca without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Pizarro’s expedition came to capture the Inca emperor in the years 1528–32. You may use the following in your answer: the death of Huayna Capac, the war between Huascar and Atahualpa. You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1528 Pizarro made a brief reconnaissance of the Inca coast at Tumbes, saw the wealth of the empire, and travelled to Spain to secure royal authority for a full conquest expedition (the Capitulation of Toledo, 1529).
• Meanwhile, smallpox — spreading south from Mexico through Indigenous trade routes ahead of the Spaniards — killed Huayna Capac and his named heir around 1527. This in turn left the throne disputed between Huascar in Cuzco and Atahualpa in Quito.
• Because of the disputed succession, the Inca empire fought a civil war from 1529 to 1532. Atahualpa’s veteran northern army defeated Huascar at the Battle of Quipaipan in spring 1532 — just weeks before Pizarro’s force began climbing into the Andes.
• This in turn meant that when Pizarro’s 168 men reached Cajamarca in November 1532, Atahualpa was a victor without a recognised state behind him — surrounded by an exhausted army of supporters but without the legitimacy of the emperor he had killed.
• Because of all this, Atahualpa accepted Pizarro’s invitation to meet in Cajamarca’s plaza unarmed. The ambush of 16 November 1532 killed thousands and seized the emperor — ending an empire of millions in a single afternoon.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Capitulation of Toledo, Quipaipan, Cajamarca).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Inca civil war (1529–32) for the Spanish conquest of Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the civil war, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The civil war split the Inca army into two warring camps and consumed the empire’s most experienced commanders just before the Spaniards arrived — weakening the state militarily at the worst possible moment.
• Atahualpa won the war only weeks before Pizarro reached Cajamarca; his authority was therefore untested, and many of Huascar’s old loyalists later allied with the Spanish against him.
• The civil war made Indigenous allies available — the Cañari, the Huanca and Huascar’s supporters joined the Spanish coalition against Atahualpa, mirroring the Tlaxcalan alliance against the Aztecs.
• The civil war meant the Inca elite were politically divided. Pizarro could exploit those divisions by installing Manco Inca, another son of Huayna Capac, as a puppet emperor in 1533.
• Without the civil war, the conquest of Peru — like Cortes’s conquest of Mexico — could not have been a coalition victory over a divided empire. The historiographical move (Restall) is that conquest required Indigenous division, not Spanish genius.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Cañari and Huanca allies, Manco Inca, Quipaipan, link to Restall’s framing).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the civil war without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the siege of Cuzco (1536–37) for Spanish rule in Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the siege, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The siege was the closest the Inca came to reversing the conquest. Manco Inca raised an army of perhaps 100,000 Indigenous warriors and trapped a small Spanish garrison in the city for ten months.
• It showed that the conquest of 1532–33 had been incomplete. The puppet emperor system was unstable; Manco Inca slipped his Spanish handlers and turned the Inca state machinery against them.
• The siege killed Juan Pizarro, exposed the small size of the Spanish force, and forced the Crown to accept that holding Peru would require a permanent military presence and a properly governed colony — not just conquistadors and puppets.
• The siege was broken because Indigenous peoples Atahualpa had crushed during the civil war switched to the Spanish side, and Almagro’s force returned from Chile in time to relieve the city. Spanish rule in Peru depended on Indigenous allies in 1537 just as it had in 1532.
• Manco Inca’s retreat to Vilcabamba founded a rump Neo-Inca state that survived until 1572 — a long-term reminder that resistance was not finished, and a recurring problem for the colonial regime.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Manco Inca, the size of his army, Juan Pizarro’s death, Almagro’s relief, Vilcabamba 1572).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the siege without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Atahualpa’s execution (26 July 1533) for the Spanish conquest of Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Atahualpa’s execution, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The execution removed the only emperor with active authority over the Inca army — Huascar had already been killed on Atahualpa’s orders — leaving the empire without a recognised central leader.
• It opened the way for the Spanish puppet emperor system. Manco Inca was installed in late 1533 with no legitimate alternative claimant alive.
• It allowed Pizarro to march on Cuzco unopposed by an organised state army; the city fell in November 1533 with relatively little resistance from the imperial centre.
• It set a brutal precedent for Spanish dealings with Indigenous rulers — even cooperation and ransom did not save Atahualpa — which would later make Indigenous leaders reluctant to negotiate.
• It created a long-term moral problem for the Crown. Charles V expressed displeasure at the execution; the legality and justice of the conquest became one of the key questions debated by Las Casas, Sepulveda and the New Laws.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Huascar, Manco Inca, Cuzco 1533, Charles V’s reaction, link to Las Casas debate).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the execution without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the way commanders found out about the enemy was different in the nineteenth century and the twenty-first century.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: Nineteenth-century commanders relied on their own eyes and on riders (1). At Balaclava in 1854 Raglan could see the Causeway Heights from a hilltop, but his cavalry in the valley could not, and his order had to be carried down by Captain Nolan (1). Twenty-first-century commanders use ISTAR systems (1). Satellite images, signals intercepts, radar and drone video are combined into one live picture, so a target can be identified and struck within minutes (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the size and make-up of British armies was different in the First World War and the Iraq War (2003).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Identify one clear point (1) and support it with precise detail from both periods (up to 3).

Example: The First World War army was a mass force of civilians in uniform (1). Volunteers and then conscripts under the 1916 Military Service Act filled millions of places, most of them in the infantry (1). The 2003 force was small and professional (1). British troops in Iraq were all volunteers on contracts, trained to use Challenger 2 tanks, Apache helicopters and satellite communications, so far fewer people delivered far more firepower (1).

Write about both periods. A point about only one period cannot reach full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why technology changed the way British forces fought in the period c1900–present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• nuclear weapons
• the Iraq War (2003).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons in 1914–18 turned battle into a contest between machines rather than between lines of men.
• Nuclear weapons from 1945 made a great-power war too destructive to fight, so British planning turned to deterrence and small professional forces.
• Computers and satellites produced precision-guided munitions, first shown to the public in the 1991 Gulf War.
• ISTAR systems cut the time between spotting a target and hitting it from days to minutes.
• In 2003 air dominance, GPS-guided artillery and Challenger 2 tanks let a small coalition force beat a much larger Iraqi army in about three weeks.
• Technology did not solve every problem: cheap IEDs in Basra neutralised much of that advantage during the insurgency that followed.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the British armed forces became smaller and more technical in the period c1900–present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1957 Defence White Paper
• the all-volunteer professional army.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Britain tested an atomic bomb in 1952 and a hydrogen bomb in 1957, so deterrence began to replace mass conventional forces.
• The 1957 Defence White Paper traded conscript numbers for the nuclear umbrella and prepared the end of National Service.
• Submarine-based deterrence, Polaris from 1968 and Trident from 1994, needed engineers, submariners and communications specialists rather than infantry battalions.
• The last conscript joined in 1960 and the last left the regulars in 1963, leaving an all-volunteer force.
• Modern equipment takes years to master, so long contracts and technical training matter more than numbers.
• Precision weapons, drones and ISTAR let small units do what once needed a division, so capability no longer depends on size.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why British forces have found some enemies hard to defeat in the period c1900–present.

You may use the following in your answer:
• guerrilla warfare
• improvised explosive devices in Iraq.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• An enemy who refuses open battle cannot be destroyed by the firepower a conventional army is built around.
• Insurgents in Iraq used cheap IEDs along supply routes, which could wreck an armoured vehicle and could not be reliably spotted by ISTAR.
• Fighters based inside the civilian population made precision weapons risky, because a strike that killed civilians turned local opinion further against the coalition.
• Counter-insurgency depends on local knowledge, language and trust, none of which a satellite or a drone can supply.
• Dissolving the Iraqi army in 2003 put roughly 400,000 trained men out of work and gave the insurgency a ready pool of recruits.
• British forces in Basra Province were stretched thin over a six-year campaign, so they could not hold ground and gather intelligence at the same time.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text:
‘Computerised high-tech warfare was the most important change in modern British warfare.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• nuclear deterrence
• the Iraq War 2003.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for high-tech warfare as most important:
• Precision-guided munitions allowed small professional units to deliver firepower beyond anything available to a Somme commander.
• ISTAR and GPS reduced the time between identifying a target and engaging it from days to minutes, transforming the operational tempo of war.
• The 2003 conventional invasion of Iraq took only three weeks against a much larger Iraqi army, demonstrating high-tech dominance.
• Drones allow British forces to loiter and strike at low risk to their own personnel, reshaping how political leaders authorise force.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Nuclear deterrence (1952–present) reshaped British force structure more fundamentally than any conventional technology, ending National Service and producing the all-volunteer army.
• The Iraq insurgency showed that low-tech IEDs and sniper attacks neutralise high-tech advantages once a war moves to street-level counter-insurgency.
• The shift to a contract-based all-volunteer professional army (1963) is a recruitment change that underlies all twenty-first-century capability — technology means little without trained operators.
• Mass communications — television in the 1991 Gulf War, embedded reporting in 2003, social media after 2010 — have made public opinion as decisive a factor in modern war as weaponry.
• Cardwell-era professionalisation produced the cadre system on which all later technical specialisation has been built — modern high-tech warfare rests on a Victorian recruitment platform.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs computerisation against nuclear deterrence, professionalisation and public opinion, uses accurate period detail (1952, 1957 White Paper, 1991 Gulf, 2003 Iraq, IEDs, Trident) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One factor dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: From the Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders (the Kerner Report), published 29 February 1968.

‘This is our basic conclusion: our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white — separate and unequal. To pursue our present course will involve the continuing polarisation of the American community and, ultimately, the destruction of basic democratic values. The alternative is not blind repression or capitulation to lawlessness. It is the realisation of common opportunities for all within a single society. White racism is essentially responsible for the explosive mixture which has been accumulating in our cities since the end of World War II.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Kerner Commission’s view of the urban riots.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘The Commission blamed white attitudes for the underlying conditions of the riots, not the rioters themselves’ supported by ‘White racism is essentially responsible for the explosive mixture which has been accumulating in our cities’ AND ‘The Commission warned that without major change the United States risked becoming permanently divided by race’ supported by ‘our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white — separate and unequal’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 2003 textbook celebrating the achievements of the civil rights era):
‘The civil rights revolution was substantially complete by 1975. The Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968 outlawed segregation in public life, voting and housing. Black voter registration in the South rose from about 23 per cent in 1964 to over 60 per cent by 1969. The number of Black elected officials rose from around 100 in 1964 to over 3,500 by 1975. The legal architecture of Jim Crow had been dismantled and Black Americans had become full citizens of the Republic.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2014 history that begins with the Kerner Report):
‘The Kerner Report’s warning of two societies had been ignored. By 1975 segregated housing, segregated schools by housing, racist policing and mass unemployment in Northern cities remained intact. Median Black household income was around 60 per cent of the white figure; Black poverty stood at almost three times the white rate. The legal revolution of 1964-65 had reached the South; the economic and Northern revolution had not begun.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the extent of progress in civil rights for Black Americans by 1975? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees civil rights as substantially achieved by 1975 through the legislative architecture of 1964-68 and the rise in Black voter registration and Black elected officials; Interpretation 2 sees civil rights as substantially incomplete by 1975 because the Kerner conditions of Northern segregation, racist policing, unemployment and Black-white income inequality remained intact) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘The civil rights revolution was substantially complete by 1975’ vs ‘the economic and Northern revolution had not begun’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the extent of civil rights progress by 1975.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 2003 textbook that draws on legislation, voter-registration statistics, and figures for Black elected officials, and so foregrounds the legal and electoral achievements of 1964-68; Interpretation 2 is from a 2014 history that draws on the Kerner Report and on income, poverty and housing-segregation statistics for Northern cities, and so foregrounds the economic and structural conditions the Kerner Commission identified. The two have different focuses (legal-political vs economic-structural) and use different bodies of evidence (legislation and registration figures vs Kerner-era social statistics), and reach different judgements as a result.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the extent of progress in civil rights for Black Americans by 1975?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across the legal and structural picture (the Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965 and Fair Housing Act 1968; the rise in Black voter registration in the South from around 23 per cent in 1964 to over 60 per cent by 1969; the growth of Black elected officials from around 100 in 1964 to over 3,500 by 1975; the urban uprisings of Watts 1965, Newark 1967 and Detroit 1967; the Kerner Report’s findings on white racism, segregated housing, unequal schools and racist policing; King’s Chicago Freedom Movement and the unenforceability of the 1966 Daley settlement; King’s 1967 Riverside Church speech against the Vietnam War; the Memphis sanitation strike and King’s assassination on 4 April 1968; the Poor People’s Campaign; the persistence of Black-white income inequality and Northern segregation by 1975), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the urban riots of 1965-67 took place.

You may use the following in your answer:
• racist policing in Northern cities
• the limits of the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. de facto housing segregation in Northern cities through redlining, which left Black families excluded from the suburbs and concentrated in declining inner-city neighbourhoods; the loss of Northern manufacturing jobs from the 1950s as factories moved to suburbs Black families could not enter; the role of specific incidents — the Marquette Frye traffic stop in Watts in August 1965, a police raid on an unlicensed Detroit bar in July 1967 — in triggering uprisings; the disproportionate Black casualty rate in Vietnam combining with poverty at home), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. Uses precise period terminology (de facto segregation, redlining, Watts, Newark, Detroit, Kerner Report).
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of the events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. A Memphis press report of Martin Luther King’s assassination, 5 April 1968.

‘Dr Martin Luther King Jr, the apostle of nonviolence in the civil rights movement, was shot to death here last night. The 39-year-old Negro leader was killed by a sniper’s bullet that struck him as he stood on the balcony of his motel room. Police found a high-powered rifle abandoned a block away. King had come to Memphis last week to lend his support to the city’s 1,300 striking sanitation workers, almost all of them Negro. By dawn this morning rioting had broken out in 60 cities. President Johnson cancelled a planned trip to Hawaii and called for a national day of mourning.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about Martin Luther King’s assassination.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘King had come to Memphis to support a specific labour dispute, not on a national tour’ supported by ‘had come to Memphis last week to lend his support to the city’s 1,300 striking sanitation workers’ AND ‘The killing produced an immediate and nationwide reaction’ supported by ‘By dawn this morning rioting had broken out in 60 cities’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Israeli invasion of Lebanon (1982) for the PLO.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. the IDF’s ten-week siege of Beirut destroyed the PLO mini-state in Lebanon and forced the evacuation of around 14,000 fighters and the Arafat leadership to Tunis, 1,500 miles from any Palestinian territory; the PLO lost the only Arab base from which it could mount cross-border operations against Israel; with the PLO sidelined, new movements filled the vacuum — Hezbollah in Lebanon and, by 1987, Hamas in Gaza — both of which would later reject Arafat’s two-state turn. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the invasion without showing why it mattered for the PLO. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Sabra and Shatila massacre (1982) for Israeli politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. about 400,000 Israelis demonstrated in Tel Aviv on 25 September 1982 — the largest protest in Israel’s history — turning Lebanon into a domestic political problem for the Begin government; the Kahan Commission’s February 1983 finding of ‘indirect responsibility’ forced Sharon to resign as Defence Minister and damaged Begin politically, contributing to his retirement later that year; for the next two decades, Israeli debates about military intervention abroad would invoke Sabra and Shatila as a warning. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the massacre without showing why it mattered for Israeli politics. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Rabat Summit (1974) for the Palestinian cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Rabat removed King Hussein of Jordan’s claim to negotiate for West Bank Palestinians and made the PLO the only Arab-recognised channel; it cleared the diplomatic ground for Arafat’s UN appearance four weeks later and the granting of permanent UN observer status; in the longer term Rabat made any West Bank settlement impossible without the PLO, which is why Israel ultimately negotiated the Oslo Accords with Arafat in 1993. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Rabat without showing why it mattered for the Palestinians. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Litani Operation (1978).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the UN Security Council passed Resolution 425 and authorised UNIFIL, deploying a peacekeeping force on the Israel-Lebanon border that has remained in place ever since; (ii) the operation left a Christian-led ‘South Lebanon Army’ in control of a six-mile buffer zone, the basis on which Israel would later expand to a wider security zone after 1982 and remain in southern Lebanon until 2000. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Israel invaded southern Lebanon in 1978 without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the rise of Hezbollah after 1982.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) Hezbollah’s suicide bombings against US Marine and French paratrooper barracks in Beirut on 23 October 1983 killed 241 American and 58 French troops and forced the multinational force out of Lebanon, leaving Israel without Western political cover; (ii) Hezbollah displaced the PLO as the leading armed challenge to Israel in Lebanon and tied down the IDF in the south Lebanon security zone until 2000, contradicting the original aim of the 1982 invasion. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Hezbollah was created without analysing its effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the PLO’s changing fortunes in the years 1974–82.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Arafat’s speech to the UN (1974)
• Operation Peace for Galilee (1982)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the Rabat recognition and Arafat’s UN speech; the PLO mini-state in southern Lebanon and reprisal raids; the Litani Operation and UNIFIL; Operation Peace for Galilee and the evacuation to Tunis). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as the Lebanese civil war, Sabra and Shatila or the Kahan Commission. Connects events through causation rather than sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Magna Carta as sealed at Runnymede in June 1215.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Fixed reliefs — the charter set the relief due from an earl or baron at £100, replacing the punitive sums John had charged on inheritances.
• The Twenty-five — clause 61 created a baronial enforcement committee with the legal right to seize royal castles and lands if the king broke the charter.
• Limits on taxation — clause 12 forbade the levy of general aid or scutage without the ‘common counsel of the realm’, except in three customary cases.
• Justice clauses — clauses 39 and 40 declared that no free man could be imprisoned or dispossessed except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land.
• Freedom of the Church — clause 1 confirmed the freedom of the English Church to elect its own bishops, the issue that had triggered the Interdict.
• Removal of foreign captains — clauses 50 and 51 ordered the dismissal of named mercenary captains such as Falkes de Bréauté and Engelard de Cigogné.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the siege of Rochester Castle in 1215.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Length and command — the siege ran from 11 October to 30 November 1215; the rebel garrison was led by William of Albini holding the keep against John’s royal army.
• Strategic importance — Rochester controlled the road from London to the Channel ports and was the strongest castle south of London.
• Use of mining — royal sappers undermined the south-east tower; according to chroniclers the foundation was destroyed by burning forty fat pigs in the mine to set the timbers alight.
• Surrender on 30 November — the garrison surrendered after the collapse of the south-east tower; John ordered them all hanged but was talked out of it, and one crossbowman was hanged.
• Political consequences — the hanging order and the king’s subsequent ‘tempest’ through the rebel north made political settlement impossible.
• Symbolic restoration — the recapture of Rochester restored royal control of the south-east in the immediate term and showed that John still possessed siege capability.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or named individuals.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature, or features unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the First Barons’ War broke out in 1215.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Pope Innocent III’s annulment of Magna Carta
• the role of Prince Louis of France
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• Annulment of Magna Carta — on 24 August 1215 Innocent III declared the charter ‘null and void’ and excommunicated the rebels; the only legal mechanism for binding John was destroyed.
• The role of Prince Louis — with no peace possible the rebel barons offered the throne to Louis of France, whose continental resources could match John’s mercenaries; Louis landed at Thanet in May 1216.
• John’s sincerity — the king sealed the charter intending to seek annulment; once the rebels realised this they had no incentive to disarm.
• Suspension of Stephen Langton — the moderate mediator was removed by the Pope, leaving the rebels without a respected go-between.
• Continued mercenary government — John refused to dismiss Falkes de Bréauté and Engelard de Cigogné in line with clauses 50–51, evidence that the king did not intend to live under the charter.
• John’s treatment of the Rochester garrison — his order to hang them all in November 1215 hardened rebel positions and showed waverers that surrender was not safe.
• Civic loyalty in London — the city held firm for the rebel cause and welcomed Louis when he arrived, providing a permanent military base.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Pope Innocent III annulled Magna Carta in August 1215.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the settlement of 1213
• clause 61 and the Twenty-five
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• The 1213 reconciliation — under the settlement at Dover, England had become a papal fief at 1,000 marks a year; Innocent III was now legally John’s overlord with a duty to defend his vassal.
• John’s appeal — within hours of leaving Runnymede the king sent envoys to Rome arguing the charter had been ‘extorted by force’ and was an injury to royal dignity.
• Threat to royal authority — clause 61’s Twenty-five enforcement committee allowed barons to seize royal castles, an arrangement Innocent III viewed as a violation of monarchical authority anywhere.
• Wider implications for kingship — the Pope feared that allowing barons to constrain a king would set a dangerous precedent across Christendom; he had already supported royal authority against rebellious subjects elsewhere.
• Conflict with the 1213 fief — if England was a papal fief, agreements binding its king without papal consent were arguably illegitimate.
• Stephen Langton’s position — Langton had mediated and not insisted that papal consent was required; Innocent suspended him and used annulment to restore papal control.
• Speed of judgement — the Pope acted within ten weeks because allowing the charter to set down roots would have made annulment harder.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Prince Louis of France was invited to invade England in 1216.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the papal annulment of Magna Carta
• the resources of the French crown
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• The papal annulment had closed the door on a constitutional settlement, leaving the rebels with no legal means to bind John.
• Louis’s claim — through his wife Blanche of Castile, granddaughter of Henry II, Louis had a thin but exploitable royal claim that could be presented as legitimate.
• Continental resources — only Capetian France could supply the soldiers, ships and credit needed to match John’s mercenary captains; rebel barons could not raise such forces alone.
• Philip II’s strategy — Philip had spent a decade dismantling the Angevin Empire; supporting his son’s English campaign continued the project that began at Bouvines.
• Domestic credibility — a recognised royal claimant gave the rebellion legitimacy that an open republic could not have claimed in 1216 England.
• London’s commitment — the citizens of London needed a king to whom they could swear loyalty without facing reprisal; Louis offered them that figurehead.
• John’s treatment of the Rochester garrison — his order to hang them all convinced wavering barons that no negotiated peace with him was safe.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Magna Carta of 1215 was more important as a baronial peace treaty than as a constitutional landmark.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• clause 61 and the Twenty-five barons
• the papal annulment of 1215
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Clause 61 and the Twenty-five — the enforcement committee was a tool to coerce one specific king and required ongoing baronial control of royal castles; this is the language of a peace treaty, not a constitution.
• The papal annulment — within ten weeks Innocent III declared the charter ‘null and void of all validity for ever’; if the document had been a foundational constitution it could not have been swept aside so easily.
• The protections applied only to ‘free men’ — perhaps a fifth of the population; villeins, the urban poor, and the Anglo-Jewish community received almost nothing.
• Specific clauses targeted current grievances — the named removal of Falkes de Bréauté and Engelard de Cigogné (clauses 50–51) shows the document was tailored to John’s government, not to permanent principles.
• The settlement collapsed — within twelve weeks the kingdom was at civil war; a successful constitutional document would have been embedded.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
