• Clauses 39 and 40 — the principle that no free man could be imprisoned or dispossessed except by lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land became the foundation for later due-process jurisprudence.
• Reissue and survival — William Marshal reissued Magna Carta in 1216 and 1217, and Henry III confirmed it in 1225; the charter became part of English law and was repeatedly reissued through to Edward I’s 1297 confirmation.
• Clause 12 and consent to taxation — the principle that scutage and aids required ‘common counsel of the realm’ foreshadowed parliamentary control of taxation in the later medieval period.
• Clause 1 and the Church — the freedom of the Church to elect its own bishops became a long-term feature of English ecclesiastical law.
• Later reputation — seventeenth-century lawyers like Sir Edward Coke used Magna Carta to argue against royal absolutism in the Stuart age; American revolutionaries cited it in turn.
• The principle that the king is under the law — however limited in 1215, this was the seed of later constitutional development.

Overall judgement: In 1215 itself Magna Carta was a baronial peace treaty — designed to bind one specific king, enforced by a committee of named barons, and annulled within ten weeks. It cannot be called a constitutional landmark in 1215. But it became one over centuries through reissue, citation and reinterpretation. A balanced judgement separates the document of 1215 (peace treaty, failed) from the legacy of Magna Carta (a foundation of constitutional argument that grew long after). On the test ‘in 1215’ the statement is largely correct; on the test ‘in long-term significance’ it is largely wrong.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (interdict, fief, scutage, demesne, papal legate, regent, peers, free men).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about Mao’s relationship with the Red Guards in 1966. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (e.g. the eight Tiananmen rallies, the ‘Bombard the Headquarters’ poster, the use of free rail travel for students). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that Mao deliberately mobilised teenagers to bypass the existing party structure. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that reads more as paraphrase than inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Red Guards descended into factional violence by 1967.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the four olds
• the Wuhan Incident
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. Mao’s licence to attack ‘capitalist roaders’ without naming them, the collapse of provincial CCP authority, rival readings of who counted as a ‘real’ revolutionary, seizure of PLA weapons, the encouragement of denunciation through struggle sessions) and shows how they interacted. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the Red Guard movement without explaining why factional violence followed; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about who controlled the Red Guards in 1966-68.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents the Red Guards as Mao’s disciplined instrument; the other presents them as a movement that quickly escaped his control). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Red Guard attacks on the ‘four olds’.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (CCP-era 1980s versus post-archival access in the 2000s); they used different evidence (state-published material versus survivor testimony and Cultural Revolution archives, e.g. Dikötter); or they had different purposes (commemorative versus critical). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why; or names a reason without supporting it. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the role of Jiang Qing in directing the Red Terror?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own knowledge — Jiang Qing’s role in the Cultural Revolution Group, the press campaign that purged Liu Shaoqi, the choreographing of struggle sessions, the targeting of cultural figures — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on Jiang Qing or the Cultural Revolution Group and barely engages with the interpretations as views; or relies on the stimulus alone. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that the Red Guard movement of 1966–68 was directed top-down by Mao throughout?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the May 16 Notification, ‘Bombard the Headquarters’, the eight Tiananmen rallies, the four olds, the role of Jiang Qing and the Cultural Revolution Group, the splitting of the Red Guards into rival factions, the January Storm and the Wuhan Incident — to test how far Mao directed the movement throughout. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (struggle session, big-character poster, capitalist roaders, four olds). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning; limited subject vocabulary. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors or no period vocabulary. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the response of Caribbean migrants to discrimination in Bristol in the 1960s was different from the response of Irish migrants to hostility in Liverpool in the 1850s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Caribbean migrants organised a public campaign aimed at changing the law: the boycott of 1963 fed directly into the Race Relations Act of 1965.
• Irish migrants in Liverpool built parallel institutions instead - Catholic parishes, schools and friendly societies - because no anti-discrimination law existed to appeal to.
• The Bristol campaign used national media coverage deliberately; nineteenth-century Irish migrants were the subject of the press rather than users of it.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Bristol bus boycott of 1963 mattered beyond Bristol.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the colour bar in employment
• the Race Relations Act (1965).

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• It broke the colour bar at a large, publicly subsidised employer: Raghbir Singh became the Bristol Omnibus Company's first non-white conductor on 17 September 1963.
• National press coverage gave Harold Wilson's incoming government a ready-made case for the Race Relations Act of 1965, the first British law against racial discrimination in public places.
• It showed that a small, well-organised local campaign could produce national policy change, a model later campaigns followed.
• It produced national figures: Paul Stephenson, Roy Hackett and Guy Bailey became recognised civil-rights leaders, and Stephenson received the OBE in 2009.
• It showed other communities that the colour bar in housing and employment was not inevitable and could be challenged directly.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which East African Asian migration to Leicester was similar to Huguenot migration to Spitalfields after 1685.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Explain One Way (Similarity or Difference)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. One mark identifies a valid similarity or difference; the rest come from supporting it with accurate detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content (any one way, fully developed):
• Both groups arrived with skills and capital rather than empty-handed, so their economic impact was fast: silk weaving in Spitalfields, and shops along Belgrave Road.
• Both concentrated in one district and reshaped its trade and streetscape within a generation.
• Both were refugees expelled or driven out by a government abroad - Louis XIV in 1685, Idi Amin in 1972 - rather than economic migrants choosing their moment.

Mastering: One clear way identified and supported with precise detail from both periods.
Secure: One clear way identified with some supporting detail from both periods.
Developing: A way identified, but the detail comes from only one period.
Emerging: A vague comparison with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘Migrants had a greater impact on Leicester than on Bristol in the post-war period.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Bristol bus boycott of 1963
• Ugandan Asians in Leicester from 1972.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree (plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 16 marks for the history, plus up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and the use of specialist terms — the only question on this paper that carries those extra marks.

Indicative content - support for greater impact on Leicester:
• Leicester became the first major British city in which no single ethnic group formed a majority, with around a third of the population of Asian origin by 2011.
• East African Asian families arrived with business experience and capital and turned Belgrave Road into the 'Golden Mile' within a generation.
• Public services and civic life changed: multilingual provision in schools, council recognition of Diwali, and Diwali lights that became the largest outside India by the early 2000s.
• The 'twice migrant' background sped everything up, because arrivals were not starting from nothing.

Indicative content - support for Bristol:
• The bus boycott of 1963 fed directly into the Race Relations Act of 1965, a national legal change Leicester cannot match.
• Paul Stephenson, Roy Hackett and Guy Bailey became national civil-rights figures whose campaign provided a model for later protest.
• The St Paul's Carnival from 1968 and the wider Caribbean cultural presence reshaped the city's identity.
• 'Impact' depends on the measure: Leicester wins on demographic and economic change, Bristol on national law.

Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs at least two factors against each other across the period, uses a factor of the student's own alongside the two prompts, and reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; a judgement is reached but less consistently supported.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; the judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail and no clear judgement.

Spelling, punctuation and grammar: accurate writing with consistent use of subject terms (colour bar, twice migrant, Race Relations Act, decolonisation).

practice_questions.text:
Explain why a colour bar operated so widely in Britain in the 1950s and 1960s.

You may use the following in your answer:
• housing and lodging houses
• trade unions.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Nothing in law forbade it: until the Race Relations Act of 1965 a landlord, publican or employer could refuse service on grounds of colour and face no penalty.
• In housing it produced advertisements specifying 'No Coloureds' alongside 'No Irish' in the windows of bedsits and lodging houses across British cities.
• In employment it kept Black and Asian workers out of customer-facing jobs; the Bristol Omnibus Company was one example among many.
• Trade unions sometimes defended it: in Bristol the local branch of the Transport and General Workers' Union initially backed the company's bar.
• Employers justified it by claiming that existing staff or customers would object, which turned private prejudice into company policy.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why East African Asian migration to Leicester had such a rapid economic impact.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the 'twice migrant' background
• Belgrave Road.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 12 marks for explaining causes. Two prompts are given and students must add information of their own.

Indicative content:
• Most arrivals were 'twice migrants' whose families had lived in East Africa for a generation or two under British rule, so they came with English, British passports and business experience.
• Many had been shopkeepers, traders or professionals in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, and brought capital that let them take premises on Belgrave and Melton Roads almost on arrival.
• Leicester's declining inner-city economy in the 1970s left affordable shop fronts and housing exactly where the Uganda Resettlement Board placed arrivals.
• Family and community networks meant that earlier arrivals of the 1960s could offer the 1972 wave contacts, information and credit.
• The Race Relations Acts of 1965, 1968 and 1976 gave a legal protection in housing, employment and credit that the Caribbean arrivals of 1948 had not had.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each developed with precise detail and tied explicitly to the question, including at least one reason of the student's own.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant detail and clear links to the question.
Developing: One reason explained, or several reasons named with little detail.
Emerging: Description of the topic with no explanation of cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the effect of technology on the definition of crime in the twentieth century was different from its effect in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Twentieth-century technology created crimes: the motor car produced a whole new branch of law in the Road Traffic Act 1930, and networked computers produced the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
• Nineteenth-century technology mostly removed crimes: turnpikes, bank notes and the railways took away the conditions that had made highway robbery possible.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why drug-related behaviour became a major area of criminal law in twentieth-century Britain.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the First World War
• the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• In 1900 cocaine, opium and cannabis were legal commerce, sold openly in chemists’ shops; Britain had no peacetime drug-control law to enforce.
• The First World War created an immediate concern about cocaine reaching soldiers, leading to the Defence of the Realm Act 1916 and then the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920 — the first peacetime drug-control statute.
• Public concern about youth drug use in the 1960s pushed Parliament towards a more comprehensive system, producing the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 with its A/B/C classification.
• Drug-funded property crime — especially burglary and street robbery from the 1980s — meant drug control was no longer a niche health issue but a major policing priority.
• International pressure (UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs 1961) and improved scientific knowledge of harm both pushed Britain towards a stronger statutory framework.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (1916, 1920, 1971, drug-funded crime, international treaties) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of drug law without explaining why it grew.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the law on crimes against the person in the twentieth century was different from the law in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Twentieth-century law began to punish motive: the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 attached higher sentences to assault, criminal damage and harassment when they were racially aggravated.
• Sixteenth-century law defined offences by belief and status instead, so heresy and vagabondage were crimes while racial hostility was not recognised in law at all.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the criminalisation of drugs in the twentieth century was similar to the criminalisation of vagabondage in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Both took behaviour that had been lawful and relabelled it as crime: opium and cocaine were sold over the counter until the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920, and wandering for work was ordinary until the 1547 Vagrancy Act.
• In both cases the state acted because it feared a social problem — addiction and drug-funded theft in one, homelessness and disorder in the other — not because the behaviour itself was new.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the legal definition of crime in Britain changed between 1900 and 2000.

You may use the following in your answer:
• new technology
• migration after 1948.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• New technologies created new crimes: the motor car required the 1930 and 1988 Road Traffic Acts; the personal computer required the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
• Migration and a multi-ethnic society after 1948 made racial discrimination a public issue; the Race Relations Acts (1965, 1968, 1976) made it illegal where it had been permitted.
• Changing scientific understanding of drugs — their addictive properties, their links to disease, their use during the First World War — led to the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920 and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.
• High-profile cases (the Stephen Lawrence murder 1993; the Macpherson Inquiry 1999) reshaped public expectations of police and law and produced statutes like the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
• International pressure from treaties on drugs, race and human rights (UN 1965 Convention on Racial Discrimination, 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs) required statutory changes domestically.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (technology, migration, science, public events, international treaties) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of changes without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
‘The twentieth century created entirely new types of crime in Britain.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• motoring offences
• cybercrime.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for accuracy and use of period-specific vocabulary.

Indicative content — arguments supporting the statement:
• Motoring offences were genuinely new: there was no offence of reckless or drink-driving before the 1930 Road Traffic Act because there were no cars to drive.
• Computer misuse, defined by the Computer Misuse Act 1990 as unauthorised access to a system, did not exist as a concept before networked computers.
• Race and hate crime law (Race Relations Acts 1965, 1968, 1976; Crime and Disorder Act 1998) created criminal categories that had not existed in earlier law.
• Drug-control statutes (1920, 1971) reclassified what had been legal commerce into crime, creating a new field of policing.

Indicative content — arguments against:
• Theft, burglary, assault and fraud remained the bulk of recorded crime; old categories continued under new statutes (Theft Act 1968, Fraud Act 2006).
• ‘Cybercrime’ is largely older crime by new means — phishing is fraud, identity theft is theft, online harassment is harassment.
• Sexual offences law (Sexual Offences Act 2003) and people-trafficking law built on legislation reaching back to the 1885 Criminal Law Amendment Act.
• Drugs themselves were not new behaviour; the change was in legal classification, not in human use.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs new categories against continuity, uses accurate period vocabulary, and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

SPaG (4 marks): Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with consistent use of subject-specific historical terminology (Road Traffic Act, Misuse of Drugs Act, Race Relations Act, racially aggravated, Computer Misuse Act, breathalyser, cybercrime).

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the American victory at Saratoga (October 1777) for the war.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: Saratoga led directly to the French treaties of alliance and commerce signed at Paris in February 1778, transforming a colonial rebellion into a global war that Britain had to fight in the West Indies, Gibraltar and the Channel; it also led to Spanish entry against Britain in June 1779 and Dutch entry in December 1780, multiplying the fronts on which Britain had to defend an empire. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the international response.
Emerging: Notes that the Americans won at Saratoga without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of George Washington’s leadership for the American war effort.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: Washington’s leadership mattered because he held the Continental Army together at Valley Forge in winter 1777–78, when 2,500 of around 11,000 troops died and the army nearly disintegrated; it also mattered because his strategy of avoiding pitched battles and preserving the army made it impossible for Britain to win the decisive engagement they expected. A third anchor might be his command at Yorktown, where his coordination with Rochambeau and de Grasse trapped Cornwallis. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus.
Emerging: Names Washington without explaining how he shaped events.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of French involvement in the War of Independence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: French involvement mattered because the treaties of February 1778 supplied an alliance, an army and a navy that Britain could not match in American waters; it also mattered because Admiral de Grasse’s victory at the Battle of the Chesapeake on 5 September 1781 sealed Cornwallis off from the sea at Yorktown. A third anchor might be the loans and direct subsidies that kept the Continental Congress financially solvent. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions French help without showing how it shaped specific outcomes.
Emerging: General references to allies without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Battle of Yorktown (October 1781) for British politics and policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: the surrender of Cornwallis’s army of around 7,000 led directly to the fall of Lord North’s ministry in March 1782, ending the war faction in London and bringing first Rockingham’s and then Lord Shelburne’s government to office; it also led Britain to seek a negotiated settlement, which produced the Peace of Paris of 1783 and the recognition of American independence. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to the political fall-out.
Emerging: Mentions Yorktown without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining why the Americans won the War of Independence in the years 1777–83. You may use the following information in your answer:
• Saratoga (1777)
• Yorktown (1781)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; weighs the four spec factors against each other rather than ranking Washington alone. Links Saratoga to French entry in 1778, French entry to Spanish entry in 1779 and Dutch entry in 1780, and the global war to Britain’s diversion of resources from the American theatre; links Washington’s leadership at Valley Forge to the survival of the Continental Army; brings in own knowledge such as Bernardo de Gálvez at Mobile and Pensacola, the French fleet at the Chesapeake, or Lord North’s fall after Yorktown. Reaches an analytical judgement.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis.
Emerging: Lists battles without explaining why America won.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Benjamin Franklin’s role in the Peace of Paris (1783).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: Franklin’s standing in Paris since 1776 mattered because it gave him personal access to the French government and persuaded Vergennes to support American negotiating goals; it also mattered because his calm management of the separate negotiations with Britain — alongside Adams and Jay — secured American territory east of the Mississippi rather than the smaller settlement France and Spain might have preferred. A third anchor might be his role in fishing rights off Newfoundland. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Names Franklin without showing how he shaped the treaty.
Emerging: General references to negotiation without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the condition of England at the time of King John’s death in October 1216.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks. Two distinct features required.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Civil war — the First Barons’ War had been running since September 1215 and divided the kingdom; Prince Louis of France controlled London and much of the south-east while loyalists held only a network of garrisoned castles.
• Empty treasury — pipe roll evidence shows revenue from rebel-held shires effectively at zero, and John’s baggage train including portable treasure had been lost crossing the tidal Wash on 12 October.
• Foreign occupation — Prince Louis of France had been acclaimed at St Paul’s in 1216 and held London, with Capetian reinforcements arriving through the Cinque Ports.
• Loyalist castles — royal authority survived in major fortresses including Dover, Windsor, Corfe and Nottingham, but not in continuous territory.
• Lost regalia — the legendary loss of the crown jewels in the Wash deprived the loyalists of the symbols needed for a normal coronation.
• Mercenary backbone — royal armies still depended on captains such as Falkes de Bréauté and Engelard de Cigogné, but their wages were chronically late.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or features blurred.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of William Marshal as Protector after 1216.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Reissue of Magna Carta — on 12 November 1216 Marshal reissued the charter in Henry III’s name, dropping the Twenty-five enforcement committee but keeping the substantive protections.
• Military leadership — aged about seventy, Marshal personally led the loyalist charge at the Battle of Lincoln on 20 May 1217.
• Papal alliance — he worked closely with the papal legates Guala Bicchieri and his successor Pandulf, using papal authority to absolve waverers and to legitimise loyalist actions.
• Negotiation of peace — he led the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Lambeth in September 1217, paying Louis 10,000 marks to leave and securing amnesty for rebel barons.
• Personal vow of loyalty — Marshal accepted the regency in his seventieth year and pledged to ‘carry the king on his shoulders’ if needed, providing the personal authority the regime required.
• Reconciliation policy — he avoided punitive vengeance against rebels after Lincoln, restoring lands and bringing the political nation back together rapidly.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or named events.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature, or features unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the loyalist cause survived the death of King John in October 1216.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the coronation of Henry III
• the reissue of Magna Carta in November 1216
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• The coronation of Henry III — on 28 October 1216 the boy king was crowned at Gloucester by Peter des Roches, with the papal legate Guala Bicchieri presiding, securing immediate legal continuity with the dynasty even without the lost regalia.
• The reissue of Magna Carta — on 12 November 1216 Marshal reissued the charter in Henry’s name, stripping the rebels of their political programme; barons fighting for the charter could no longer claim the king was against it.
• Papal protection — Henry did homage to Honorius III, placing the kingdom under papal overlordship; the papal legate excommunicated the rebels and absolved waverers.
• William Marshal’s prestige — the most respected knight of the Anglo-Norman world acted as Protector, providing the personal authority a regency required.
• The legitimacy contrast — Henry’s direct Plantagenet descent contrasted with Louis’s thin claim through his wife Blanche of Castile; many waverers preferred a continuity king to a foreign prince.
• Loyalist castles — Dover under Hubert de Burgh, Windsor, Corfe and Nottingham held; rebels could not secure England without taking them.
• Tactical victories — the Battle of Lincoln on 20 May 1217 and the destruction of the French fleet off Sandwich on 24 August 1217 broke Louis’s military position.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on causation; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive.
Emerging: General narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why William Marshal’s reissue of Magna Carta in November 1216 was politically important.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the demands of the rebel barons
• the boy king Henry III
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• It removed the rebels’ programme — the barons had taken up arms over Magna Carta; with the charter reissued in the king’s name there was no political reason left to fight.
• It separated the document from John’s personality — under a boy king with no record of arbitrary government, the charter could be a constitutional norm rather than a peace treaty for one hated ruler.
• The clauses targeting John specifically — the Twenty-five committee, the named foreign captains — were dropped, making the charter sustainable as ongoing law rather than a one-off settlement.
• Papal endorsement — with Innocent III dead and Honorius III now in office, the new pope did not annul the reissue; what had been illegitimate in 1215 was now legal.
• Drawing in waverers — moderates who had supported the rebels for the charter could now return to the loyalist side without abandoning their principles.
• Legal continuity — the 1216 reissue was followed by another in 1217 (with the separate Charter of the Forest) and by Henry III’s 1225 confirmation; this is the version that became part of English law.
• Magna Carta’s long-term survival — the document was repeatedly reissued through to Edward I’s 1297 confirmation; without the 1216 reissue Magna Carta would probably have died with John.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained causation.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations thin.
Emerging: Narrative description with little focus on why.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Henry III was crowned at Gloucester rather than Westminster in October 1216.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Prince Louis of France
• the loss of the regalia
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Westminster was in rebel hands — Prince Louis of France held London and the rebel-controlled clergy of Westminster Abbey could not be trusted with the ceremony.
• Speed mattered — the loyalist council had nine days from John’s death to secure a coronation; an immediate ceremony at the nearest secure cathedral closed off Louis’s rival claim.
• Gloucester’s strategic position — the city sat in the loyalist heartland of the south-west, close to Bristol and to Marshal’s own lands in Wales.
• Practical accessibility — Henry was hidden at Devizes; Gloucester was reachable without crossing rebel territory.
• Symbolic substitution for the regalia — with the crown jewels lost in the Wash, a circle of gold from Isabella of Angoulême had to be borrowed; this was easier in a familiar regional cathedral than in the great national space of Westminster.
• Papal endorsement — Guala Bicchieri, the papal legate, was on hand at Gloucester to preside over the ceremony, lending it the authority of Rome.
• Avoiding rebel disruption — a coronation at Westminster could have been physically attacked or boycotted; Gloucester was safe.

Mastering: Five or more reasons each clearly explained with specific evidence.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped.
Emerging: Narrative with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘King John’s reign was a disaster for England by the time of his death in 1216.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the loss of Normandy in 1204
• the role of William Marshal after 1216
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Loss of Normandy in 1204 — the Angevin Empire of 1199 was dismantled; Normandy, Anjou and Maine fell to Philip II, ending the cross-Channel monarchy that had defined English kingship since 1066.
• Financial exhaustion — eleven scutages, punitive feudal ‘fines’, the 1207 thirteenth and the 1210 Bristol Tallage of 66,000 marks on the Jewish community had drained the kingdom; Bouvines in 1214 wasted the proceeds.
• Religious crisis — six years of Interdict 1208–14 had stopped public worship across England; submission to Innocent III made England a papal fief at 1,000 marks a year.
• Civil war — the First Barons’ War was raging at his death; half the kingdom including London was in rebel and French hands.
• Loss of the legendary regalia — the baggage train sunk in the Wash on 12 October 1216 deprived the kingdom of its most symbolic possessions.
• Personal humiliation — the murder of Arthur of Brittany in 1203, the breach of chivalry at Rochester in 1215, and the dependence on foreign mercenaries had reduced royal prestige to a low never seen since 1066.

Arguments for alternative explanations or qualifications:
• Survival of the dynasty — Henry III was crowned within ten days at Gloucester; the Plantagenet line continued and Henry would rule for fifty-six years.
• The role of William Marshal — Marshal’s regency saved the cause; reissued Magna Carta on 12 November 1216 to win over moderates; led the loyalist victory at the Battle of Lincoln in May 1217 and negotiated the Treaty of Lambeth in September 1217.
• Magna Carta survived — the charter that John had sealed in 1215 became, after 1216 and 1217 reissues, part of English law and was confirmed by Edward I in 1297.
• Administrative legacy — modern historians (W. L. Warren onwards) have stressed the energetic personal kingship John exercised: itinerant justice, detailed pipe-roll record-keeping, the 1207 thirteenth as an experimental tax on movables.
• Tactical brilliance of the 1213 reconciliation — turning Innocent III from enemy to protector enabled the papal annulment of Magna Carta and helped the dynasty survive 1216 by binding England to Rome.
• Limits of John’s personal control — Bouvines was decided in Flanders by another army; the loss of Normandy depended partly on Philip II’s strategic skill.

Overall judgement: On the immediate measure of October 1216 the statement is largely correct. John left a kingdom at war, half-occupied, financially ruined, and led by a child. But on the longer arc — the survival of the dynasty under Marshal, the entrenchment of Magna Carta, and the energetic administrative methods that even modern revisionists credit — the disaster was partial and recoverable. A balanced judgement weighs the catastrophic state of the kingdom in October 1216 against the survival of monarchy, charter and dynasty by September 1217. John was a disastrous king for England in his lifetime; he was not the end of England.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout (regent, papal legate, scutage, fief, demesne, interdict).
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: From a press conference given by President Dwight D. Eisenhower at the White House on 7 April 1954.

‘You have a row of dominoes set up, you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly. So you could have a beginning of a disintegration that would have the most profound influences. We have got to look at this thing in the largest sense. The possible consequences of the loss are just incalculable to the free world.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the reasons for US involvement in Vietnam.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear inferences each supported by a quoted detail. (e.g. ‘Eisenhower presented Vietnam as part of a global Cold War contest, not a local problem’ supported by ‘We have got to look at this thing in the largest sense’ or ‘the most profound influences’ AND ‘Eisenhower expected one country’s fall to communism would lead to the rapid fall of others’ supported by ‘you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why US involvement in Vietnam escalated between 1954 and 1964.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the domino theory
• the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor, and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The full picture connects: Eisenhower’s 1954 domino theory; the Geneva Accords and Diem’s refusal to hold the 1956 reunification elections; the structural weakness of the Diem government (Catholic-Mandarin regime, reversed land reform, Madame Nhu and the secret police, the Buddhist crisis of 1963); Kennedy’s expansion of advisers from around 800 to over 16,000 and the failure of the Strategic Hamlets Programme; the November 1963 coup against Diem and the political instability of nine successive juntas; the rising threat of the Vietcong from 1960 supplied via the Ho Chi Minh Trail; the disputed second Gulf of Tonkin engagement and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of 7 August 1964 that authorised escalation. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of events without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1995 textbook of the Cold War):
‘The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of August 1964 was the moment American escalation in Vietnam became inevitable. Once Congress had given Johnson open-ended authority to use force, the path to Operation Rolling Thunder in March 1965 and to half a million ground troops by 1968 was set. Without Tonkin, Johnson could not have escalated; with Tonkin, he could not avoid it.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 study of US decision-making before 1965):
‘The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution mattered as a legal vehicle, not as a turning point. The structural decisions had already been taken: Eisenhower’s 1954 commitment to a non-communist South Vietnam, Kennedy’s 1961-63 escalation of advisers from 800 to over 16,000, the Strategic Hamlets failure of 1962-63 and the November 1963 coup. By August 1964 the choice was not whether to escalate but how to formalise it.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the importance of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution as the decisive turning point that made full escalation possible and inevitable; Interpretation 2 sees Tonkin as a legal vehicle for decisions already taken under Eisenhower and Kennedy and so not the real turning point) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the moment American escalation in Vietnam became inevitable’ vs ‘Tonkin mattered as a legal vehicle, not as a turning point’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the importance of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1995 textbook of the Cold War that frames Vietnam as a single escalation episode and uses the dramatic moment of Tonkin to anchor its narrative arc; Interpretation 2 is from a 2010 study of US decision-making that draws on declassified policy papers from the Eisenhower, Kennedy and early Johnson administrations and so foregrounds the structural commitments of 1954-63. The two have different focuses (a moment of legal escalation vs the longer-run policy commitments) and use different bodies of evidence (a Cold War narrative vs presidential policy archives), and reach different judgements on Tonkin’s significance.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the importance of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across the period (Eisenhower’s domino theory of April 1954; the Geneva Accords; Diem’s refusal of the 1956 elections and the structural weaknesses of the Republic of Vietnam; the founding of the Vietcong in 1960; Kennedy’s expansion of advisers to over 16,000 and the Strategic Hamlets Programme of 1962-63; the Buddhist crisis and the November 1963 coup; the disputed second Gulf of Tonkin engagement of 4 August 1964 and the Resolution of 7 August 1964; Operation Rolling Thunder from March 1965 and the deployment of US ground combat troops; the political instability of nine juntas after the coup), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 2. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. A record of a conversation between US ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge and Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson in October 1963, on whether to back a coup against Diem.

‘Mr Lodge said that the Diem regime had lost the support of the Vietnamese people. The Strategic Hamlets Programme had alienated the peasants. The Buddhist crisis of the summer had destroyed Diem’s international standing. The South Vietnamese generals were now ready to act against Diem if assured the United States would not oppose them. Mr Johnson said that he was uneasy: removing Diem might leave South Vietnam more politically unstable than before. Mr Lodge replied that without a change of regime South Vietnam would fall to communism by the spring.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about US thinking on the Diem coup.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Senior US officials concluded by October 1963 that Diem could no longer hold South Vietnam against the Vietcong’ supported by ‘without a change of regime South Vietnam would fall to communism by the spring’ AND ‘Some US officials worried that removing Diem might create more problems than it solved’ supported by ‘removing Diem might leave South Vietnam more politically unstable than before’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the New Laws of 1542.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples was banned, and many Indigenous workers held as slaves were freed across the Spanish Americas in the years that followed.
• The encomenderos — especially in Peru — rebelled. In January 1546 Gonzalo Pizarro’s men killed the first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, at the Battle of Añaquito.
• Charles V was forced to compromise: although the rebellion was eventually broken and Gonzalo Pizarro executed in 1548, the inheritance clause was quietly repealed. Existing encomiendas could now be inherited.
• The New Laws established the principle that Indigenous peoples had legal personality and rights as vassals of the crown, opening the way for the 1550–51 Valladolid debate between Las Casas and Sepulveda.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the New Laws without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the establishment of the viceroyalties of New Spain (1535) and Peru (1542).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• The crown finally had a single representative on each continent able to exercise royal authority directly — ending the era of independent conquistador governors and centralising power in the Crown’s appointees.
• The first Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, used his fifteen-year tenure (1535–50) to centralise royal authority over the conquistadors, the encomienda and the audiencia.
• Each viceroyalty was supported by an audiencia — a royal court of judges — that supervised local governors and heard appeals, creating a layered bureaucracy quite unlike the personal rule of Cortes or Pizarro.
• The first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, was killed by encomenderos at the Battle of Añaquito in 1546 — showing that the viceroy system was not yet fully accepted on the ground.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the viceroyalties without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Bartolome de las Casas in the period c1514–1552.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Las Casas, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Las Casas was the most persistent Spanish critic of the encomienda. As a former encomendero who renounced his grant in 1514, he had inside knowledge of the system — making his testimony harder to dismiss.
• He was made ‘Protector of the Indians’ at the Spanish court in 1516 and used the position for fifty years of lobbying, travelling repeatedly between the Americas and Spain.
• His memoranda to Charles V were the political pressure that produced the New Laws of 1542 — the first European law banning the outright enslavement of an Indigenous population.
• His Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552) was reprinted across Protestant Europe and became the basis for the ‘Black Legend’ of Spanish cruelty — weaponised against Spain, but also a real moral indictment.
• He confronted the theologian Juan Gines de Sepulveda at the Valladolid debate of 1550–51, defending the position that Indigenous peoples were not ‘natural slaves’. The debate established the principle that Indigenous peoples had rights, even if the encomienda survived in practice.
• The historiographical move (Restall) is to see Las Casas as evidence that the conquest was contested by Spaniards in real time — not unanimously celebrated.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (renunciation 1514, Protector 1516, New Laws 1542, Brief Account 1552, Valladolid 1550–51).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Las Casas without explaining his importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the encomienda system in the Spanish Empire by 1542.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the encomienda, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The encomienda was the everyday economic basis of the empire. Tens of thousands of Indigenous people in Mexico and Peru paid tribute and laboured under Spanish encomenderos — supplying food, cloth, building work and (later) labour for the mines.
• It created a colonial aristocracy. Conquistadors who had served in 1521 or 1532 were rewarded with encomiendas in lieu of cash, becoming wealthy landowners with hereditary expectations.
• It tied the missions to the labour system. Encomenderos were nominally responsible for the religious instruction of their workers, which gave the Franciscans and Dominicans access to Indigenous communities — including Las Casas himself.
• It became the central political problem of the empire. Las Casas’s campaign and the New Laws of 1542 were direct responses to encomienda abuses; the 1546 Peru rebellion was a direct defence of encomendero privilege.
• It demonstrated continuity rather than novelty. The encomienda often inherited Aztec and Inca tribute structures wholesale — the same workers paid the same tribute, but to a Spaniard rather than to Tenochtitlan or Cuzco.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (the link to missions, the link forward to the New Laws and the 1546 rebellion, the inheritance from Aztec and Inca tribute).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the encomienda without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the role of the viceroy in the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the viceroy, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The viceroy was the personal representative of the king in the colony, holding executive, judicial and military authority — allowing the Crown to govern at a distance of 9,000 kilometres.
• The first Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, used his fifteen-year tenure (1535–50) to centralise royal authority over the conquistadors and the encomienda system, ending the era of personal conquistador rule.
• The viceroyalty system replaced the audiencia of 1528 with a single royal authority on the ground, supported by a permanent audiencia of judges underneath.
• The system spread the empire’s administration: Viceroyalty of New Spain (1535) for North and Central America, Viceroyalty of Peru (1542) for South America. Eighteenth-century New Granada and Rio de la Plata followed the same template.
• The system also exposed the limits of royal power. The first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, was killed by encomenderos in 1546 — showing that even royal authority needed military backing on the ground.
• The viceroys connect the period to the silver economy of the second half of the century. Viceroy Toledo of Peru (1569–81) would extend the mita forced-labour rota to feed the Potosi mines.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Mendoza, Nunez Vela, the audiencia layer, link forward to Toledo).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the viceroy without explaining the role’s importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spain attempted to reform the treatment of Indigenous peoples in the years 1511–46. You may use the following in your answer: Las Casas’s renunciation of his encomienda (1514), the New Laws (1542). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1511 the Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos preached the famous sermon on Hispaniola — ‘Are these not men?’ — the first public Spanish protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples. This in turn placed the question on the political agenda at the Spanish court.
• Because of this growing pressure, the encomendero Bartolome de las Casas heard the same arguments and renounced his own encomienda in 1514, freeing the Indigenous workers tied to it. He was made Protector of the Indians at court in 1516.
• This in turn fuelled fifty years of memoranda and lobbying. By 1542 Las Casas had gathered the testimony into a long memorandum (the Brevisima relacion) for Charles V, describing the cruelty of conquest and encomienda.
• Because of this lobbying, Charles V signed the New Laws on 20 November 1542. They banned outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples, banned new encomiendas, and required existing ones to expire on the holder’s death.
• This in turn provoked open rebellion. In 1546 the encomenderos of Peru rose under Gonzalo Pizarro and killed the first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, at the Battle of Añaquito — forcing the Crown to repeal the inheritance clause and accept that reform on the ground would be partial.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Montesinos, Protector of the Indians, Añaquito).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the Five-Year Plans on Soviet workers in the 1930s. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, the introduction of internal passports in December 1932, the labour-discipline law making one day’s absenteeism a sackable offence, the falling real wages, the fanfare around Stakhanov, the rationing of bread until 1935, or the use of foreign engineers). Inferences go beyond surface description to explain what the detail reveals about regime methods or worker experience. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Stalin launched the First Five-Year Plan in 1928.
You may use the following in your answer:
• fear of foreign attack
• the failings of the New Economic Policy
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — e.g. defence against the industrial powers of Europe and Japan; autarky and the impossibility of importing on credit; the ideological need for an industrial working class to make socialism real; the failings of the NEP exposed by the 1927–28 grain procurement crisis; and the political logic of breaking with Bukharin’s Right Opposition. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Gosplan, NEP, Politburo, Sovnarkom. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the Five-Year Plan without explaining why Stalin launched it. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the success of the Five-Year Plans by 1941.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation argues that the Plans were a remarkable success in turning a peasant country into the third largest industrial economy in the world by 1941, ready to fight Nazi Germany; the other argues that the published figures were inflated, real wages fell, the showpiece projects relied on Gulag labour, and the Stakhanovite movement was a propaganda lever rather than a real productivity gain). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Stakhanovite movement.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (published Soviet productivity figures and propaganda articles versus shop-floor memoirs and Smolensk Archive party records); they wrote at different times (Cold War-era surveys versus post-1991 archival studies such as Khlevniuk and Fitzpatrick); or they had different purposes (assessing Soviet industrial performance from the regime’s own statistics versus reconstructing worker experience and resistance). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the achievements of the First Five-Year Plan, 1928–32?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the First Plan — Magnitogorsk, the Dnieper Dam, the Belomor Canal and its Gulag labour, the doubling of coal output, foreign engineers, the introduction of internal passports in 1932 and the collapse of real wages — weighed against the propaganda character of headline figures and the unevenness of regional and sectoral progress. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the success of Soviet industrialisation by 1941 was bought at an unacceptable human cost?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — falling real wages 1928–32, ration cards until 1935, the Belomor Canal’s Gulag death toll, the labour-discipline laws, internal passports, the resentment of Stakhanovites on the shop floor, the squeezing of consumer goods after 1935 — weighed against the genuine industrial achievement: coal, steel, oil and machine-tool output rising sharply, the new Urals industrial base that carried the Soviet war effort after 1941, and the social mobility of working-class families into engineering and managerial posts (Fitzpatrick). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Gosplan, Sovnarkom, Stakhanovite, Magnitogorsk, Politburo). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Arafat’s renunciation of terrorism (1988) for attempts to find a solution in the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. within hours of the Geneva speech the United States opened direct dialogue with the PLO, ending nearly two decades of diplomatic isolation; the renunciation, paired with the Algiers Declaration’s implicit acceptance of partition, made the two-state solution the formal Palestinian position; this provided the legal and political basis for the Madrid Conference of 1991 and the Oslo Accords of 1993, neither of which would have been possible without a PLO recognised as a diplomatic partner. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the speech without showing why it mattered for finding a solution. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the First Intifada (1987–88) for Israeli attitudes to the occupied territories.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. nightly television footage of Israeli soldiers confronting unarmed Palestinian children imposed political and reputational costs that the IDF’s ‘iron fist’ could not contain, eroding Israel’s post-1967 claim to a relatively benign occupation; the cost calculus of holding the territories shifted on the Israeli left, forming the constituency that would back Yitzhak Rabin’s 1992 election victory and his decision to negotiate the Oslo Accords; for the Israeli right and the army, the Intifada confirmed security concerns and the need for tighter control, hardening the politics that opposed Oslo from 1993 onwards. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the Intifada without showing why it mattered for Israeli attitudes. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the founding of Hamas (1987) for Palestinian politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Hamas’s 1988 charter rejected the recognition of Israel and provided an Islamist alternative for Palestinians who distrusted secular nationalist PLO leadership; its mosque- and welfare-based network in Gaza built a constituency the PLO could not command and would later use to win the 2006 Palestinian elections (post-spec but rooted in this period); from 1988 onwards Hamas’s rejection of Arafat’s two-state turn meant any Palestinian-Israeli agreement would lack the support of a major Palestinian movement, weakening every later peace effort. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Hamas’s founding without showing why it mattered for Palestinian politics. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Algiers Declaration of Independence (November 1988).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) by citing UN Resolution 181 the PLO implicitly accepted the 1947 partition and so the existence of an Israeli state alongside a Palestinian one, transforming the official Palestinian position; (ii) within a month around eighty states recognised the declaration, ending the PLO’s diplomatic isolation and creating the international platform on which Arafat’s December 1988 Geneva speech and the US-PLO dialogue could rest. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that the PLO declared a state without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Israeli ‘iron fist’ response to the First Intifada.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) the mass arrests, school closures and Rabin’s January 1988 ‘break the bones’ instruction produced international television coverage that shifted Western opinion against Israel and undermined the post-1967 image of Israel as the smaller actor in the conflict; (ii) the policy did not stop the uprising but did persuade a section of the Israeli political class — ultimately including Rabin himself by 1992–93 — that occupation was unsustainable, contributing to the political shift that produced the Oslo negotiations. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates the ‘iron fist’ without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the First Intifada and Arafat’s political turn in the years 1987–88.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Jabaliya incident (December 1987)
• Arafat’s Geneva speech (December 1988)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the spread of the uprising from Jabaliya through Gaza and the West Bank; the founding of Hamas and the parallel Islamist track; King Hussein’s renunciation of the West Bank in July 1988; the Algiers Declaration of Independence; the Geneva renunciation and US-PLO dialogue). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as Rabin’s ‘iron fist’ or the Beit Sahour tax revolt. Connects events through causation rather than sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Operation Pied Piper, the British evacuation plan of September 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Beginning on 1 September 1939, around 1.5 million British civilians, including roughly 800,000 from London, were moved by special trains and buses to reception areas.
• Evacuees were drawn from priority groups: school children, pregnant women, mothers with babies, the blind and other disabled people.
