• Children travelled with luggage labels tied to their coats, gas-mask boxes round their necks, and a small bag of clothing prepared by their families.
• They were billeted with host families in rural reception areas such as Devon, Somerset, Wales and East Anglia, organised by local authorities under the Civil Defence Act.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to evacuation without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Anderson shelter.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Anderson shelter was made of curved corrugated steel sheets bolted together into a tunnel shape and partly buried in the back garden under a covering of earth.
• It was distributed from 1939 free to families earning less than £250 a year, and sold for £7 to those above that income line.
• Around 1.5 million had been distributed by the outbreak of war and another 2.1 million followed during the war.
• It was named after Sir John Anderson, the Lord Privy Seal who then became Home Secretary in September 1939, and was designed to protect a family from blast and shrapnel.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to a shelter without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: Sources A and B below are composed for practice. They are not real archive documents; in the exam you are given two genuine sources.

Source A: a photograph taken at a London railway station on 1 September 1939. A line of schoolchildren stands on the platform beside a teacher. Each child has a luggage label tied to a coat and a gas-mask box on a string round the neck. A porter is loading small cases into a carriage.

Source B: written guidance sent to local authorities in January 1939, setting out the evacuation plan.
‘The plan rests on the assumption that the bombing of major cities will begin within hours of the outbreak of war. Local authorities must be ready to send away the priority groups — school children, mothers with babies, the disabled — as soon as the codeword is given. Reception areas have been allocated and billets surveyed. Success depends on speed, and on the willingness of householders to accept the evacuees allotted to them.’

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the British government’s preparations to protect civilians in London in 1939?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Weigh both sources together: what each one says, who made it and why, and what you know about the context.

Indicative content:
• Source A shows what evacuation looked like on the day: labels, gas-mask boxes and small cases, with the school as the unit of organisation.
• A photograph freezes one platform at one moment, and pictures of this kind were often taken for the press, so it cannot show how billeting worked at the other end.
• Source B gives the planning behind the picture: priority groups, a codeword, allocated reception areas and surveyed billets.
• As internal guidance to local authorities, Source B was written to be acted on rather than published, so it is good evidence of official intentions before any bombing.
• Both sources are about intention and departure, not about what happened next; neither shows the cold houses, prejudice and drift home that Mass Observation recorded.
• Context to bring in: Operation Pied Piper began on 1 September 1939 and moved around 1.5 million people in three days, about 800,000 of them from London; many drifted home during the Phoney War.

Mastering: Both sources judged on content and on who made them and why, supported by precise contextual knowledge, with a clear verdict on usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Both sources considered, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: Simple comments on what the sources show; provenance or context is thin.
Emerging: Describes the sources without judging their usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B again.

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about how well billeting worked for London evacuees in the reception areas?

Give the detail in Source B you would follow up, the question you would ask, the type of source you could use, and how it would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Give a coherent chain: a detail in Source B, the question it raises, the type of source you could use, and how that source would help.

Indicative example:
• Detail in Source B: success ‘depends on … the willingness of householders to accept the evacuees allotted to them’.
• Question: how willing were householders in the reception areas to take London evacuees in autumn 1939?
• Type of source: diaries kept by people living in reception-area villages, such as those collected by Mass Observation.
• How it helps: private diaries record what hosts actually thought and did, which official planning documents cannot show.

Other chains are equally creditable, for example following up the priority groups, the codeword, or the expectation of bombing ‘within hours’, using borough council evacuation records, a local newspaper such as the Hackney Gazette, or oral-history recordings of former evacuees.

Mastering: All four steps clear, with the source type matched to the question.
Secure: A sound question and source type, briefly explained.
Developing: A question or a source type given, but the link to Source B is weak.
Emerging: A source type or question suggested that is not grounded in Source B.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of British civil defence preparations in London by September 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Around 1.5 million Anderson shelters had been distributed by the outbreak of war, free to households earning under £250 a year.
• About 38 million civilian gas masks had been distributed nationally by spring 1939, including brightly coloured ‘Mickey Mouse’ masks for small children.
• A network of ARP (Air Raid Precautions) wardens had been recruited as part-time volunteers organised by sector under the Civil Defence Act of 1939.
• Operation Pied Piper had moved roughly 800,000 Londoners (children, pregnant women, the disabled) to reception areas in the first three days of war.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to civil defence without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
‘Governments did far more to protect civilians in wartime by 1945 than in any earlier period.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• evacuation and Anderson shelters in 1939
• the impact of war on civilians in the medieval period.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments that protection improved enormously:
• Operation Pied Piper moved around 1.5 million people out of the cities in three days from 1 September 1939, about 800,000 of them Londoners.
• About 1.5 million Anderson shelters had been given out by the outbreak of war, free to households earning under £250 a year.
• Around 38 million gas masks had been distributed by spring 1939, with ‘Mickey Mouse’ masks for small children and helmets for babies.
• The Civil Defence Act of 1939 made local authorities responsible for air-raid precautions, and over a million wardens and rescue workers were in place by 1940.
• From October 1940 the government equipped 79 Tube stations as shelters, and the Morrison shelter followed in 1941 for homes without a garden.

Indicative content — arguments that the change is smaller than it looks:
• In earlier centuries governments did not try to protect civilians at all: medieval purveyance took their food, and free quarter in the 1640s put soldiers in their houses.
• Protection in 1939–45 was uneven: Anderson shelters suited suburban gardens, not the flat-roofed terraces of Stepney and Bethnal Green.
• The government banned Tube shelter at first, and Londoners forced the change themselves.
• Planning failed in practice at South Hallsville School in 1940 and at Bethnal Green in 1943.
• Resources went to the gas threat that never came, while the real danger of high-explosive and incendiary bombing was underestimated.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that compares government action across several periods, uses accurate detail (Pied Piper, Anderson shelters, gas masks, purveyance, free quarter) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) in Notting Hill in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• They were large Victorian houses on streets such as Powis Square and Colville Terrace, carved into 8-12 separate bedsits.
• Several families shared one kitchen and one bathroom, sometimes with a dozen tenants in the house.
• Conditions were often dangerous: damp walls, faulty wiring, blocked drains and broken sash windows.
• Rents were high relative to earnings, because landlords could charge a premium while the colour bar closed off the rest of London.
• Most occupants were Caribbean families, since the housing colour bar restricted where they could rent.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Sources A and B.

Source A: A photograph published in a London newspaper in 1959. It shows the front of a lodging house in Powis Square, Notting Hill, with a broken sash window, peeling paint and damp staining on the brickwork above the entrance.

Source B: From a letter written in 1960 by a Caribbean tenant in Notting Hill to a local housing charity. 'There are nine of us on this landing and one tap between us. The rent is thirty-five shillings a week for one room. I have asked the landlord three times about the window. He tells me that if I do not like it I can find somewhere else, and he knows there is nowhere else that will have me.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the housing conditions of Caribbean tenants in Notting Hill in the late 1950s and early 1960s?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 8 marks for an answer that weighs content, provenance and own knowledge for both sources against the stated enquiry.

Indicative content:
• Content of A: visible disrepair on a house in Powis Square, one of the streets where Peter Rachman was active, and bad enough to be newsworthy in 1959.
• Content of B: nine people to one tap, thirty-five shillings a week for a single room, and a landlord who knows the tenant has no alternative because of the colour bar.
• Provenance of A: a newspaper photograph shows one front elevation at one moment. It cannot show interior conditions, the rent charged, or how the landlord treated tenants.
• Provenance of B: a tenant's own letter gives the experience from inside, but it is one household's account written to a charity that the writer hoped would help.
• Own knowledge: Caribbean tenants were concentrated in houses of multiple occupation around Powis Square because the colour bar excluded them from most of London.
• Own knowledge: Rachman owned around 100 properties in the area by 1959 and used the Rent Act of 1957 to clear regulated tenants and re-let at three or four times the rent.
• Own knowledge: Ruth Glass's 1960 study Newcomers documented the same conditions across the district, so both sources fit a well-evidenced pattern.

Mastering: Content, provenance and own knowledge weighed for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Both sources used, with two of the three strands developed and a judgement reached.
Developing: The sources are described rather than weighed; provenance is noted but not linked to usefulness.
Emerging: One source described, with little or no own knowledge.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Source B.

The rent is thirty-five shillings a week for one room. I have asked the landlord three times about the window. He tells me that if I do not like it I can find somewhere else, and he knows there is nowhere else that will have me.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the way landlords treated Caribbean tenants in Notting Hill?

In your answer, you must give the question you would ask and the type of source you could use.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — How Could You Follow Up
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks for a coherent chain: a detail in the source, the question that detail raises, and a type of source that could answer it.

Indicative content (any one, fully developed):
• Detail: 'thirty-five shillings a week for one room'. Question: how did rents in Notting Hill compare with rents for similar rooms elsewhere in London in 1960? Source type: rent books, tenancy agreements and rent tribunal records for the borough.
• Detail: 'nine of us on this landing and one tap'. Question: how many houses in the Colville and Powis streets were recorded as overcrowded? Source type: council housing inspectorate records for the borough of Kensington.
• Detail: 'he knows there is nowhere else that will have me'. Question: how widespread was the colour bar in London lettings? Source type: contemporary lodging-house advertisements in local newspapers, and the reports of housing charities.

Mastering: A coherent chain — a specific detail picked out, a precise question, and a type of source that could realistically answer it.
Secure: Detail and question are sensible; the source type is named but generic.
Developing: The detail or the question is vague; the source type is generic.
Emerging: No clear chain from the source to an enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Peter Rachman’s housing business in Notting Hill in the late 1950s and early 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Rachman owned around 100 properties in Notting Hill by 1959, mostly on Powis Square, Colville Terrace and Powis Terrace.
• He exploited the Rent Act of 1957, which lifted rent controls on a property once it fell vacant.
• He used intimidation to clear regulated tenants: removing front doors, cutting off services, sending heavies and moving in disruptive lodgers.
• He re-let the vacated rooms to Caribbean families at three or four times the regulated rent, because the colour bar left them nowhere else to go.
• His name entered the language as 'Rachmanism' after his death in 1962 and the press coverage of the Profumo affair in 1963.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Bruce Kenrick's response to the housing crisis in Notting Hill.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• He founded the Notting Hill Housing Trust in 1963, a charitable housing association that bought and refurbished cheap property.
• The Trust let its homes to low-income tenants regardless of race, in direct contrast to the colour bar operating around it.
• It raised its money by charitable donation rather than from rents alone, and owned hundreds of properties across the borough within five years.
• Kenrick went on to co-found the national homelessness charity Shelter in 1966, which took the issue to a national audience.
• The Trust's model of renovating older stock for low-income tenants became a template for the housing-association movement from the late 1960s.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the methods used to catch criminals in the twentieth century were different from the methods used in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Twentieth-century police used science and records: a fingerprint bureau from 1901, the Police National Computer from 1974 and DNA fingerprinting from 1984.
• Nineteenth-century detectives had none of these; the 1888 Whitechapel investigation ran on door-to-door interviews, witness statements and sketches alone.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the death penalty was abolished in Britain in 1965.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Derek Bentley case
• Sydney Silverman.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• High-profile, controversial executions undermined public confidence in the system: Timothy Evans (hanged 1950, later pardoned because John Christie was the real killer), Derek Bentley (hanged 1953 although his accomplice fired the shot) and Ruth Ellis (hanged 1955, the last woman executed in Britain).
• A long parliamentary campaign by the Labour MP Sydney Silverman, who introduced four abolition Bills before the 1965 success, kept the issue on the political agenda for over a decade.
• Public opinion shifted as press coverage of these cases drew attention to mistakes that could not be reversed once a sentence had been carried out.
• Wider penal reform — open prisons (1946), borstals, probation — had already shifted punishment away from physical retribution towards reform and management of offenders.
• Comparable countries had already abolished or suspended capital punishment, increasing pressure on Britain to align with international practice.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (Bentley, Evans, Ellis, Silverman, broader penal reform) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of abolition without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the punishment of people who refused to obey the state in the twentieth century was different from their punishment in the seventeenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Twentieth-century conscientious objectors went before tribunals that could grant absolute exemption, alternative civilian work or non-combatant service; about 6,000 were imprisoned in the First World War and around 5,000 in the Second.
• Seventeenth-century defiance of the state was answered with death: the Gunpowder Plotters were hanged, drawn and quartered in 1606, and Catholic priests were executed as traitors.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why attitudes to the death penalty changed in Britain between 1900 and 1965.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Derek Bentley case
• miscarriages of justice.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks for an explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail. Students may use the two stimulus points, but the top band needs at least one reason of their own.

Indicative content:
• The case dramatised the unfairness of joint-enterprise murder convictions: Bentley was already under arrest when Christopher Craig fired the fatal shot at PC Sidney Miles, and Bentley had a mental age of around 10.
• Public reaction was unprecedented: 200 MPs signed a motion against the execution, and the campaign for abolition gathered organised political support.
• The case gave Sydney Silverman a high-profile injustice to point to in the parliamentary debates that led to his Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965.
• It exposed a deeper problem: an irreversible punishment cannot be corrected, a point reinforced by Timothy Evans (hanged 1950, pardoned 1966) and Ruth Ellis (hanged 1955).
• The case retained its symbolic force after abolition: Bentley was granted a posthumous pardon for his sentence in 1993 and his conviction was quashed by the Court of Appeal in 1998 — a final endorsement of the campaigners’ arguments.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of at least two reasons with specific detail (joint enterprise, MPs’ motion, Silverman, posthumous pardon, conviction quashed) and explicit links to abolition.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the case without explaining importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the part played by ordinary people in preventing crime in the late twentieth century was similar to the part they played in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Up to 2 marks for identifying a valid point of similarity or difference; up to 2 further marks for supporting detail drawn from both periods.

Indicative content:
• Neighbourhood Watch, begun at Mollington in Cheshire in 1982, asked neighbours to watch each other's homes and report anything suspicious to the police.
• Anglo-Saxon tithings and the hue and cry placed the same duty on neighbours by law, making them answerable for each other's behaviour and obliged to join the chase.

Top band: one clear point, supported with accurate detail from both periods.
Mid band: one clear point, supported from one period only.
Low band: a point stated with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text:
‘The use of science and technology was the most important development in twentieth-century British policing.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• DNA evidence
• Neighbourhood Watch.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments supporting science and technology as the most important development:
• Fingerprint identification (Met bureau 1901; first conviction 1902) gave police a reliable way to identify offenders for the first time.
• Police radio (1934 Met trial; standard by 1960s) and the Police National Computer (1974) revolutionised communication and record-keeping nationally.
• DNA fingerprinting, developed by Alec Jeffreys in 1984 and first used to convict Colin Pitchfork in 1986, made it possible to identify offenders from biological traces invisible to the eye.
• Forensic science transformed the investigation of serious crime — murder, sexual offences, terrorism — in ways that beat policing alone could never have achieved.

Indicative content — arguments against (other developments mattered as much or more):
• Specialisation produced new branches that science alone did not deliver: Special Branch (1883, expanded post-1945), Fraud Squad (1946), drug squads (1960s), Armed Response Vehicles (1991).
• Crime prevention — Neighbourhood Watch (1982), CCTV from the 1980s, target hardening, community policing — arguably reduced crime more than detection did.
• Non-custodial alternatives (open prisons 1946, probation, community service 1972, electronic tagging 1989) reshaped what happened after offending and reduced reoffending pressure on the police.
• Public consent and visibility — the unarmed beat constable, the ‘bobby’ image dating back to Peel — remained the visible face of policing and was as important to legitimacy as any forensic tool.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs science against at least one other factor (specialisation, prevention, non-custodial alternatives) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Red Cloud’s War (1866–68) for relations between the US Government and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Red Cloud’s War, supported by specific period detail.

Indicative content:
• Red Cloud’s War was the only major nineteenth-century war the US Government settled by accepting Indigenous demands — the second Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) closed the Bozeman Trail and abandoned Forts Reno, Phil Kearny and C.F. Smith.
• Because the US recognised the Black Hills and Powder River country as Lakota territory in writing, the war set a legal benchmark that later treaty-breaking (the 1874 gold strike, the 1876 ultimatum) could be measured against.
• The Fetterman Fight of 21 December 1866 — in which Crazy Horse’s decoy party led Captain Fetterman’s 80 men into ambush — was the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until Little Bighorn, shaking the Army’s confidence in lightly held forts.
• Because the war showed that a coalition of Oglala, Hunkpapa, Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters could close a strategic trail for two years, federal policy shifted towards reservation containment over open military pressure for the rest of the 1860s.
• The treaty fed directly into the conditions of the next decade: when gold was struck in the Black Hills in 1874, the Lakota could point to a federal promise less than six years old — making the resulting Little Bighorn campaign a war over a treaty the Government itself had signed.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1866–68, 21 December 1866, 1868) and specialist vocabulary (Bozeman Trail, Powder River country, Oglala Lakota, unceded territory).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the war without explanation of importance for US–Indigenous relations.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the deterioration of relations between the US Government and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains in the years 1862–1868.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Sand Creek Massacre (1864)
• the Fetterman Fight (1866)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1862 the Santee Sioux of Minnesota were starving because annuities promised under earlier treaties had been withheld; the agent Andrew Myrick’s reported ‘eat grass’ remark triggered Little Crow’s rising and the killing of around 500 settlers, ending in the Mankato execution of 38 Dakota men in December 1862.
• Because the Pikes Peak gold rush had drawn miners deep into Cheyenne and Arapaho hunting land guaranteed by the 1851 treaty, tensions in Colorado built up across 1863–64 and culminated on 29 November 1864 in Colonel Chivington’s attack on Black Kettle’s peaceful camp under a US flag at Sand Creek — about 150 were killed, mostly women, children and elderly.
• Because Sand Creek made ‘peaceful’ treaty arrangements look worthless, allied Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota raids spread across the central Plains in 1865 and pushed younger Indigenous leaders — including the Oglala Lakota war leader Red Cloud — towards organised armed resistance.
• Because Congress had authorised the Bozeman Trail and the US Army began building forts through Powder River country in 1866, Red Cloud walked out of negotiations and launched a coalition war; on 21 December 1866 Crazy Horse’s decoy party led Captain Fetterman’s 80 men into ambush outside Fort Phil Kearny — the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until 1876.
• By 1868 the cost of garrisoning forts that could not be safely supplied forced Washington to accept terms: the Bozeman Trail closed, the forts abandoned, and the Black Hills recognised as Lakota territory in the second Fort Laramie Treaty — the closing point of a six-year deterioration that had begun with starving Santee in Minnesota.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1862, 1864, 1866, 1868), specialist vocabulary (annuities, Bozeman Trail, Powder River, Oglala Lakota), both stimulus points covered and integrated with own knowledge.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Sand Creek Massacre (1864) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Sand Creek killed around 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho on 29 November 1864 — mostly women, children and elderly — despite Black Kettle flying both a US flag and a white flag of truce; the loss of so many non-combatants weakened the Cheyenne nation in the central Plains for a generation.
• Because the federal investigation of 1865 condemned the attack but no one was prosecuted, Sand Creek showed that ‘peaceful’ treaty status offered no real protection — pushing more Indigenous leaders towards armed resistance rather than negotiation.
• The massacre triggered an immediate wave of allied Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota raids across the central Plains throughout 1865, lengthening the cycle of violence that fed directly into Red Cloud’s War.
• Because survivors brought the story north into Lakota territory, Sand Creek hardened the resolve of younger leaders such as Red Cloud and Crazy Horse, who would not trust unprotected camps near US forts.
• Black Kettle’s death four years later at the Washita River — again under a US flag — underlined the pattern Sand Creek had established: peace chiefs who trusted federal protection could be killed without consequence.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (29 November 1864, around 150 killed, federal investigation 1865) and specialist vocabulary (Cheyenne, Arapaho, peace chief, Colorado Volunteers).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how Red Cloud’s War unfolded in the years 1866–1868.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Bozeman Trail forts
• the Fetterman Fight (1866)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1866 the US Army began building three forts — Reno, Phil Kearny and C.F. Smith — along the Bozeman Trail to protect miners heading from the Oregon Trail to the Montana goldfields; the trail cut straight through Powder River country guaranteed to the Lakota by the 1851 treaty.
• Because the forts were built without Lakota consent, Red Cloud walked out of the 1866 negotiations and organised a coalition of Oglala, Hunkpapa, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors that effectively blockaded the trail.
• Because Captain William Fetterman led 80 men out of Fort Phil Kearny against orders on 21 December 1866 in pursuit of a small decoy party led by Crazy Horse, his entire column was destroyed in around 30 minutes by a much larger waiting force — the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until 1876.
• Because the forts could not be safely supplied through a contested winter and public opinion in the East was hardening against the cost of the war, Washington opened peace negotiations through 1867 and into 1868.
• By 1868 the war ended on Lakota terms: the Bozeman Trail was closed, the forts abandoned and burned, and the second Fort Laramie Treaty recognised the Black Hills and Powder River country as Lakota territory — a rare Indigenous victory written into US law.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1866, 21 December 1866, 1868), specialist vocabulary (Bozeman Trail, Oglala Lakota, Powder River, decoy).
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Little Crow’s War (1862) for relations between the US Government and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Little Crow’s War showed how easily withheld annuities could push a treaty-bound nation into open war — the agent Andrew Myrick’s reported ‘eat grass’ remark made it clear that paper guarantees meant nothing without the food and money the treaties had promised.
• Because around 500 settlers were killed in the Minnesota River valley, eastern public opinion swung sharply against Indigenous nations on the Plains, hardening political support for harsher policy and a larger frontier military presence.
• Because President Lincoln personally reviewed the 392 trials and confirmed 38 hangings, the Mankato execution on 26 December 1862 became the largest mass execution in US history, setting a federal precedent for swift mass punishment after Indigenous risings.
• Because the surviving Santee were stripped of their Minnesota reservation and pushed into Dakota Territory, the war began the wider movement of Indigenous peoples onto reservations west of the Mississippi.
• Because news of starvation, withheld annuities and mass execution spread through Plains nations, Little Crow’s War contributed to the deepening distrust that fed into Sand Creek (1864) and Red Cloud’s War (1866–68).

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1862, 26 December 1862, 38 men hanged, around 500 settlers killed) and specialist vocabulary (Santee Sioux, annuities, Indian agent).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Sand Creek Massacre (1864).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the massacre to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that allied Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota raids spread across the central Plains throughout 1865, lengthening the cycle of violence and feeding directly into Red Cloud’s War (1866–68).
• Another consequence was that surviving Cheyenne carried the story north into Lakota country, hardening the resolve of younger leaders such as Red Cloud and Crazy Horse who would refuse to camp unprotected near US forts.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named feature or event (e.g. Red Cloud’s War, Indigenous coalition).
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Cromwell’s reform of royal finance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Court of Augmentations — the new department created to channel monastic income from the dissolution to the crown.
• Court of First Fruits and Tenths — managed church revenues such as the first year’s income from a benefice paid to the crown.
• Court of Wards — administered feudal incomes from the heirs of tenants-in-chief.
• Court of General Surveyors — supervised crown lands and existing royal estates.
• Specialist staff — each department had permanent officers and account books separate from the medieval Exchequer.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the marriage to Anne of Cleves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Diplomatic purpose — the match was arranged by Cromwell in 1539 to build a Protestant alliance after Charles V and Francis I had signed the Truce of Nice.
• Anne’s background — she was the sister of the Duke of Cleves, a Protestant prince on the Lower Rhine.
• The Holbein portrait — the king relied on Hans Holbein the Younger’s 1539 painting and ambassadorial reports before agreeing to the match.
• The Rochester meeting — Henry made a surprise visit in disguise on New Year’s Day 1540 and found Anne plain-looking and awkward.
• The annulment — the marriage was declared void on 9 July 1540 with Anne’s cooperation; she was rewarded with manors and the title ‘the king’s sister’.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Anne Boleyn fell from power in 1536.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Thomas Cromwell
• the failure to produce a male heir
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Clash with Cromwell — Anne and Cromwell disagreed over how monastic wealth should be spent (charity vs crown finance).
• Foreign policy disagreement — after Catherine of Aragon’s death in January 1536, Cromwell wanted reconciliation with Charles V; Anne preferred the French alliance.
• Failure to produce a male heir — Anne’s January 1536 miscarriage of a son weighed heavily on Henry, who needed a Tudor male heir.
• Henry’s infatuation with Jane Seymour — the king’s eye had moved on by spring 1536.
• Charges of adultery and incest — Cromwell engineered the case using forced confessions (Mark Smeaton) and the testimony of court enemies.
• Family abandonment — even her uncle, the Duke of Norfolk, sat on the jury that convicted her, showing the Boleyn faction had collapsed.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
‘Cromwell’s changes to government amounted to a revolution.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Privy Council
• parliamentary statute
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the case for revolution against the case for gradual change and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments that the changes were revolutionary:
• Cromwell turned the Principal Secretary into the central coordinating office of government.
• A smaller Privy Council of around nineteen named councillors met with formal agendas and clerks taking minutes.
• New revenue departments — Augmentations, First Fruits and Tenths, Wards, General Surveyors — had permanent staff and books separate from the medieval Exchequer.
• Parliamentary statute replaced royal proclamation as the engine of policy in religion and government.
• Geoffrey Elton argued in 1953 that this amounted to a Tudor revolution in government.

Arguments that the changes were gradual:
• John Guy and David Starkey argue the reforms answered immediate problems rather than following a plan.
• Some of the revenue courts were only completed after Cromwell’s death, so the design was not finished by him.
• Henry VIII remained the source of all authority, as Cromwell’s own fall in 1540 demonstrated.
• Parliament had passed major statutes before 1532; what changed was the scale rather than the principle.
• The household and the court still decided careers, as the conservative capture of the Privy Chamber in 1540 showed.

Overall judgement: government in 1540 looked very different from government in 1509, but it grew out of immediate need rather than a plan, and the king still decided what mattered. Top-band answers weigh these readings and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell fell from power in 1540.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the marriage to Anne of Cleves
• the Duke of Norfolk
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cleves marriage failure — Henry found Anne plain-looking and awkward; the marriage humiliated him personally and discredited Cromwell’s diplomatic judgement.
• Conservative faction — the Duke of Norfolk, Bishop Stephen Gardiner and Catherine Howard’s family worked together against Cromwell.
• Catherine Howard — presented to Henry at Norfolk’s Lambeth house, the teenage Howard cousin gave the king a personal motive to be free of Cleves and Cromwell.
• Henry’s religious conservatism — the Act of Six Articles (1539) had already shown Henry was uncomfortable with Cromwell’s evangelical pace.
• Cromwell’s low-born status — his April 1540 promotion to Earl of Essex provoked further conservative anger that a commoner sat above old peers.
• Use of attainder — Cromwell was condemned without trial, by the same Act of Attainder weapon he had used against the Nun of Kent and Anne Boleyn.
• The diplomatic context — the feared Charles V–Francis I coalition turned out to be less imminent than Cromwell had argued, weakening the case for Cleves.
• Henry’s personal authority — the king demonstrated by Cromwell’s fall that even his most powerful minister served at royal pleasure.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for Cromwell’s fall in 1540 was the failure of the marriage to Anne of Cleves.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Duke of Norfolk
• Cromwell’s religious convictions
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the Cleves marriage against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The Cleves marriage humiliated Henry personally on New Year’s Day 1540 and tied Cromwell to that humiliation.
• Cromwell’s ambassadors had reported favourably on Anne; the failure was a direct intelligence failure on his part.
• The marriage produced no heir and damaged Cromwell’s standing in just six months.
• The annulment process kept Cromwell alive only as a witness for the king’s case.
• The diplomatic justification weakened: the feared Charles V–Francis I coalition had stalled.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• The Duke of Norfolk and Bishop Gardiner had been working against Cromwell for years and only needed an opportunity.
• Catherine Howard — the king’s infatuation gave the conservative faction a Howard candidate to put forward.
• Religious conviction — Cromwell had pushed evangelical reform faster than Henry wanted; the 1539 Act of Six Articles was already a corrective signal.
• Faction politics — the conservative court had blamed Cromwell for monastic suppression and the Pilgrimage of Grace casualties.
• Cromwell’s low-born status — his elevation to Earl of Essex in April 1540 antagonised noble rivals.
• Use of his own methods — the Act of Attainder he was condemned by was a weapon he had perfected.
• Henry’s personality — Diarmaid MacCulloch and G.W. Bernard agree the king himself decided to drop Cromwell once the political price became higher than the value.

Overall judgement: the Cleves marriage was the trigger that turned a long-running political vulnerability into a fatal crisis. Cromwell’s religious agenda, his low-born status, and the conservative faction’s patience all mattered more for explaining why he was vulnerable in the first place. A top-band answer weighs these factors and reaches a substantiated conclusion using precise Tudor vocabulary.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the position of Lin Biao within the CCP between 1969 and 1971. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (e.g. Lin’s naming as successor in the 1969 constitution, the dispute over the post of state chairman, the 13 September 1971 plane crash). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that Lin’s formal status as successor was real but conditional on Mao’s personal trust. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that reads more as paraphrase than inference. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Gang of Four were arrested in October 1976.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the death of Zhou Enlai
• Hua Guofeng
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. the Tiananmen Incident of April 1976 and public hostility to the radicals, the loss of Mao as protector, Hua Guofeng’s appointment as Mao’s chosen successor, the support of veteran marshals like Ye Jianying, the radicals’ isolation from the PLA, the political vacuum after Zhou’s death) and shows how they interacted. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the political situation in 1976 without explaining why the arrest happened; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about Mao’s political control between 1971 and 1976.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents Mao as still firmly in command until his death; the other presents him as ailing and outflanked by rival factions). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Lin Biao affair of September 1971.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (Cold War-era versus post-1990s archival access); they used different evidence (CCP-published material versus survivor testimony or US intelligence reports); or they had different purposes (commemorative versus critical). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the role of the PLA in ending the Red Guard movement after 1967?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own knowledge — the PLA ‘mass support’ teams in factories and schools, the xiaxiang campaign that sent c.17 million urban youth to the countryside, the role of revolutionary committees chaired by army officers, the army’s growing political weight at the Ninth Party Congress — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 that the death of Zhou Enlai in January 1976 was the turning point that ended the Cultural Revolution?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — Zhou’s recall of Deng in 1973, the Four Modernisations of 1975, the Tiananmen Incident of April 1976, the radicals’ second purge of Deng, Mao’s death on 9 September 1976, Hua Guofeng’s arrest of the Gang of Four on 6 October 1976 — to test how far Zhou’s death alone explains the end. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (xiaxiang, Gang of Four, Four Modernisations, Tiananmen Incident). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate with some period vocabulary. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning; limited subject vocabulary. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe, 1577–80.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks. Indicative content: • It was a secret raid on Spanish shipping — Drake left Plymouth in December 1577 with five ships under cover of a Mediterranean voyage but a private commission from Elizabeth to attack Spanish silver in the Pacific. • He captured the Spanish treasure ship Cacafuego — off the coast of Peru in March 1579, taking 26 tons of silver, 80 pounds of gold and chests of jewels. • It produced enormous profits for investors — on his return in September 1580 every £1 invested returned roughly £47, including a large secret share for Elizabeth. • Elizabeth knighted Drake on the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581 — a deliberate provocation of Philip II that horrified the Spanish ambassador. Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail. Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed. Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature. Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1585 Roanoke settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It was financed by Sir Walter Raleigh under a 1584 royal charter — named ‘Virginia’ in honour of the Virgin Queen, although Raleigh himself never sailed.
• It was led by Ralph Lane — a soldier rather than a farmer — and numbered only about 100 men, largely soldiers and gentlemen with very few experienced cultivators or craftsmen.
• It was sited on Roanoke Island, off the coast of present-day North Carolina — reached by a 1584 scouting voyage that brought back two Algonquian men, Manteo and Wanchese, to London.
• Relations with the Indigenous Roanoke people broke down — after the killing of Wingina in 1586 trade for food collapsed, and Drake evacuated the surviving colonists in summer 1586.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Elizabethans began to explore further than before.
You may use the following in your answer:
• new ship and navigation technology
• Spanish American silver
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• New ship and navigation technology (stimulus) — the English galleon developed by Hawkins was longer, lower and more manoeuvrable than earlier carracks; astrolabes and quadrants allowed accurate latitude readings; Mercator’s 1569 projection helped plot long ocean courses.
• Spanish American silver (stimulus) — bullion fleets carried huge wealth from Mexico and Peru to Seville every year, making Spanish shipping a tempting target for privateers like Drake and a strategic threat the Privy Council wanted to weaken.
• Disruption of the Antwerp cloth market (own knowledge) — religious wars in the Netherlands in the 1560s damaged England’s main trade route, pushing merchants to seek new markets in the Baltic, Mediterranean, Russia and West Africa through chartered companies.
• Search for a north-west passage (own knowledge) — men such as Sir Humphrey Gilbert, Martin Frobisher and John Davis sought an Arctic route to Asia’s spice trade that bypassed Spanish and Portuguese controls.
• Patriotic and Protestant rivalry with Spain (own knowledge) — Hakluyt argued in 1582 for English colonies as bases against Catholic Spain and as a source of national greatness; Elizabeth’s personal investment in Drake reflected the same calculation.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the first English settlement at Roanoke failed.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the choice of colonists
• the killing of Wingina
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links.

Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own):
• Unsuitable colonists — the 1585 settlement was led by Ralph Lane, a soldier, and made up largely of soldiers and gentlemen; few colonists could farm or trade, so food ran out within months.
• Breakdown of Indigenous relations — after Lane killed Wingina in 1586 the Roanoke people stopped supplying food and the colony lost its only practical food source.
• Poor harbour and supply lines — Roanoke Island had shallow waters making resupply difficult; expected relief from England was delayed.
• Wider Spanish war — English shipping was diverted to confront Spain in the Caribbean and to defend against the Armada in 1588, leaving the colony unsupported at the critical moment.

Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: ‘The main reason Drake’s circumnavigation of 1577–80 was significant was the wealth it brought to England.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. You may use the following in your answer: • the capture of the Cacafuego • Drake’s knighthood at Deptford You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor. Arguments supporting the statement (wealth as main reason): • Capture of the Cacafuego (stimulus) — off Peru in March 1579, taking 26 tons of silver, 80 pounds of gold and chests of jewels; this single prize transformed the voyage’s economics. • Investor returns — every £1 invested in the voyage produced roughly £47, including a large secret share for Elizabeth that strengthened Crown finances. • The wealth made future privateering attractive — private capital flowed into voyages such as the 1587 Cadiz raid and helped fund the fleet that fought the Armada. Arguments against (other factors more important): • Drake’s knighthood at Deptford (stimulus) — Elizabeth’s public knighting in April 1581 was a deliberate political insult to Philip II that turned the voyage into a diplomatic event with consequences far beyond money. • Strategic and navigational achievement (own knowledge) — Drake had sailed through the Strait of Magellan, raided Pacific coasts the Spanish had thought safe, and proved that English seamanship could match Spain’s; this shaped naval thinking ahead of 1588. • Boost to national prestige and morale (own knowledge) — only the second captain in history to circumnavigate the globe; Drake became a national hero whose later command at Cadiz and against the Armada drew on this reputation. • Wider Anglo-Spanish rivalry (own knowledge) — the voyage hardened Philip II’s view that war with England was inevitable; in that sense its long-term significance was diplomatic and strategic, not just financial. Justified judgement: The wealth was real and shifted Crown finances, but Drake’s circumnavigation mattered just as much as a strategic and political event — the knighthood, the navigational achievement and the impact on Spain’s view of England all flowed from it. A strong response weighs financial return against political and strategic significance and reaches a defended overall view. Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed. Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors. Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Sir Walter Raleigh chose to attempt a colony in North America.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Raleigh’s 1584 charter
• rivalry with Spain
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons, using both stimulus points and information of your own, with clear causal links. Indicative content (use both stimulus points and add at least one of your own): • Royal charter and political ambition — in 1584 Elizabeth granted Raleigh a six-year monopoly on colonising unclaimed North American land, giving him the legal and financial framework to launch the voyages. • Strategic rivalry with Spain — English colonies on the North American coast could serve as bases for raids on Spanish shipping returning from the Caribbean, fitting the same anti-Spanish strategy as Drake’s privateering. • Patriotic and propaganda arguments — Richard Hakluyt’s 1582 Divers Voyages Touching the Discoverie of America argued that England needed colonies for trade, prestige and Protestant evangelism; Raleigh was a court favourite who absorbed and acted on these arguments. • Expected wealth from natural resources — backers hoped Virginia would provide timber, furs, naval stores and a possible route to gold or precious metals to rival Spain’s American silver. Mastering: Three reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links. Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail. Developing: Two reasons explained, or three reasons identified without explanation. Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the methods used by the NKVD during the Great Terror. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, the use of regional quotas under Order 00447, the ‘conveyor’ sleep-deprivation interrogations, family threats, denunciations by neighbours, or the staged confessions of the Show Trials). Each inference goes beyond surface description to explain why the detail mattered for how the Terror functioned. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Stalin launched the Great Terror in the 1930s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the murder of Kirov
• the Old Bolsheviks
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — Kirov’s December 1934 assassination as pretext and Stalin’s personal interrogation of Nikolayev; the destruction of the Old Bolshevik generation that had defeated Stalin’s rivals in the 1920s (Zinoviev and Kamenev in 1936, Bukharin in 1938); the bureaucratic logic of quotas under Yezhov and Order 00447 of July 1937; the German intelligence forgery against Tukhachevsky and the targeting of the Red Army officer corps; and the role of denunciations by ordinary citizens. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — NKVD, Yezhovshchina, Gulag, Politburo. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans heavily on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists Show Trial defendants without explaining why each was targeted. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the reasons for the Great Terror in the Soviet Union.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation argues the Terror was driven from the top by Stalin’s personal will and the totalitarian logic of the dictatorship, while the other argues it was driven by chaotic centre-and-periphery dynamics, denunciations from below, and local NKVD officers raising their own quotas to demonstrate zeal). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Great Terror.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (Cold War-era memoirs and high-estimate victim figures versus post-1991 NKVD archives and quota documents); they wrote at different times (Conquest’s 1968 totalitarian reading versus Fitzpatrick’s 1990s revisionist work versus Khlevniuk’s post-archival biographies); or they had different purposes (defending or rebutting the totalitarian school). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of Stalin’s personal direction of the Great Terror?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of Stalin’s overnight train to Leningrad after Kirov’s killing, the orchestration of the three Moscow Show Trials, the personal targeting of Bukharin, and Order 00447 — weighed against revisionist evidence of bottom-up denunciations, regional NKVD chiefs petitioning to raise their quotas, and the chaotic dynamics of the Yezhovshchina. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the Great Terror was driven by denunciations from below as much as by Stalin’s orders from above?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — NKVD Order 00447 of July 1937 and its ‘Category 1’ and ‘Category 2’ quotas, regional NKVD chiefs petitioning upwards for higher targets, denunciations of neighbours and colleagues, the apartment-and-job-grab dynamic identified by Sheila Fitzpatrick — weighed against the top-down evidence of Stalin’s personal direction (the night train to Leningrad after Kirov, the orchestration of Bukharin’s confession, Stalin’s belief in the German forgery against Tukhachevsky). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (NKVD, Yezhovshchina, Gulag, Order 00447, Old Bolsheviks). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
