practice_questions.text: Describe two features of housing in Whitechapel in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two valid features):
• The rookeries — densely packed slum streets such as Flower and Dean Street and Dorset Street, where houses had been subdivided into single rooms shared by many families.
• Common lodging houses (‘doss-houses’) — private businesses that let beds in shared dormitories at fourpence a night, with no register of guests.
• The Whitechapel Union workhouse — state-run Poor Law institution where the destitute received food and shelter in exchange for hard labour, with separate casual wards for one-night admissions.
• The Peabody Estate on Commercial Street (1881) — a charitable model housing development of brick blocks with sanitary flats, intended to replace one of the worst rookeries.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support (named streets, named institutions, named years).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature identified with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to ‘the slums’ without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Jewish migration into Whitechapel after 1881.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It followed the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in March 1881 and the antisemitic pogroms across the Russian Empire, Lithuania and Ukraine that came after it.
• Migrants settled in a tight area around Brick Lane, Wentworth Street and Goulston Street, where an established Jewish community already had synagogues, kosher shops and Yiddish newspapers.
• Many worked in the sweated trades — tailoring workshops, cigarette making and boot finishing — for long hours and very low pay.
• Jewish migrants and their British-born children were a large minority, not a majority: most Whitechapel residents were British-born poor.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources A and B.

Source A (composed for this exercise — not a real document): a description of a common lodging house in Whitechapel, written in the style of a social-investigation article of the late 1880s.
'The room is filled with low wooden beds set close together. Each bed costs fourpence; the price is paid in advance to the deputy at the door, who asks no name and gives no receipt. By midnight every bed is taken, and on the floor between them men and women lie down in their clothes for a halfpenny.'

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): notes by an officer of the Whitechapel Union workhouse about its casual ward, written in the style of Poor Law records of the 1880s.
'Every applicant is bathed and his clothing taken from him. He sleeps on a plank, and in the morning breaks his allotted quantity of stone before he is discharged. Many prefer an archway or a staircase to our ward, and we see the same faces again within the week.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into where the poorest people in Whitechapel slept in the late 1880s?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Both sources must be judged for the named enquiry, and the answer should weave together what each source says, who made it and why, and the student's own knowledge of Whitechapel.

Indicative content:
• Content: what each source tells the enquiry, and what it leaves out.
• Provenance: who wrote it, when, for whom and why, and what that does to its usefulness — bias does not make a source useless, it tells you what the source is good for.
• Own knowledge: named Whitechapel detail used to test, support or qualify what the sources say.

Top band: content, provenance and own knowledge integrated for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the enquiry into where the poorest people in Whitechapel slept.
Mid band: both sources used with own knowledge, or one source fully analysed, with a judgement.
Low band: the sources described, with little own knowledge and no judgement.

Subject-specific pointers:
• Source A gives prices (fourpence a bed, a halfpenny for the floor) and the absence of any register — the detail that mattered when police tried to trace people.
• Source B gives the price of a workhouse bed in labour: a bath, a plank, and stone-breaking before release, which is why many slept rough instead.
• Both are composed for practice, so provenance here is a scenario to reason about, not a real archive reference; students should say what kind of record would carry this information and how far it could be trusted.
• Own knowledge: over 200 common lodging houses sleeping more than 8,000 people a night; the Whitechapel Union workhouse at South Grove; the Peabody Estate of 1881, which excluded the very poorest because it required regular work; Booth's 1889 map colouring the worst streets black.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): notes by an officer of the Whitechapel Union workhouse about its casual ward, written in the style of Poor Law records of the 1880s.
'Every applicant is bathed and his clothing taken from him. He sleeps on a plank, and in the morning breaks his allotted quantity of stone before he is discharged. Many prefer an archway or a staircase to our ward, and we see the same faces again within the week.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the casual wards of the Whitechapel workhouse?

In your answer you must give:
• the detail in Source B that you would follow up
• the question you would ask
• what type of source you could use
• how that source might help answer your question.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a relevant detail taken from Source B, 1 for a question that follows from it, 1 for a named type of source, and 1 for explaining how that source would help.

Indicative content (any one complete chain):
• Detail: 'He sleeps on a plank, and in the morning breaks his allotted quantity of stone.' Question: how much stone did a casual-ward inmate have to break, and how long did it take? Source type: Whitechapel Union workhouse casual-ward records and Poor Law Board rules. How it helps: the rules set the task in writing, so they show whether the officer's account matched official policy.
• Detail: 'We see the same faces again within the week.' Question: how many people used the casual ward more than once in a month? Source type: workhouse admission and discharge registers. How it helps: the registers name each admission with a date, so repeat stays can be counted.
• Detail: 'Many prefer an archway or a staircase to our ward.' Question: how many people slept rough in Whitechapel rather than enter the workhouse? Source type: police records of the beat constables who moved rough sleepers on, and Charles Booth's survey notebooks. How it helps: both recorded where people were found sleeping, street by street.

Top band: all four links present, with a source type that could realistically answer the question.
Mid band: detail and question sound, but the source type is generic.
Low band: no clear chain from the source to the enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the environment of Whitechapel that made policing difficult in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• The rookeries — Flower and Dean Street, Thrawl Street and Dorset Street — were served by alleys and enclosed courts only a foot or two wide, where a constable could lose sight of a suspect at once.
• Gas lamps did not reach into the courts, and fog and coal smoke routinely cut visibility on the lit streets to a few yards.
• Around 200 common lodging houses slept more than 8,000 people a night with no register of guests, so anyone could disappear overnight.
• Around 78,000 people were packed into roughly one square mile, so most life was lived in the street and casual labour left thousands with no fixed address.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of provision for the poor in Whitechapel in the 1880s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Whitechapel Union workhouse — a state-run Poor Law institution where inmates were segregated by sex, made to wear uniforms and given food and shelter in return for hard labour such as breaking stones or picking oakum.
• The casual ward — a section of the workhouse for one-night admissions, where the homeless had to bathe, sleep on a wooden plank and complete several hours of labour before release.
• The Peabody Estate on Commercial Street (1881) — charitable model housing built by the Peabody Trust to replace one of the worst rookeries with sanitary brick flats, though only available to those in regular work.
• Common lodging houses — not strictly poor relief, but the cheapest paid shelter for those just above destitution at fourpence per bed.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail (named institutions, named years, specific rules).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to ‘help for the poor’ without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. Guidance of the kind given to US soldiers arriving in South Vietnam, 1967.

‘In the country areas where you will operate, you cannot tell the Vietcong from the ordinary peasant. The enemy wears no uniform. He may be the man working in the rice paddy by day and the man laying a booby trap by night. The peasant village is therefore the battlefield. You must search every hut, every well, every haystack. You must measure success not by the ground you hold but by the enemy you have killed. The body count is your scorecard. Trust no one outside your unit.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about US tactics in South Vietnam.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘US commanders measured success in enemy dead rather than territory held’ supported by ‘measure success not by the ground you hold but by the enemy you have killed’ AND ‘US tactics treated the peasant village itself as a target, blurring the line between civilians and Vietcong’ supported by ‘The peasant village is therefore the battlefield’ or ‘Trust no one outside your unit’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why US military tactics failed to defeat the Vietcong between 1965 and 1968.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Operation Rolling Thunder
• the Ho Chi Minh Trail

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. search-and-destroy and the body count, the use of Agent Orange and napalm, Vietcong tunnel networks, integration with the peasant population), and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The full picture connects: Rolling Thunder’s 643,000 tons of bombs and around 900 US aircraft lost; the Trail’s repair by hand through Laos and Cambodia; search-and-destroy producing tactical victories such as Ia Drang while a 1967 Pentagon study found two new Vietcong recruits per one killed; Agent Orange’s 4.5 million defoliated acres and the refugees this generated; the Cu Chi tunnels (around 250 km) that allowed the Vietcong to vanish from ‘cleared’ ground; the strategic mismatch between an industrial firepower war and a rural political war.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of US tactics without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1985 history of US strategy in Vietnam):
‘US tactics in Vietnam failed because the wrong tactics were chosen. Search and destroy mistook a political war for a body-count contest. Operation Rolling Thunder bombed an agricultural country as if it were industrial Germany. With clear-and-hold tactics, support for South Vietnamese village government and a stop to indiscriminate firepower, the United States could have won.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2005 study of insurgency warfare):
‘US tactics in Vietnam failed because no Western tactics could have succeeded. The Vietcong’s guerrilla war — ambush, tunnel networks, integration with the peasant population and supply through Laos and Cambodia — turned American firepower into a strategic liability. The Republic of Vietnam had no rural legitimacy. There were no ‘right tactics’ to win a war the South Vietnamese state could not have won politically.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about why US military tactics failed in Vietnam? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees failure as a problem of tactical choice that better US tactics — clear-and-hold, support for village government — could have fixed; Interpretation 2 sees failure as structural, rooted in Vietcong guerrilla war and the political weakness of South Vietnam, so that no Western tactics could have won) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the wrong tactics were chosen’ vs ‘no Western tactics could have succeeded’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about why US military tactics failed in Vietnam.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1985 history of US strategy that focuses on choices made in Washington and Saigon and treats Vietnam as a tactical case study, so foregrounds tactical alternatives such as clear-and-hold; Interpretation 2 is from a 2005 study of insurgency warfare with a comparative database of guerrilla conflicts, so reads Vietcong tactics, the Ho Chi Minh Trail and the rural illegitimacy of South Vietnam as structural conditions no Western tactic could overcome. The two have different focuses (US choices vs guerrilla war as a category) and use different bodies of evidence (US strategic archives vs comparative insurgency studies), and so reach different verdicts on whether better tactics could have won.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the reasons US military tactics failed in Vietnam?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across 1965-68 (Operation Rolling Thunder’s 643,000 tons of bombs and around 900 US aircraft lost; the failure to close the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia; Westmoreland’s search-and-destroy and the body-count metric; the 1967 Pentagon study finding around two new Vietcong recruits per one killed; Operation Ranch Hand’s 19 million gallons of herbicide and roughly 4.5 million defoliated acres; napalm and the political cost of civilian images; the Cu Chi tunnels and Vietcong integration with the peasant population), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 2. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 2. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From the testimony of a US infantry sergeant before a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on the conduct of the war, 1971.

‘We would go into a village in the morning. By midday we had taken three killed and four wounded from booby traps and small-arms fire we never saw. We never saw the men who fired on us. We saw farmers in the rice paddy and old women in the doorways and children running through the lanes. We could not tell who was Vietcong. The captain told us to count every body as VC. By evening we were back at base and the village was reported cleared. By morning the Vietcong walked back in. The next month a different company did the same operation in the same village.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the limits of US ground tactics in Vietnam.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘US troops could rarely identify the Vietcong they were fighting’ supported by ‘We never saw the men who fired on us’ or ‘We could not tell who was Vietcong’ AND ‘Search-and-destroy could not hold ground — clearings were temporary and had to be repeated’ supported by ‘By morning the Vietcong walked back in’ or ‘The next month a different company did the same operation in the same village’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the decline of the open-range cattle industry in the years 1876–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the patenting of barbed wire (1874)
• the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• Through the late 1870s and early 1880s the open range looked like easy money; British and eastern investors poured capital into Wyoming, Montana and Dakota herds, encouraged by refrigerated railcars and the London beef market.
• Because grass was treated as a free common resource, ranchers overstocked their ranges; by 1885 some Wyoming counties carried herds far above the land’s carrying capacity, and the dry summer of 1886 left grass thin going into winter.
• Because Joseph Glidden’s 1874 barbed wire patent had made cheap fencing possible, homesteaders were already enclosing claims across the Plains during the boom — reducing the open range available to drives and water access for the largest herds.
• Because the winter of 1886–87 brought blizzards and temperatures of around −40°C across the northern Plains, cattle drifted south, piled into draws and froze in such numbers that some ranches lost 90% of their stock and British investors pulled out within months.
• By 1890 the surviving ranchers had switched to smaller fenced ranches with hay-fed winters and higher-quality breeds; the era of long drives and unbranded mavericks was over, and the changed industry would soon collide with homesteaders and small ranchers in the Johnson County War of 1892.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1874, 1886–87, 1890), specialist vocabulary (open range, barbed wire, bonanza farm, maverick), both stimulus points covered and integrated with own knowledge.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 for the cattle industry of the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Die-Up killed 50–90% of cattle in some Wyoming and Montana herds, bankrupting many ranches and triggering the immediate withdrawal of British and eastern American investors who had funded the boom.
• Because surviving ranchers could not afford another such loss, the industry shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay cut in summer for winter feed — ending the open-range model.
• Because barbed wire (patented by Glidden in 1874) was already being used to enclose homestead claims, the post-Die-Up shift to enclosure was technically straightforward and accelerated rapidly.
• Because the long drive depended on continuous grass between Texas and the railheads, the move to smaller fenced ranches ended the long drive and the era of the unbranded maverick — every animal now had an owner.
• Because the Die-Up bankrupted small operators while leaving large incorporated ranches intact, it widened the gap between cattle barons and small ranchers that fed directly into the Johnson County War of April 1892.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (winter 1886–87, 50–90% losses, 1892) and specialist vocabulary (open range, barbed wire, maverick, range war).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Johnson County War (1892) for understanding law and order on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Johnson County War showed that, even thirty years into Wyoming’s settled frontier, large landowners could still hire 50 Texas gunmen to kill suspected rustlers and outrun the elected sheriff — the elected law could not restrain organised wealth.
• Because President Benjamin Harrison had to order the US Cavalry to break the siege at the TA Ranch, the war revealed that local law on the Plains still depended on federal force to function in extremis.
• Because the trial was packed with friendly jurors paid for by the Wyoming Stock Growers Association and every defendant was acquitted, the case showed how frontier court law could be bent by money and political connections.
• Because the state legislature, dominated by ranchers, blocked further investigation, the war demonstrated that the rise of statehood (Wyoming admitted 1890) had not by itself produced impartial law.
• Because the war became a national scandal — covered by eastern newspapers as a betrayal of frontier ideals — it strengthened the political case for federal grazing reform and the long-term curbing of the cattle barons’ influence.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (April 1892, 50 gunmen, Wyoming Stock Growers Association, Harrison) and specialist vocabulary (range war, packed jury, statehood).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how law and order on the late frontier was tested in the years 1878–1892.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the OK Corral (1881)
• the Johnson County War (1892)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1878 the Lincoln County War in New Mexico Territory pitted two rival merchant-rancher factions against one another; both sides used elected sheriffs and federal contracts as weapons, producing the conditions in which Henry McCarty — Billy the Kid — rose as an outlaw before Sheriff Pat Garrett killed him in 1881.
• Because Tombstone, Arizona, by 1881 had a silver-boom population of about 7,000 and rival rural cattle and town saloon interests, the friction between the Clantons and McLaurys and the Earp brothers exploded into the OK Corral gunfight on 26 October 1881 — thirty seconds of fire, three deaths, and two competing legal hearings that cleared the Earps.
• Because the law could not produce a clear verdict in feuds of that scale, frontier disputes increasingly depended on which side held the badge or the better-paid lawyers — even where formal courts were now in place.
• Because the Big Die-Up (1886–87) had bankrupted small operators while leaving large incorporated ranches intact, by the early 1890s Wyoming’s cattle barons faced rising homesteader fences and elected sheriffs they could no longer rely on.
• In April 1892 the Wyoming Stock Growers Association hired about 50 Texas gunmen to kill suspected rustlers in Johnson County; only US Cavalry intervention and a packed jury kept it from being a massacre, completing the story of how late-frontier law could still be bent by organised wealth even after statehood.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1878, 1881, 1886–87, April 1892), specialist vocabulary (range war, Stock Growers Association, town marshal), both stimulus points covered.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of barbed wire for the development of farming and ranching on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Joseph Glidden’s 1874 patent made fencing the Plains affordable for the first time — cheaper and faster than wood or stone in a region with neither — which let homesteaders enclose 160-acre claims they could not otherwise have defended.
• Because barbed wire enclosed homestead claims, it began separating farming from ranching on what had been continuous open grass; the open-range cattle model was already under pressure before the Big Die-Up.
• Because barbed wire could exclude cattle from rivers and waterholes, it shifted bargaining power towards homesteaders and small ranchers who could now block the long drive and the open-range herd from key water sources.
• Because barbed wire made the smaller, fenced ranch viable, after the 1886–87 winter ranchers could enclose hay meadows and rebuild on a model that did not depend on free grass.
• Because barbed wire reduced the value of unbranded mavericks (every animal on a fenced ranch had an owner), it changed the economics of cattle theft and helped trigger the cattle-baron political backlash that ended in the Johnson County War of 1892.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1874 patent, 160-acre homestead, 1886–87, 1892) and specialist vocabulary (open range, maverick, range war).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 for the cattle industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the Die-Up to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that surviving ranchers shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay-fed winters and higher-quality breeds — the open range and the long drive ended within a few years.
• Another consequence was that British and eastern American investors withdrew their capital from the cattle industry, ending the speculative boom that had drawn outside money onto the open Plains during the early 1880s.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named feature (e.g. fenced ranching, withdrawal of investment).
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Caribbean cafes and restaurants in Notting Hill in the 1950s and 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• They were small, family-run businesses serving Caribbean food that mainstream London restaurants did not cook.
• They served late-night customers such as taxi drivers and shift workers, because London pubs closed at 11pm and the colour bar shut Black customers out of many venues.
• They acted as community meeting places: Frank Crichlow's El Rio on Westbourne Park Road, and later his Mangrove Restaurant on All Saints Road.
• They clustered around Portobello Road and All Saints Road, producing a visible Caribbean high street.
• They depended on the Caribbean grocers of Portobello Road for ingredients that mainstream shops did not stock.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of pardner schemes used by Caribbean households in Notting Hill.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• They were rotating-credit savings clubs: roughly twelve to twenty trusted members each paid in a fixed sum every week and one took the whole pot in turn.
• They ran on community trust alone, with no contracts and no legal remedy if a member defaulted.
• They replaced the banking system, which would not open accounts for or lend to Caribbean migrants in the 1950s.
• They funded specific goals: a deposit on a house, a family fare from the Caribbean, the rent on a shop, or a sound system.
• They were managed by a banker, a trusted neighbour who collected the weekly payments and held the pot until handover day.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Sources A and B.

Source A: From an oral history interview recorded in 1961 for an inner-London local history project. The speaker, a Caribbean shopkeeper who opened a grocery on Portobello Road in 1955, says: 'I came to Notting Hill in 1953. The bank wouldn't take my money, the pubs wouldn't take my custom, the landlord wouldn't take my reference. So we made our own - pardner for the deposit, friends for the labour, my wife for the till. By 1959 we had two shops.'

Source B: From an article in a west London community newspaper, 1962, on saving clubs among Caribbean families. 'Twelve of us pay in every Friday and one of us draws the hand. There are no forms and no manager. That is how the corner shop was paid for, and how my sister's fare from Kingston was found.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into Caribbean self-help in Notting Hill in the 1950s and early 1960s?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 8 marks for an answer that weighs content, provenance and own knowledge for both sources against the stated enquiry.

Indicative content:
• Content of A: names the three exclusions Caribbean migrants met - banks, pubs and landlords - and names the pardner scheme as the source of the shop deposit.
• Content of A: tracks one shop in 1955 becoming two by 1959, which shows how parallel institutions could compound.
• Content of B: sets out how a pardner actually worked, week by week, and what it paid for.
• Provenance of A: a first-person account recorded six years after the events, for a project whose interviewer was probably sympathetic; it is one man's memory, not a measure of scale.
• Provenance of B: a community newspaper wrote for the community it described, so it is close to the practice but not a neutral observer of it.
• Own knowledge: high-street banks would not open accounts for Caribbean migrants, which is exactly why pardner schemes spread across Notting Hill.
• Own knowledge: Caribbean grocers reshaped Portobello Road from the early 1950s, and Ruth Glass's 1960 study Newcomers recorded similar household histories.

Mastering: Content, provenance and own knowledge weighed for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Both sources used, with two of the three strands developed and a judgement reached.
Developing: The sources are described rather than weighed; provenance is noted but not linked to usefulness.
Emerging: One source described, with little or no own knowledge.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Source B.

Source B: From an article in a west London community newspaper, 1962, on saving clubs among Caribbean families. 'Twelve of us pay in every Friday and one of us draws the hand. There are no forms and no manager. That is how the corner shop was paid for, and how my sister's fare from Kingston was found.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about how Caribbean families in Notting Hill financed their businesses?

In your answer, you must give the question you would ask and the type of source you could use.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — How Could You Follow Up
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks for a coherent chain: a detail in the source, the question that detail raises, and a type of source that could answer it.

Indicative content (any one, fully developed):
• Detail: 'that is how the corner shop was paid for'. Question: how many Caribbean-owned businesses opened around Portobello Road and All Saints Road between 1955 and 1965? Source type: local trade directories for the borough, checked against oral history collections held by Black community archives.
• Detail: 'there are no forms and no manager'. Question: how far did London banks refuse accounts to Caribbean customers in the 1950s? Source type: bank branch records for west London, and the case files of organisations that took up complaints of discrimination.
• Detail: 'my sister's fare from Kingston'. Question: how many Caribbean families used pooled savings to bring relatives to Britain? Source type: shipping passenger lists alongside recorded interviews with Caribbean families in London.

Mastering: A coherent chain — a specific detail picked out, a precise question, and a type of source that could realistically answer it.
Secure: Detail and question are sensible; the source type is named but generic.
Developing: The detail or the question is vague; the source type is generic.
Emerging: No clear chain from the source to an enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of shebeens and blues dances in Notting Hill in the 1950s and 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• A shebeen was an unlicensed late-night club, usually run from a basement flat or back room.
• They served Caribbean food, rum and music to a Caribbean clientele after the pubs had closed at 11pm.
• Many hosted blues dances, with sound systems playing ska, rocksteady, American rhythm and blues, and later reggae.
• They existed because most pubs around Notting Hill would not serve Black customers, so social life moved indoors and underground.
• Being unlicensed made them a standing target for Metropolitan Police licensing and drugs raids, which fed the policing tensions of the late 1960s.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

Study Source A.

Source A: From an oral history interview recorded in 1961 for an inner-London local history project. The speaker, a Caribbean shopkeeper who opened a grocery on Portobello Road in 1955, says: 'I came to Notting Hill in 1953. The bank wouldn't take my money, the pubs wouldn't take my custom, the landlord wouldn't take my reference. So we made our own - pardner for the deposit, friends for the labour, my wife for the till. By 1959 we had two shops.'

How could you follow up Source A to find out more about the colour bar in Notting Hill in the 1950s?

In your answer, you must give the question you would ask and the type of source you could use.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — How Could You Follow Up
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks for a coherent chain: a detail in the source, the question that detail raises, and a type of source that could answer it.

Indicative content (any one, fully developed):

• Detail: 'the bank wouldn't take my money'. Question: did any London bank open accounts for Caribbean customers before 1960? Source type: bank branch records and the correspondence of organisations that campaigned against the colour bar.

Mastering: A coherent chain — a specific detail picked out, a precise question, and a type of source that could realistically answer it.
Secure: Detail and question are sensible; the source type is named but generic.
Developing: The detail or the question is vague; the source type is generic.
Emerging: No clear chain from the source to an enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of American independence for the institution of slavery in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly identified consequences each with supporting detail. For example: independence led directly to a wave of Northern abolition laws — Vermont (1777), Pennsylvania’s Gradual Abolition Act (1780) and the Massachusetts court rulings (1781–83) — that began to divide the new republic into free and slave states; it also led to the 1787 Constitution’s three-fifths clause, which counted three out of every five enslaved people for representation, giving slaveholding states extra political weight in Congress while granting the enslaved no rights at all. Equal attention to both with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences identified, each with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to abolition laws or the Constitution.
Emerging: Notes that slavery existed without showing how independence shaped it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of American independence for the position of Indigenous peoples in North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to clearly identified developments. For example: independence mattered because the Peace of Paris of 1783 ceded territory east of the Mississippi to the United States without consulting the Indigenous nations who lived there, removing the protection that the 1763 Proclamation Line had offered; it also mattered because the new United States treated Indigenous peoples as a defeated people whose lands were forfeit, extracting cessions through treaties under duress at Fort Stanwix (1784) and Fort McIntosh (1785). A third anchor might be the migration of Joseph Brant’s Mohawks to the Haldimand Tract in the Niagara region. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: Importance explained with relevant detail and at least two developments identified.
Developing: General claim of importance without sustained focus.
Emerging: Mentions Indigenous peoples without explaining how independence affected them.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the war for the Loyalists.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two specific consequences with development. For example: state Confiscation Acts after the war seized Loyalist estates with little prospect of restitution despite the Peace of Paris recommending it, driving around 60,000 to 80,000 colonists into exile; resettlement schemes carried around 30,000 white Loyalists and 3,000 Black Loyalists to Nova Scotia, with New Brunswick carved out as a separate colony in 1784 to accommodate them and the Niagara peninsula receiving others under what became Upper Canada in 1791. Each developed with explicit causal verbs.
Secure: Two consequences with at least one supporting detail each.
Developing: Two general consequences without specific reference to confiscation or resettlement.
Emerging: Mentions Loyalists without showing consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Black Loyalists for the post-war settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance shown in relation to identified developments. For example: the Black Loyalists mattered because tens of thousands of enslaved people had run to British lines after Dunmore’s 1775 proclamation and Clinton’s 1779 Philipsburg Proclamation, the largest single act of resistance to slavery in colonial America; their evacuation in the 1783 Book of Negroes mattered because around 3,000 free Black Loyalists were carried to Nova Scotia, where their experience of inferior land grants and the 1784 Shelburne riot drove around 1,200 of them to migrate under Thomas Peters in 1792 to found Freetown in Sierra Leone — one of the first organised returns to Africa by people of African descent. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions Black Loyalists without showing the wider significance.
Emerging: General references to enslaved people without specific examples.

practice_questions.text:
Write an analytical narrative explaining how the war shaped the lives of enslaved people, Indigenous peoples and Loyalists in the years 1775–83. You may use the following information in your answer:
• Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation (1775)
• The Haldimand Tract
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses connections between events using causation and consequence; explains how each group’s experience flowed from specific decisions rather than narrating in sequence. Links Dunmore’s 1775 proclamation and Clinton’s 1779 Philipsburg Proclamation to the flight of tens of thousands of enslaved people and the Black Loyalist evacuation of 1783; links the Iroquois split, Joseph Brant’s alliance with Britain, and the post-war Haldimand Tract to the dispossession of Indigenous nations on the American side of the new border; brings in own knowledge such as the Confiscation Acts, the three-fifths clause, the Loyalist Claims Commission, or the Vermont and Pennsylvania abolition laws. Reaches an analytical judgement about who actually won.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical links between events; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Mostly chronological description with limited analysis.
Emerging: Lists groups without explaining how the war shaped their experience.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the 1787 United States Constitution for the future of slavery in the new republic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Importance anchored to identified developments. For example: the three-fifths clause mattered because it counted three out of every five enslaved people for representation in Congress, giving the slaveholding states a permanent political bonus that protected slavery from federal abolition; the 1808 slave-trade clause mattered because it forbade Congress from ending the transatlantic slave trade for twenty years, allowing tens of thousands more Africans to be enslaved before the door closed. A third anchor might be the contrast with the Northern abolition laws of the same period, which made the Constitution’s pro-slavery provisions a regional fault line that the Civil War would eventually fight over. Specific anchors developed.
Secure: At least two developments explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Mentions the Constitution without showing how it shaped slavery.
Emerging: General references to slavery without specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the role of the Little Red Book in Chinese daily life during the late 1960s. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail (e.g. soldiers reading the book at morning study sessions, workers raising it at ‘asking instructions’ rituals, Red Guards waving it at Tiananmen rallies). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that the book was used to structure daily routine and produce visible loyalty, or that political ritual had absorbed activities once shaped by family or religion. [4]
Secure: Two supported inferences with one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the cult of Mao reached its peak between 1966 and 1969.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Little Red Book
• the Red Guards and the Tiananmen rallies
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. Lin Biao’s deliberate construction of the cult inside the PLA from 1964, the propaganda template established by the Lei Feng campaign in 1963, the launch of the Cultural Revolution in May 1966 which removed CCP rivals (Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping) who might have moderated the cult, the mass mobilisation of Red Guards at the eight Tiananmen rallies (August–November 1966), and Mao’s own use of the cult to bypass the party hierarchy. Uses stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative of the cult without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the importance of propaganda in maintaining Communist control over China.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues that propaganda worked because the regime imposed it through loudspeakers, censorship and forced ritual; the other argues that propaganda worked because much of it was genuinely internalised, especially by younger Chinese). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the cult of Mao.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (revisionists like Frank Dikötter writing after PRC archives opened in the 1990s vs sympathetic accounts like Mobo Gao’s village-level oral histories), used different evidence (state propaganda material vs personal memoir and survivor testimony), or had different purposes (holding Mao personally responsible vs reassessing the era’s real social gains). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the laogai ‘Reform Through Labour’ system in maintaining Communist control?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the formalisation of laogai in 1951, the camps’ mixing of political and criminal prisoners, the economic role of forced labour in Qinghai and Xinjiang, the silencing effect of the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign that fed the camps, alongside alternative explanations of control such as propaganda saturation, the danwei work unit, the personal dossier, and the cult of Mao. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the cult of Mao was the most important reason the CCP maintained control over Chinese society between 1949 and 1976?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — Lin Biao’s 1964 Little Red Book, the 12 million Red Guards at the eight Tiananmen rallies, the Lei Feng campaign of 1963, Jiang Qing’s eight model operas, alongside alternative mechanisms such as laogai, danwei surveillance, the dossier, the Ministry of Culture and the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign. Engages with the historiographical debate (Dikötter and MacFarquhar on top-down construction; Mobo Gao on internalisation and genuine social gains). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (laogai, danwei, dossier, four olds, struggle session). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Oslo Accords (1993) for the Palestinian issue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Israel formally recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people for the first time, ending decades of refusal to deal with it; the establishment of the Palestinian National Authority in May 1994 created the first Palestinian self-governing body since 1948 and brought Arafat back to Gaza in July 1994; the deferral of final-status issues (refugees, Jerusalem, settlements, borders) meant Oslo did not deliver a Palestinian state and left every later flare-up rooted in disputes the agreement deliberately did not settle. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions Oslo without showing why it mattered for the Palestinian issue. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the end of the Cold War for peacemaking in the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. Syria and other rejectionist Arab states lost their Soviet patron and political cover, removing the alternative on which decades of refusal to negotiate had rested; the United States entered a ‘unipolar moment’ in which it could co-host the Madrid Conference of October 1991 without a Soviet veto, bringing Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and a Palestinian delegation to one table for the first time; without these conditions the bilateral tracks that produced the Oslo Declaration of Principles in 1993 and the Israel-Jordan peace treaty in 1994 would not have been politically possible. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the Cold War ending without showing why it mattered for peacemaking. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Gulf War (1991) for changing superpower policies in the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific consequences explained, e.g. UN Resolution 678 produced a thirty-five-state coalition that included Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Morocco alongside the NATO allies, demonstrating that Arab states would now accept US-led action against another Arab state — a Cold War impossibility; Israeli restraint under Scud bombardment, achieved by US Patriot deployment, gave the Bush and Clinton administrations a political debt they used in 1991–93 to push Israel into the Madrid and Oslo tracks; Arafat’s alignment with Saddam cost the PLO its Gulf state funding and forced it to negotiate from weakness. Distinguishes immediate from longer-term effects. [7–8]
Secure: Two or three consequences explained with relevant period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Identifies relevant facts but explanation is descriptive. [3–4]
Emerging: Mentions the Gulf War without showing why it mattered for superpower policy. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of Arafat’s support for Iraq during the 1990–91 Gulf crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the Gulf Cooperation Council ended their financial backing for the PLO and Kuwait expelled around 350,000 Palestinian guest workers after liberation, costing the PLO an estimated $300 million a year and a major source of remittance income; (ii) the financial squeeze, combined with the political damage of being on the losing side, made Arafat far more willing by 1992–93 to accept a deal he would have rejected in 1989, opening the door to the Oslo back-channel. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Arafat backed Saddam without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin (November 1995).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed consequences. For example: (i) it removed the Israeli politician most strongly identified with the Oslo process at the moment when implementation was most fragile, depriving the agreement of its main domestic Israeli champion; (ii) Shimon Peres lost the 1996 election by a fraction of a percent to Benjamin Netanyahu, who had campaigned against Oslo; the political momentum behind the Accords largely ended in 1995–96, even though the legal framework remained in place. [7–8]
Secure: Two consequences identified, both explained but unevenly. [5–6]
Developing: One supported consequence and a second that is closer to description. [3–4]
Emerging: Restates that Rabin was killed without analysing the effects. [1–2]

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the road from the end of the Cold War to the Oslo Accords in the years 1989–93.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Gulf War (1991)
• the Madrid Conference (1991)
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A coherent analytical narrative covering at least three aspects (e.g. the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the loss of Arab rejectionism’s patron; the Gulf War coalition and the PLO’s loss of Gulf funding; the Madrid Conference’s bilateral tracks; Rabin’s 1992 election win; the Norwegian back-channel and the September 1993 Declaration of Principles). Uses both stimulus points and adds independent material such as the mutual-recognition letters or the ‘unipolar moment’. Connects events through causation rather than sequencing. [7–8]
Secure: Three aspects addressed with clear analytical links; uses both stimulus points; some period detail. [5–6]
Developing: Covers the period but leans heavily on the stimulus and addresses fewer than three aspects (capped at this band per the cap rule). [3–4]
Emerging: A descriptive sequence with little or no analysis of how events connected. [1–2]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Black Saturday raid on London on 7 September 1940.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Around 350 German bombers, escorted by some 600 fighters, crossed the Kent coast on the afternoon of 7 September 1940 and attacked the Royal Docks and East End riverside.
• The first wave used incendiary bombs to set the docks and warehouses on fire so that a second wave of bombers could be guided in through the night by the glow on the Thames.
• The raid killed around 430 Londoners and seriously injured around 1,600 in a single night, with the heaviest losses in Silvertown, Canning Town and West Ham.
• It opened the Blitz: 57 consecutive nights of bombing followed, with raids continuing on London until May 1941.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to bombing without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the V1 and V2 weapons used against London in 1944–45.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• The V1 was a pulse-jet flying bomb that arrived from June 1944, launched from ramps in northern France; its engine made a buzzing sound that earned it the nickname ‘doodlebug’, and it could be shot down by RAF fighters, anti-aircraft guns and barrage balloons.
• The V2, first launched on London on 8 September 1944, was the world’s first ballistic missile, travelling faster than the speed of sound so it gave no warning of its approach.
• Around 6,000 Londoners were killed by V1s in summer 1944 and a further 2,700 by V2s, with V2 launch sites finally captured in the Netherlands by April 1945.
• The most lethal single V2 strike on London hit the Woolworth’s store in New Cross Road, Deptford on 25 November 1944, killing 168 shoppers and staff in seconds.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to V-weapons without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: Sources A and B below are composed for practice. They are not real archive documents; in the exam you are given two genuine sources.

Source A: a photograph taken on the night of 7 September 1940 from the south bank of the Thames. Warehouses along the Surrey Docks are burning from end to end and the river is lit by the flames. Two firemen play a single hose on a wall of fire.

Source B: the diary of an ARP warden in Stepney, written on the night of 7–8 September 1940.
‘The river is on fire from the docks down to the Tower. We have lost two streets in Limehouse already and Bow Common has gone — not damaged, gone. The first lot dropped firesticks; while we were running for the buckets, the heavy stuff started. The fire crews can’t get through — mains are split everywhere. People are walking out west with prams. I do not see how we can do this every night.’

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the impact of Black Saturday on the East End of London?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Weigh both sources together: what each one says, who made it and why, and what you know about the context.

Indicative content:
• Source A shows the scale of the dock fires and how few crews there were to fight them; the glow on the river is what guided the second wave of bombers in.
• A photograph taken at night shows one stretch of river only, and pictures like this were often taken for official use, so it cannot show the streets behind the docks.
• Source B confirms the two-stage tactic — ‘firesticks’ first, then ‘the heavy stuff’ — and shows that broken water mains crippled fire-fighting from the start.
• Source B also captures street-level loss (‘Bow Common has gone’), the first movement of people out of the East End, and strain on a warden’s own morale.
• A warden’s diary is a private record by someone who was there, so it is not curated propaganda, but it covers one sector on one night only.
• Context to bring in: around 350 bombers attacked on 7 September 1940, about 430 people were killed and 1,600 seriously injured, and Stepney lost more than 40 per cent of its housing across the Blitz.

Mastering: Both sources judged on content and on who made them and why, supported by precise contextual knowledge, with a clear verdict on usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Both sources considered, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: Simple comments on what the sources show; provenance or context is thin.
Emerging: Describes the sources without judging their usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B again.

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about what happened to East End families made homeless on Black Saturday?

Give the detail in Source B you would follow up, the question you would ask, the type of source you could use, and how it would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Give a coherent chain: a detail in Source B, the question it raises, the type of source you could use, and how that source would help.

Indicative example:
• Detail in Source B: ‘People are walking out west with prams’ on the first night of the Blitz.
• Question: how many East End families left their homes after Black Saturday, and where did they go?
• Type of source: borough Civil Defence and rest-centre returns for September and October 1940.
• How it helps: these were compiled daily for officials to act on, so they record numbers of homeless people and billeting requests that a diary cannot give.

Other chains are equally creditable, for example following up the split water mains, the incendiary clusters or the warden’s doubts about morale, using fire-brigade records, a local newspaper such as the East London Advertiser, or oral-history recordings of East Enders.

Mastering: All four steps clear, with the source type matched to the question.
Secure: A sound question and source type, briefly explained.
Developing: A question or a source type given, but the link to Source B is weak.
Emerging: A source type or question suggested that is not grounded in Source B.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Second World War had a greater impact on British civilians than the First World War.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the bombing of London
• conscription and the Home Front.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments that the Second World War affected civilians more:
• Bombing made civilians targets: around 20,000 Londoners were killed in the Blitz of 1940–41 and roughly 1.4 million were made homeless at some point.
• Black Saturday on 7 September 1940 opened 57 consecutive nights of raids on the capital.
• The V1 from June 1944 and the supersonic V2 from September 1944 killed thousands more and reached boroughs that had escaped in 1940–41.
• Civilians were organised as well as attacked: evacuation, gas masks, shelters, the blackout, rationing and Dig for Victory reached every household.
• Conscription applied to women for the first time from December 1941.

Indicative content — arguments for the First World War, or for continuity:
• The First World War introduced conscription in 1916 and took men from almost every family, with casualty lists that reached every street.
• Zeppelin and Gotha raids had already brought bombing to British towns before 1918, so the principle was not new in 1940.
• Rationing, censorship and government control of industry began in the First World War and were rebuilt, not invented, in 1939.
• Civilians in earlier centuries suffered heavily too, through purveyance, billeting and free quarter, so the twentieth century is a change of scale rather than of kind.
• The Second World War Home Front was better organised, so some effects were softened as well as widened.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that compares the two wars and reaches back into earlier periods where useful, with accurate detail (Black Saturday, V-weapons, conscription, rationing) and a clear judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One war dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the German bombing of the East End docks in 1940–41.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Raids were aimed at the Royal Albert, Royal Victoria, King George V and Surrey docks, which handled food, oil, timber and munitions.
• Bombers dropped incendiaries first so that the fires would guide the night waves in by the glow on the Thames, then high explosives to wreck buildings and water mains.
• The industry around the docks was also targeted: Tate & Lyle’s sugar refinery, gasometers, chemical works and ship-repair yards in Silvertown and Canning Town.
• Because dockers and factory workers lived beside their work, terraced housing in Stepney, Bethnal Green, Poplar and West Ham was destroyed with the targets.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to bombing without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the discovery of silver at Potosi (1545) and Zacatecas (1546).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8. 1–2 marks for identifying a relevant consequence; further marks for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Spain became the financial superpower of 16th-century Europe. Potosi alone produced roughly 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the century, with the crown taking a 20% royal fifth (quinto real).
• The foundation of La Paz in 1548 as a stopover on the silver road from Potosi to the Pacific coast reorganised Andean geography around extraction.
• Indigenous labour conditions worsened. The mita system — formalised from 1573 but rooted in this period’s encomienda labour — sent one in seven Andean men into the mines for four months a year with appalling mortality.
• Silver flooding into Europe drove a century of inflation — the price revolution — which actually hollowed out Spanish manufacturing rather than enriching ordinary Spaniards.
• The crown’s share of silver went largely to German bankers (the Fuggers) to service Charles V’s European war debts, deepening Spain’s long-term dependence on extraction.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on silver without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the asiento system (from 1518) for the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 8.

Indicative content (any two):
• It legally formalised the Atlantic shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas, creating the contractual framework that would underwrite three centuries of the transatlantic slave trade.
• It supplied labour for the early Caribbean sugar plantations, the silver mines and urban Spanish households — partially replacing the collapsing Indigenous Caribbean population.
• It exposed a moral inconsistency in Spanish reform: the New Laws of 1542 banned the outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples but did not extend the same protection to enslaved Africans — an inconsistency Las Casas himself eventually came to regret.
• It bound Spain’s American economy into Atlantic networks of trade, finance and migration that would shape European colonial economies for the next two centuries.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on the slave trade without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of silver from the ‘New World’ for the Spanish Empire in the period 1545–c1555.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of silver, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Silver from Potosi (1545) and Zacatecas (1546) made Spain the financial superpower of 16th-century Europe. Potosi alone produced about 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the century.
• The crown’s 20% tax (the quinto real) on every ounce mined became the biggest single source of royal revenue, financing Charles V’s wars in Italy, Germany, the Mediterranean and the Netherlands.
• Silver flowed almost as fast as it arrived to the Fugger banking family of Augsburg, who had financed Charles V’s election as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. Spain’s European wars were paid for by Andean miners.
• Silver flooding into Europe drove the price revolution — a century of inflation that actually weakened Spanish manufacturing because Spanish goods became uncompetitive abroad.
• The human cost was extracted from Indigenous Andeans through forced labour rotas (which would be formalised as the mita from 1573), and from enslaved Africans shipped in under the asiento system.
• The historiographical move (J.H. Elliott) is that silver made Spain powerful and dependent at the same time — the empire was a great-power machine, not a national prosperity machine.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Potosi, the quinto, the Fuggers, the price revolution, the mita).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of silver mining without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Council of the Indies (1524) and the Casa de Contratacion (1503) for the government of the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of these two bodies, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The Council of the Indies (founded 1524) was the supreme governing body for Spanish America. It issued laws, appointed viceroys and audiencia judges, supervised colonial finances and heard final appeals — centralising authority over a continent at the Spanish court.
• The Casa de Contratacion (founded 1503) was the House of Trade in Seville. It regulated all shipping, trade, taxation, navigation and migration between Spain and the Americas. Every ship, passenger and ounce of silver was supposed to be registered there.
• Together the two bodies created the most centralised European colonial bureaucracy of the 16th century — quite unlike the personal rule of Cortes or Pizarro that they replaced.
• They allowed the Crown to enforce key reforms at scale, including the New Laws of 1542 and the assignment of viceroys to New Spain (1535) and Peru (1542).
• They were also slow, paper-heavy and limited by distance — orders from Seville often took months to reach Lima — explaining why the 1546 Peru rebellion succeeded for several years before being broken.
• The architecture endured: Latin American government and law would still be running on Spanish institutional templates two and a half centuries later.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (foundation dates, link to viceroyalties, link to the New Laws, the limits of distance).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the bodies without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of enslaved African labour for the Spanish Empire in the period c1518–c1555.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of enslaved African labour, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• From 1518 the asiento system licensed the shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas, creating the legal framework that would underwrite three centuries of the transatlantic slave trade.
• Enslaved Africans worked in the silver mines, on the early Caribbean sugar plantations and as urban servants — supplying labour as Indigenous Caribbean populations collapsed under disease and forced labour.
• African labour partially replaced the Tainos in Hispaniola and Cuba; by mid-century the demographic shift in the Caribbean was already underway.
• The asiento bound Spain’s American economy into Atlantic networks of trade and finance that would shape European colonial economies for the next two centuries.
• It also exposed the moral limits of the New Laws (1542): the laws banned enslavement of Indigenous peoples but not of Africans — an inconsistency that Las Casas eventually came to regret in his old age.
• Numbers in the period 1518–55 were small compared to the later trade, but the legal structures, shipping routes and contractual templates that would later move millions of enslaved Africans were now in place.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (asiento, the Caribbean shift, the moral limits of the New Laws, the link forward to later centuries).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the slave trade without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the ‘New World’ transformed the Spanish economy in the years 1503–c1555. You may use the following in your answer: the foundation of the Casa de Contratacion (1503), the discovery of silver at Potosi (1545). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1503 the crown founded the Casa de Contratacion in Seville to regulate all shipping, trade, taxation and migration to the Americas. This created the institutional framework for transatlantic commerce that would later channel a flood of bullion.
• In 1518 the first asiento licences began the legalised shipping of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean, supplying plantation and household labour as the Taino population collapsed.
• In 1521 the conquest of Tenochtitlan and the encomiendas Cortes granted there created a tribute economy that fed Spanish settlers from Indigenous labour without paying for it.
• This in turn drew Spanish settlers and capital across the Atlantic in greater numbers, supporting the further conquests of Peru (1532–33) and the foundation of Lima (1535).
• Because of this expansion, the discovery of silver at Potosi in 1545 had a system ready to move and tax it: mule trains down to the Pacific coast, ships to Panama, treasure fleets across the Caribbean to Seville, the quinto real recorded by the Casa de Contratacion.
• This in turn flooded Europe with silver, fuelling Charles V’s wars, enriching the Fugger bankers, but driving the price revolution that hollowed out Spanish manufacturing — making the empire both more powerful and more dependent.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (asientos, Tenochtitlan, Lima, the Fuggers).
