Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Notting Hill riots of August–September 1958.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• The attacks were largely white-led: crowds of up to 400 men, including teddy boys travelling in from outside, attacked Caribbean homes around Bramley Road and Latimer Road.
• The violence ran night after night from 29 August to 5 September 1958, with iron bars, knives, milk bottles and homemade petrol bombs.
• Around 140 people were arrested, and nine white men were each given five years in prison and a £500 order by Mr Justice Salmon.
• Caribbean residents organised defence committees to protect homes; their action was reactive rather than a coordinated counter-attack.
• Metropolitan Police files released in 2002 show senior officers telling the Home Secretary there was little racial motive, against the evidence of individual officers.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Sources A and B.

Source A: From a report in a London daily newspaper, 3 September 1958. 'For the fourth night running, crowds gathered in the Bramley Road area. Bottles and iron bars were thrown at houses known to be occupied by West Indian families. Police made further arrests in the early hours.'

Source B: From a recorded interview with a Caribbean resident of Notting Hill, made in 1988, remembering the summer of 1958. 'We stopped going out after dark. The men took it in turns to sit up at the front window with the light off. The police came, but they came late, and when they came they asked us what we had done to bring it on ourselves.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the 1958 attacks on Caribbean homes in Notting Hill?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 8 marks for an answer that weighs content, provenance and own knowledge for both sources against the stated enquiry.

Indicative content:
• Content of A: names the Bramley Road area, describes crowds and weapons, and confirms the attacks ran for successive nights.
• Content of B: gives the experience from inside a Caribbean household, including the defence watch at the window and the response of the police.
• Provenance of A: a newspaper report written during the disturbances is close to events but relies on what reporters and police said at the time.
• Provenance of B: an interview recorded thirty years later carries the weight of lived experience but also of hindsight and selective memory.
• Own knowledge: the attacks ran from 29 August to 5 September 1958, with crowds of up to 400 men, many travelling in from outside the area.
• Own knowledge: around 140 people were arrested and nine white men were each given five years and a £500 order by Mr Justice Salmon.
• Own knowledge: Metropolitan Police files released in 2002 show senior officers telling the Home Secretary there was little racial motive, which supports Source B's account of how residents were treated.

Mastering: Content, provenance and own knowledge weighed for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Both sources used, with two of the three strands developed and a judgement reached.
Developing: The sources are described rather than weighed; provenance is noted but not linked to usefulness.
Emerging: One source described, with little or no own knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Oswald Mosley’s 1959 election campaign in North Kensington.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Mosley stood as the Union Movement candidate in North Kensington, the constituency that covered most of Notting Hill.
• His platform called for the compulsory repatriation of Black and Caribbean residents and a ban on further Commonwealth migration.
• He campaigned door to door across Notting Hill and addressed public meetings that drew audiences in the hundreds.
• He took 2,821 votes, around 8% of the total, at the October 1959 general election, finishing fourth of four and losing his deposit.
• The result was far higher than commentators had predicted, in a seat Labour held by only 877 votes.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Source B.

Source B: From a recorded interview with a Caribbean resident of Notting Hill, made in 1988, remembering the summer of 1958. 'We stopped going out after dark. The men took it in turns to sit up at the front window with the light off. The police came, but they came late, and when they came they asked us what we had done to bring it on ourselves.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about how the police responded to the 1958 attacks?

In your answer, you must give the question you would ask and the type of source you could use.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — How Could You Follow Up
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks for a coherent chain: a detail in the source, the question that detail raises, and a type of source that could answer it.

Indicative content (any one, fully developed):
• Detail: 'they came late'. Question: how quickly did police reach the streets under attack on each night? Source type: Metropolitan Police divisional occurrence books and duty records for the district, released to the National Archives.
• Detail: 'what we had done to bring it on ourselves'. Question: how did senior officers describe the cause of the disturbances at the time? Source type: the Home Office and Metropolitan Police correspondence released in 2002, including the advice given to the Home Secretary.
• Detail: 'the men took it in turns to sit up at the front window'. Question: how organised were the Caribbean defence committees? Source type: contemporary reports in Black newspapers, and recorded interviews with residents held in community archives.

Mastering: A coherent chain — a specific detail picked out, a precise question, and a type of source that could realistically answer it.
Secure: Detail and question are sensible; the source type is named but generic.
Developing: The detail or the question is vague; the source type is generic.
Emerging: No clear chain from the source to an enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the policing of Caribbean Notting Hill in the 1960s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Metropolitan Police used the sus law, the 1824 Vagrancy Act offence of being a suspected person loitering with intent, against young Black men without any complaint of an actual offence.
• Caribbean cafes, shebeens and, from 1968, the Mangrove Restaurant on All Saints Road were repeatedly raided on drugs warrants that produced no evidence.
• The unsolved murder of Kelso Cochrane in May 1959 left a standing grievance, since the killing was widely understood as racist and no one was charged.
• Each raid was officially routine, but the cumulative effect was a force that treated residents as suspects rather than as the public it served.
• The pattern led directly to the protest march of 9 August 1970 and the Mangrove Nine trial of 1971.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the murder of Kelso Cochrane and the response to it in Notting Hill.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Kelso Cochrane, a 32-year-old Antiguan carpenter, was attacked by a group of white youths near the junction of Southam Street and Golborne Road in the early hours of 17 May 1959 and died in hospital.
• The murder came nine months after the 1958 attacks and was widely understood at the time as a racist killing.
• The Metropolitan Police investigated for months but no one was ever charged, and the case remains formally unsolved.
• His funeral procession on 6 June 1959 drew around 1,200 mourners and was the largest the area had seen.
• Caribbean leaders, including those around the West Indian Gazette, used the funeral and the press coverage to demand stronger anti-discrimination law.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. Defense Secretary Clark Clifford advising President Johnson on the Tet Offensive, March 1968.

‘The Tet Offensive cannot be read as a military defeat for the United States. Vietcong losses are catastrophic and the urban territory briefly seized has been almost wholly recovered, including Hue. The political effect, however, has been the reverse. The American people had been told the enemy was on the verge of collapse. They have now seen Vietcong soldiers in the grounds of the embassy in Saigon and house-to-house fighting in a city most had never heard of. We must assume that another six months of escalation is not politically available to us.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the impact of the Tet Offensive.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Senior US officials judged Tet a tactical victory’ supported by ‘Vietcong losses are catastrophic’ or ‘urban territory briefly seized has been almost wholly recovered’ AND ‘Tet had broken the political case for further military escalation’ supported by ‘another six months of escalation is not politically available to us’ or ‘The American people had been told the enemy was on the verge of collapse’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Tet Offensive shifted American public opinion against the Vietnam War in 1968.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Walter Cronkite’s broadcast (27 February 1968)
• the fighting in Hue

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the credibility gap and Westmoreland’s November 1967 ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line; the Vietcong commando raid on the US embassy in Saigon; Johnson’s 31 March 1968 withdrawal; the wider role of TV coverage and the draft system) and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The argument connects the gap between official optimism and televised reality to the changing balance of US public opinion through 1968. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of Tet without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1990 history of the American media in Vietnam):
‘The Tet Offensive was a defeat for the United States because the public believed it was. Walter Cronkite’s broadcast of 27 February 1968 told a country that the war would ‘end in stalemate’, and within five weeks Johnson had withdrawn from the presidential race. Tet was, above all, a media event — a contradiction of the ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line that the political class could not survive.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2005 study of US military operations in Vietnam):
‘The Tet Offensive was a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory of the first order. Around 40,000 Vietcong fighters died; the southern uprising Hanoi expected did not occur; Hue was recaptured after twenty-five days of urban fighting. The Vietcong were so depleted that the North Vietnamese Army carried the rest of the war. To call Tet a US defeat is to mistake the political reaction in Washington for the military reality in South Vietnam.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the Tet Offensive? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees Tet as a US defeat because of its political and media impact at home, captured by Cronkite’s broadcast and Johnson’s withdrawal; Interpretation 2 sees Tet as a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory in South Vietnam itself, with the ‘defeat’ reading mistaking Washington politics for military reality) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘Tet was, above all, a media event’ vs ‘a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory of the first order’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the Tet Offensive.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1990 history of the American media in Vietnam, foregrounding the role of television, Cronkite’s broadcast and the Johnson withdrawal, and so reads Tet through the lens of US public opinion; Interpretation 2 is from a 2005 study of US military operations focused on Vietcong casualties, the recapture of Hue and the depletion of the southern insurgency, and so reads Tet through the lens of the South Vietnamese battlefield. The two have different focuses (US politics and media vs South Vietnamese military outcomes) and use different bodies of evidence (US press archives and the Cronkite broadcast vs operational reports from Vietnam), and so reach different verdicts on whether Tet was a US defeat.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the Tet Offensive?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across 1967-68 (Westmoreland’s November 1967 ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line; the Tet Offensive of 30 January 1968 and the more than 100 attacks; the Vietcong raid on the US embassy in Saigon; the twenty-five-day battle for Hue and around 40,000 Vietcong dead; the credibility gap; Cronkite’s 27 February broadcast; Johnson’s 31 March withdrawal; later wider home-front events such as My Lai, the Calley trial, Kent State and the silent majority that show how divided the political fallout actually was), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Written for this exercise. A Kent State University professor writing to a colleague at another Ohio campus shortly after the 4 May 1970 shootings.

‘The killings here have changed how the country argues about Vietnam. Within hours of Mr Filo’s photograph reaching the wires we had calls from professors in California and Texas asking how to keep their own campuses calm. By the end of that week the universities had effectively closed for the term. The President describes the protesters as bums; New York construction workers attacked our students in lower Manhattan; my own colleagues are split between those who believe the country has had enough of the war and those who believe it has had enough of student protest.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the impact of the Kent State shootings on the United States.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Kent State produced a national wave of campus protest and shutdowns’ supported by ‘By the end of that week the universities had effectively closed for the term’ AND ‘Kent State did not unite the country against the war but deepened a divide between anti-war and pro-war Americans’ supported by ‘my own colleagues are split between those who believe the country has had enough of the war and those who believe it has had enough of student protest’ or ‘New York construction workers attacked our students’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Metropolitan Police’s H Division in Whitechapel in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two valid features):
• Headquartered at Leman Street police station — the central building from which beat patrols and detective work in Whitechapel and Spitalfields were directed.
• Around 500 officers in total — the great majority uniformed beat constables, with a small CID detective contingent.
• Beat constables walked fixed routes at two and a half miles per hour, in nine-hour shifts, day and night.
• Bordered the separate City of London Police force at Aldgate — an organisational split that complicated investigations crossing the boundary.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support (named station, specific numbers, specific procedures).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to ‘the police’ without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the work of a beat constable in Whitechapel in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• He walked a fixed route, usually about half a mile of streets and alleys in central Whitechapel, marked on a map at Leman Street.
• He walked it at a regulation two and a half miles an hour, day and night, in shifts of nine hours, and a sergeant met him at set points to check he had not strayed.
• He wore a heavy blue uniform, helmet and cape and carried a truncheon, a whistle and a bullseye lantern; he was unarmed as a matter of force policy.
• His job was prevention by visible presence rather than investigation; serious enquiry work went to the small CID, founded only in 1878.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources A and B.

Source A (composed for this exercise — not a real document): a Whitechapel constable's account of night duty, written in the style of a late-Victorian police memoir.
'My beat was half a mile of streets and courts, walked at the regulation pace so that the sergeant could meet me at the corner at the appointed minute. In the courts the lamps do not reach, and on a foggy night a man twenty yards off is a shadow. Every corner boy in Dorset Street knew the minute I should pass.'

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): a letter to a London newspaper from a Whitechapel shopkeeper, autumn 1888.
'We are told the Force is strengthened, yet the same young constables pass my door and they are gone within the month. Twenty-four shillings will not keep a married man in this parish. The detective gentlemen come out from Scotland Yard and know nothing of our alleys.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the difficulties of policing Whitechapel in 1888?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Both sources must be judged for the named enquiry, and the answer should weave together what each source says, who made it and why, and the student's own knowledge of Whitechapel.

Indicative content:
• Content: what each source tells the enquiry, and what it leaves out.
• Provenance: who wrote it, when, for whom and why, and what that does to its usefulness — bias does not make a source useless, it tells you what the source is good for.
• Own knowledge: named Whitechapel detail used to test, support or qualify what the sources say.

Top band: content, provenance and own knowledge integrated for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the enquiry into the difficulties of policing Whitechapel in 1888.
Mid band: both sources used with own knowledge, or one source fully analysed, with a judgement.
Low band: the sources described, with little own knowledge and no judgement.

Subject-specific pointers:
• Source A gives the physical problem: the fixed pace that locals could time, unlit courts and fog.
• Source B gives the human problem: low pay, heavy turnover and detectives who did not know the district.
• Both are composed for practice, so treat provenance as a scenario: a constable writing later may defend his own record, and a shopkeeper writing during the murders may be angry rather than accurate.
• Own knowledge: H Division's roughly 500 officers based at Leman Street; a recruit's wage of about 24 shillings a week; only a few weeks' training; around a quarter of recruits leaving in the first year; the separate City of London Police across the Aldgate boundary.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): a letter to a London newspaper from a Whitechapel shopkeeper, autumn 1888.
'We are told the Force is strengthened, yet the same young constables pass my door and they are gone within the month. Twenty-four shillings will not keep a married man in this parish. The detective gentlemen come out from Scotland Yard and know nothing of our alleys.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the recruitment and retention of Metropolitan Police constables in the 1880s?

In your answer you must give:
• the detail in Source B that you would follow up
• the question you would ask
• what type of source you could use
• how that source might help answer your question.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a relevant detail taken from Source B, 1 for a question that follows from it, 1 for a named type of source, and 1 for explaining how that source would help.

Indicative content (any one complete chain):
• Detail: 'They are gone within the month.' Question: how many H Division constables left within a year of joining, and why? Source type: Metropolitan Police divisional personnel registers and dismissal books. How it helps: they record each officer's joining and leaving date with the reason given.
• Detail: 'Twenty-four shillings will not keep a married man.' Question: how did constable pay compare with other Whitechapel wages? Source type: Charles Booth's survey of London labour and life, which recorded incomes street by street. How it helps: it lets the constable's wage be set against dock labour and sweated tailoring.
• Detail: 'The detective gentlemen come out from Scotland Yard.' Question: how many CID officers were attached to H Division in 1888? Source type: Metropolitan Police establishment returns and CID records. How it helps: they list posts by division, showing how thin detective cover really was.

Top band: all four links present, with a source type that could realistically answer the question.
Mid band: detail and question sound, but the source type is generic.
Low band: no clear chain from the source to the enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the problems the Metropolitan Police had in recruiting and keeping constables in the 1880s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Pay was low: a new recruit earned around 24 shillings a week in 1888, less than a skilled tradesman.
• Training was thin: recruits had only a few weeks of basic instruction before being put on a beat.
• Turnover was heavy: around a quarter of new constables left within their first year.
• Drunkenness on duty was the commonest reason for dismissal, so many beats were walked by inexperienced replacements.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of crime in Whitechapel in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Drunkenness and street fighting filled the casebooks, helped by the very large number of public houses in the district.
• Prostitution was widespread, and the lodging-house economy, with no register of guests, made it almost untraceable.
• Protection rackets were run by organised gangs such as the Bessarabian Tigers and the Odessians, who demanded payments from shopkeepers and publicans.
• Pickpocketing and street theft were common in crowded markets such as Petticoat Lane, and attacks on Jewish residents rose after 1881.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the use of London Underground stations as shelters during the Blitz.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Home Office initially banned Tube shelter use in 1940 because of fears of ‘deep shelter mentality’, but Londoners overrode the ban by buying day-return tickets and refusing to leave the platforms.
• By October 1940 the government had accepted Tube shelter as official policy, equipping 79 stations with bunks, lighting, chemical toilets and refreshment trains.
• At peak around 177,000 Londoners slept in Tube stations every night.
• Tube shelter was popular but not safe: direct hits at Balham (October 1940) and Bank (January 1941) killed shelterers, and the worst Tube disaster (Bethnal Green, 1943) happened in a station that was never bombed.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to Tube shelter without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Bethnal Green tube shelter disaster of 3 March 1943.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• 173 people, including 62 children, died of crush asphyxiation on the staircase at Bethnal Green Tube station as crowds rushed in after the air-raid sirens.
• The panic was triggered not by bombing but by the misidentified noise of a Z-battery anti-aircraft rocket test in nearby Victoria Park; no bomb fell on the station that night.
• The disaster was censored by the government until 1945 to protect morale and avoid blame on the LCC for the inadequate staircase design (no central handrail, poor lighting).
• The first death in the crush was a woman who slipped on the wet steps near the front, while the crowd behind kept pushing forward.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to the disaster without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: Sources A and B below are composed for practice. They are not real archive documents; in the exam you are given two genuine sources.

Source A: a photograph taken on a London Underground platform in the autumn of 1940. Whole families are lying on blankets along the platform edge and on the stairs. A child is asleep on a coat and an older woman is pouring tea from a flask. There is no bunk or bedding provided.

Source B: the diary of a 28-year-old shop assistant in Stepney, written in October 1940.
‘The Tube is full again tonight. Mrs C. brought her three down and they have a good corner near the lift. Mickey is in his shelter at the Exchange — he has the children’s milk now and a doctor on Tuesdays. The Hallsville rumour will not go away — people in our court say it was hundreds, not the figure in the paper. The wireless does not say. Whoever lost the buses ought to swing for it.’

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how East End Londoners coped with shelter during the Blitz?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Weigh both sources together: what each one says, who made it and why, and what you know about the context.

Indicative content:
• Source A shows how crowded and improvised Tube shelter was before the government equipped the stations, with families bringing their own bedding and food.
• A photograph shows one platform at one moment and nothing of the surface shelters, basements or homes that most Londoners used.
• Source B shows the same shelter as a routine: families claiming the same corner night after night, and community provision at ‘Mickey’s shelter’ with milk and a weekly doctor.
• Source B also records what people believed about South Hallsville, official silence (‘The wireless does not say’) and anger at the failure of the buses.
• A private diary is not curated propaganda, but it is one young East End woman’s view and its rumour about the death toll is unverified within the source.
• Context to bring in: the Home Office banned Tube shelter at first, 79 stations were equipped from October 1940, around 177,000 people slept underground at the peak, and ‘Mickey’s shelter’ held about 5,000.

Mastering: Both sources judged on content and on who made them and why, supported by precise contextual knowledge, with a clear verdict on usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Both sources considered, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: Simple comments on what the sources show; provenance or context is thin.
Emerging: Describes the sources without judging their usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B again.

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about what East End Londoners believed about the South Hallsville School disaster?

Give the detail in Source B you would follow up, the question you would ask, the type of source you could use, and how it would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Give a coherent chain: a detail in Source B, the question it raises, the type of source you could use, and how that source would help.

Indicative example:
• Detail in Source B: the rumour that the death toll ‘was hundreds, not the figure in the paper’, and that ‘the wireless does not say’.
• Question: how widely did people in the East End believe the official Hallsville figure was false?
• Type of source: the weekly reports on civilian morale that government officers compiled for ministers in the autumn of 1940.
• How it helps: they were written for internal use, not for the public, so they record the rumours officials were hearing as well as the official figures.

Other chains are equally creditable, for example following up the Tube routine, ‘Mickey’s shelter’ or the anger about the buses, using borough Civil Defence records, a local newspaper such as the Hackney Gazette, or oral-history recordings of East End survivors.

Mastering: All four steps clear, with the source type matched to the question.
Secure: A sound question and source type, briefly explained.
Developing: A question or a source type given, but the link to Source B is weak.
Emerging: A source type or question suggested that is not grounded in Source B.

practice_questions.text:
‘The state protected civilians far better in the twentieth century than in earlier centuries.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• air-raid shelters in the Blitz
• billeting and free quarter in earlier centuries.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments that protection improved:
• Before the twentieth century governments did not try to protect civilians at all; medieval purveyance took their food and Civil War free quarter put soldiers in their homes.
• By 1939 the state issued gas masks, buried Anderson shelters, planned evacuation and made local councils responsible for air-raid precautions.
• From October 1940 the government equipped 79 Tube stations with bunks, lighting and chemical toilets, and added the indoor Morrison shelter in 1941.
• Rest centres, billeting and homelessness returns were reorganised after the South Hallsville failure so that bombed-out families could be moved faster.
• Officials tracked civilian morale daily, so problems in one borough could be answered with extra resources.

Indicative content — arguments that protection was patchy:
• The government banned Tube shelter at first and only accepted it after Londoners forced the issue themselves.
• Anderson shelters suited suburban gardens, not the flat-roofed East End terraces where many homes had no garden.
• South Hallsville School (9–10 September 1940) killed at least 73 homeless people because the buses meant to move them went to the wrong address.
• Bethnal Green (3 March 1943) killed 173 people on a council staircase with no central handrail, in a station no bomb had hit.
• Community effort filled the gaps: Mickey Davis ran a shelter for about 5,000 people in Spitalfields with no government structure behind it.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that compares state action across several periods, uses accurate detail (purveyance, free quarter, Anderson shelters, Tube stations, Hallsville, Bethnal Green) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why British governments tried to control what the public was told about war in the period c1800–1945.

You may use the following in your answer:
• reporting of the Crimean War
• censorship during the Blitz.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 12 marks.

Mastering: Several reasons analysed and linked into a clear line of reasoning, with precise period detail.
Secure: Two or more reasons explained with accurate supporting detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Simple statements about the topic with little supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Once William Howard Russell could telegraph from the Crimea, governments lost control of the story and learned that bad news travelled in days.
• Reporting could bring down ministers, so controlling it became a political necessity as much as a military one.
• In wartime, casualty figures and bomb damage could be used by the enemy, so the Hallsville, Balham and Bethnal Green losses were withheld.
• Officials believed that news of mass-casualty disasters would spread panic and damage morale, which they tracked daily.
• Censorship also protected secrets: weather, troop movements, the Cabinet War Rooms and the Z-battery rockets in Victoria Park.
• Positive propaganda worked alongside censorship: ‘London Can Take It!’ and Dig for Victory framed the war as a shared national effort.

Use both printed prompts and add at least one reason of your own.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the 1950 Marriage Law on women in rural China. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail (e.g. women queueing for divorce, husbands or mothers-in-law violently opposing it, courts handling huge case volumes, local cadres refusing to enforce). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that the law’s legal change ran far ahead of rural attitudes, or that women were exposed to family violence when they tried to use it. [4]
Secure: Two supported inferences with one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the 1950 Marriage Law produced backlash in the Chinese countryside.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the bride price and arranged marriage
• the role of local CCP cadres
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. the law’s threat to the rural household economy (a divorced wife could leave with property), the loss of bride price as a family asset, the resistance of clan elders and mothers-in-law to changes in family hierarchy, the unwillingness of local cadres (themselves rural patriarchs) to enforce against their own communities, and the gulf between Beijing’s legal change and rural Confucian attitudes. Uses stimulus and adds independent knowledge (e.g. 1953 ‘Marriage Law Implementation Month’, reports of beatings and suicides). Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the impact of communes on family life in Mao’s China.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues that communal mess halls and collective childcare freed women from the ‘double burden’ and broke patriarchal household authority; the other argues that the communes disrupted the rural household economy, contributed to famine and were widely resisted, with most reforms quietly reversed after 1962). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the status of women under Mao.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (revisionist Western writing after PRC archives opened, e.g. Dikötter, vs sympathetic accounts comparing the Mao era favourably with the post-1978 reform era, e.g. Mobo Gao), used different evidence (CCP enforcement reports of rural backlash vs literacy and labour-force statistics), or had different purposes (highlighting the gulf between rhetoric and reality vs reassessing genuine gains). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the 1950 Marriage Law in changing the status of women in China?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the 1950 minimum marriage ages, the bans on bride price and concubinage, the c.1.1 million divorce cases of 1953, the role of Deng Yingchao, the rural backlash and the 1953 Implementation Month, alongside other drivers of change such as the end of foot binding, the literacy drives, and the iron-girl workforce mobilisation. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the lives of Chinese women were transformed by Mao’s policies between 1949 and 1976?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the Marriage Law of 1 May 1950, the end of foot binding, the rise in female literacy, the c.90% urban female labour participation by 1976, the iron-girls campaign, alongside limits such as the work-points pay gap (often 7 to 10), the double burden, the male-dominated Politburo and the post-1976 retreat from radical gender propaganda. Engages with the historiography (Dikötter on the gulf between rhetoric and rural reality; Mobo Gao on the Mao era’s genuine gains compared with the reform era). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (Marriage Law, work points, iron girls, double burden, commune, mess hall). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Dawes Act (1887) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Dawes Act broke up reservations into 160-acre family allotments and declared the rest ‘surplus’ for sale to white settlers — the mechanism by which Indigenous landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934.
• Because allotment forced families onto plots too small to support horse-buffalo traditions and undermined communal landholding, it dismantled long-established Plains social structures faster than any military defeat had done.
• Because the ‘surplus’ lands were sold to white settlers, the Act was a vehicle for continued settler expansion long after the official end of the Plains wars — it functioned as continuing dispossession dressed as reform.
• Because citizenship was promised to those who took allotments, the Act tied legal personhood to the abandonment of communal Indigenous identity — aligned with Carlisle’s ‘Kill the Indian, Save the Man’ philosophy.
• Because the Act sat alongside Wounded Knee (1890) and the closure of the frontier (1890 Census), it gave a legal frame to a wider end-of-frontier policy: the West was now to be a settler society, with Indigenous nations remade as small-acreage farmers under federal supervision.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1887, 138 million → 48 million acres, 160-acre allotment) and specialist vocabulary (allotment, surplus, reservation, Carlisle).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the destruction of the Indigenous Plains way of life in the years 1874–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876)
• the Dawes Act (1887)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1874 a US Army expedition led by Custer struck gold in the Black Hills — land guaranteed to the Lakota by the second Fort Laramie Treaty just six years earlier; Washington ordered all Lakota and Cheyenne onto smaller reservations by 31 January 1876.
• Because many bands refused, a coalition under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse gathered in the Powder River country; on 25–26 June 1876 they destroyed Custer’s 7th Cavalry column at the Little Bighorn — around 268 US soldiers killed.
• Because the federal response was overwhelming, by 1881 the Lakota leadership was broken: Crazy Horse killed in custody (1877), Sitting Bull surrendered after exile in Canada; meanwhile General Sheridan’s endorsement of buffalo extermination collapsed the herd from millions to around 1,000 by 1890.
• Because Indigenous nations were now ration-dependent on shrinking reservations, the 1887 Dawes Act could break those reservations into 160-acre allotments and sell the ‘surplus’ to white settlers — landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934.
• By the end of 1890 the destruction was effectively complete: the Ghost Dance had spread; Sitting Bull was killed during a botched arrest on 15 December; Big Foot’s band was massacred at Wounded Knee on 29 December — around 250–300 Lakota dead, the great majority unarmed, marking the end of armed resistance on the Plains.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1874, 25–26 June 1876, 1887, 29 December 1890), specialist vocabulary (allotment, ration, Ghost Dance), both stimulus points covered and integrated with own knowledge.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the extermination of the buffalo for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The buffalo’s collapse from around 30 million in 1850 to about 1,000 by 1890 destroyed the food, shelter, fuel, clothing and trade base of horse-buffalo culture in a single generation.
• Because Plains nations had built mobility on horseback around following a moving herd, removing the herd removed the practical possibility of independent life away from reservations.
• Because the slaughter was openly endorsed by General Sheridan as a strategy to subdue the Plains nations, it was a form of war by other means — producing surrender and confinement that the army alone had not achieved.
• Because reservation life depended on government rations rather than on hunting, food shortages, malnutrition and disease became routine; the conditions in which the Ghost Dance spread in 1890 grew directly out of this dependence.
• Because the buffalo’s removal cleared the High Plains of its dominant grazer, it also opened the land to the long drives and the open-range cattle industry of the 1870s and 1880s — tying Indigenous loss directly to settler economic gain.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (around 30 million in 1850, 1,000 by 1890, Sheridan) and specialist vocabulary (horse-buffalo culture, reservation, ration).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how the Plains wars came to an end in the years 1876–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876)
• the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In June 1876 the coalition under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse destroyed Custer’s 7th Cavalry column at the Little Bighorn, killing around 268 US soldiers — a real Indigenous victory but one that triggered an overwhelming federal response.
• Because federal forces poured into the Powder River country and Black Hills through 1876–81, organised Lakota resistance was broken: Crazy Horse was killed in custody at Fort Robinson (1877), Sitting Bull surrendered after exile in Canada (1881).
• Because General Sheridan had endorsed buffalo extermination as a strategy, the herd had collapsed from around 30 million in 1850 to about 1,000 by 1890 — ending horse-buffalo culture and forcing Indigenous Plains nations onto government rations on shrinking reservations.
• Because reservation rations were short and crops failed, the Paiute prophet Wovoka’s 1889 Ghost Dance vision spread quickly through 1890 — offering hope of the buffalo’s return and ancestors’ rising; among the Lakota it took on a more militant edge that alarmed federal Indian agents.
• On 15 December 1890 Sitting Bull was killed in a botched arrest at Standing Rock; on 29 December the 7th Cavalry massacred around 250–300 Lakota at Wounded Knee, mostly unarmed — the effective end of armed Indigenous resistance on the Plains.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1876, 1877, 1881, 15 and 29 December 1890), specialist vocabulary (Ghost Dance, ration, reservation, 7th Cavalry), both stimulus points covered and integrated with own knowledge.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Wounded Knee killed around 250–300 Lakota on 29 December 1890, the great majority of them unarmed and including women and children — a heavier loss in a single morning than any of the open-Plains battles of the previous decade.
• Because Big Foot’s band had already surrendered when the massacre began, the event made clear that surrender no longer guaranteed protection — ending hopes that the Ghost Dance would coexist with federal authority.
• Because Wounded Knee was the effective end of armed Indigenous resistance on the Plains, it closed a 28-year cycle of conflict that had begun with Little Crow’s War in 1862.
• Because the 7th Cavalry was the same regiment Custer had led at the Little Bighorn, the massacre carried a sense of revenge for the army; twenty Medals of Honor were awarded to soldiers involved — a federal blessing of what was a non-combatant slaughter.
• Because Wounded Knee occurred two months after the 1890 Census declared the frontier ‘closed’, it became the symbolic end-point of the period — a moment that Limerick and other historians have read as completed conquest dressed as ‘the end of the frontier’.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (29 December 1890, around 250–300 killed, 7th Cavalry, 20 Medals of Honor) and specialist vocabulary (Ghost Dance, reservation, Pine Ridge).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Dawes Act (1887).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for two separately developed consequences (up to 4 each), each linking the Act to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that Indigenous landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934 — the ‘surplus’ land sold to white settlers became the legal mechanism of continued dispossession after the end of the Plains wars.
• Another consequence was that allotment forced families onto plots too small to sustain horse-buffalo traditions and broke up communal Plains landholding — aligning Indigenous policy with Carlisle’s ‘Kill the Indian, Save the Man’ assimilation philosophy.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named feature (e.g. land loss to 1934, communal landholding).
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about how the Soviet regime used culture and propaganda in the 1930s. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, the use of doctored photographs, the writer as ‘engineer of the human soul’, the rewriting of school textbooks, the closure of churches, or the Stalingrad place-name). Each inference goes beyond surface description to explain why the detail mattered for the regime’s control. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises the source rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Stalin built up a Cult of Stalin in the 1930s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Lenin cult
• the Show Trials
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — the existing Lenin cult of 1924 as a template (Mausoleum, embalmed body, Petrograd renamed Leningrad); the destruction of the Old Bolsheviks in the Moscow Show Trials of 1936–38, leaving Stalin as the only public face of October; the need to stabilise a society in violent flux during collectivisation, industrialisation and the Terror; and the foreign-policy function of the paternal Stalin of the 1936 Constitution. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — Politburo, Sovnarkom, Pravda, Komsomol, Stakhanovite. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans heavily on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of the cult without explaining why each was needed. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the nature of Stalinist propaganda and the Cult of Stalin.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation argues the cult was a top-down imposition driven by Stalin’s personal will and the destruction of rivals, while the other argues that ordinary Soviets actively welcomed and helped construct a paternal image of Stalin after years of upheaval). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the Cult of Stalin.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (Cold War defector memoirs versus Soviet diaries and letters opened in the 1990s); they wrote at different times (Conquest’s 1968 totalitarian reading versus Fitzpatrick’s revisionist work versus Kotkin’s post-archival biography); or they had different purposes (defending or rebutting the totalitarian-school reading). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of the Cult of Stalin in legitimising Stalin’s rule by 1941?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the Cult’s features (statues, place-names like Stalingrad and Stalin Peak, doctored photographs, the title ‘Wise Father’), its Lenin-cult template, and its role after the Show Trials had killed the Old Bolsheviks — weighed against rival explanations of legitimisation: the 1936 Constitution as paper democracy, Socialist Realism in literature and cinema, the rewritten school textbooks, the antireligious campaign, and the Stakhanovite movement. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that Soviet propaganda in the 1930s succeeded mainly because ordinary citizens accepted and helped to construct the official image of Stalin?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge of the bottom-up evidence (Soviet diaries showing genuine belief in Gorky and Eisenstein, the demand for a fatherly leader after years of upheaval that Kotkin identifies, Stakhanovite enthusiasm, Komsomol ceremonies) weighed against the top-down evidence (the 1932 decree dissolving artistic associations, Glavlit censorship, the Shostakovich denunciation in Pravda in 1936, the Yezhovshchina punishing dissent, doctored photographs erasing the purged). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (Sovnarkom, Politburo, Komsomol, Pravda, Glavlit, Socialist Realism, Stakhanovite). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about working and living conditions in Stalin’s USSR. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences anchored to specific quoted details (for example, the kommunalka and shared kitchen, bread rationing, the internal passport stamp, factory piece rates, criminal absenteeism, the Stakhanovite’s closed shop, or the kolkhoz labour-day). Each inference goes beyond surface description to explain why the detail mattered for daily life. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail; one may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises the source rather than infers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why life in Stalin’s USSR varied so sharply between social groups by 1941.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Stakhanovites
• the kolkhoz
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes — the Stakhanovite reward system from 1935 (bonuses, larger flats, closed shops); the kolkhoz system that paid peasants in labour-days and tied them to the farm via internal-passport rules; the bureaucratic and NKVD elite that lived above the rationed economy; the new women’s position in industry and the professions alongside the 1936 Family Code rollback; and the pre-war deportations of ethnic minorities that placed whole communities outside ordinary Soviet life. Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge; reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — kolkhoz, sovkhoz, Stakhanovite, NKVD, kommunalka. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one beyond the stimulus; some attempt at weighing causes; judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans heavily on the stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists groups without explaining why their experience differed. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the position of women in Stalin’s USSR.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (for example, one interpretation argues that Stalinism produced real gains for Soviet women in industry, education and the professions, while the other argues that the 1936 Family Code reversed the radical early-Bolshevik settlement and re-traditionalised women’s domestic role). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side more thinly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified but supported from only one interpretation. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about life in Stalin’s USSR.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — for example, the historians used different evidence (Soviet women’s magazines and propaganda films versus diaries and family-court records); they wrote at different times (Cold War surveys versus post-1991 social-history work by Sheila Fitzpatrick or Lynne Viola); or they had different purposes (assessing Soviet propaganda claims versus reconstructing private life). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified but with limited explanation of how it produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the impact of the 1936 Family Code on the position of Soviet women?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the 1936 Family Code (abortion banned, divorce made expensive, awards for mothers of large families, criminalised non-payment of child support) and the early Bolshevik record under Kollontai (legal abortion 1920, easy divorce, civil marriage) — weighed against the genuine gains made by Soviet women in industry and the professions (a clear majority of doctors female by 1940, ten million women joining the urban workforce 1928–40). Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the persecution of ethnic minorities in the USSR was a long-running pre-war policy rather than a wartime emergency?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the deportation of around 172,000 Soviet Koreans in 1937 with Japan as the named threat; the ‘national operations’ of 1937–38 against Poles, Germans, Latvians, Estonians, Finns and Greeks; around 350,000 arrested and roughly two thirds shot — weighed against the wartime evidence (the 440,000 Volga Germans deported after Barbarossa in 1941; the 1943–44 deportation of Crimean Tatars, Chechens, Ingush and Kalmyks). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (NKVD, kolkhoz, internal passport, special settlement, autonomous republic). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the work of the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee in 1888.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two valid features):
• Formed in September 1888 by local tradesmen under chairman George Lusk, a master builder, in response to public alarm after the Chapman murder.
• Organised civilian patrols of the rookeries at night, particularly around Flower and Dean Street and Dorset Street.
• Hired private detectives and lobbied the Home Office to offer a public reward, which Home Secretary Henry Matthews refused to authorise.
• Received a parcel on 16 October 1888 containing half a human kidney and the so-called ‘From Hell’ letter addressed to Lusk — one of the most striking pieces of contemporary evidence.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support (named individuals, named dates, specific actions).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to ‘a vigilante group’ without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources A and B.

Source A: a cartoon by John Tenniel published in Punch magazine on 29 September 1888, titled 'The Nemesis of Neglect'. It shows a hooded phantom holding a knife, gliding down a dark Whitechapel alley; the figure is labelled 'CRIME'. The verse printed beneath it begins: 'There floats a phantom on the slum's foul air, / Shaping, to eyes which have the gift of seeing, / Into the Spectre of that loathly lair. / Face it — for vain is fleeing!'

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): an appeal from the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee to the Home Secretary, October 1888, written in the style of the Committee's letters.
'The people of this district have lost their confidence in the police. Our members patrol the courts nightly at their own cost, and we have engaged two private officers. We again ask the Government to offer a reward, which we believe would loosen tongues that will not speak to a constable.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into public attitudes towards the police in Whitechapel in the autumn of 1888?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Both sources must be judged for the named enquiry, and the answer should weave together what each source says, who made it and why, and the student's own knowledge of Whitechapel.

Indicative content:
• Content: what each source tells the enquiry, and what it leaves out.
• Provenance: who wrote it, when, for whom and why, and what that does to its usefulness — bias does not make a source useless, it tells you what the source is good for.
• Own knowledge: named Whitechapel detail used to test, support or qualify what the sources say.

Top band: content, provenance and own knowledge integrated for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the enquiry into public attitudes towards the police in Whitechapel in the autumn of 1888.
Mid band: both sources used with own knowledge, or one source fully analysed, with a judgement.
Low band: the sources described, with little own knowledge and no judgement.

Subject-specific pointers:
• Source A is a real cartoon of 29 September 1888, published between the Chapman murder and the 'double event'. It blames neglected slums as much as the police, and it is an opinion piece for a middle-class readership — which is exactly why it is useful for mood rather than for what officers actually did.
• Source B is composed for practice, so treat its provenance as a scenario: a body asking the Government for something has a reason to paint the police as failing.
• Own knowledge: confidence had already been damaged by Bloody Sunday on 13 November 1887; H Division constables earned about 24 shillings a week with a few weeks' training; Henry Matthews refused a public reward; Sir Charles Warren resigned on 8 November 1888.
• A strong answer notes that neither source tells us what Whitechapel's poorest residents thought, only what a national magazine and a committee of tradesmen said.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B (composed for this exercise — not a real document): an appeal from the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee to the Home Secretary, October 1888, written in the style of the Committee's letters.
'The people of this district have lost their confidence in the police. Our members patrol the courts nightly at their own cost, and we have engaged two private officers. We again ask the Government to offer a reward, which we believe would loosen tongues that will not speak to a constable.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the work of the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee?

In your answer you must give:
• the detail in Source B that you would follow up
• the question you would ask
• what type of source you could use
• how that source might help answer your question.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a relevant detail taken from Source B, 1 for a question that follows from it, 1 for a named type of source, and 1 for explaining how that source would help.

Indicative content (any one complete chain):
• Detail: 'We have engaged two private officers.' Question: what did the Committee's private detectives actually do, and did the police work with them? Source type: the Committee's own minutes and its correspondence with the Home Office. How it helps: the minutes record decisions and spending, and the letters show how the police replied.
• Detail: 'We again ask the Government to offer a reward.' Question: why did Henry Matthews keep refusing a reward? Source type: Home Office files and Hansard reports of parliamentary questions in autumn 1888. How it helps: they set out the Government's stated policy that rewards produced false information.
• Detail: 'Our members patrol the courts nightly at their own cost.' Question: how many men patrolled, and which streets did they cover? Source type: London newspaper reports of Committee meetings, such as those in The Star and The Times. How it helps: the press reported the meetings in detail, including numbers and routes.

Top band: all four links present, with a source type that could realistically answer the question.
Mid band: detail and question sound, but the source type is generic.
Low band: no clear chain from the source to the enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the difficulties the police faced in investigating the Whitechapel murders.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Detective methods were limited to witness statements, sketches, photographs of the victims and post-mortems by surgeons such as Thomas Bond; there was no fingerprinting, no blood-typing and no central record of suspects.
• The Met and the City of London Police were separate forces, so the 'double event' of 30 September 1888 crossed a boundary and evidence had to pass through two chains of command.
• Sir Charles Warren had the Goulston Street writing scrubbed off before it could be photographed, which removed possible evidence and angered the City force.
• The lodging-house economy kept no register of guests, so witnesses moved on and could be untraceable within a week.

Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the reporting of the Whitechapel murders in the press.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• The murders were covered daily by a new mass-circulation press: The Star was a halfpenny evening paper selling around 300,000 copies by 1888.
• The 'Dear Boss' letter, received by the Central News Agency on 27 September 1888, gave the killer his name in every paper; the police came to believe it was a journalist's hoax.
• Punch ran satirical cartoons attacking Sir Charles Warren and the Met, including Tenniel's 'The Nemesis of Neglect' on 29 September 1888.
• Reporting fed rumours that the killer was a Jewish migrant, which is why Warren had the Goulston Street writing erased before daylight.
