Top band: two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Mid band: two features identified with brief support, or one feature fully supported.
Low band: features named without support.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of detective methods used in the Metropolitan Police investigation of the Whitechapel murders.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Door-to-door interviews with Whitechapel residents, recorded as written witness statements in H Division case papers.
• Police sketches drawn from witness descriptions of suspects and circulated in the press.
• Crime-scene photography — Catherine Eddowes’ body in Mitre Square was photographed by the City of London Police on 30 September 1888.
• Post-mortem examinations by police surgeons such as Thomas Bond, who produced detailed forensic notes on the wounds and what they implied about the killer.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail (named individuals, named locations, specific procedures).
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to ‘the police investigated’ without identifying a specific method.

practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the work of barefoot doctors in rural Chinese communes during the late 1960s. Support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted or paraphrased detail (e.g. short training period, basic medical kit, vaccinations, family-planning advice, treating illnesses no doctor had previously seen). Inferences move beyond what the source states — e.g. that the system reached communities previously without any medical care, or that the barefoot doctor combined healthcare with political education on hygiene and contraception. [4]
Secure: Two supported inferences with one weaker. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a paraphrase. [2]
Emerging: Summary or unsupported point. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Chinese adult literacy rose so sharply between 1949 and 1976.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the introduction of Pinyin in 1958
• simplified characters
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighted explanation drawing on at least three causes — e.g. the technical reform of the script (Pinyin 1958, simplified characters from 1956), the targeted adult campaigns in winter village classes and factory worker classes, the rise in primary school enrolment to c.80% by 1965, the propaganda demand for citizens able to read posters and the Little Red Book, and the explicit targeting of women and girls. Uses stimulus and adds independent knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. [10–12]
Secure: Three causes explained; some weighing; partial judgement. [7–9]
Developing: Causes named but mainly described; relies on stimulus. [4–6]
Emerging: Narrative without causation focus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the impact of the Cultural Revolution on Chinese education.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise central difference (e.g. one interpretation argues that the Cultural Revolution destroyed Chinese education by closing schools and universities and abolishing the gaokao; the other argues that primary literacy classes continued in villages and that the era reached more peasants than Republican-era schools ever had). Each side supported with detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified, supported by detail from both interpretations but unevenly. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported from only one. [2]
Emerging: One interpretation summarised without comparison. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about religion in Mao’s China.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A reason explained with supporting detail — e.g. the historians used different evidence (state inventories of destroyed temples and Tibetan exile records vs village-level oral histories of underground ancestor worship), wrote at different times (Cold War-era accounts focused on overt persecution vs reform-era accounts noting religious revival after 1976), or had different purposes (highlighting state repression vs measuring popular resilience). The reason is linked specifically to the difference between the views. [4]
Secure: Relevant reason explained with some detail. [3]
Developing: Reason identified but loosely linked. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the views differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the importance of barefoot doctors in transforming healthcare in Mao’s China?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views and tests them with own knowledge — the c.1 million barefoot doctors formalised 1965, their three- to six-month training, the rise in life expectancy from c.36 to c.66 by 1976, the fall in rural infant mortality, alongside limits such as the forced relocation of urban specialists, the loss of city hospital capacity, and the political suppression of the 1959–62 famine death rates. Reaches a substantiated judgement on ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed with own knowledge; uneven cross-referencing or implicit judgement. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation favoured; own knowledge in patches; judgement asserted. [5–8]
Emerging: A general essay; little engagement with interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the destruction of traditional culture was the most damaging legacy of Mao’s rule on Chinese society between 1949 and 1976?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the ‘four olds’ campaign of May 1966, the Red Guard desecration of Confucius’s tomb in November 1966, the destruction of c.6,000 Tibetan monasteries (with damage continuing from the 1959 uprising), Jiang Qing’s eight model operas displacing classical theatre, alongside competing legacies such as the famine death toll of 1959–62, the closure of universities, the c.17 million sent-down youth, and the reverse case of genuine social gains in literacy and rural healthcare. Engages with the historiography (Dikötter on cultural destruction; Mobo Gao on social gains). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate with confident period vocabulary (four olds, gaokao, xiaxiang, model operas, danwei, barefoot doctors, Pinyin). [13–16 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge; clear judgement, reasoning thin in places. SPaG: mostly accurate. [9–12 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [5–8 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–4 + 0–1 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Written for this exercise. Henry Kissinger advising President Nixon on the prospects for the Paris peace talks, September 1971.

‘Hanoi’s position has hardened since Lam Son 719. The North Vietnamese have concluded that the South Vietnamese army cannot hold the country alone and that the United States will not stay. We must therefore exit on terms that protect the appearance of an honourable settlement and that buy a sufficient interval before the inevitable test of South Vietnam’s independent capacity. The bombing of the North, if necessary on a far heavier scale than yet attempted, may be the lever required to bring Le Duc Tho back to the table.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about US thinking on the peace talks in 1971.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘US officials privately doubted that South Vietnam could survive on its own once US forces left’ supported by ‘the South Vietnamese army cannot hold the country alone’ or ‘a sufficient interval before the inevitable test’ AND ‘Kissinger saw the bombing of North Vietnam as a tool to force concessions in Paris rather than to win the war’ supported by ‘the bombing of the North … may be the lever required to bring Le Duc Tho back to the table’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Vietnamisation failed to secure South Vietnam between 1969 and 1975.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Cambodia incursion (1970)
• the fall of Saigon (1975)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the political weakness of South Vietnam, ARVN corruption and the failure of Lam Son 719, the impact of Watergate and congressional aid cuts in 1974-75, the terms of the Paris Peace Agreement that left around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops inside South Vietnam) and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The argument connects withdrawal of US troops from over 540,000 in 1969 to around 24,000 by the end of 1972 with the structural weaknesses of the South Vietnamese state. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of Vietnamisation without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1985 study of the Vietnam War):
‘The United States lost the war in Vietnam mainly because of the strength of the enemy. The Vietcong’s guerrilla tactics, the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia, integration with the peasant population and Russian and Chinese material support gave Hanoi a strategic depth no Western army could counter. The fall of Saigon in 1975 was the consequence of an enemy whose patience and political capacity always exceeded America’s.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 study of US strategy in Indochina):
‘The United States lost the war in Vietnam mainly because of its own strategic and political failures. The body-count tactics of search and destroy, the bombing campaigns that radicalised the home front, the political collapse of South Vietnam under an army with no rural legitimacy, the credibility gap after Tet 1968, and the congressional aid cuts after Watergate all turned American power against itself. The Vietcong did not defeat the United States; the United States defeated itself.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about why the United States lost the Vietnam War? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 explains American defeat as the consequence of North Vietnamese and Vietcong strength — guerrilla tactics, the Trail, peasant integration, Russian and Chinese support; Interpretation 2 explains American defeat as the consequence of US strategic and political failures — search and destroy, bombing, the credibility gap, the political weakness of South Vietnam, congressional aid cuts) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the consequence of an enemy whose patience and political capacity always exceeded America’s’ vs ‘the United States defeated itself’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about why the United States lost the Vietnam War.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1985 study of the Vietnam War, written when Cold War framing dominated and when Vietcong and North Vietnamese strengths were the natural focus, drawing on military operations and supply-line evidence; Interpretation 2 is from a 2010 study of US strategy in Indochina, written after the opening of the Pentagon archives and the Watergate-era papers, drawing on US presidential records and so foregrounding the failures of search and destroy, the credibility gap, ARVN weakness and the impact of Watergate. The two have different focuses (enemy strength vs US strategic and political failure) and use different bodies of evidence (Vietcong operations vs US strategy archives), and so reach different verdicts on why the United States lost.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about why the United States lost the Vietnam War?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.

In your answer you should:
• give arguments for and against Interpretation 1
• use both interpretations and your own knowledge of the historical context
• reach a substantiated judgement

Marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar will be awarded for this answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across 1969-75 (Vietnamisation and US troop withdrawal from over 540,000 to around 24,000; the Nixon Doctrine of July 1969; ARVN corruption and the failure of Operation Lam Son 719 in 1971; the Cambodia incursion of 1970 and Kent State; Operation Linebacker II of December 1972; the Paris Peace Agreement of 27 January 1973 and the around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops left inside the South; the Vietcong’s guerrilla tactics and the Ho Chi Minh Trail; Russian and Chinese support; congressional aid cuts after Watergate in 1974-75; the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently and writes with sustained accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar (full SPaG band).
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated; SPaG generally accurate.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit; SPaG inconsistent.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1; SPaG limits clarity. [20 marks — 16 content + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From a 1975 retrospective interview with a former South Vietnamese army officer recorded for a US oral history project shortly after the fall of Saigon.

‘The Americans gave us helicopters, M16 rifles and tanks. They could not give us a country. After 1973 they were gone, and in 1974 the Congress in Washington cut the money. Our generals were political appointees; many of them ran when the offensive came in March 1975. The peasants in the highlands had no reason to fight for Saigon. We were left with everything except the only thing that mattered — a state the people would defend.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about why South Vietnam fell in 1975.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Equipment and aid alone could not compensate for the political weakness of the South Vietnamese state’ supported by ‘They could not give us a country’ or ‘everything except the only thing that mattered — a state the people would defend’ AND ‘The collapse of ARVN leadership accelerated the South’s defeat in 1975’ supported by ‘Our generals were political appointees; many of them ran when the offensive came in March 1975’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the West Indian Gazette under Claudia Jones.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It was the first major Black newspaper in Britain, founded by Claudia Jones in March 1958, six months before the Notting Hill attacks.
• It covered Caribbean politics, the colour bar in housing and employment, and anti-colonial movements across Africa and Asia.
• It was edited from a small office above a barber's shop on Brixton Road, with contributors across Britain and the Caribbean.
• It was used to organise the Caribbean response to the 1958 attacks and the murder of Kelso Cochrane in 1959.
• It ran until Jones's death from heart failure on Christmas Eve 1964.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1959 Caribbean Carnival organised by Claudia Jones.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It was held indoors at St Pancras Town Hall in January 1959, four months after the Notting Hill attacks.
• It was organised by Claudia Jones, founder of the West Indian Gazette, as a deliberate cultural response to the violence.
• It featured steel bands, calypso singers and dancers in Caribbean dress, and the BBC televised highlights.
• Jones described the event in the Gazette with the line that a people's art is the genesis of their freedom.
• It is seen as the seed of the later open-air Notting Hill Carnival, which grew from Rhaune Laslett's 1966 local festival on Tavistock Road.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Mangrove Restaurant between 1968 and 1970.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Frank Crichlow, a Trinidadian who had run the El Rio cafe on Westbourne Park Road, opened it at 8 All Saints Road in 1968.
• It served Caribbean food but quickly became a community hub, drawing writers, musicians, lawyers and activists including Darcus Howe.
• Its customers included the writer Sam Selvon, the cricketer Garfield Sobers and the singer Diana Ross.
• From 1969 the Metropolitan Police raided it repeatedly on drugs warrants - nine raids in eighteen months by Crichlow's count - and found nothing.
• It sat at the centre of a cluster of Caribbean shops, barbershops, cafes and shebeens along All Saints Road.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Sources A and B.

Source A: From a letter written in November 1970 by a Caribbean resident of Notting Hill to a Black newspaper in London, after the Mangrove protest march. 'The Mangrove is not just a restaurant. It is the only place around here where we can sit, eat our food, hear our music and talk among ourselves without a uniform watching. The police know that. That is why they raid it. The march was not about a restaurant. It was about being treated like criminals on our own street.'

Source B: From a Metropolitan Police statement to the press, August 1970. 'Officers attended All Saints Road on the afternoon of 9 August in numbers sufficient to keep the peace. The premises in question have been the subject of a number of lawful searches under warrant. The force does not accept that any community in this district is policed differently from any other.'

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into the relationship between Caribbean Notting Hill and the Metropolitan Police around 1970?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 8 marks for an answer that weighs content, provenance and own knowledge for both sources against the stated enquiry.

Indicative content:
• Content of A: frames the Mangrove as a community hub rather than a business, and reads the raids as targeting that function rather than evidence of crime.
• Content of B: sets out the official position that the searches were lawful and the policing even-handed, which is exactly the claim Source A denies.
• Provenance of A: written by a resident days after the march, for a paper already sympathetic to the Mangrove; strong on feeling, weak as a measure of how widely the view was held.
• Provenance of B: a press statement written to defend the force, so it says what the Met wanted the public to believe rather than what officers did.
• Using them together is the point: the two sources state the disagreement that the 1971 trial then tested in court.
• Own knowledge: Crichlow recorded nine drugs raids in eighteen months with no drugs found, and the sus law fell heavily on young Black men across Notting Hill.
• Own knowledge: the march of 9 August 1970 led to the Mangrove Nine trial; in December 1971 all nine were acquitted of incitement to riot and the judge acknowledged evidence of racial hatred, which weighs against Source B.

Mastering: Content, provenance and own knowledge weighed for both sources, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Both sources used, with two of the three strands developed and a judgement reached.
Developing: The sources are described rather than weighed; provenance is noted but not linked to usefulness.
Emerging: One source described, with little or no own knowledge.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: the source material below is composed for practice. It is not an archive document, and the wording should not be quoted as evidence.

Study Source B.

Source B: From a Metropolitan Police statement to the press, August 1970. 'Officers attended All Saints Road on the afternoon of 9 August in numbers sufficient to keep the peace. The premises in question have been the subject of a number of lawful searches under warrant. The force does not accept that any community in this district is policed differently from any other.'

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the policing of All Saints Road around 1970?

In your answer, you must give the question you would ask and the type of source you could use.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — How Could You Follow Up
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks for a coherent chain: a detail in the source, the question that detail raises, and a type of source that could answer it.

Indicative content (any one, fully developed):
• Detail: 'a number of lawful searches under warrant'. Question: how many warrants were issued for the Mangrove between 1969 and 1970, and what did the searches find? Source type: magistrates' court warrant registers and Metropolitan Police records for the district.
• Detail: 'in numbers sufficient to keep the peace'. Question: how many officers were deployed on 9 August 1970, and on whose order? Source type: Metropolitan Police deployment records and the evidence given at the Mangrove Nine trial in 1971.
• Detail: 'policed differently from any other'. Question: how often was the sus law used against Black residents in the district compared with white residents? Source type: court registers for the local magistrates' court, and Home Office statistics on Vagrancy Act charges.

Mastering: A coherent chain — a specific detail picked out, a precise question, and a type of source that could realistically answer it.
Secure: Detail and question are sensible; the source type is named but generic.
Developing: The detail or the question is vague; the source type is generic.
Emerging: No clear chain from the source to an enquiry.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Mangrove Nine trial of 1971.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: up to 2 for each feature. One mark identifies a valid feature; a second adds supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It opened at the Old Bailey on 5 October 1971 and ran for 55 days, one of the longest trials of its kind.
• Darcus Howe and Althea Jones-LeCointe defended themselves and used the trial to put the policing of Notting Hill on trial alongside their own actions.
• The demand for an all-Black jury was refused, but the defence challenged 63 potential jurors, which left two Black jurors on the panel.
• All nine were acquitted of the most serious charge of incitement to riot; five were cleared of every charge and four received suspended sentences.
• Judge Edward Clarke acknowledged evidence of racial hatred on both sides, the first such judicial acknowledgement in British legal history; the Met tried and failed to have the remark withdrawn.

Mastering: Two features identified, each with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features identified with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: A vague statement that does not identify a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Cabinet War Rooms in London during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Located beneath the New Public Offices on Horse Guards Road in Westminster, the complex was reinforced from June 1940 with steel girders and a thick concrete ‘slab’.
• The site contained the Cabinet meeting room, a Map Room manned around the clock, communication centres for the Navy, RAF and Army and a transatlantic telephone room used by Winston Churchill to call President Roosevelt.
• In all, 115 Cabinet meetings were held there, the last on 28 March 1945.
• The site was a closely-guarded secret throughout the war — most ministers were unaware it existed in advance — and was kept on twenty-four-hour standby until 16 August 1945.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to the War Rooms without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Dig for Victory campaign in London during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Launched in October 1939, Dig for Victory encouraged civilians to grow vegetables and keep chickens or rabbits on private gardens and converted public land to reduce reliance on Atlantic food imports.
• By 1943 around 1.4 million allotments had been created across Britain, producing roughly half of all the country’s vegetables and fruit.
• In London, the dry medieval moat of the Tower of London was turned into vegetable allotments worked by Tower staff and volunteers, a striking image distributed worldwide as Ministry of Information propaganda.
• Sections of Victoria Park in the East End were converted to allotments alongside a Z-battery anti-aircraft rocket battery; Hyde Park grew potatoes and Kensington Gardens kept pigs.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to Dig for Victory without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
NOTE: Sources A and B below are composed for practice. They are not real archive documents; in the exam you are given two genuine sources.

Source A: a Ministry of Information poster issued in 1939. Above a crown, large capital letters read ‘YOUR COURAGE, YOUR CHEERFULNESS, YOUR RESOLUTION WILL BRING US VICTORY’. There is no picture of damage and no mention of casualties.

Source B: an internal memorandum written for the Ministry of Information in October 1940, recommending wider distribution of the documentary ‘London Can Take It!’.
‘The film, narrated by the American journalist Mr Reynolds, presents one full night of the present air war on London. It avoids any reference to the casualty figures or to the disposition of damage by borough. Its purpose is to communicate to American audiences the resilience of the civilian population and the continuity of national life. We recommend its distribution at home as a counterweight to the recent dip in public confidence in the East End.’

How useful are Sources A and B for an enquiry into how the British government used propaganda to manage civilian feeling during the Blitz?

Explain your answer, using Sources A and B and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Are Sources A and B
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks. Weigh both sources together: what each one says, who made it and why, and what you know about the context.

Indicative content:
• Source A shows the tone the government wanted: civilian feeling itself framed as a weapon, with no damage and no casualties shown.
• As a public poster, Source A tells you what people were meant to see, but nothing about whether it worked; posters of this kind were widely mocked at the time.
• Source B explains the thinking behind the films: the American audience, the deliberate omission of casualty figures and damage by borough.
• Source B admits a ‘recent dip in public confidence in the East End’, which is strong evidence that officials knew morale was uneven.
• An internal memorandum was written to be acted on rather than published, so it captures intentions that public material hides; but it covers film policy only.
• Context to bring in: the Ministry of Information worked from Senate House and censored under the 1939 Defence Regulations; Mass Observation recorded panic, looting and class resentment alongside resilience.

Mastering: Both sources judged on content and on who made them and why, supported by precise contextual knowledge, with a clear verdict on usefulness for this enquiry.
Secure: Both sources considered, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: Simple comments on what the sources show; provenance or context is thin.
Emerging: Describes the sources without judging their usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B again.

How could you follow up Source B to find out more about the ‘dip in public confidence in the East End’ that the memorandum mentions?

Give the detail in Source B you would follow up, the question you would ask, the type of source you could use, and how it would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Give a coherent chain: a detail in Source B, the question it raises, the type of source you could use, and how that source would help.

Indicative example:
• Detail in Source B: the admission of a ‘recent dip in public confidence in the East End’ in October 1940.
• Question: what caused that loss of confidence, and how widespread was it?
• Type of source: the weekly reports on civilian morale that government officers compiled for ministers in the autumn of 1940.
• How it helps: they were written for internal use and summarised feeling borough by borough, so they show whether the dip was general or local.

Other chains are equally creditable, for example following up the omission of casualty figures, the American audience for the film, or the use of film as policy, using Mass Observation diaries, a local newspaper such as the Hackney Gazette, or oral-history recordings of East Enders.

Mastering: All four steps clear, with the source type matched to the question.
Secure: A sound question and source type, briefly explained.
Developing: A question or a source type given, but the link to Source B is weak.
Emerging: A source type or question suggested that is not grounded in Source B.

practice_questions.text:
‘Propaganda was the most important way British governments shaped attitudes to war.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Ministry of Information in the Second World War
• war reporting in the nineteenth century.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for propaganda:
• The Ministry of Information packaged a single night as cheerful resilience in ‘London Can Take It!’ (1940), narrated by Quentin Reynolds, and aimed it at American opinion.
• Posters such as ‘Your Courage, Your Cheerfulness, Your Resolution Will Bring Us Victory’ framed civilian feeling as part of the war effort.
• Censorship worked with propaganda: casualty figures from Hallsville, Balham and Bethnal Green were withheld to protect morale.
• Dig for Victory and the Royal Family’s East End visits made participation feel obligatory and shared.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Independent reporting could set attitudes against the government: Russell’s telegraphed Crimean dispatches exposed supply failure and forced Nightingale’s mission and army reform.
• Photography and then film gave the public evidence of their own, from Fenton in 1855 to newsreels in the 1940s.
• Real experience mattered more than any film: bombed streets, rationing and the loss of relatives shaped what people believed.
• Material provision changed feeling: 79 Tube stations equipped from October 1940 did more for confidence than a poster.
• Mass Observation shows people distinguishing between the official story and what they saw around them, so propaganda framed attitudes without controlling them.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs propaganda against independent reporting and lived experience across more than one century, with accurate detail (Russell, Fenton, the Ministry of Information, censorship) and a clear judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the part played by the Royal Family in London during the Blitz.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• King George VI and Queen Elizabeth refused to leave London, and Buckingham Palace was bombed nine times during the war.
• The strike of 13 September 1940 fell within about thirty metres of the King and Queen while they were in residence.
• Queen Elizabeth said afterwards that being bombed made her feel she could ‘look the East End in the face’, a remark reported everywhere.
• The royal couple visited bomb sites across London, including the East End the day after Black Saturday, and Coventry after the raid of November 1940.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to the Royal Family without identifying a feature.
